title: Writing Integers as Rational Numbers
snippet: Writing Integers as Rational Numbers: Write each of the following as a rational number. ⓐ7 ⓑ0 ⓒ–8 Write a fraction with the integer in the numerator and 1 in the denominator. ⓐ 7 = \frac{7}{1} ⓑ 0 = \frac{0}{1} ⓒ -8 = - \frac{8}{1}
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Writing Integers as Rational Numbers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write each of the following as a rational number.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ7</item>
        <item>ⓑ0</item>
        <item>ⓒ–8</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Write a fraction with the integer in the numerator and 1 in the denominator.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$7 = \frac{7}{1}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$0 = \frac{0}{1}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$-8 = - \frac{8}{1}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Identifying Rational Numbers
snippet: Identifying Rational Numbers: Write each of the following rational numbers as either a terminating or repeating decimal. ⓐ - \frac{5}{7} ⓑ \frac{15}{5} ⓒ \frac{13}{25} Write each fraction as a decimal by dividing the numerator by the...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Identifying Rational Numbers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write each of the following rational numbers as either a terminating or repeating decimal.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$- \frac{5}{7}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\frac{15}{5}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\frac{13}{25}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Write each fraction as a decimal by dividing the numerator by the denominator.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$- \frac{5}{7} = -0.\overset{ \text{———} }{714285},$$ a repeating decimal</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\frac{15}{5} = 3$$ (or 3.0), a terminating decimal</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\frac{13}{25} = 0.52,$$ a terminating decimal</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Differentiating Rational and Irrational Numbers
snippet: Differentiating Rational and Irrational Numbers: Determine whether each of the following numbers is rational or irrational. If it is rational, determine whether it is a terminating or repeating decimal. ⓐ \sqrt{25} ⓑ \frac{33}{9} ⓒ...
body_xml:
<example number="3" title="Differentiating Rational and Irrational Numbers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine whether each of the following numbers is rational or irrational. If it is rational, determine whether it is a terminating or repeating decimal.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\sqrt{25}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\frac{33}{9}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\sqrt{11}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\frac{17}{34}$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$0.3033033303333\ldots$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\sqrt{25}:$$ This can be simplified as $$\sqrt{25} = 5.$$ Therefore, $$\sqrt{25}$$ is rational.</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\frac{33}{9}:$$ Because it is a fraction of integers, $$\frac{33}{9}$$ is a rational number. Next, simplify and divide. $$\frac{33}{9} = \frac{\overset{11}{33}}{\underset{3}{9}} = \frac{11}{3} = 3.\overline{6}$$ So, $$\frac{33}{9}$$ is rational and a repeating decimal.</item>
        <item>ⓒ $${\sqrt{11}:}\sqrt{11}$$ is irrational because 11 is not a perfect square and $$\sqrt{11}$$ cannot be expressed as a fraction.</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\frac{17}{34}:$$ Because it is a fraction of integers, $$\frac{17}{34}$$ is a rational number. Simplify and divide. $$\frac{17}{34} = \frac{\overset{1}{17}}{\underset{2}{34}} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5$$ So, $$\frac{17}{34}$$ is rational and a terminating decimal.</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$0.3033033303333\ldots$$ is not a terminating decimal. Also note that there is no repeating pattern because the group of 3s increases each time. Therefore it is neither a terminating nor a repeating decimal and, hence, not a rational number. It is an irrational number.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Classifying Real Numbers
snippet: Classifying Real Numbers: Classify each number as either positive or negative and as either rational or irrational. Does the number lie to the left or the right of 0 on the number line? ⓐ - \frac{10}{3} ⓑ \sqrt{5} ⓒ - \sqrt{289} ⓓ -6\pi ⓔ...
body_xml:
<example number="4" title="Classifying Real Numbers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Classify each number as either positive or negative and as either rational or irrational. Does the number lie to the left or the right of 0 on the number line?</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$- \frac{10}{3}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\sqrt{5}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$- \sqrt{289}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$-6\pi$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$0.615384615384\ldots$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$- \frac{10}{3}$$ is negative and rational. It lies to the left of 0 on the number line.</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\sqrt{5}$$ is positive and irrational. It lies to the right of 0.</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$- \sqrt{289} = - \sqrt{17^{2}} = -17$$ is negative and rational. It lies to the left of 0.</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$-6\pi$$ is negative and irrational. It lies to the left of 0.</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$0.615384615384\ldots$$ is a repeating decimal so it is rational and positive. It lies to the right of 0.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Sets of Numbers
snippet: Sets of Numbers: The set of natural numbers includes the numbers used for counting: \left\{ {1,2,3,...} \right\}. The set of whole numbers is the set of natural numbers plus zero: \left\{ {0,1,2,3,...} \right\}. The set of integers adds...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Sets of Numbers" title="Sets of Numbers">
    <paragraph>The set of natural numbers includes the numbers used for counting: $$\left\{ {1,2,3,...} \right\}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The set of whole numbers is the set of natural numbers plus zero: $$\left\{ {0,1,2,3,...} \right\}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The set of integers adds the negative natural numbers to the set of whole numbers: $$\left\{ {...,-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3,...} \right\}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The set of rational numbers includes fractions written as $$\left\{ {\left. {\frac{m}{n}} \right|m \text{and} n \text{are integers and} n \neq 0} \right\}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The set of irrational numbers is the set of numbers that are not rational, are nonrepeating, and are nonterminating: $$\left\{ {\left. h \right|h \text{is not a rational number} } \right\}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Using the Order of Operations
snippet: Using the Order of Operations: Use the order of operations to evaluate each of the following expressions. ⓐ \left( {3 \cdot 2} \right)^{2} - 4\left( {6 + 2} \right) ⓑ \frac{5^{2} - 4}{7} - \sqrt{11 - 2} ⓒ 6 - \left| {5 - 8} \right| +...
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Using the Order of Operations">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the order of operations to evaluate each of the following expressions.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\left( {3 \cdot 2} \right)^{2} - 4\left( {6 + 2} \right)$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\frac{5^{2} - 4}{7} - \sqrt{11 - 2}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$6 - \left| {5 - 8} \right| + 3\left( {4 - 1} \right)$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\frac{14 - 3 \cdot 2}{2 \cdot 5 - 3^{2}}$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$7\left( {5 \cdot 3} \right) - 2\left\lbrack {\left( {6 - 3} \right) - 4^{2}} \right\rbrack + 1$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {{(3 \cdot 2)}^{2} - 4(6 + 2)} & = & {{(6)}^{2} - 4(8)} & { \text{Simplify parentheses.} } \\ & = & {36 - 4(8)} & { \text{Simplify exponent.} } \\ & = & {36 - 32} & { \text{Simplify multiplication.} } \\ & = & 4 & { \text{Simplify subtraction.} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {\frac{5^{2} - 4}{7} - \sqrt{11 - 2}} & = & {\frac{5^{2} - 4}{7} - \sqrt{9}} & { \text{Simplify grouping symbols (radical).} } \\ & = & {\frac{5^{2} - 4}{7} - 3} & { \text{Simplify radical.} } \\ & = & {\frac{25 - 4}{7} - 3} & { \text{Simplify exponent.} } \\ & = & {\frac{21}{7} - 3} & { \text{Simplify subtraction in numerator.} } \\ & = & {3 - 3} & { \text{Simplify division.} } \\ & = & 0 & { \text{Simplify subtraction.} } \end{array}$$ Note that in the first step, the radical is treated as a grouping symbol, like parentheses. Also, in the third step, the fraction bar is considered a grouping symbol so the numerator is considered to be grouped.</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\begin{array}{ccll} \left. 6 - \middle| 5 - 8 \middle| + 3 \middle| 4 - 1 \right| & = & \left. 6 - \middle| -3 \middle| + 3(3) \right. & { \text{Simplify inside grouping symbols.} } \\ & = & {6 - (3) + 3(3)} & { \text{Simplify absolute value.} } \\ & = & {6 - 3 + 9} & { \text{Simplify multiplication.} } \\ & = & 12 & { \text{Simplify addition.} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\begin{array}{ccll} \frac{14 - 3 \cdot 2}{2 \cdot 5 - 3^{2}} & = & \frac{14 - 3 \cdot 2}{2 \cdot 5 - 9} & { \text{Simplify exponent.} } \\ & = & \frac{14 - 6}{10 - 9} & { \text{Simplify products.} } \\ & = & \frac{8}{1} & { \text{Simplify differences.} } \\ & = & 8 & { \text{Simplify quotient.} } \end{array}$$ In this example, the fraction bar separates the numerator and denominator, which we simplify separately until the last step.</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {7\left( {5 \cdot 3} \right) - 2\left\lbrack {\left( {6 - 3} \right) - 4^{2}} \right\rbrack + 1} & = & {7(15) - 2\left\lbrack {(3) - 4^{2}} \right\rbrack + 1} & { \text{Simplify inside parentheses.} } \\ & = & {7(15) - 2\left( {3 - 16} \right) + 1} & { \text{Simplify exponent.} } \\ & = & {7(15) - 2(-13) + 1} & { \text{Subtract.} } \\ & = & {105 + 26 + 1} & { \text{Multiply.} } \\ & = & 132 & { \text{Add.} } \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Properties of Real Numbers
snippet: Properties of Real Numbers: The following properties hold for real numbers a, b, and c. Addition Multiplication Commutative Property a + b = b + a a \cdot b = b \cdot a Associative Property a + \left( {b + c} \right) = \left( {a + b}...
body_xml: The following properties hold for real numbers a, b, and c. Addition Multiplication Commutative Property $$a + b = b + a$$ $$a \cdot b = b \cdot a$$ Associative Property $$a + \left( {b + c} \right) = \left( {a + b} \right) + c$$ $$a\left( {bc} \right) = \left( {ab} \right)c$$ Distributive Property $$a \cdot \left( {b + c} \right) = a \cdot b + a \cdot c$$ Identity Property There exists a unique real number called the additive identity, 0, such that, for any real number a $$a + 0 = a$$ There exists a unique real number called the multiplicative identity, 1, such that, for any real number a $$a \cdot 1 = a$$ Inverse Property Every real number a has an additive inverse, or opposite, denoted –a, such that $$a + \left( {- a} \right) = 0$$ Every nonzero real number a has a multiplicative inverse, or reciprocal, denoted $$\frac{1}{a},$$ such that $$a \cdot \left( \frac{1}{a} \right) = 1$$

title: Using Properties of Real Numbers
snippet: Using Properties of Real Numbers: Use the properties of real numbers to rewrite and simplify each expression. State which properties apply. ⓐ 3 \cdot 6 + 3 \cdot 4 ⓑ \left( {5 + 8} \right) + (-8) ⓒ 6 - \left( {15 + 9} \right) ⓓ \frac{4}{7}...
body_xml:
<example number="7" title="Using Properties of Real Numbers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the properties of real numbers to rewrite and simplify each expression. State which properties apply.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$3 \cdot 6 + 3 \cdot 4$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\left( {5 + 8} \right) + (-8)$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$6 - \left( {15 + 9} \right)$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\frac{4}{7} \cdot \left( {\frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{7}{4}} \right)$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$100 \cdot \left\lbrack {0.75 + (-2.38)} \right\rbrack$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {3 \cdot 6 + 3 \cdot 4} & = & {3 \cdot (6 + 4)} & { \text{Distributive property.} } \\ & = & {3 \cdot 10} & { \text{Simplify.} } \\ & = & 30 & { \text{Simplify.} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\begin{array}{cclc} {(5 + 8) + (-8)} & = & {5 + \lbrack 8 + (-8)\rbrack} & { \text{Associative property of addition.} } \\ & = & {5 + 0} & { \text{Inverse property of addition.} } \\ & = & 5 & { \text{Identity property of addition.} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {6 - (15 + 9)} & = & {6 + \lbrack(-15) + (-9)\rbrack} & { \text{Distributive property.} } \\ & = & {6 + (-24)} & { \text{Simplify.} } \\ & = & -18 & { \text{Simplify.} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {\frac{4}{7} \cdot \left( {\frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{7}{4}} \right)} & = & {\frac{4}{7} \cdot \left( {\frac{7}{4} \cdot \frac{2}{3}} \right)} & { \text{Commutative property of multiplication.} } \\ & = & {\left( {\frac{4}{7} \cdot \frac{7}{4}} \right) \cdot \frac{2}{3}} & { \text{Associative property of multiplication.} } \\ & = & {1 \cdot \frac{2}{3}} & { \text{Inverse property of multiplication.} } \\ & = & \frac{2}{3} & { \text{Identity property of multiplication.} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$\begin{array}{cclc} {100 \cdot \lbrack 0.75 + ( - 2.38)\rbrack} & = & {100 \cdot 0.75 + 100 \cdot (-2.38)} & { \text{Distributive property.} } \\ & = & {75 + (-238)} & { \text{Simplify.} } \\ & = & -163 & { \text{Simplify.} } \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Evaluating an Algebraic Expression at Different Values
snippet: Evaluating an Algebraic Expression at Different Values: Evaluate the expression 2x - 7 for each value for x. ⓐ x = 0 ⓑ x = 1 ⓒ x = \frac{1}{2} ⓓ x = -4 ⓐ Substitute 0 for x. \begin{matrix} {2x - 7} & = & {2(0) - 7} \\ & = & {0 - 7} \\ & =...
body_xml:
<example number="9" title="Evaluating an Algebraic Expression at Different Values">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate the expression $$2x - 7$$ for each value for x.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$x = 0$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$x = 1$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$x = \frac{1}{2}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$x = -4$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ Substitute 0 for $$x.$$ $$\begin{matrix} {2x - 7} & = & {2(0) - 7} \\ & = & {0 - 7} \\ & = & -7 \end{matrix}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑSubstitute 1 for $$x.$$ $$\begin{array}{ccl} {2x - 7} & = & {2(1) - 7} \\ & = & {2 - 7} \\ & = & -5 \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ Substitute $$\frac{1}{2}$$ for $$x.$$ $$\begin{array}{ccl} {2x - 7} & = & {2\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) - 7} \\ & = & {1 - 7} \\ & = & -6 \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓSubstitute $$-4$$ for $$x.$$ $$\begin{matrix} {2x - 7} & = & {2( - 4) - 7} \\ & = & {- 8 - 7} \\ & = & -15 \end{matrix}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Evaluating Algebraic Expressions
snippet: Evaluating Algebraic Expressions: Evaluate each expression for the given values. ⓐ x + 5 for x = -5 ⓑ \frac{t}{2t-1} for t = 10 ⓒ \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} for r = 5 ⓓ a + ab + b for a = 11,b = -8 ⓔ \sqrt{2m^{3}n^{2}} for m = 2,n = 3 ⓐ...
body_xml:
<example number="10" title="Evaluating Algebraic Expressions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate each expression for the given values.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$x + 5$$ for $$x = -5$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\frac{t}{2t-1}$$ for $$t = 10$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$$ for $$r = 5$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$a + ab + b$$ for $$a = 11,b = -8$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$\sqrt{2m^{3}n^{2}}$$ for $$m = 2,n = 3$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ Substitute $$-5$$ for $$x.$$ $$\begin{array}{ccl} {x + 5} & = & {(-5) + 5} \\ & = & 0 \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ Substitute 10 for $$t.$$ $$\begin{array}{ccl} \frac{t}{2t - 1} & = & \frac{(10)}{2(10) - 1} \\ & = & \frac{10}{20 - 1} \\ & = & \frac{10}{19} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ Substitute 5 for $$r.$$ $$\begin{matrix} {\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}} & = & {\frac{4}{3}\pi{(5)}^{3}} \\ & = & {\frac{4}{3}\pi(125)} \\ & = & {\frac{500}{3}\pi} \end{matrix}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ Substitute 11 for $$a$$ and –8 for $$b.$$ $$\begin{matrix} {a + ab + b} & = & {(11) + (11)(-8) + (-8)} \\ & = & {11 - 88 - 8} \\ & = & -85 \end{matrix}$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ Substitute 2 for $$m$$ and 3 for $$n.$$ $$\begin{array}{ccl} \sqrt{2m^{3}n^{2}} & = & \sqrt{2{(2)}^{3}{(3)}^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{2(8)(9)} \\ & = & \sqrt{144} \\ & = & 12 \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml: A right circular cylinder with radius $$h$$ and height $$S$$ has the surface area $$S = 2\pi r\left( {r + h} \right).$$ (in square units) given by the formula $$\pi.$$ See Figure 3. Find the surface area of a cylinder with radius 6 in. and height 9 in. Leave the answer in terms of $$2\pi r\left( {r + h} \right)$$ Evaluate the expression $$r = 6$$ for $$h = 9.$$ and $$\begin{array}{ccl} S & = & {2\pi r(r + h)} \\ & = & {2\pi(6)\lbrack(6) + (9)\rbrack} \\ & = & {2\pi(6)(15)} \\ & = & {180\pi} \end{array}$$ $$180\pi$$ The surface area is $$A = \left( {L + 16} \right)\left( {W + 16} \right) - L \cdot W.$$ square inches.

body_xml:
<example number="12" title="Simplifying Algebraic Expressions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Simplify each algebraic expression.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$2r - 5\left( {3 - r} \right) + 4$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\left( {4t - \frac{5}{4}s} \right) - \left( {\frac{2}{3}t + 2s} \right)$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$2mn - 5m + 3mn + n$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {3x - 2y + x - 3y - 7} & = & {3x + x - 2y - 3y - 7} & { \text{Commutative property of addition.} } \\ & = & {4x - 5y - 7} & { \text{Simplify.} } \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {2r - 5(3 - r) + 4} & = & {2r - 15 + 5r + 4} & { \text{Distributive property.} } \\ & = & {2r + 5r - 15 + 4} & { \text{Commutative property of addition.} } \\ & = & {7r - 11} & { \text{Simplify.} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {\left( {4t - \frac{5}{4}s} \right) - \left( {\frac{2}{3}t + 2s} \right)} & = & {4t - \frac{5}{4}s - \frac{2}{3}t - 2s} & { \text{Distributive property.} } \\ & = & {4t - \frac{2}{3}t - \frac{5}{4}s - 2s} & { \text{Commutative property of addition.} } \\ & = & {\frac{10}{3}t - \frac{13}{4}s} & { \text{Simplify.} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\begin{array}{cccl} {2mn - 5m + 3mn + n} & = & {2mn + 3mn - 5m + n} & { \text{Commutative property of addition.} } \\ & = & { 5mn - 5m + n} & { \text{Simplify.} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\frac{2}{3}y - 2\left( {\frac{4}{3}y + z} \right)$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using the Product Rule

body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Using the Product Rule">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write each of the following products with a single base. Do not simplify further.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$t^{5} \cdot t^{3}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$(-3)^{5} \cdot (-3)$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$x^{2} \cdot x^{5} \cdot x^{3}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use the product rule to simplify each expression.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$t^{5} \cdot t^{3} = t^{5 + 3} = t^{8}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$(-3)^{5} \cdot (-3) = (-3)^{5} \cdot (-3)^{1} = (-3)^{5 + 1} = (-3)^{6}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$x^{2} \cdot x^{5} \cdot x^{3}$$</item>
      </list>
      <paragraph>At first, it may appear that we cannot simplify a product of three factors. However, using the associative property of multiplication, begin by simplifying the first two.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x^{2} \cdot x^{5} \cdot x^{3} = \left( {x^{2} \cdot x^{5}} \right) \cdot x^{3} = \left( x^{2 + 5} \right) \cdot x^{3} = x^{7} \cdot x^{3} = x^{7 + 3} = x^{10}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice we get the same result by adding the three exponents in one step.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x^{2} \cdot x^{5} \cdot x^{3} = x^{2 + 5 + 3} = x^{10}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Using the Zero Exponent Rule: Simplify each expression using the zero exponent rule of exponents. ⓐ \frac{c^{3}}{c^{3}} ⓑ \frac{-3x^{5}}{x^{5}} ⓒ \frac{\left( {j^{2}k} \right)^{4}}{\left( {j^{2}k} \right) \cdot \left( {j^{2}k} \right)^{3}}...
body_xml:
<example number="4" title="Using the Zero Exponent Rule">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Simplify each expression using the zero exponent rule of exponents.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\frac{c^{3}}{c^{3}}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\frac{-3x^{5}}{x^{5}}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\frac{\left( {j^{2}k} \right)^{4}}{\left( {j^{2}k} \right) \cdot \left( {j^{2}k} \right)^{3}}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\frac{5\left( {rs^{2}} \right)^{2}}{\left( {rs^{2}} \right)^{2}}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use the zero exponent and other rules to simplify each expression.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓐ $$\begin{array}{ccl} \frac{c^{3}}{c^{3}} & = & c^{3 - 3} \\ & = & c^{0} \\ & = & 1 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓑ $$\begin{array}{ccl} \frac{-3x^{5}}{x^{5}} & = & {-3 \cdot \frac{x^{5}}{x^{5}}} \\ & = & {-3 \cdot x^{5 - 5}} \\ & = & {-3 \cdot x^{0}} \\ & = & {-3 \cdot 1} \\ & = & -3 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓒ $$\begin{array}{cclc} \frac{\left( j^{2}k \right)^{4}}{\left( j^{2}k \right) \cdot \left( j^{2}k \right)^{3}} & = & \frac{\left( j^{2}k \right)^{4}}{\left( j^{2}k \right)^{1 + 3}} & { \text{Use the product rule in the denominator} .} \\ & = & \frac{\left( j^{2}k \right)^{4}}{\left( j^{2}k \right)^{4}} & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ & = & \left( j^{2}k \right)^{4 - 4} & { \text{Use the quotient rule} .} \\ & = & \left( j^{2}k \right)^{0} & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ & = & 1 & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓓ $$\begin{array}{ccll} \frac{5\left( rs^{2} \right)^{2}}{\left( rs^{2} \right)^{2}} & = & {5\left( rs^{2} \right)^{2 - 2}} & { \text{Use the quotient rule} .} \\ & = & {5\left( rs^{2} \right)^{0}} & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ & = & {5 \cdot 1} & { \text{Use the zero exponent rule} .} \\ & = & 5 & { \text{Simplify} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="5" title="Using the Negative Exponent Rule">

<example number="7" title="Using the Power of a Product Rule">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Simplify each of the following products as much as possible using the power of a product rule. Write answers with positive exponents.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\left( {ab^{2}} \right)^{3}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\left( {2t} \right)^{15}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\left( {-2w^{3}} \right)^{3}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\frac{1}{\left( {-7z} \right)^{4}}$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$\left( {e^{-2}f^{2}} \right)^{7}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use the product and quotient rules and the new definitions to simplify each expression.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\left( {ab^{2}} \right)^{3} = (a)^{3} \cdot \left( b^{2} \right)^{3} = a^{1 \cdot 3} \cdot b^{2 \cdot 3} = a^{3}b^{6}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\left( {2t} \right)^{15} = (2)^{15} \cdot (t)^{15} = 2^{15}t^{15} = 32,768t^{15}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\left( {-2w^{3}} \right)^{3} = (-2)^{3} \cdot \left( w^{3} \right)^{3} = -8 \cdot w^{3 \cdot 3} = -8w^{9}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\frac{1}{\left( {-7z} \right)^{4}} = \frac{1}{(-7)^{4} \cdot (z)^{4}} = \frac{1}{2,401z^{4}}$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$\left( {e^{-2}f^{2}} \right)^{7} = \left( e^{-2} \right)^{7} \cdot \left( f^{2} \right)^{7} = e^{-2 \cdot 7} \cdot f^{2 \cdot 7} = e^{-14}f^{14} = \frac{f^{14}}{e^{14}}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Using the Power of a Quotient Rule: Simplify each of the following quotients as much as possible using the power of a quotient rule. Write answers with positive exponents. ⓐ \left( \frac{4}{z^{11}} \right)^{3} ⓑ \left( \frac{p}{q^{3}}...
body_xml:
<example number="8" title="Using the Power of a Quotient Rule">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Simplify each of the following quotients as much as possible using the power of a quotient rule. Write answers with positive exponents.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\left( \frac{4}{z^{11}} \right)^{3}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\left( \frac{p}{q^{3}} \right)^{6}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\left( \frac{-1}{t^{2}} \right)^{27}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\left( {j^{3}k^{-2}} \right)^{4}$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$\left( {m^{-2}n^{-2}} \right)^{3}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\left( \frac{4}{z^{11}} \right)^{3} = \frac{(4)^{3}}{\left( z^{11} \right)^{3}} = \frac{64}{z^{11 \cdot 3}} = \frac{64}{z^{33}}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\left( \frac{p}{q^{3}} \right)^{6} = \frac{(p)^{6}}{\left( q^{3} \right)^{6}} = \frac{p^{1 \cdot 6}}{q^{3 \cdot 6}} = \frac{p^{6}}{q^{18}}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\left( \frac{-1}{t^{2}} \right)^{27} = \frac{(-1)^{27}}{\left( t^{2} \right)^{27}} = \frac{-1}{t^{2 \cdot 27}} = \frac{-1}{t^{54}} = - \frac{1}{t^{54}}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\left( {j^{3}k^{-2}} \right)^{4} = \left( \frac{j^{3}}{k^{2}} \right)^{4} = \frac{\left( j^{3} \right)^{4}}{\left( k^{2} \right)^{4}} = \frac{j^{3 \cdot 4}}{k^{2 \cdot 4}} = \frac{j^{12}}{k^{8}}$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$\left( {m^{-2}n^{-2}} \right)^{3} = \left( \frac{1}{m^{2}n^{2}} \right)^{3} = \frac{(1)^{3}}{\left( {m^{2}n^{2}} \right)^{3}} = \frac{1}{\left( m^{2} \right)^{3}\left( n^{2} \right)^{3}} = \frac{1}{m^{2 \cdot 3} \cdot n^{2 \cdot 3}} = \frac{1}{m^{6}n^{6}}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Simplifying Exponential Expressions
snippet: Simplifying Exponential Expressions: Simplify each expression and write the answer with positive exponents only. ⓐ \left( {6m^{2}n^{-1}} \right)^{3} ⓑ 17^{5} \cdot 17^{-4} \cdot 17^{-3} ⓒ \left( \frac{u^{-1}v}{v^{-1}} \right)^{2} ⓓ \left(...
body_xml:
<example number="9" title="Simplifying Exponential Expressions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Simplify each expression and write the answer with positive exponents only.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\left( {6m^{2}n^{-1}} \right)^{3}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$17^{5} \cdot 17^{-4} \cdot 17^{-3}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\left( \frac{u^{-1}v}{v^{-1}} \right)^{2}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\left( {-2a^{3}b^{-1}} \right)\left( {5a^{-2}b^{2}} \right)$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$\left( {x^{2}\sqrt{2}} \right)^{4}\left( {x^{2}\sqrt{2}} \right)^{-4}$$</item>
        <item>ⓕ $$\frac{\left( {3w^{2}} \right)^{5}}{\left( {6w^{-2}} \right)^{2}}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\begin{array}{ccll} \left( 6m^{2}n^{-1} \right)^{3} & = & {{(6)}^{3}\left( m^{2} \right)^{3}\left( n^{-1} \right)^{3}} & { \text{The power of a product rule} } \\ & = & {6^{3}m^{2 \cdot 3}n^{-1 \cdot 3}} & { \text{The power rule} } \\ & = & { 216m^{6}n^{-3}} & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ & = & \frac{216m^{6}}{n^{3}} & { \text{The negative exponent rule} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {17^{5} \cdot 17^{-4} \cdot 17^{-3}} & = & 17^{5 - 4 - 3} & { \text{The product rule} } \\ & = & 17^{-2} & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ & = & {\frac{1}{17^{2}} \text{or} \frac{1}{289}} & { \text{The negative exponent rule} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\begin{array}{cccl} \left( \frac{u^{-1}v}{v^{-1}} \right)^{2} & = & \frac{{(u^{-1}v)}^{2}}{{(v^{-1})}^{2}} & { \text{The power of a quotient rule} } \\ & = & \frac{u^{-2}v^{2}}{v^{-2}} & { \text{The power of a product rule} } \\ & = & {u^{-2}v^{2 - (-2)}} & { \text{The quotient rule} } \\ & = & {u^{-2}v^{4}} & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ & = & \frac{v^{4}}{u^{2}} & { \text{The negative exponent rule} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {\left( -2a^{3}b^{- 1} \right)\left( 5a^{-2}b^{2} \right)} & = & {-2 \cdot 5 \cdot a^{3} \cdot a^{-2} \cdot b^{-1} \cdot b^{2}} & { \text{Commutative and associative laws of multiplication} } \\ & = & {-10 \cdot a^{3 - 2} \cdot b^{-1 + 2}} & { \text{The product rule} } \\ & = & {-10ab} & { \text{Simplify} .} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {\left( x^{2}\sqrt{2} \right)^{4}\left( x^{2}\sqrt{2} \right)^{-4}} & = & \left( x^{2}\sqrt{2} \right)^{4 - 4} & { \text{The product rule} } \\ & = & {\left( x^{2}\sqrt{2} \right)^{0}} & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ & = & 1 & { \text{The zero exponent rule} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓕ $$\begin{array}{ccll} \frac{{(3w^{2})}^{5}}{{(6w^{-2})}^{2}} & = & \frac{{(3)}^{5} \cdot {(w^{2})}^{5}}{{(6)}^{2} \cdot {(w^{-2})}^{2}} & { \text{The power of a product rule} } \\ & = & \frac{3^{5}w^{2 \cdot 5}}{6^{2}w^{-2 \cdot 2}} & { \text{The power rule} } \\ & = & \frac{243w^{10}}{36w^{-4}} & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ & = & \frac{27w^{10 - (-4)}}{4} & { \text{The quotient rule and reduce fraction} } \\ & = & \frac{27w^{14}}{4} & { \text{Simplify} .} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

      <paragraph>Write each number in scientific notation.</paragraph>

      <paragraph>ⓑDiameter of Andromeda Galaxy: 1,300,000,000,000,000,000,000 m</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓒNumber of stars in Andromeda Galaxy: 1,000,000,000,000</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓓDiameter of electron: 0.00000000000094 m</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓔProbability of being struck by lightning in any single year: 0.00000143</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>ⓐ $$\begin{array}{l} {24,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 \text{m} } \\ \underset{\leftarrow 22 \text{places} }{\underset{}{24,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 \text{m} }} \\ {2.4 \times 10^{22} \text{m} } \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓑ $$\begin{array}{l} {1,300,000,000,000,000,000,000 \text{m} } \\ \underset{\leftarrow 21 \text{places} }{\underset{}{1,300,000,000,000,000,000,000 \text{m} }} \\ {1.3 \times 10^{21} \text{m} } \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓒ $$\begin{array}{l} 1,000,000,000,000 \\ \underset{\leftarrow 12 \text{places} }{\underset{}{1,000,000,000,000}} \\ {1 \times 10^{12}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓓ $$\begin{array}{l} {0.00000000000094 \text{m} } \\ \underset{\rightarrow 13 \text{places} }{\underset{}{0.00000000000094 \text{m} }} \\ {9.4 \times 10^{-13} \text{m} } \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓔ $$\begin{array}{l} 0.00000143 \\ \underset{\rightarrow 6 \text{places} }{\underset{}{0.00000143}} \\ {1.43 \times 10^{-6}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>Observe that, if the given number is greater than 1, as in examples a–c, the exponent of 10 is positive; and if the number is less than 1, as in examples d–e, the exponent is negative.</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="12" title="Using Scientific Notation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Perform the operations and write the answer in scientific notation.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\left( {8.14 \times 10^{-7}} \right)\left( {6.5 \times 10^{10}} \right)$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\left( {4 \times 10^{5}} \right) \div \left( {-1.52 \times 10^{9}} \right)$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\left( {2.7 \times 10^{5}} \right)\left( {6.04 \times 10^{13}} \right)$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\left( {1.2 \times 10^{8}} \right) \div \left( {9.6 \times 10^{5}} \right)$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$\left( {3.33 \times 10^{4}} \right)\left( {-1.05 \times 10^{7}} \right)\left( {5.62 \times 10^{5}} \right)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {\left( {8.14 \times 10^{-7}} \right)\left( {6.5 \times 10^{10}} \right)} & = & {(8.14 \times 6.5)\left( {10^{-7} \times 10^{10}} \right)} & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Commutative and associative} } \\ { \text{properties of multiplication} } \end{array} \\ & = & {(52.91)\left( 10^{3} \right)} & { \text{Product rule of exponents} } \\ & = & {5.291 \times 10^{4}} & { \text{Scientific notation} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {\left( {4 \times 10^{5}} \right) \div \left( {-1.52 \times 10^{9}} \right)} & = & {\left( \frac{4}{-1.52} \right)\left( \frac{10^{5}}{10^{9}} \right)} & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Commutative and associative} } \\ { \text{properties of multiplication} } \end{array} \\ & \approx & {(-2.63)\left( 10^{-4} \right)} & { \text{Quotient rule of exponents} } \\ & = & {-2.63 \times 10^{-4}} & { \text{Scientific notation} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {\left( {2.7 \times 10^{5}} \right)\left( {6.04 \times 10^{13}} \right)} & = & {(2.7 \times 6.04)\left( {10^{5} \times 10^{13}} \right)} & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Commutative and associative} } \\ { \text{properties of multiplication} } \end{array} \\ & = & {(16.308)\left( 10^{18} \right)} & { \text{Product rule of exponents} } \\ & = & {1.6308 \times 10^{19}} & { \text{Scientific notation} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\begin{array}{ccll} {\left( {1.2 \times 10^{8}} \right) \div \left( {9.6 \times 10^{5}} \right)} & = & {\left( \frac{1.2}{9.6} \right)\left( \frac{10^{8}}{10^{5}} \right)} & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Commutative and associative} } \\ { \text{properties of multiplication} } \end{array} \\ & = & {(0.125)\left( 10^{3} \right)} & { \text{Quotient rule of exponents} } \\ & = & {1.25 \times 10^{2}} & { \text{Scientific notation} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓔ $$\begin{array}{ccl} {\left( {3.33 \times 10^{4}} \right)\left( {-1.05 \times 10^{7}} \right)\left( {5.62 \times 10^{5}} \right)} & = & {\lbrack 3.33 \times (-1.05) \times 5.62\rbrack\left( {10^{4} \times 10^{7} \times 10^{5}} \right)} \\ & \approx & {(-19.65)\left( 10^{16} \right)} \\ & = & {-1.965 \times 10^{17}} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Applying Scientific Notation to Solve Problems
snippet: Applying Scientific Notation to Solve Problems: In April 2014, the population of the United States was about 308,000,000 people. The national debt was about \$17,547,000,000,000. Write each number in scientific notation, rounding figures...
body_xml:
<example number="13" title="Applying Scientific Notation to Solve Problems">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>In April 2014, the population of the United States was about 308,000,000 people. The national debt was about \$17,547,000,000,000. Write each number in scientific notation, rounding figures to two decimal places, and find the amount of the debt per U.S. citizen. Write the answer in both scientific and standard notations.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The population was $$308,000,000 = 3.08 \times 10^{8}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The national debt was $$\$17,547,000,000,000 \approx \$1.75 \times 10^{13}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To find the amount of debt per citizen, divide the national debt by the number of citizens.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} {\left( 1.75 \times 10^{13} \right) \div \left( 3.08 \times 10^{8} \right)} & = & {\left( \frac{1.75}{3.08} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{10^{13}}{10^{8}} \right)} \\ & \approx & {0.57 \times 10^{5}} \\ & = & {5.7 \times 10^{4}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The debt per citizen at the time was about $$\$5.7 \times 10^{4},$$ or \$57,000.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

        <item>ⓓ $$\sqrt{49} - \sqrt{81}$$</item>
      </list>

    <solution>

        <item>ⓐ $$\sqrt{100} = 10$$ because $$10^{2} = 100$$</item>

snippet: The Product Rule for Simplifying Square Roots: If a and b are nonnegative, the square root of the product ab is equal to the product of the square roots of a and b. \sqrt{ab} = \sqrt{a} \cdot \sqrt{b}

snippet: Adding Square Roots: Add 5\sqrt{12} + 2\sqrt{3}. We can rewrite 5\sqrt{12} as 5\sqrt{4 \cdot 3}. According the product rule, this becomes 5\sqrt{4}\sqrt{3}. The square root of \sqrt{4} is 2, so the expression becomes 5(2)\sqrt{3}, which is...

<example number="6" title="Adding Square Roots">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Add $$5\sqrt{12} + 2\sqrt{3}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We can rewrite $$5\sqrt{12}$$ as $$5\sqrt{4 \cdot 3}.$$ According the product rule, this becomes $$5\sqrt{4}\sqrt{3}.$$ The square root of $$\sqrt{4}$$ is 2, so the expression becomes $$5(2)\sqrt{3},$$ which is $$10\sqrt{3}.$$ Now the terms have the same radicand so we can add.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$10\sqrt{3} + 2\sqrt{3} = 12\sqrt{3}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>

<example number="7" title="Subtracting Square Roots">

      <paragraph>Subtract $$20\sqrt{72a^{3}b^{4}c} - 14\sqrt{8a^{3}b^{4}c}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Factor 9 out of the first term so that both terms have equal radicands.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cclcl} {20\sqrt{72a^{3}b^{4}c}} & = & {20\sqrt{9 \cdot 8a^{3}b^{4}c}} & = & {20\sqrt{9}\sqrt{8a^{3}b^{4}c}} \\ & = & {20(3)\sqrt{8a^{3}b^{4}c}} & = & {60\sqrt{8a^{3}b^{4}c}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {20\sqrt{72a^{3}b^{4}c} - 14\sqrt{8a^{3}b^{4}c}} \\ {= 60\sqrt{8a^{3}b^{4}c} - 14\sqrt{8a^{3}b^{4}c}} \\ {= 46\sqrt{8a^{3}b^{4}c}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

<example number="10" title="Simplifying nth Roots">

      <paragraph>Simplify each of the following:</paragraph>

        <item>ⓑ $$\sqrt[4]{4} \cdot \sqrt[4]{1,024}$$</item>

        <item>ⓓ $$8\sqrt[4]{3} - \sqrt[4]{48}$$</item>

    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\sqrt[5]{-32} = -2$$ because $${(-2)}^{5} = -32$$</item>

        <item>ⓒ $$\begin{array}{ll} \frac{- \sqrt[3]{8x^{6}}}{\sqrt[3]{125}} & { \text{Write as quotient of two radical expressions} .} \\ \frac{- 2x^{2}}{5} & { \text{Simplify} .} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\begin{array}{ll} {8\sqrt[4]{3} - 2\sqrt[4]{3}} & { \text{Simplify to get equal radicands} .} \\ {6\sqrt[4]{3} } & { \text{Add} .} \end{array}$$</item>

    </solution>
  </example>

title: Writing Rational Exponents as Radicals
snippet: Writing Rational Exponents as Radicals: Write 343^{\frac{2}{3}} as a radical. Simplify. The 2 tells us the power and the 3 tells us the root. 343^{\frac{2}{3}} = \left( \sqrt[3]{343} \right)^{2} = \sqrt[3]{343^{2}} We know that...

<example number="11" title="Writing Rational Exponents as Radicals">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write $$343^{\frac{2}{3}}$$ as a radical. Simplify.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The 2 tells us the power and the 3 tells us the root.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$343^{\frac{2}{3}} = \left( \sqrt[3]{343} \right)^{2} = \sqrt[3]{343^{2}}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We know that $$\sqrt[3]{343} = 7$$ because $$7^{3} = 343.$$ Because the cube root is easy to find, it is easiest to find the cube root before squaring for this problem. In general, it is easier to find the root first and then raise it to a power.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$343^{\frac{2}{3}} = \left( \sqrt[3]{343} \right)^{2} = 7^{2} = 49$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Writing Radicals as Rational Exponents
snippet: Writing Radicals as Rational Exponents: Write \frac{4}{\sqrt[7]{a^{2}}} using a rational exponent. The power is 2 and the root is 7, so the rational exponent will be \frac{2}{7}. We get \frac{4}{a^{\frac{2}{7}}}. Using properties of...

<example number="12" title="Writing Radicals as Rational Exponents">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write $$\frac{4}{\sqrt[7]{a^{2}}}$$ using a rational exponent.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The power is 2 and the root is 7, so the rational exponent will be $$\frac{2}{7}.$$ We get $$\frac{4}{a^{\frac{2}{7}}}.$$ Using properties of exponents, we get $$\frac{4}{\sqrt[7]{a^{2}}} = 4a^{\frac{-2}{7}}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Polynomials: A polynomial is an expression that can be written in the form a_{n}x^{n} + ... + a_{2}x^{2} + a_{1}x + a_{0} Each real number ai is called a coefficient. The number a_{0} that is not multiplied by a variable is called a...

<note type="rule" source_type="Polynomials" title="Polynomials">
    <paragraph>A polynomial is an expression that can be written in the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$a_{n}x^{n} + ... + a_{2}x^{2} + a_{1}x + a_{0}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Each real number ai is called a coefficient. The number $$a_{0}$$ that is not multiplied by a variable is called a constant. Each product $$a_{i}x^{i}$$ is a term of a polynomial. The highest power of the variable that occurs in the polynomial is called the degree of a polynomial. The leading term is the term with the highest power, and its coefficient is called the leading coefficient.</paragraph>
  </note>

    <problem>
      <paragraph>For the following polynomials, identify the degree, the leading term, and the leading coefficient.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$3 + 2x^{2} - 4x^{3}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$5t^{5} - 2t^{3} + 7t$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$6p - p^{3} - 2$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐThe highest power of x is 3, so the degree is 3. The leading term is the term containing that degree, $$-4x^{3}.$$ The leading coefficient is the coefficient of that term, $$-4.$$</item>
        <item>ⓑThe highest power of t is $$5,$$ so the degree is $$5.$$ The leading term is the term containing that degree, $$5t^{5}.$$ The leading coefficient is the coefficient of that term, $$5.$$</item>
        <item>ⓒThe highest power of p is $$3,$$ so the degree is $$3.$$ The leading term is the term containing that degree, $$- p^{3},$$ The leading coefficient is the coefficient of that term, $$-1.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>

<example number="3" title="Subtracting Polynomials">

      <paragraph>$$\left( {7x^{4} - x^{2} + 6x + 1} \right) - \left( {5x^{3} - 2x^{2} + 3x + 2} \right)$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{ll} {7x^{4} - x^{2} + 6x + 1 - 5x^{3} + 2x^{2} - 3x - 2} & { \text{Distribute negative sign.} } \\ {7x^{4} - 5x^{3} + x^{2} + 6x - 3x + 1 - 2} & { \text{Group like terms.} } \\ {7x^{4} - 5x^{3} + x^{2} + 3x - 1} & { \text{Combine/simplify.} } \end{array}$$</paragraph>

title: Factoring the Greatest Common Factor
snippet: Factoring the Greatest Common Factor: Factor 6x^{3}y^{3} + 45x^{2}y^{2} + 21xy. First, find the GCF of the expression. The GCF of 6, 45, and 21 is 3. The GCF of x^{3},x^{2} , and x is x . (Note that the GCF of a set of expressions in the...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Factoring the Greatest Common Factor">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Factor $$6x^{3}y^{3} + 45x^{2}y^{2} + 21xy.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, find the GCF of the expression. The GCF of 6, 45, and 21 is 3. The GCF of $$x^{3},x^{2}$$ , and $$x$$ is $$x$$ . (Note that the GCF of a set of expressions in the form $$x^{n}$$ will always be the exponent of lowest degree.) And the GCF of $$y^{3},y^{2}$$ , and $$y$$ is $$y$$ . Combine these to find the GCF of the polynomial, $$3xy$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, determine what the GCF needs to be multiplied by to obtain each term of the polynomial. We find that $$3xy\left( 2x^{2}y^{2} \right) = 6x^{3}y^{3},3xy(15xy) = 45x^{2}y^{2}$$ , and $$3xy(7) = 21xy.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Finally, write the factored expression as the product of the GCF and the sum of the terms we needed to multiply by.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$(3xy)\left( 2x^{2}y^{2} + 15xy + 7 \right)$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>After factoring, we can check our work by multiplying. Use the distributive property to confirm that $$(3xy)\left( 2x^{2}y^{2} + 15xy + 7 \right) = 6x^{3}y^{3} + 45x^{2}y^{2} + 21xy.$$</paragraph>
  </example>

Factor $$x^{2} + 2x - 15.$$ We have a trinomial with leading coefficient $$1,b = 2,$$ and $$c = -15.$$ We need to find two numbers with a product of $$-15$$ and a sum of $$2.$$ In the table below, we list factors until we find a pair with the desired sum. Factors of $$-15$$ Sum of Factors $$1,-15$$ $$-14$$ $$-1,15$$ 14 $$3,-5$$ $$-2$$ $$-3,5$$ 2
Now that we have identified $$p$$ and $$q$$ as $$-3$$ and $$5,$$ write the factored form as $$(x - 3)(x + 5).$$ We can check our work by multiplying. Use FOIL to confirm that $$(x - 3)(x + 5) = x^{2} + 2x - 15.$$

title: Factoring a Trinomial by Grouping
snippet: Factoring a Trinomial by Grouping: Factor 5x^{2} + 7x - 6 by grouping. We have a trinomial with a = 5,b = 7, and c = -6. First, determine ac = -30. We need to find two numbers with a product of -30 and a sum of 7. In the table below, we...
body_xml:
Factor $$5x^{2} + 7x - 6$$ by grouping. We have a trinomial with $$a = 5,b = 7,$$ and $$c = -6.$$ First, determine $$ac = -30.$$ We need to find two numbers with a product of $$-30$$ and a sum of $$7.$$ In the table below, we list factors until we find a pair with the desired sum. Factors of $$-30$$ Sum of Factors $$1,-30$$ $$-29$$ $$-1,30$$ 29 $$2,-15$$ $$-13$$ $$-2,15$$ 13 $$3,-10$$ $$-7$$ $$-3,10$$ 7
So $$p = -3$$ and $$q = 10.$$ $$\begin{array}{ll} {5x^{2} - 3x + 10x - 6 } & { \text{Rewrite the original expression as} ax^{2} + px + qx + c.} \\ {x(5x - 3) + 2(5x - 3)} & { \text{Factor out the GCF of each part} .} \\ {(5x - 3)(x + 2)} & { \text{Factor out the GCF} \text{of the expression} .} \end{array}$$ We can check our work by multiplying. Use FOIL to confirm that $$(5x - 3)(x + 2) = 5x^{2} + 7x - 6.$$

title: Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial
snippet: Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial: Factor 25x^{2} + 20x + 4. Notice that 25x^{2} and 4 are perfect squares because 25x^{2} = {(5x)}^{2} and 4 = 2^{2}. Then check to see if the middle term is twice the product of 5x and 2. The middle...

<example number="4" title="Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Factor $$25x^{2} + 20x + 4.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Notice that $$25x^{2}$$ and $$4$$ are perfect squares because $$25x^{2} = {(5x)}^{2}$$ and $$4 = 2^{2}.$$ Then check to see if the middle term is twice the product of $$5x$$ and $$2.$$ The middle term is, indeed, twice the product: $$2(5x)(2) = 20x.$$ Therefore, the trinomial is a perfect square trinomial and can be written as $${(5x + 2)}^{2}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{2x^{2} + x - 6}{x^{2} - 1} \div \frac{x^{2} - 4}{x^{2} + 2x + 1}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>

title: Adding Rational Expressions
snippet: Adding Rational Expressions: Add the rational expressions: \frac{5}{x} + \frac{6}{y} First, we have to find the LCD. In this case, the LCD will be xy. We then multiply each expression by the appropriate form of 1 to obtain xy as the...
body_xml:
<example number="4" title="Adding Rational Expressions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Add the rational expressions:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{5}{x} + \frac{6}{y}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, we have to find the LCD. In this case, the LCD will be $$xy.$$ We then multiply each expression by the appropriate form of 1 to obtain $$xy$$ as the denominator for each fraction.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{5}{x} \cdot \frac{y}{y} + \frac{6}{y} \cdot \frac{x}{x}} \\ {\frac{5y}{xy} + \frac{6x}{xy}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now that the expressions have the same denominator, we simply add the numerators to find the sum.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{6x + 5y}{xy}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>Multiplying by $$\frac{y}{y}$$ or $$\frac{x}{x}$$ does not change the value of the original expression because any number divided by itself is 1, and multiplying an expression by 1 gives the original expression.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Subtracting Rational Expressions
snippet: Subtracting Rational Expressions: Subtract the rational expressions: \frac{6}{x^{2} + 4x + 4} - \frac{2}{x^{2}-4} \begin{array}{ll} {\frac{6}{{(x + 2)}^{2}} - \frac{2}{(x + 2)(x - 2)}} & { \text{Factor} .} \\ {\frac{6}{{(x + 2)}^{2}} \cdot...

<example number="5" title="Subtracting Rational Expressions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Subtract the rational expressions:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{6}{x^{2} + 4x + 4} - \frac{2}{x^{2}-4}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {\frac{6}{{(x + 2)}^{2}} - \frac{2}{(x + 2)(x - 2)}} & { \text{Factor} .} \\ {\frac{6}{{(x + 2)}^{2}} \cdot \frac{x - 2}{x - 2} - \frac{2}{(x + 2)(x - 2)} \cdot \frac{x + 2}{x + 2}} & { \text{Multiply each fraction to get LCD as denominator} .} \\ {\frac{6(x - 2)}{{(x + 2)}^{2}(x - 2)} - \frac{2(x + 2)}{{(x + 2)}^{2}(x - 2)}} & { \text{Multiply} .} \\ \frac{6x - 12 - (2x + 4)}{{(x + 2)}^{2}(x - 2)} & { \text{Apply distributive property} .} \\ \frac{4x - 16}{{(x + 2)}^{2}(x - 2)} & { \text{Subtract} .} \\ \frac{4(x - 4)}{{(x + 2)}^{2}(x - 2)} & { \text{Simplify} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Simplifying Complex Rational Expressions
snippet: Simplifying Complex Rational Expressions: Simplify: \frac{y + \frac{1}{x}}{\frac{x}{y}} . Begin by combining the expressions in the numerator into one expression. \begin{array}{lc} {y \cdot \frac{x}{x} + \frac{1}{x}} & { \text{Multiply by}...
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Simplifying Complex Rational Expressions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Simplify: $$\frac{y + \frac{1}{x}}{\frac{x}{y}}$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Begin by combining the expressions in the numerator into one expression.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lc} {y \cdot \frac{x}{x} + \frac{1}{x}} & { \text{Multiply by} \frac{x}{x} \text{to get LCD as denominator} .} \\ {\frac{xy}{x} + \frac{1}{x}} & \\ \frac{xy + 1}{x} & { \text{Add numerators} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now the numerator is a single rational expression and the denominator is a single rational expression.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\frac{xy + 1}{x}}{\frac{x}{y}}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We can rewrite this as division, and then multiplication.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lc} {\frac{xy + 1}{x} \div \frac{x}{y}} & \\ {\frac{xy + 1}{x} \cdot \frac{y}{x}} & { \text{Rewrite as multiplication} .} \\ \frac{y(xy + 1)}{x^{2}} & { \text{Multiply} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Plotting Points in a Rectangular Coordinate System: Plot the points \left( {-2,4} \right), \left( {3,3} \right), and \left( {0,-3} \right) in the plane. To plot the point \left( {-2,4} \right), begin at the origin. The x-coordinate is –2,...
body_xml: Plot the points $$\left( {-2,4} \right),$$ $$\left( {3,3} \right),$$ and $$\left( {0,-3} \right)$$ in the plane. To plot the point $$\left( {-2,4} \right),$$ begin at the origin. The x-coordinate is –2, so move two units to the left. The y-coordinate is 4, so then move four units up in the positive y direction. To plot the point $$\left( {3,3} \right),$$ begin again at the origin. The x-coordinate is 3, so move three units to the right. The y-coordinate is also 3, so move three units up in the positive y direction. To plot the point $$\left( {0,-3} \right),$$ begin again at the origin. The x-coordinate is 0. This tells us not to move in either direction along the x-axis. The y-coordinate is –3, so move three units down in the negative y direction. See the graph in Figure 5. Note that when either coordinate is zero, the point must be on an axis. If the x-coordinate is zero, the point is on the y-axis. If the y-coordinate is zero, the point is on the x-axis.

title: Finding the Distance between Two Locations
snippet: Finding the Distance between Two Locations: Let’s return to the situation introduced at the beginning of this section. Tracie set out from Elmhurst, IL, to go to Franklin Park. On the way, she made a few stops to do errands. Each stop is...
body_xml:
Let’s return to the situation introduced at the beginning of this section. Tracie set out from Elmhurst, IL, to go to Franklin Park. On the way, she made a few stops to do errands. Each stop is indicated by a red dot in Figure 1. Find the total distance that Tracie traveled. Compare this with the distance between her starting and final positions. The first thing we should do is identify ordered pairs to describe each position. If we set the starting position at the origin, we can identify each of the other points by counting units east (right) and north (up) on the grid. For example, the first stop is 1 block east and 1 block north, so it is at $$\left( {1,1} \right).$$ The next stop is 5 blocks to the east, so it is at $$\left( {5,1} \right).$$ After that, she traveled 3 blocks east and 2 blocks north to $$\left( {8,3} \right).$$ Lastly, she traveled 4 blocks north to $$\left( {8,7} \right).$$ We can label these points on the grid as in Figure 15. Next, we can calculate the distance. Note that each grid unit represents 1,000 feet. From her starting location to her first stop at $$\left( {1,1} \right),$$ Tracie might have driven north 1,000 feet and then east 1,000 feet, or vice versa. Either way, she drove 2,000 feet to her first stop. Her second stop is at $$\left( {5,1} \right).$$ So from $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {5,1} \right),$$ Tracie drove east 4,000 feet. Her third stop is at $$\left( {8,3} \right).$$ There are a number of routes from $$\left( {5,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {8,3} \right).$$ Whatever route Tracie decided to use, the distance is the same, as there are no angular streets between the two points. Let’s say she drove east 3,000 feet and then north 2,000 feet for a total of 5,000 feet. Tracie’s final stop is at $$\left( {8,7} \right).$$ This is a straight drive north from $$\left( {8,3} \right)$$ for a total of 4,000 feet. Next, we will add the distances listed in Table 3. From/To Number of Feet Driven $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ 2,000 $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {5,1} \right)$$ 4,000 $$\left( {5,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {8,3} \right)$$ 5,000 $$\left( {8,3} \right)$$ to $$\left( {8,7} \right)$$ 4,000 Total 15,000
The total distance Tracie drove is 15,000 feet, or 2.84 miles. This is not, however, the actual distance between her starting and ending positions. To find this distance, we can use the distance formula between the points $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {8,7} \right).$$ $$\begin{array}{l} {d = \sqrt{{(8 - 0)}^{2} + {(7 - 0)}^{2}}} \\ { = \sqrt{64 + 49}} \\ { = \sqrt{113}} \\ { \approx 10.63 \text{units} } \end{array}$$ At 1,000 feet per grid unit, the distance between Elmhurst, IL, to Franklin Park is 10,630.14 feet, or 2.01 miles. The distance formula results in a shorter calculation because it is based on the hypotenuse of a right triangle, a straight diagonal from the origin to the point $$\left( {8,7} \right).$$ Perhaps you have heard the saying “as the crow flies,” which means the shortest distance between two points because a crow can fly in a straight line even though a person on the ground has to travel a longer distance on existing roadways.

<example number="8" title="Finding the Center of a Circle">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The diameter of a circle has endpoints $$\left( {-1,-4} \right)$$ and $$\left( {5,-4} \right).$$ Find the center of the circle.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The center of a circle is the center, or midpoint, of its diameter. Thus, the midpoint formula will yield the center point.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} \left( {\frac{x_{1} + x_{2}}{2},\frac{y_{1} + y_{2}}{2}} \right) \\ {\left( {\frac{- 1 + 5}{2},\frac{- 4 - 4}{2}} \right) = \left( {\frac{4}{2}, - \frac{8}{2}} \right) = (2,-4)} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given a linear equation in one variable, use algebra to solve it. The following steps are used to manipulate an equation and isolate the unknown variable, so that the last line reads x = \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_,} if x is the...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given a linear equation in one variable, use algebra to solve it.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The following steps are used to manipulate an equation and isolate the unknown variable, so that the last line reads $$x = \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_,}$$ if x is the unknown. There is no set order, as the steps used depend on what is given:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>We may add, subtract, multiply, or divide an equation by a number or an expression as long as we do the same thing to both sides of the equal sign. Note that we cannot divide by zero.</item>
      <item>Apply the distributive property as needed: $$a\left( {b + c} \right) = ab + ac.$$</item>
      <item>Isolate the variable on one side of the equation.</item>
      <item>When the variable is multiplied by a coefficient in the final stage, multiply both sides of the equation by the reciprocal of the coefficient.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Solving an Equation in One Variable
snippet: Solving an Equation in One Variable: Solve the following equation: 2x + 7 = 19. This equation can be written in the form ax + b = 0 by subtracting 19 from both sides. However, we may proceed to solve the equation in its original form by...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Solving an Equation in One Variable">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the following equation: $$2x + 7 = 19.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This equation can be written in the form $$ax + b = 0$$ by subtracting $$19$$ from both sides. However, we may proceed to solve the equation in its original form by performing algebraic operations.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rclc} {2x + 7} & = & 19 & \\ {2x} & = & 12 & { \text{Subtract 7 from both sides} .} \\ x & = & 6 & { \text{Multiply both sides by} \frac{1}{2} \text{or divide by 2} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solution is 6.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving an Equation Algebraically When the Variable Appears on Both Sides
snippet: Solving an Equation Algebraically When the Variable Appears on Both Sides: Solve the following equation: 4\left( {x-3} \right) + 12 = 15-5\left( {x + 6} \right). Apply standard algebraic properties. \begin{array}{cclc} {4(x - 3) + 12} & =...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Solving an Equation Algebraically When the Variable Appears on Both Sides">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the following equation: $$4\left( {x-3} \right) + 12 = 15-5\left( {x + 6} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Apply standard algebraic properties.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cclc} {4(x - 3) + 12} & = & {15 - 5(x + 6)} & \\ {4x - 12 + 12} & = & {15 - 5x - 30} & { \text{Apply the distributive property} .} \\ {4x} & = & {-15 - 5x} & { \text{Combine like terms} .} \\ {9x} & = & -15 & { \text{Place} x \text{-terms on one side and simplify} .} \\ x & = & {- \frac{15}{9}} & { \text{Multiply both sides by} \frac{1}{9} \text{, the reciprocal of 9} .} \\ x & = & {- \frac{5}{3}} & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>This problem requires the distributive property to be applied twice, and then the properties of algebra are used to reach the final line, $$x = - \frac{5}{3}.$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Solving a Rational Equation
snippet: Solving a Rational Equation: Solve the rational equation: \frac{7}{2x} - \frac{5}{3x} = \frac{22}{3}. We have three denominators; 2x,3x, and 3. The LCD must contain 2x,3x, and 3. An LCD of 6x contains all three denominators. In other...
body_xml:
<example number="3" title="Solving a Rational Equation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the rational equation: $$\frac{7}{2x} - \frac{5}{3x} = \frac{22}{3}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have three denominators; $$2x,3x,$$ and 3. The LCD must contain $$2x,3x,$$ and 3. An LCD of $$6x$$ contains all three denominators. In other words, each denominator can be divided evenly into the LCD. Next, multiply both sides of the equation by the LCD $$6x.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rclc} {(6x)\left( {\frac{7}{2x} - \frac{5}{3x}} \right)} & = & {\left( \frac{22}{3} \right)(6x)} & \\ {(6x)\left( \frac{7}{2x} \right) - (6x)\left( \frac{5}{3x} \right)} & = & {\left( \frac{22}{3} \right)(6x)} & { \text{Use the distributive property} .} \\ {({6x})\left( \frac{7}{2x} \right) - ({6x})\left( \frac{5}{3x} \right)} & = & {\left( \frac{22}{3} \right)(6x)} & { \text{Cancel out the common factors} .} \\ {3(7) - 2(5)} & = & {22(2x)} & { \text{Multiply remaining factors by each numerator} .} \\ {21 - 10} & = & {44x} & \\ 11 & = & {44x} & \\ \frac{11}{44} & = & x & \\ \frac{1}{4} & = & x & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given a rational equation, solve it.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Factor all denominators in the equation.</item>
      <item>Find and exclude values that set each denominator equal to zero.</item>
      <item>Find the LCD.</item>
      <item>Multiply the whole equation by the LCD. If the LCD is correct, there will be no denominators left.</item>
      <item>Solve the remaining equation.</item>
      <item>Make sure to check solutions back in the original equations to avoid a solution producing zero in a denominator.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Solving a Rational Equation without Factoring
snippet: Solving a Rational Equation without Factoring: Solve the following rational equation: \frac{2}{x} - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{7}{2x} We have three denominators: x, 2, and 2x. No factoring is required. The product of the first two denominators is...
body_xml:
<example number="4" title="Solving a Rational Equation without Factoring">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the following rational equation:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{2}{x} - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{7}{2x}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have three denominators: $$x,$$ $$2,$$ and $$2x.$$ No factoring is required. The product of the first two denominators is equal to the third denominator, so, the LCD is $$2x.$$ Only one value is excluded from a solution set, 0. $$2x.$$ Next, multiply the whole equation (both sides of the equal sign) by $$\begin{matrix} {2x\left( {\frac{2}{x} - \frac{3}{2}} \right)} & = & {\left( \frac{7}{2x} \right)2x} & \\ {2x\left( \frac{2}{x} \right) - 2x\left( \frac{3}{2} \right)} & = & {\left( \frac{7}{2x} \right){2x}} & { \text{Distribute} 2x.} \\ {2(2) - 3x} & = & 7 & { \text{Denominators cancel out} .} \\ {4 - 3x} & = & 7 & \\ {-3x} & = & 3 & \\ x & = & -1 & \\ & & { \text{or} \left\{ -1 \right\}} & \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$-1,$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The proposed solution is −1, $$\left\{ -1 \right\}$$ which is not an excluded value, so the solution set contains one number, $$\frac{2}{3x} = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{6x}.$$ or $$\frac{1}{x} = \frac{1}{10} - \frac{3}{4x}.$$ written in set notation.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving a Rational Equation by Factoring the Denominator
snippet: Solving a Rational Equation by Factoring the Denominator: Solve the following rational equation: 4x = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot x. First find the common denominator. The three denominators in factored form are 20x. and x = 0 The smallest expression...
body_xml:
<example number="5" title="Solving a Rational Equation by Factoring the Denominator">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the following rational equation: $$4x = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot x.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First find the common denominator. The three denominators in factored form are $$20x.$$ and $$x = 0$$ The smallest expression that is divisible by each one of the denominators is $$20x.$$ Only $$\begin{array}{rcl} {20x\left( \frac{1}{x} \right)} & = & {\left( {\frac{1}{10} - \frac{3}{4x}} \right)20x} \\ 20 & = & {2x - 15} \\ 35 & = & {2x} \\ \frac{35}{2} & = & x \end{array}$$ is an excluded value. Multiply the whole equation by $$\frac{35}{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$- \frac{5}{2x} + \frac{3}{4x} = - \frac{7}{4}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solution is $$\frac{3}{x - 6} = \frac{5}{x}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving Rational Equations with a Binomial in the Denominator
snippet: Solving Rational Equations with a Binomial in the Denominator: Solve the following rational equations and state the excluded values: ⓐ \frac{x}{x - 2} = \frac{5}{x - 2} - \frac{1}{2} ⓑ x ⓒ x - 6 ⓐThe denominators x\left( {x - 6} \right)....
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Solving Rational Equations with a Binomial in the Denominator">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the following rational equations and state the excluded values:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\frac{x}{x - 2} = \frac{5}{x - 2} - \frac{1}{2}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$x$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$x - 6$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐThe denominators $$x\left( {x - 6} \right).$$ and $$\begin{array}{rclc} \frac{3}{x - 6} & = & \frac{5}{x} & \\ {3x} & = & {5(x - 6)} & { \text{Distribute} .} \\ {3x} & = & {5x - 30} & \\ {-2x} & = & -30 & \\ x & = & 15 & \end{array}$$ have nothing in common. Therefore, the LCD is the product $$6$$ However, for this problem, we can cross-multiply. $$0.$$ The solution is 15. $$2\left( {x - 3} \right).$$ The excluded values are $$2\left( {x - 3} \right).$$ and $$\begin{array}{rcl} {2(x - 3)\left( \frac{x}{x - 3} \right)} & = & {\left( {\frac{5}{x - 3} - \frac{1}{2}} \right)2(x - 3)} \\ \frac{2{(x - 3)}x}{x - 3} & = & {\frac{2{(x - 3)}5}{x - 3} - \frac{2(x - 3)}{2}} \\ {2x} & = & {10 - (x - 3)} \\ {2x} & = & {10 - x + 3} \\ {2x} & = & {13 - x} \\ {3x} & = & 13 \\ x & = & \frac{13}{3} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ The LCD is $$\frac{13}{3}.$$ Multiply both sides of the equation by $$3.$$ $$2\left( {x - 2} \right).$$ The solution is $$2\left( {x - 2} \right).$$ The excluded value is $$\begin{array}{rcl} {2(x - 2)\left( \frac{x}{x - 2} \right)} & = & {\left( {\frac{5}{x - 2} - \frac{1}{2}} \right)2(x - 2)} \\ {2x} & = & {10 - (x - 2)} \\ {2x} & = & {12 - x} \\ {3x} & = & 12 \\ x & = & 4 \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒThe least common denominator is $$2.$$ Multiply both sides of the equation by $$\frac{- 3}{2x + 1} = \frac{4}{3x + 1}.$$ $$\frac{2}{x + 1} - \frac{1}{x - 1} = \frac{2x}{x^{2} - 1}.$$ The solution is 4. The excluded value is $$x^{2}-1.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving a Rational Equation with Factored Denominators and Stating Excluded Values
snippet: Solving a Rational Equation with Factored Denominators and Stating Excluded Values: Solve the rational equation after factoring the denominators: \left( {x - 1} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right). State the excluded values. We must factor the...
body_xml:
<example number="7" title="Solving a Rational Equation with Factored Denominators and Stating Excluded Values">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the rational equation after factoring the denominators: $$\left( {x - 1} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right).$$ State the excluded values.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We must factor the denominator $$\begin{array}{rcl} {(x - 1)(x + 1)\left( {\frac{2}{x + 1} - \frac{1}{x - 1}} \right)} & = & {\left( \frac{2x}{(x - 1)(x + 1)} \right)(x - 1)(x + 1)} \\ {2(x - 1) - 1(x + 1)} & = & {2x} \\ {2x - 2 - x - 1} & = & {2x \text{Distribute the negative sign} .} \\ {-3 - x} & = & 0 \\ -3 & = & x \end{array}$$ We recognize this as the difference of squares, and factor it as $$-3.$$ Thus, the LCD that contains each denominator is $$1$$ Multiply the whole equation by the LCD, cancel out the denominators, and solve the remaining equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$-1.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solution is $$\frac{2}{x - 2} + \frac{1}{x + 1} = \frac{1}{x^{2} - x - 2}.$$ The excluded values are $$y = mx + b,$$ and $$m = \text{slope}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} m & = & \frac{3 - (-1)}{-5 - 2} \\ & = & \frac{4}{-7} \\ & = & {- \frac{4}{7}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

<example number="9" title="Identifying the Slope and y-intercept of a Line Given an Equation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Identify the slope and y-intercept, given the equation $$b = -4.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>As the line is in $$x = 0.$$ form, the given line has a slope of $$x = 0$$ The y-intercept is $$y - y_{1} = m\left( {x - x_{1}} \right)$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>The y-intercept is the point at which the line crosses the y-axis. On the y-axis, $$y - y_{1} = m\left( {x - x_{1}} \right)$$ We can always identify the y-intercept when the line is in slope-intercept form, as it will always equal b. Or, just substitute $$m = -3$$ and solve for y.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Finding the Equation of a Line Given the Slope and One Point

<example number="10" title="Finding the Equation of a Line Given the Slope and One Point">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write the equation of the line with slope $$\left( {4,8} \right)$$ and passing through the point $$\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right).$$ Write the final equation in slope-intercept form.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Using the point-slope formula, substitute $$\begin{array}{rcl} {y - y_{1}} & = & {m(x - x_{1})} \\ {y - 8} & = & {-3(x - 4)} \\ {y - 8} & = & {-3x + 12} \\ y & = & {-3x + 20} \end{array}$$ for m and the point $$m = 4,$$ for $$\left( {2,5} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {3,4} \right)$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>Note that any point on the line can be used to find the equation. If done correctly, the same final equation will be obtained.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Finding the Equation of a Line Passing Through Two Given Points
snippet: Finding the Equation of a Line Passing Through Two Given Points: Find the equation of the line passing through the points \frac{7}{3}, and \left( {3,4} \right) Write the final equation in slope-intercept form. First, we calculate the slope...

<example number="11" title="Finding the Equation of a Line Passing Through Two Given Points">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the equation of the line passing through the points $$\frac{7}{3},$$ and $$\left( {3,4} \right)$$ Write the final equation in slope-intercept form.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, we calculate the slope using the slope formula and two points.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, we use the point-slope formula with the slope of $$\begin{array}{rcl} {y - 4} & = & {\frac{7}{3}(x - 3)} \\ {y - 4} & = & {\frac{7}{3}x - 7 \text{Distribute the} \frac{7}{3}.} \\ y & = & {\frac{7}{3}x - 3} \end{array}$$ and either point. Let’s pick the point $$y = \frac{7}{3}x - 3.$$ for $$\left( {0,-3} \right)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {y - ( - 3)} & = & {\frac{7}{3}(x - 0)} \\ {y + 3} & = & {\frac{7}{3}x} \\ y & = & {\frac{7}{3}x - 3} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>In slope-intercept form, the equation is written as $$Ax + By = C$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>To prove that either point can be used, let us use the second point $$A,$$ and see if we get the same equation.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$B,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We see that the same line will be obtained using either point. This makes sense because we used both points to calculate the slope.</paragraph>
  </example>

First equation: $$2y - x = 10$$ Second equation: $$2y = x + 4.$$ See the graph of both lines in Figure 6 From the graph, we can see that the lines appear perpendicular, but we must compare the slopes. $$5x + 3y = 1$$ The slopes are negative reciprocals of each other, confirming that the lines are perpendicular.

title: Writing the Equation of a Line Parallel to a Given Line Passing Through a Given Point
snippet: Writing the Equation of a Line Parallel to a Given Line Passing Through a Given Point: Write the equation of line parallel to a m = - \frac{5}{3}. and passing through the point \frac{1}{3}, First, we will write the equation in...
body_xml: Write the equation of line parallel to a $$m = - \frac{5}{3}.$$ and passing through the point $$\frac{1}{3},$$ First, we will write the equation in slope-intercept form to find the slope. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {y - 5} & = & {- \frac{5}{3}(x - 3)} \\ {y - 5} & = & {- \frac{5}{3}x + 5} \\ y & = & {- \frac{5}{3}x + 10} \end{array}$$ The slope is $$y = - \frac{5}{3}x + 10.$$ The y-intercept is $$5x = 7 + y$$ but that really does not enter into our problem, as the only thing we need for two lines to be parallel is the same slope. The one exception is that if the y-intercepts are the same, then the two lines are the same line. The next step is to use this slope and the given point with the point-slope formula. $$\left( {-1,-2} \right).$$ The equation of the line is $$5x - 3y + 4 = 0$$ See Figure 7.

title: Finding the Equation of a Line Perpendicular to a Given Line Passing Through a Given Point
snippet: Finding the Equation of a Line Perpendicular to a Given Line Passing Through a Given Point: Find the equation of the line perpendicular to m = \frac{5}{3}. and passing through the point - \frac{3}{5}. The first step is to write the...
body_xml:
<example number="16" title="Finding the Equation of a Line Perpendicular to a Given Line Passing Through a Given Point">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the equation of the line perpendicular to $$m = \frac{5}{3}.$$ and passing through the point $$- \frac{3}{5}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The first step is to write the equation in slope-intercept form.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {y - 1} & = & {- \frac{3}{5}\left( {x - (-4)} \right)} \\ {y - 1} & = & {- \frac{3}{5}x - \frac{12}{5}} \\ y & = & {- \frac{3}{5}x - \frac{12}{5} + \frac{5}{5}} \\ y & = & {- \frac{3}{5}x - \frac{7}{5}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We see that the slope is $$y = 4x + 3,$$ This means that the slope of the line perpendicular to the given line is the negative reciprocal, or $$\frac{2}{x - 5} = \frac{4}{x + 1}$$ Next, we use the point-slope formula with this new slope and the given point.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x = 5$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>
