title: Modeling a Linear Equation to Solve an Unknown Number Problem
snippet: Modeling a Linear Equation to Solve an Unknown Number Problem: Find a linear equation to solve for the following unknown quantities: One number exceeds another number by 17 and their sum is 31. Find the two numbers. Let x equal the first...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Modeling a Linear Equation to Solve an Unknown Number Problem">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find a linear equation to solve for the following unknown quantities: One number exceeds another number by $$17$$ and their sum is $$31.$$ Find the two numbers.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$x$$ equal the first number. Then, as the second number exceeds the first by 17, we can write the second number as $$x + 17.$$ The sum of the two numbers is 31. We usually interpret the word is as an equal sign.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} {x + (x + 17)} & = & 31 \\ {2x + 17} & = & {31 \text{Simplify and solve} .} \\ {2x} & = & 14 \\ x & = & 7 \\ {x + 17} & = & {7 + 17} \\ & = & 24 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The two numbers are $$7$$ and $$24.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Setting Up a Linear Equation to Solve a Real-World Application
snippet: Setting Up a Linear Equation to Solve a Real-World Application: There are two cell phone companies that offer different packages. Company A charges a monthly service fee of \$34 plus \$.05/min talk-time. Company B charges a monthly service...
body_xml: There are two cell phone companies that offer different packages. Company A charges a monthly service fee of \$34 plus \$.05/min talk-time. Company B charges a monthly service fee of \$40 plus \$.04/min talk-time. ⓐWrite a linear equation that models the packages offered by both companies. ⓑ If the average number of minutes used each month is 1,160, which company offers the better plan? ⓒIf the average number of minutes used each month is 420, which company offers the better plan? ⓓHow many minutes of talk-time would yield equal monthly statements from both companies? ⓐThe model for Company A can be written as $$A = 0.05x + 34.$$ This includes the variable cost of $$0.05x$$ plus the monthly service charge of \$34. Company B’s package charges a higher monthly fee of \$40, but a lower variable cost of $$0.04x.$$ Company B’s model can be written as $$B = 0.04x + \$40.$$ ⓑIf the average number of minutes used each month is 1,160, we have the following: $$\begin{array}{ccl} { \text{Company} A} & = & {0.05(1,160) + 34} \\ & = & {58 + 34} \\ & = & 92 \\ { \text{Company} B} & = & {0.04(1,160) + 40} \\ & = & {46.4 + 40} \\ & = & 86.4 \end{array}$$ So, Company B offers the lower monthly cost of \$86.40 as compared with the \$92 monthly cost offered by Company A when the average number of minutes used each month is 1,160. ⓒIf the average number of minutes used each month is 420, we have the following: $$\begin{array}{ccl} { \text{Company} A} & = & {0.05(420) + 34} \\ & = & {21 + 34} \\ & = & 55 \\ { \text{Company} B} & = & {0.04(420) + 40} \\ & = & {16.8 + 40} \\ & = & 56.8 \end{array}$$ If the average number of minutes used each month is 420, then Company A offers a lower monthly cost of \$55 compared to Company B’s monthly cost of \$56.80. ⓓTo answer the question of how many talk-time minutes would yield the same bill from both companies, we should think about the problem in terms of $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ coordinates: At what point are both the x-value and the y-value equal? We can find this point by setting the equations equal to each other and solving for x. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {0.05x + 34} & = & {0.04x + 40} \\ {0.01x} & = & 6 \\ x & = & 600 \end{array}$$ Check the x-value in each equation. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {0.05(600) + 34} & = & 64 \\ {0.04(600) + 40} & = & 64 \end{array}$$ Therefore, a monthly average of 600 talk-time minutes renders the plans equal. See Figure 2

title: Solving an Application Using a Formula
snippet: Solving an Application Using a Formula: It takes Andrew 30 min to drive to work in the morning. He drives home using the same route, but it takes 10 min longer, and he averages 10 mi/h less than in the morning. How far does Andrew drive to...
body_xml:
It takes Andrew 30 min to drive to work in the morning. He drives home using the same route, but it takes 10 min longer, and he averages 10 mi/h less than in the morning. How far does Andrew drive to work? This is a distance problem, so we can use the formula $$d = rt,$$ where distance equals rate multiplied by time. Note that when rate is given in mi/h, time must be expressed in hours. Consistent units of measurement are key to obtaining a correct solution. First, we identify the known and unknown quantities. Andrew’s morning drive to work takes 30 min, or $$\frac{1}{2}$$ h at rate $$r.$$ His drive home takes 40 min, or $$\frac{2}{3}$$ h, and his speed averages 10 mi/h less than the morning drive. Both trips cover distance $$d.$$ A table, such as Table 2, is often helpful for keeping track of information in these types of problems. $$d$$ $$r$$ $$t$$ To Work $$d$$ $$r$$ $$\frac{1}{2}$$ To Home $$d$$ $$r - 10$$ $$\frac{2}{3}$$
Write two equations, one for each trip. $$\begin{array}{rcll} d & = & {r\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)} & { \text{To work} } \\ d & = & {(r - 10)\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)} & { \text{To home} } \end{array}$$ As both equations equal the same distance, we set them equal to each other and solve for r. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {r\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)} & = & {(r - 10)\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)} \\ {\frac{1}{2}r} & = & {\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{20}{3}} \\ {\frac{1}{2}r - \frac{2}{3}r} & = & {- \frac{20}{3}} \\ {- \frac{1}{6}r} & = & {- \frac{20}{3}} \\ r & = & {- \frac{20}{3}(-6)} \\ r & = & 40 \end{array}$$ We have solved for the rate of speed to work, 40 mph. Substituting 40 into the rate on the return trip yields 30 mi/h. Now we can answer the question. Substitute the rate back into either equation and solve for d. $$\begin{array}{ccl} d & = & {40\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)} \\ & = & 20 \end{array}$$ The distance between home and work is 20 mi. Note that we could have cleared the fractions in the equation by multiplying both sides of the equation by the LCD to solve for $$r.$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} {r\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)} & = & {(r - 10)\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)} \\ {6 \times r\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)} & = & {6 \times (r - 10)\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)} \\ {3r} & = & {4(r - 10)} \\ {3r} & = & {4r - 40} \\ {- r} & = & -40 \\ r & = & 40 \end{array}$$

title: Solving a Perimeter Problem
snippet: Solving a Perimeter Problem: The perimeter of a rectangular outdoor patio is 54 ft. The length is 3 ft greater than the width. What are the dimensions of the patio? The perimeter formula is standard: P = 2L + 2W. We have two unknown...
body_xml: The perimeter of a rectangular outdoor patio is $$54$$ ft. The length is $$3$$ ft greater than the width. What are the dimensions of the patio? The perimeter formula is standard: $$P = 2L + 2W.$$ We have two unknown quantities, length and width. However, we can write the length in terms of the width as $$L = W + 3.$$ Substitute the perimeter value and the expression for length into the formula. It is often helpful to make a sketch and label the sides as in Figure 3. Now we can solve for the width and then calculate the length. $$\begin{array}{rcl} P & = & {2L + 2W} \\ 54 & = & {2(W + 3) + 2W} \\ 54 & = & {2W + 6 + 2W} \\ 54 & = & {4W + 6} \\ 48 & = & {4W} \\ 12 & = & W \\ {(12 + 3)} & = & L \\ 15 & = & L \end{array}$$ The dimensions are $$L = 15$$ ft and $$W = 12$$ ft.

title: Solving an Area Problem
snippet: Solving an Area Problem: The perimeter of a tablet of graph paper is 48 in. The length is 6 in. more than the width. Find the area of the graph paper. The standard formula for area is A = LW; however, we will solve the problem using the...
body_xml:
<example number="5" title="Solving an Area Problem">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The perimeter of a tablet of graph paper is 48 in. The length is $$6$$ in. more than the width. Find the area of the graph paper.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The standard formula for area is $$A = LW;$$ however, we will solve the problem using the perimeter formula. The reason we use the perimeter formula is because we know enough information about the perimeter that the formula will allow us to solve for one of the unknowns. As both perimeter and area use length and width as dimensions, they are often used together to solve a problem such as this one.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We know that the length is 6 in. more than the width, so we can write length as $$L = W + 6.$$ Substitute the value of the perimeter and the expression for length into the perimeter formula and find the length.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} P & = & {2L + 2W} \\ 48 & = & {2(W + 6) + 2W} \\ 48 & = & {2W + 12 + 2W} \\ 48 & = & {4W + 12} \\ 36 & = & {4W} \\ 9 & = & W \\ {(9 + 6)} & = & L \\ 15 & = & L \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now, we find the area given the dimensions of $$L = 15$$ in. and $$W = 9$$ in.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} A & = & {LW} \\ A & = & {15(9)} \\ & = & {135 \text{in} .^{2}} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The area is $$135$$ in.2.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving a Volume Problem
snippet: Solving a Volume Problem: Find the dimensions of a shipping box given that the length is twice the width, the height is 8 inches, and the volume is 1,600 in.3. The formula for the volume of a box is given as V = LWH, the product of length,...
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Solving a Volume Problem">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the dimensions of a shipping box given that the length is twice the width, the height is $$8$$ inches, and the volume is 1,600 in.3.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The formula for the volume of a box is given as $$V = LWH,$$ the product of length, width, and height. We are given that $$L = 2W,$$ and $$H = 8.$$ The volume is $$1,600$$ cubic inches.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} V & = & {LWH} \\ {1,600} & = & {(2W)W(8)} \\ {1,600} & = & {16W^{2}} \\ 100 & = & W^{2} \\ 10 & = & W \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The dimensions are $$L = 20$$ in., $$W = 10$$ in., and $$H = 8$$ in.</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>Note that the square root of $$W^{2}$$ would result in a positive and a negative value. However, because we are describing width, we can use only the positive result.</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Complex Numbers: Addition and Subtraction" title="Complex Numbers: Addition and Subtraction">
    <paragraph>Adding complex numbers:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {a + bi} \right) + \left( {c + di} \right) = \left( {a + c} \right) + \left( {b + d} \right)i$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Subtracting complex numbers:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {a + bi} \right) - \left( {c + di} \right) = \left( {a - c} \right) + \left( {b - d} \right)i$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Adding and Subtracting Complex Numbers
snippet: Adding and Subtracting Complex Numbers: Add or subtract as indicated. ⓐ \left( {3 - 4i} \right) + \left( {2 + 5i} \right) ⓑ \left( {-5 + 7i} \right) - \left( {-11 + 2i} \right) We add the real parts and add the imaginary parts. ⓐ...
body_xml:
<example number="3" title="Adding and Subtracting Complex Numbers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Add or subtract as indicated.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\left( {3 - 4i} \right) + \left( {2 + 5i} \right)$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\left( {-5 + 7i} \right) - \left( {-11 + 2i} \right)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We add the real parts and add the imaginary parts.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\begin{array}{ccl} {(3 - 4i) + (2 + 5i)} & = & {3 - 4i + 2 + 5i} \\ & = & {3 + 2 + (-4i) + 5i} \\ & = & {(3 + 2) + (-4 + 5)i} \\ & = & {5 + i} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\begin{array}{ccl} {(-5 + 7i) - (-11 + 2i)} & = & {-5 + 7i + 11 - 2i} \\ & = & {-5 + 11 + 7i - 2i} \\ & = & {(-5 + 11) + (7 - 2)i} \\ & = & {6 + 5i} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: The Complex Conjugate
snippet: The Complex Conjugate: The complex conjugate of a complex number a + bi is a - bi. It is found by changing the sign of the imaginary part of the complex number. The real part of the number is left unchanged. When a complex number is...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="The Complex Conjugate" title="The Complex Conjugate">
    <paragraph>The complex conjugate of a complex number $$a + bi$$ is $$a - bi.$$ It is found by changing the sign of the imaginary part of the complex number. The real part of the number is left unchanged.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>When a complex number is multiplied by its complex conjugate, the result is a real number.</item>
      <item>When a complex number is added to its complex conjugate, the result is a real number.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Finding Complex Conjugates
snippet: Finding Complex Conjugates: Find the complex conjugate of each number. ⓐ 2 + i\sqrt{5} ⓑ - \frac{1}{2}i ⓐThe number is already in the form a + bi. The complex conjugate is a - bi, or 2 - i\sqrt{5}. ⓑWe can rewrite this number in the form a...
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Finding Complex Conjugates">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the complex conjugate of each number.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$2 + i\sqrt{5}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$- \frac{1}{2}i$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐThe number is already in the form $$a + bi.$$ The complex conjugate is $$a - bi,$$ or $$2 - i\sqrt{5}.$$</item>
        <item>ⓑWe can rewrite this number in the form $$a + bi$$ as $$0 - \frac{1}{2}i.$$ The complex conjugate is $$a - bi,$$ or $$0 + \frac{1}{2}i.$$ This can be written simply as $$\frac{1}{2}i.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>Although we have seen that we can find the complex conjugate of an imaginary number, in practice we generally find the complex conjugates of only complex numbers with both a real and an imaginary component. To obtain a real number from an imaginary number, we can simply multiply by $$i.$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Dividing Complex Numbers
snippet: Dividing Complex Numbers: Divide: \left( {2 + 5i} \right) by \left( {4 - i} \right). We begin by writing the problem as a fraction. \frac{\left( {2 + 5i} \right)}{\left( {4 - i} \right)} Then we multiply the numerator and denominator by...
body_xml:
<example number="7" title="Dividing Complex Numbers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Divide: $$\left( {2 + 5i} \right)$$ by $$\left( {4 - i} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We begin by writing the problem as a fraction.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\left( {2 + 5i} \right)}{\left( {4 - i} \right)}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then we multiply the numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{(2 + 5i)}{(4 - i)} \cdot \frac{(4 + i)}{(4 + i)}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To multiply two complex numbers, we expand the product as we would with polynomials (using FOIL).</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cclc} {\frac{(2 + 5i)}{(4 - i)} \cdot \frac{(4 + i)}{(4 + i)}} & = & \frac{8 + 2i + 20i + 5i^{2}}{16 + 4i - 4i - i^{2}} & \\ & = & \frac{8 + 2i + 20i + 5(-1)}{16 + 4i - 4i - (-1)} & { \text{Because} i^{2} = -1.} \\ & = & \frac{3 + 22i}{17} & \\ & = & {\frac{3}{17} + \frac{22}{17}i} & { \text{Separate real and imaginary parts} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Note that this expresses the quotient in standard form.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Simplifying Powers of i i
snippet: Simplifying Powers of i i: Evaluate: i^{35}. Since i^{4} = 1, we can simplify the problem by factoring out as many factors of i^{4} as possible. To do so, first determine how many times 4 goes into 35: 35 = 4 \cdot 8 + 3. i^{35} = i^{4...
body_xml:
<example number="8" title="Simplifying Powers of i i">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate: $$i^{35}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since $$i^{4} = 1,$$ we can simplify the problem by factoring out as many factors of $$i^{4}$$ as possible. To do so, first determine how many times 4 goes into 35: $$35 = 4 \cdot 8 + 3.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$i^{35} = i^{4 \cdot 8 + 3} = i^{4 \cdot 8} \cdot i^{3} = \left( i^{4} \right)^{8} \cdot i^{3} = 1^{8} \cdot i^{3} = i^{3} = - i$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <paragraph>where a and b are real numbers or algebraic expressions.</paragraph>

    <paragraph math="block">$$ax^{2} + bx + c = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where a, b, and c are real numbers, and if $$a \neq 0,$$ it is in standard form.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Factoring and Solving a Quadratic with Leading Coefficient of 1
snippet: Factoring and Solving a Quadratic with Leading Coefficient of 1: Factor and solve the equation: x^{2} + x - 6 = 0. To factor x^{2} + x - 6 = 0, we look for two numbers whose product equals -6 and whose sum equals 1. Begin by looking at the...
body_xml: Factor and solve the equation: $$x^{2} + x - 6 = 0.$$ To factor $$x^{2} + x - 6 = 0,$$ we look for two numbers whose product equals $$-6$$ and whose sum equals 1. Begin by looking at the possible factors of $$-6.$$ $$\begin{matrix} {1 \cdot (-6)} \\ {(-6) \cdot 1} \\ {2 \cdot (-3)} \\ {3 \cdot (-2)} \end{matrix}$$ The last pair, $$3 \cdot (-2)$$ sums to 1, so these are the numbers. Note that only one pair of numbers will work. Then, write the factors. $$\left( {x - 2} \right)\left( {x + 3} \right) = 0$$ To solve this equation, we use the zero-product property. Set each factor equal to zero and solve. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {\left( {x - 2} \right)\left( {x + 3} \right)} & = & 0 \\ \left( {x - 2} \right) & = & 0 \\ x & = & 2 \\ \left( {x + 3} \right) & = & 0 \\ x & = & -3 \end{array}$$ The two solutions are $$2$$ and $$-3.$$ We can see how the solutions relate to the graph in Figure 2. The solutions are the x-intercepts of $$y = x^{2} + x - 6 = 0.$$

title: Solve the Quadratic Equation by Factoring
snippet: Solve the Quadratic Equation by Factoring: Solve the quadratic equation by factoring: x^{2} + 8x + 15 = 0. Find two numbers whose product equals 15 and whose sum equals 8. List the factors of 15. \begin{array}{l} {1 \cdot 15} \\ {3 \cdot...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Solve the Quadratic Equation by Factoring">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the quadratic equation by factoring: $$x^{2} + 8x + 15 = 0.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Find two numbers whose product equals $$15$$ and whose sum equals $$8.$$ List the factors of $$15.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {1 \cdot 15} \\ {3 \cdot 5} \\ {(-1) \cdot (-15)} \\ {(-3) \cdot (-5)} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The numbers that add to 8 are 3 and 5. Then, write the factors, set each factor equal to zero, and solve.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\left( {x + 3} \right)\left( {x + 5} \right)} & = & 0 \\ \left( {x + 3} \right) & = & 0 \\ x & = & -3 \\ \left( {x + 5} \right) & = & 0 \\ x & = & -5 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solutions are $$-3$$ and $$-5.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using the Zero-Product Property to Solve a Quadratic Equation Written as the Difference of Squares
snippet: Using the Zero-Product Property to Solve a Quadratic Equation Written as the Difference of Squares: Solve the difference of squares equation using the zero-product property: x^{2} - 9 = 0. Recognizing that the equation represents the...
body_xml:
<example number="3" title="Using the Zero-Product Property to Solve a Quadratic Equation Written as the Difference of Squares">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the difference of squares equation using the zero-product property: $$x^{2} - 9 = 0.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Recognizing that the equation represents the difference of squares, we can write the two factors by taking the square root of each term, using a minus sign as the operator in one factor and a plus sign as the operator in the other. Solve using the zero-factor property.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {x^{2} - 9} & = & 0 \\ {\left( {x - 3} \right)\left( {x + 3} \right)} & = & 0 \\ \left( {x - 3} \right) & = & 0 \\ x & = & 3 \\ \left( {x + 3} \right) & = & 0 \\ x & = & -3 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solutions are $$3$$ and $$-3.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving a Quadratic Equation Using Grouping
snippet: Solving a Quadratic Equation Using Grouping: Use grouping to factor and solve the quadratic equation: 4x^{2} + 15x + 9 = 0. First, multiply ac:4(9) = 36. Then list the factors of 36. \begin{array}{l} {1 \cdot 36} \\ {2 \cdot 18} \\ {3...
body_xml: Use grouping to factor and solve the quadratic equation: $$4x^{2} + 15x + 9 = 0.$$ First, multiply $$ac:4(9) = 36.$$ Then list the factors of $$36.$$ $$\begin{array}{l} {1 \cdot 36} \\ {2 \cdot 18} \\ {3 \cdot 12} \\ {4 \cdot 9} \\ {6 \cdot 6} \end{array}$$ The only pair of factors that sums to $$15$$ is $$3 + 12.$$ Rewrite the equation replacing the b term, $$15x,$$ with two terms using 3 and 12 as coefficients of x. Factor the first two terms, and then factor the last two terms. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {4x^{2} + 3x + 12x + 9} & = & 0 \\ {x(4x + 3) + 3(4x + 3)} & = & 0 \\ {(4x + 3)(x + 3)} & = & 0 \end{array}$$ Solve using the zero-product property. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {(4x + 3)(x + 3)} & = & 0 \\ {(4x + 3)} & = & 0 \\ x & = & {- \frac{3}{4}} \\ {(x + 3)} & = & 0 \\ x & = & {- 3} \end{array}$$ The solutions are $$- \frac{3}{4},$$ and $$-3.$$ See Figure 3.

title: Solving a Polynomial of Higher Degree by Factoring
snippet: Solving a Polynomial of Higher Degree by Factoring: Solve the equation by factoring: -3x^{3} - 5x^{2} - 2x = 0. This equation does not look like a quadratic, as the highest power is 3, not 2. Recall that the first thing we want to do when...
body_xml:
<example number="5" title="Solving a Polynomial of Higher Degree by Factoring">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the equation by factoring: $$-3x^{3} - 5x^{2} - 2x = 0.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This equation does not look like a quadratic, as the highest power is 3, not 2. Recall that the first thing we want to do when solving any equation is to factor out the GCF, if one exists. And it does here. We can factor out $$- x$$ from all of the terms and then proceed with grouping.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {-3x^{3} - 5x^{2} - 2x} & = & 0 \\ {- x\left( 3x^{2} + 5x + 2 \right)} & = & 0 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Use grouping on the expression in parentheses.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {- x\left( 3x^{2} + 3x + 2x + 2 \right)} & = & 0 \\ {- x\lbrack 3x(x + 1) + 2(x + 1)\rbrack} & = & 0 \\ {- x(3x + 2)(x + 1)} & = & 0 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now, we use the zero-product property. Notice that we have three factors.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {- x} & = & 0 \\ x & = & 0 \\ {3x + 2} & = & 0 \\ x & = & {- \frac{2}{3}} \\ {x + 1} & = & 0 \\ x & = & -1 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solutions are $$0,$$ $$- \frac{2}{3},$$ and $$-1.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: The Square Root Property: With the x^{2} term isolated, the square root property states that: \text{if} x^{2} = k, \text{then} x = \pm \sqrt{k} where k is a nonzero real number.

    <paragraph math="block">$$\text{if} x^{2} = k, \text{then} x = \pm \sqrt{k}$$</paragraph>

title: Solving a Simple Quadratic Equation Using the Square Root Property
snippet: Solving a Simple Quadratic Equation Using the Square Root Property: Solve the quadratic using the square root property: x^{2} = 8. Take the square root of both sides, and then simplify the radical. Remember to use a \pm sign before the...
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Solving a Simple Quadratic Equation Using the Square Root Property">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the quadratic using the square root property: $$x^{2} = 8.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Take the square root of both sides, and then simplify the radical. Remember to use a $$\pm$$ sign before the radical symbol.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} x^{2} & = & 8 \\ x & = & {\pm \sqrt{8}} \\ & = & {\pm 2\sqrt{2}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solutions are $$2\sqrt{2},$$ $$-2\sqrt{2}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving a Quadratic Equation Using the Square Root Property
snippet: Solving a Quadratic Equation Using the Square Root Property: Solve the quadratic equation: 4x^{2} + 1 = \text{7.} First, isolate the x^{2} term. Then take the square root of both sides. \begin{array}{rcl} {4x^{2} + 1} & = & 7 \\ {4x^{2}} &...
body_xml:
<example number="7" title="Solving a Quadratic Equation Using the Square Root Property">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the quadratic equation: $$4x^{2} + 1 = \text{7.}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, isolate the $$x^{2}$$ term. Then take the square root of both sides.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {4x^{2} + 1} & = & 7 \\ {4x^{2}} & = & 6 \\ x^{2} & = & \frac{6}{4} \\ x & = & {\pm \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solutions are $$\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2},$$ and $$- \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving a Quadratic by Completing the Square
snippet: Solving a Quadratic by Completing the Square: Solve the quadratic equation by completing the square: x^{2} - 3x - 5 = 0. First, move the constant term to the right side of the equal sign. x^{2} - 3x = 5 Then, take \frac{1}{2} of the b term...
body_xml:
<example number="8" title="Solving a Quadratic by Completing the Square">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the quadratic equation by completing the square: $$x^{2} - 3x - 5 = 0.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, move the constant term to the right side of the equal sign.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x^{2} - 3x = 5$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then, take $$\frac{1}{2}$$ of the b term and square it.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\frac{1}{2}(-3)} & = & {- \frac{3}{2}} \\ \left( {- \frac{3}{2}} \right)^{2} & = & \frac{9}{4} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Add the result to both sides of the equal sign.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {x^{2} - 3x + \left( {- \frac{3}{2}} \right)^{2}} & = & {5 + \left( {- \frac{3}{2}} \right)^{2}} \\ {x^{2} - 3x + \frac{9}{4}} & = & {5 + \frac{9}{4}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Factor the left side as a perfect square and simplify the right side.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {x - \frac{3}{2}} \right)^{2} = \frac{29}{4}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Use the square root property and solve.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} \sqrt{\left( {x - \frac{3}{2}} \right)^{2}} & = & {\pm \sqrt{\frac{29}{4}}} \\ \left( {x - \frac{3}{2}} \right) & = & {\pm \frac{\sqrt{29}}{2}} \\ x & = & {\frac{3}{2} \pm \frac{\sqrt{29}}{2}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solutions are $$\frac{3 + \sqrt{29}}{2}$$ and $$\frac{3 - \sqrt{29}}{2}$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: The Quadratic Formula

<example number="9" title="Solve the Quadratic Equation Using the Quadratic Formula">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the quadratic equation: $$x^{2} + 5x + 1 = 0.$$</paragraph>

      <paragraph>Identify the coefficients: $$a = 1,b = 5,c = 1.$$ Then use the quadratic formula.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} x & = & \frac{- (5) \pm \sqrt{{(5)}^{2} - 4(1)(1)}}{2(1)} \\ & = & \frac{- 5 \pm \sqrt{25 - 4}}{2} \\ & = & \frac{- 5 \pm \sqrt{21}}{2} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>

title: Solving a Quadratic Equation with the Quadratic Formula

<example number="10" title="Solving a Quadratic Equation with the Quadratic Formula">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the quadratic formula to solve $$x^{2} + x + 2 = 0.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, we identify the coefficients: $$a = 1,b = 1,$$ and $$c = 2.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substitute these values into the quadratic formula.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} x & = & \frac{- b \pm \sqrt{b^{2} - 4ac}}{2a} \\ & = & \frac{- (1) \pm \sqrt{{(1)}^{2} - (4) \cdot (1) \cdot (2)}}{2 \cdot 1} \\ & = & \frac{- 1 \pm \sqrt{1 - 8}}{2} \\ & = & \frac{- 1 \pm \sqrt{- 7}}{2} \\ & = & \frac{- 1 \pm i\sqrt{7}}{2} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solutions to the equation are $$\frac{- 1 + i\sqrt{7}}{2}$$ and $$\frac{- 1 - i\sqrt{7}}{2}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: The Discriminant

<note type="rule" source_type="The Discriminant" title="The Discriminant">
    <paragraph>For $$ax^{2} + bx + c = 0$$ , where $$a$$ , $$b$$ , and $$c$$ are real numbers, the discriminant is the expression under the radical in the quadratic formula: $$b^{2} - 4ac.$$ It tells us whether the solutions are real numbers or complex numbers and how many solutions of each type to expect.</paragraph>

title: Using the Discriminant to Find the Nature of the Solutions to a Quadratic Equation
snippet: Using the Discriminant to Find the Nature of the Solutions to a Quadratic Equation: Use the discriminant to find the nature of the solutions to the following quadratic equations: ⓐ x^{2} + 4x + 4 = 0 ⓑ 8x^{2} + 14x + 3 = 0 ⓒ 3x^{2} - 5x -...
body_xml:
<example number="11" title="Using the Discriminant to Find the Nature of the Solutions to a Quadratic Equation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the discriminant to find the nature of the solutions to the following quadratic equations:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$x^{2} + 4x + 4 = 0$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$8x^{2} + 14x + 3 = 0$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$3x^{2} - 5x - 2 = 0$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$3x^{2} - 10x + 15 = 0$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Calculate the discriminant $$b^{2} - 4ac$$ for each equation and state the expected type of solutions.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$x^{2} + 4x + 4 = 0$$ $$b^{2} - 4ac = (4)^{2} - 4(1)(4) = 0.$$ There will be one rational double solution.</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$8x^{2} + 14x + 3 = 0$$ $$b^{2} - 4ac = (14)^{2} - 4(8)(3) = 100.$$ As $$100$$ is a perfect square, there will be two rational solutions.</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$3x^{2} - 5x - 2 = 0$$ $$b^{2} - 4ac = (-5)^{2} - 4(3)(-2) = 49.$$ As $$49$$ is a perfect square, there will be two rational solutions.</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$3x^{2}-10x + 15 = 0$$ $$b^{2} - 4ac = (-10)^{2} - 4(3)(15) = -80.$$ There will be two complex solutions.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Rational Exponents
snippet: Rational Exponents: A rational exponent indicates a power in the numerator and a root in the denominator. There are multiple ways of writing an expression, a variable, or a number with a rational exponent: a^{\frac{m}{n}} = \left(...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Rational Exponents" title="Rational Exponents">
    <paragraph>A rational exponent indicates a power in the numerator and a root in the denominator. There are multiple ways of writing an expression, a variable, or a number with a rational exponent:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$a^{\frac{m}{n}} = \left( a^{\frac{1}{n}} \right)^{m} = \left( a^{m} \right)^{\frac{1}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{a^{m}} = \left( \sqrt[n]{a} \right)^{m}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Evaluating a Number Raised to a Rational Exponent
snippet: Evaluating a Number Raised to a Rational Exponent: Evaluate 8^{\frac{2}{3}}. Whether we take the root first or the power first depends on the number. It is easy to find the cube root of 8, so rewrite 8^{\frac{2}{3}} as \left(...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Evaluating a Number Raised to a Rational Exponent">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$8^{\frac{2}{3}}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Whether we take the root first or the power first depends on the number. It is easy to find the cube root of 8, so rewrite $$8^{\frac{2}{3}}$$ as $$\left( 8^{\frac{1}{3}} \right)^{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} \left( 8^{\frac{1}{3}} \right)^{2} & = & {(2)}^{2} \\ & = & 4 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solve the Equation Including a Variable Raised to a Rational Exponent
snippet: Solve the Equation Including a Variable Raised to a Rational Exponent: Solve the equation in which a variable is raised to a rational exponent: x^{\frac{5}{4}} = 32. The way to remove the exponent on x is by raising both sides of the...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Solve the Equation Including a Variable Raised to a Rational Exponent">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the equation in which a variable is raised to a rational exponent: $$x^{\frac{5}{4}} = 32.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The way to remove the exponent on x is by raising both sides of the equation to a power that is the reciprocal of $$\frac{5}{4},$$ which is $$\frac{4}{5}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cclc} x^{\frac{5}{4}} & = & 32 & \\ \left( x^{\frac{5}{4}} \right)^{\frac{4}{5}} & = & {(32)}^{\frac{4}{5}} & \\ x & = & {(2)}^{4} & { \text{The fifth root of 32 is 2.} } \\ & = & 16 & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving an Equation Involving Rational Exponents and Factoring
snippet: Solving an Equation Involving Rational Exponents and Factoring: Solve 3x^{\frac{3}{4}} = x^{\frac{1}{2}}. This equation involves rational exponents as well as factoring rational exponents. Let us take this one step at a time. First, put...
body_xml:
<example number="3" title="Solving an Equation Involving Rational Exponents and Factoring">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve $$3x^{\frac{3}{4}} = x^{\frac{1}{2}}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This equation involves rational exponents as well as factoring rational exponents. Let us take this one step at a time. First, put the variable terms on one side of the equal sign and set the equation equal to zero.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {3x^{\frac{3}{4}} - \left( x^{\frac{1}{2}} \right)} & = & {x^{\frac{1}{2}} - \left( x^{\frac{1}{2}} \right)} \\ {3x^{\frac{3}{4}} - x^{\frac{1}{2}}} & = & 0 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now, it looks like we should factor the left side, but what do we factor out? We can always factor the term with the lowest exponent. Rewrite $$x^{\frac{1}{2}}$$ as $$x^{\frac{2}{4}}.$$ Then, factor out $$x^{\frac{2}{4}}$$ from both terms on the left.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {3x^{\frac{3}{4}} - x^{\frac{2}{4}}} & = & 0 \\ {x^{\frac{2}{4}}\left( {3x^{\frac{1}{4}} - 1} \right)} & = & 0 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Where did $$x^{\frac{1}{4}}$$ come from? Remember, when we multiply two numbers with the same base, we add the exponents. Therefore, if we multiply $$x^{\frac{2}{4}}$$ back in using the distributive property, we get the expression we had before the factoring, which is what should happen. We need an exponent such that when added to $$\frac{2}{4}$$ equals $$\frac{3}{4}.$$ Thus, the exponent on x in the parentheses is $$\frac{1}{4}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Let us continue. Now we have two factors and can use the zero factor theorem.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rclc} {x^{\frac{2}{4}}\left( {3x^{\frac{1}{4}} - 1} \right)} & = & 0 & \\ x^{\frac{2}{4}} & = & 0 & \\ x & = & 0 & \\ {3x^{\frac{1}{4}} - 1} & = & 0 & \\ {3x^{\frac{1}{4}}} & = & 1 & \\ x^{\frac{1}{4}} & = & \frac{1}{3} & { \text{Divide both sides by 3} .} \\ \left( x^{\frac{1}{4}} \right)^{4} & = & \left( \frac{1}{3} \right)^{4} & { \text{Raise both sides to the reciprocal of} \frac{1}{4}.} \\ x & = & \frac{1}{81} & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The two solutions are $$0$$ and $$\frac{1}{81}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Polynomial Equations
snippet: Polynomial Equations: A polynomial of degree n is an expression of the type a_{n}x^{n} + a_{n - 1}x^{n - 1} + \cdot \cdot \cdot + a_{2}x^{2} + a_{1}x + a_{0} where n is a positive integer and a_{n},\ldots,a_{0} are real numbers and a_{n}...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Polynomial Equations" title="Polynomial Equations">
    <paragraph>A polynomial of degree n is an expression of the type</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$a_{n}x^{n} + a_{n - 1}x^{n - 1} + \cdot \cdot \cdot + a_{2}x^{2} + a_{1}x + a_{0}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where n is a positive integer and $$a_{n},\ldots,a_{0}$$ are real numbers and $$a_{n} \neq 0.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Setting the polynomial equal to zero gives a polynomial equation. The total number of solutions (real and complex) to a polynomial equation is equal to the highest exponent n.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Solving a Polynomial by Factoring
snippet: Solving a Polynomial by Factoring: Solve the polynomial by factoring: 5x^{4} = 80x^{2}. First, set the equation equal to zero. Then factor out what is common to both terms, the GCF. \begin{array}{rcl} {5x^{4} - 80x^{2}} & = & 0 \\...
body_xml: Solve the polynomial by factoring: $$5x^{4} = 80x^{2}.$$ First, set the equation equal to zero. Then factor out what is common to both terms, the GCF. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {5x^{4} - 80x^{2}} & = & 0 \\ {5x^{2}\left( x^{2} - 16 \right)} & = & 0 \end{array}$$ Notice that we have the difference of squares in the factor $$x^{2} - 16,$$ which we will continue to factor and obtain two solutions. The first term, $$5x^{2},$$ generates, technically, two solutions as the exponent is 2, but they are the same solution. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {5x^{2}} & = & 0 \\ x & = & 0 \\ {x^{2} - 16} & = & 0 \\ {(x - 4)(x + 4)} & = & 0 \\ x & = & 4 \\ x & = & -4 \end{array}$$ The solutions are $$0 \text{(double solution),}$$ $$4,$$ and $$-4.$$ We can see the solutions on the graph in Figure 1. The x-coordinates of the points where the graph crosses the x-axis are the solutions—the x-intercepts. Notice on the graph that at the solution $$0,$$ the graph touches the x-axis and bounces back. It does not cross the x-axis. This is typical of double solutions.

title: Solve a Polynomial by Grouping
snippet: Solve a Polynomial by Grouping: Solve a polynomial by grouping: x^{3} + x^{2} - 9x - 9 = 0. This polynomial consists of 4 terms, which we can solve by grouping. Grouping procedures require factoring the first two terms and then factoring...
body_xml: Solve a polynomial by grouping: $$x^{3} + x^{2} - 9x - 9 = 0.$$ This polynomial consists of 4 terms, which we can solve by grouping. Grouping procedures require factoring the first two terms and then factoring the last two terms. If the factors in the parentheses are identical, we can continue the process and solve, unless more factoring is suggested. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {x^{3} + x^{2} - 9x - 9} & = & 0 \\ {x^{2}(x + 1) - 9(x + 1)} & = & 0 \\ {\left( x^{2} - 9 \right)(x + 1)} & = & 0 \end{array}$$ The grouping process ends here, as we can factor $$x^{2} - 9$$ using the difference of squares formula. $$\begin{array}{ccl} {\left( x^{2} - 9 \right)(x + 1)} & = & 0 \\ {(x - 3)(x + 3)(x + 1)} & = & 0 \\ x & = & 3 \\ x & = & -3 \\ x & = & -1 \end{array}$$ The solutions are $$3,$$ $$-3,$$ and $$-1.$$ Note that the highest exponent is 3 and we obtained 3 solutions. We can see the solutions, the x-intercepts, on the graph in Figure 2. We looked at solving quadratic equations by factoring when the leading coefficient is 1. When the leading coefficient is not 1, we solved by grouping. Grouping requires four terms, which we obtained by splitting the linear term of quadratic equations. We can also use grouping for some polynomials of degree higher than 2, as we saw here, since there were already four terms.

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given a radical equation, solve it. Isolate the radical expression on one side of the equal sign. Put all remaining terms on the other side. If the radical is a square root, then square both sides of the equation. If it is a cube...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given a radical equation, solve it.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Isolate the radical expression on one side of the equal sign. Put all remaining terms on the other side.</item>
      <item>If the radical is a square root, then square both sides of the equation. If it is a cube root, then raise both sides of the equation to the third power. In other words, for an nth root radical, raise both sides to the nth power. Doing so eliminates the radical symbol.</item>
      <item>Solve the remaining equation.</item>
      <item>If a radical term still remains, repeat steps 1–2.</item>
      <item>Confirm solutions by substituting them into the original equation.</item>
    </list>

title: Solving an Equation with One Radical
snippet: Solving an Equation with One Radical: Solve \sqrt{15 - 2x} = x. The radical is already isolated on the left side of the equal side, so proceed to square both sides. \begin{array}{rcl} \sqrt{15 - 2x} & = & x \\ \left( \sqrt{15 - 2x}...
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Solving an Equation with One Radical">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve $$\sqrt{15 - 2x} = x.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The radical is already isolated on the left side of the equal side, so proceed to square both sides.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} \sqrt{15 - 2x} & = & x \\ \left( \sqrt{15 - 2x} \right)^{2} & = & {(x)}^{2} \\ {15 - 2x} & = & x^{2} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We see that the remaining equation is a quadratic. Set it equal to zero and solve.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} 0 & = & {x^{2} + 2x - 15} \\ & = & {(x + 5)(x - 3)} \\ x & = & -5 \\ x & = & 3 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The proposed solutions are $$-5$$ and $$3.$$ Let us check each solution back in the original equation. First, check $$x = -5.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} \sqrt{15 - 2x} & = & x \\ \sqrt{15 - 2( - 5)} & = & -5 \\ \sqrt{25} & = & -5 \\ 5 & \neq & {-5} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This is an extraneous solution. While no mistake was made solving the equation, we found a solution that does not satisfy the original equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Check $$x = 3.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} \sqrt{15 - 2x} & = & x \\ \sqrt{15 - 2(3)} & = & 3 \\ \sqrt{9} & = & 3 \\ 3 & = & 3 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solution is $$3.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving a Radical Equation Containing Two Radicals
snippet: Solving a Radical Equation Containing Two Radicals: Solve \sqrt{2x + 3} + \sqrt{x - 2} = 4. As this equation contains two radicals, we isolate one radical, eliminate it, and then isolate the second radical. \begin{array}{rclc} {\sqrt{2x +...
body_xml:
<example number="7" title="Solving a Radical Equation Containing Two Radicals">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve $$\sqrt{2x + 3} + \sqrt{x - 2} = 4.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>As this equation contains two radicals, we isolate one radical, eliminate it, and then isolate the second radical.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rclc} {\sqrt{2x + 3} + \sqrt{x - 2}} & = & 4 & \\ \sqrt{2x + 3} & = & {4 - \sqrt{x - 2}} & { \text{Subtract} \sqrt{x - 2} \text{from both sides} .} \\ \left( \sqrt{2x + 3} \right)^{2} & = & \left( 4 - \sqrt{x - 2} \right)^{2} & { \text{Square both sides} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Use the perfect square formula to expand the right side: $$\left( {a - b} \right)^{2} = a^{2}-2ab + b^{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rclc} {2x + 3} & = & {{(4)}^{2} - 2(4)\sqrt{x - 2} + \left( \sqrt{x - 2} \right)^{2}} & \\ {2x + 3} & = & {16 - 8\sqrt{x - 2} + (x - 2)} & \\ {2x + 3} & = & {14 + x - 8\sqrt{x - 2}} & { \text{Combine like terms} .} \\ {x - 11} & = & {-8\sqrt{x - 2}} & { \text{Isolate the second radical} .} \\ {(x - 11)}^{2} & = & \left( -8\sqrt{x - 2} \right)^{2} & { \text{Square both sides} .} \\ {x^{2} - 22x + 121} & = & {64(x - 2)} & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now that both radicals have been eliminated, set the quadratic equal to zero and solve.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rclc} {x^{2} - 22x + 121} & = & {64x - 128} & \\ {x^{2} - 86x + 249} & = & 0 & \\ {(x - 3)(x - 83)} & = & 0 & { \text{Factor and solve} .} \\ x & = & 3 & \\ x & = & 83 & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The proposed solutions are $$3$$ and $$83.$$ Check each solution in the original equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\sqrt{2x + 3} + \sqrt{x - 2}} & = & 4 \\ \sqrt{2x + 3} & = & {4 - \sqrt{x - 2}} \\ \sqrt{2(3) + 3} & = & {4 - \sqrt{(3) - 2}} \\ \sqrt{9} & = & {4 - \sqrt{1}} \\ 3 & = & 3 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>One solution is $$3.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Check $$x = 83.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\sqrt{2x + 3} + \sqrt{x - 2}} & = & 4 \\ \sqrt{2x + 3} & = & {4 - \sqrt{x - 2}} \\ \sqrt{2(83) + 3} & = & {4 - \sqrt{(83 - 2)}} \\ \sqrt{169} & = & {4 - \sqrt{81}} \\ 13 & \neq & {- 5} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The only solution is $$3.$$ We see that $$83$$ is an extraneous solution.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Absolute Value Equations
snippet: Absolute Value Equations: The absolute value of x is written as |x|. It has the following properties: \begin{array}{l} \left. \text{If} x \geq 0, \text{then} \middle| x \middle| = x. \right. \\ \left. \text{If} x < 0, \text{then} \middle|...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Absolute Value Equations" title="Absolute Value Equations">
    <paragraph>The absolute value of x is written as $$|x|.$$ It has the following properties:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} \left. \text{If} x \geq 0, \text{then} \middle| x \middle| = x. \right. \\ \left. \text{If} x < 0, \text{then} \middle| x \middle| = -x. \right. \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For real numbers $$A$$ and $$B,$$ an equation of the form $$|A| = B,$$ with $$B \geq 0,$$ will have solutions when $$A = B$$ or $$A = - B.$$ If $$B < 0,$$ the equation $$|A| = B$$ has no solution.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>An absolute value equation in the form $$\left| {ax + b} \right| = c$$ has the following properties:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} \left. \text{If} c < 0, \middle| ax + b \middle| = c \text{has no solution} . \right. \\ \left. \text{If} c = 0, \middle| ax + b \middle| = c \text{has one solution} . \right. \\ \left. \text{If} c > 0, \middle| ax + b \middle| = c \text{has two solutions} . \right. \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

    <list type="ordered">

      <item>If $$c > 0,$$ write and solve two equations: $$ax + b = c$$ and $$ax + b = - c.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Solving Absolute Value Equations
snippet: Solving Absolute Value Equations: Solve the following absolute value equations: ⓐ \left| {6x + 4} \right| = 8 ⓑ \left| {3x + 4} \right| = -9 ⓒ \left| {3x - 5} \right| - 4 = 6 ⓓ \left| {-5x + 10} \right| = 0 ⓐ \left| {6x + 4} \right| = 8...
body_xml:
<example number="8" title="Solving Absolute Value Equations">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the following absolute value equations:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\left| {6x + 4} \right| = 8$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\left| {3x + 4} \right| = -9$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\left| {3x - 5} \right| - 4 = 6$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$\left| {-5x + 10} \right| = 0$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\left| {6x + 4} \right| = 8$$ Write two equations and solve each: $$\begin{array}{rclcrcl} {6x + 4} & = & 8 & & {6x + 4} & = & -8 \\ {6x} & = & 4 & & {6x} & = & -12 \\ x & = & \frac{2}{3} & & x & = & -2 \end{array}$$ The two solutions are $$\frac{2}{3}$$ and $$-2.$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\left| {3x + 4} \right| = -9$$ There is no solution as an absolute value cannot be negative.</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\left| {3x - 5} \right| - 4 = 6$$ Isolate the absolute value expression and then write two equations. $$\begin{matrix} & & & {\left| {3x - 5} \right| - 4} & = & 6 & & & \\ & & & \left| {3x - 5} \right| & = & 10 & & & \\ {3x - 5} & = & 10 & & & & {3x - 5} & = & -10 \\ {3x} & = & 15 & & & & {3x} & = & -5 \\ x & = & 5 & & & & x & = & {- \frac{5}{3}} \end{matrix}$$ There are two solutions: $$5,$$ and $$- \frac{5}{3}.$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ(d) $$\left| {-5x + 10} \right| = 0$$ The equation is set equal to zero, so we have to write only one equation. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {-5x + 10} & = & 0 \\ {-5x} & = & -10 \\ x & = & 2 \end{array}$$ There is one solution: $$2.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving a Fourth-degree Equation in Quadratic Form
snippet: Solving a Fourth-degree Equation in Quadratic Form: Solve this fourth-degree equation: 3x^{4} - 2x^{2} - 1 = 0. This equation fits the main criteria, that the power on the leading term is double the power on the middle term. Next, we will...
body_xml:
<example number="9" title="Solving a Fourth-degree Equation in Quadratic Form">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve this fourth-degree equation: $$3x^{4} - 2x^{2} - 1 = 0.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This equation fits the main criteria, that the power on the leading term is double the power on the middle term. Next, we will make a substitution for the variable term in the middle. Let $$u = x^{2}.$$ Rewrite the equation in u.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$3u^{2} - 2u - 1 = 0$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now solve the quadratic.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {3u^{2} - 2u - 1} & = & 0 \\ {\left( {3u + 1} \right)\left( {u - 1} \right)} & = & 0 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Solve each factor and replace the original term for u.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {3u + 1} & = & 0 \\ {3u} & = & -1 \\ u & = & {- \frac{1}{3}} \\ x^{2} & = & {- \frac{1}{3}} \\ x & = & {\pm i\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {u - 1} & = & 0 \\ u & = & 1 \\ x^{2} & = & 1 \\ x & = & \pm 1 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solutions are $$\pm i\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}$$ and $$\pm 1.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving an Equation in Quadratic Form Containing a Binomial
snippet: Solving an Equation in Quadratic Form Containing a Binomial: Solve the equation in quadratic form: \left( {x + 2} \right)^{2} + 11\left( {x + 2} \right) - 12 = 0. This equation contains a binomial in place of the single variable. The...
body_xml:
<example number="10" title="Solving an Equation in Quadratic Form Containing a Binomial">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the equation in quadratic form: $$\left( {x + 2} \right)^{2} + 11\left( {x + 2} \right) - 12 = 0.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This equation contains a binomial in place of the single variable. The tendency is to expand what is presented. However, recognizing that it fits the criteria for being in quadratic form makes all the difference in the solving process. First, make a substitution, letting $$u = x + 2.$$ Then rewrite the equation in u.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {u^{2} + 11u - 12} & = & 0 \\ {(u + 12)(u - 1)} & = & 0 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Solve using the zero-factor property and then replace u with the original expression.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {u + 12} & = & 0 \\ u & = & -12 \\ {x + 2} & = & -12 \\ x & = & -14 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The second factor results in</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {u - 1} & = & 0 \\ u & = & 1 \\ {x + 2} & = & 1 \\ x & = & -1 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We have two solutions: $$-14,$$ and $$-1.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving a Rational Equation Leading to a Quadratic
snippet: Solving a Rational Equation Leading to a Quadratic: Solve the following rational equation: \frac{- 4x}{x - 1} + \frac{4}{x + 1} = \frac{- 8}{x^{2} - 1}. We want all denominators in factored form to find the LCD. Two of the denominators...
body_xml:
<example number="11" title="Solving a Rational Equation Leading to a Quadratic">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the following rational equation: $$\frac{- 4x}{x - 1} + \frac{4}{x + 1} = \frac{- 8}{x^{2} - 1}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We want all denominators in factored form to find the LCD. Two of the denominators cannot be factored further. However, $$x^{2}-1 = \left( {x + 1} \right)\left( {x - 1} \right).$$ Then, the LCD is $$\left( {x + 1} \right)\left( {x - 1} \right).$$ Next, we multiply the whole equation by the LCD.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {(x + 1)(x - 1)\left\lbrack {\frac{-4x}{x - 1} + \frac{4}{x + 1}} \right\rbrack} & = & {\left\lbrack \frac{-8}{(x + 1)(x - 1)} \right\rbrack(x + 1)(x - 1)} \\ {-4x(x + 1) + 4(x - 1)} & = & -8 \\ {-4x^{2} - 4x + 4x - 4} & = & -8 \\ {-4x^{2} + 4} & = & 0 \\ {-4\left( {x^{2} - 1} \right)} & = & 0 \\ {-4(x + 1)(x - 1)} & = & 0 \\ x & = & -1 \\ x & = & 1 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>In this case, either solution produces a zero in the denominator in the original equation. Thus, there is no solution.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Using Interval Notation to Express All Real Numbers Less Than or Equal to a or Greater Than or Equal to b: Write the interval expressing all real numbers less than or equal to -1 or greater than or equal to 1. We have to write two...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Using Interval Notation to Express All Real Numbers Less Than or Equal to a or Greater Than or Equal to b">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write the interval expressing all real numbers less than or equal to $$-1$$ or greater than or equal to $$1.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have to write two intervals for this example. The first interval must indicate all real numbers less than or equal to 1. So, this interval begins at $$- \infty$$ and ends at $$-1,$$ which is written as $$\left( {- \infty,-1} \right\rbrack.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The second interval must show all real numbers greater than or equal to $$1,$$ which is written as $$\left\lbrack {1,\infty} \right).$$ However, we want to combine these two sets. We accomplish this by inserting the union symbol, $$\cup ,$$ between the two intervals.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {- \infty,-1} \right\rbrack \cup \left\lbrack {1,\infty} \right)$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Demonstrating the Addition Property
snippet: Demonstrating the Addition Property: Illustrate the addition property for inequalities by solving each of the following: ⓐ x - 15 < 4 ⓑ 6 \geq x - 1 ⓒ x + 7 > 9 The addition property for inequalities states that if an inequality exists,...
body_xml:
<example number="3" title="Demonstrating the Addition Property">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Illustrate the addition property for inequalities by solving each of the following:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$x - 15 < 4$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$6 \geq x - 1$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$x + 7 > 9$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The addition property for inequalities states that if an inequality exists, adding or subtracting the same number on both sides does not change the inequality.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\begin{array}{ll} { x - 15 < 4} & \\ {x - 15 + 15 < 4 + 15} & { \text{Add 15 to both sides} .} \\ { x < 19} & \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\begin{array}{ll} { 6 \geq x - 1} & \\ {6 + 1 \geq x - 1 + 1} & { \text{Add 1 to both sides} .} \\ { 7 \geq x} & \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\begin{array}{ll} { x + 7 > 9} & \\ {x + 7 - 7 > 9 - 7} & { \text{Subtract 7 from both sides} .} \\ { x > 2} & \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="4" title="Demonstrating the Multiplication Property">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Illustrate the multiplication property for inequalities by solving each of the following:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$3x < 6$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$-2x - 1 \geq 5$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$5 - x > 10$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\begin{array}{l} { 3x < 6} \\ {\frac{1}{3}(3x) < (6)\frac{1}{3}} \\ { x < 2} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\begin{array}{ll} { - 2x - 1 \geq 5} & \\ { - 2x \geq 6} & \\ {\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)( - 2x) \geq (6)\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)} & { \text{Multiply by} - \frac{1}{2}.} \\ { x \leq - 3} & { \text{Reverse the inequality} .} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$\begin{array}{ll} { 5 - x > 10} & \\ { - x > 5} & \\ {( - 1)( - x) > (5)( - 1)} & { \text{Multiply by} - 1.} \\ { x < - 5} & { \text{Reverse the inequality} .} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>

snippet: Solving an Inequality Algebraically: Solve the inequality: 13 - 7x \geq 10x - 4. Solving this inequality is similar to solving an equation up until the last step. \begin{array}{ll} { 13 - 7x \geq 10x - 4} & \\ {13 - 17x \geq -4} & {...
body_xml:
<example number="5" title="Solving an Inequality Algebraically">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the inequality: $$13 - 7x \geq 10x - 4.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Solving this inequality is similar to solving an equation up until the last step.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} { 13 - 7x \geq 10x - 4} & \\ {13 - 17x \geq -4} & { \text{Move variable terms to one side of the inequality} .} \\ {-17x \geq -17} & { \text{Isolate the variable term} .} \\ { x \leq 1} & { \text{Dividing both sides by} -17 \text{reverses the inequality} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solution set is given by the interval $$\left( {- \infty,1} \right\rbrack,$$ or all real numbers less than and including 1.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving an Inequality with Fractions
snippet: Solving an Inequality with Fractions: Solve the following inequality and write the answer in interval notation: - \frac{3}{4}x \geq - \frac{5}{8} + \frac{2}{3}x. We begin solving in the same way we do when solving an equation....

<example number="6" title="Solving an Inequality with Fractions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the following inequality and write the answer in interval notation: $$- \frac{3}{4}x \geq - \frac{5}{8} + \frac{2}{3}x.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We begin solving in the same way we do when solving an equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} { - \frac{3}{4}x \geq - \frac{5}{8} + \frac{2}{3}x} & \\ { - \frac{3}{4}x - \frac{2}{3}x \geq - \frac{5}{8}} & { \text{Put variable terms on one side} .} \\ {- \frac{9}{12}x - \frac{8}{12}x \geq - \frac{5}{8}} & { \text{Write fractions with common denominator} .} \\ { - \frac{17}{12}x \geq - \frac{5}{8}} & \\ { x \leq - \frac{5}{8}\left( {- \frac{12}{17}} \right)} & { \text{Multiplying by a negative number reverses the inequality} .} \\ { x \leq \frac{15}{34}} & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solution set is the interval $$\left( {- \infty,\frac{15}{34}} \right\rbrack.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>

title: Solving a Compound Inequality
snippet: Solving a Compound Inequality: Solve the compound inequality: 3 \leq 2x + 2 < 6. The first method is to write two separate inequalities: 3 \leq 2x + 2 and 2x + 2 < 6. We solve them independently. \begin{array}{lll} {3 \leq 2x + 2} & {...
body_xml:
<example number="7" title="Solving a Compound Inequality">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the compound inequality: $$3 \leq 2x + 2 < 6.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The first method is to write two separate inequalities: $$3 \leq 2x + 2$$ and $$2x + 2 < 6.$$ We solve them independently.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lll} {3 \leq 2x + 2} & { \text{and} } & {2x + 2 < 6} \\ {1 \leq 2x} & & { 2x < 4} \\ {\frac{1}{2} \leq x} & & { x < 2} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then, we can rewrite the solution as a compound inequality, the same way the problem began.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{1}{2} \leq x < 2$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>In interval notation, the solution is written as $$\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2},2} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The second method is to leave the compound inequality intact, and perform solving procedures on the three parts at the same time.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {3 \leq 2x + 2 < 6} & \\ {1 \leq 2x < 4} & { \text{Isolate the variable term, and subtract 2 from all three parts} .} \\ {\frac{1}{2} \leq x < 2} & { \text{Divide through all three parts by 2} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We get the same solution: $$\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2},2} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml: Solve the compound inequality with variables in all three parts: $$3 + x > 7x - 2 > 5x - 10.$$ Let's try the first method. Write two inequalities: $$\begin{array}{lll} {3 + x > 7x - 2} & { \text{and} } & {7x - 2 > 5x - 10} \\ { 3 > 6x - 2} & & {2x - 2 > -10} \\ { 5 > 6x} & & { 2x > -8} \\ {\frac{5}{6} > x} & & { x > -4} \\ { x < \frac{5}{6}} & & {-4 < x} \end{array}$$ The solution set is $$-4 < x < \frac{5}{6}$$ or in interval notation $$\left( {-4,\frac{5}{6}} \right).$$ Notice that when we write the solution in interval notation, the smaller number comes first. We read intervals from left to right, as they appear on a number line. See Figure 3.

<note type="rule" source_type="Absolute Value Inequalities" title="Absolute Value Inequalities">
    <paragraph>For an algebraic expression X, and $$k > 0,$$ an absolute value inequality is an inequality of the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {|X| < k \text{is equivalent to} - k < X < k} \\ {|X| > k \text{is equivalent to} X < - k \text{or} X > k} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

title: Determining a Number within a Prescribed Distance
snippet: Determining a Number within a Prescribed Distance: Describe all values x within a distance of 4 from the number 5. We want the distance between x and 5 to be less than or equal to 4. We can draw a number line, such as in Figure 4, to...
body_xml: Describe all values $$x$$ within a distance of 4 from the number 5. We want the distance between $$x$$ and 5 to be less than or equal to 4. We can draw a number line, such as in Figure 4, to represent the condition to be satisfied. The distance from $$x$$ to 5 can be represented using an absolute value symbol, $$\left| {x - 5} \right|.$$ Write the values of $$x$$ that satisfy the condition as an absolute value inequality. $$\left| {x - 5} \right| \leq 4$$ We need to write two inequalities as there are always two solutions to an absolute value equation. $$\begin{array}{lll} {x - 5 \leq 4} & { \text{and} } & {x - 5 \geq - 4} \\ { x \leq 9} & & { x \geq 1} \end{array}$$ If the solution set is $$x \leq 9$$ and $$x \geq 1,$$ then the solution set is an interval including all real numbers between and including 1 and 9. So $$\left| {x - 5} \right| \leq 4$$ is equivalent to $$\left\lbrack {1,9} \right\rbrack$$ in interval notation.

title: Using a Graphical Approach to Solve Absolute Value Inequalities
snippet: Using a Graphical Approach to Solve Absolute Value Inequalities: Given the equation \left. y = - \frac{1}{2} \middle| 4x - 5 \middle| + 3, \right. determine the x-values for which the y-values are negative. We are trying to determine where...
body_xml: Given the equation $$\left. y = - \frac{1}{2} \middle| 4x - 5 \middle| + 3, \right.$$ determine the x-values for which the y-values are negative. We are trying to determine where $$y < 0,$$ which is when $$\left. - \frac{1}{2} \middle| 4x - 5 \middle| + 3 < 0. \right.$$ We begin by isolating the absolute value. $$\begin{array}{ll} \left. - \frac{1}{2} \middle| 4x - 5 \middle| < - 3 \right. & { \text{Multiply both sides by –2, and reverse the inequality} .} \\ {\left| 4x - 5 \middle| > 6 \right.} & \end{array}$$ Next, we solve for the equality $$\left| 4x - 5 \middle| = 6. \right.$$ $$\begin{array}{lll} {4x - 5 = 6} & & {4x - 5 = - 6} \\ { 4x = 11} & { \text{or} } & { 4x = - 1} \\ { x = \frac{11}{4}} & & { x = - \frac{1}{4}} \end{array}$$ Now, we can examine the graph to observe where the y-values are negative. We observe where the branches are below the x-axis. Notice that it is not important exactly what the graph looks like, as long as we know that it crosses the horizontal axis at $$x = - \frac{1}{4}$$ and $$x = \frac{11}{4},$$ and that the graph opens downward. See Figure 5.

title: Function
snippet: Function: A function is a relation in which each possible input value leads to exactly one output value. We say “the output is a function of the input.” The input values make up the domain, and the output values make up the range.

<note type="rule" source_type="Function" title="Function">
    <paragraph>A function is a relation in which each possible input value leads to exactly one output value. We say “the output is a function of the input.”</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The input values make up the domain, and the output values make up the range.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Determining If Menu Price Lists Are Functions
snippet: Determining If Menu Price Lists Are Functions: The coffee shop menu, shown below, consists of items and their prices. ⓐ Is price a function of the item? ⓑ Is the item a function of the price? ⓐ Let’s begin by considering the input as the...
body_xml: The coffee shop menu, shown below, consists of items and their prices. ⓐ Is price a function of the item? ⓑ Is the item a function of the price? ⓐ Let’s begin by considering the input as the items on the menu. The output values are then the prices. Each item on the menu has only one price, so the price is a function of the item. ⓑ Two items on the menu have the same price. If we consider the prices to be the input values and the items to be the output, then the same input value could have more than one output associated with it. See the image below. Therefore, the item is a not a function of price.

title: Determining If Class Grade Rules Are Functions
snippet: Determining If Class Grade Rules Are Functions: In a particular math class, the overall percent grade corresponds to a grade point average. Is grade point average a function of the percent grade? Is the percent grade a function of the...
body_xml:
In a particular math class, the overall percent grade corresponds to a grade point average. Is grade point average a function of the percent grade? Is the percent grade a function of the grade point average? Table 1 shows a possible rule for assigning grade points. Percent grade 0–56 57–61 62–66 67–71 72–77 78–86 87–91 92–100 Grade point average 0.0 1.0 1.5 2.0 2.5 3.0 3.5 4.0
For any percent grade earned, there is an associated grade point average, so the grade point average is a function of the percent grade. In other words, if we input the percent grade, the output is a specific grade point average. In the grading system given, there is a range of percent grades that correspond to the same grade point average. For example, students who receive a grade point average of 3.0 could have a variety of percent grades ranging from 78 all the way to 86. Thus, percent grade is not a function of grade point average.

    <paragraph>The notation $$y = f(x)$$ defines a function named $$f.$$ This is read as $$``y$$ is a function of $$x."$$ The letter $$x$$ represents the input value, or independent variable. The letter $$y,$$ or $$f(x),$$ represents the output value, or dependent variable.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Using Function Notation for Days in a Month
snippet: Using Function Notation for Days in a Month: Use function notation to represent a function whose input is the name of a month and output is the number of days in that month. Assume that the domain does not include leap years. The number of...
body_xml: Use function notation to represent a function whose input is the name of a month and output is the number of days in that month. Assume that the domain does not include leap years. The number of days in a month is a function of the name of the month, so if we name the function $$f,$$ we write $$\text{days} = f( \text{month} )$$ or $$d = f(m).$$ The name of the month is the input to a “rule” that associates a specific number (the output) with each input. For example, $$f\left( \text{March} \right) = 31,$$ because March has 31 days. The notation $$d = f(m)$$ reminds us that the number of days, $$d$$ (the output), is dependent on the name of the month, $$m$$ (the input). Note that the inputs to a function do not have to be numbers; function inputs can be names of people, labels of geometric objects, or any other element that determines some kind of output. However, most of the functions we will work with in this book will have numbers as inputs and outputs.

Input Output –3 5 0 1 4 5

Table 6 and Table 7 define functions. In both, each input value corresponds to exactly one output value. Table 8 does not define a function because the input value of 5 corresponds to two different output values. When a table represents a function, corresponding input and output values can also be specified using function notation. title: Evaluating Functions at Specific Values
snippet: Evaluating Functions at Specific Values: Evaluate f(x) = x^{2} + 3x - 4 at: ⓐ 2 ⓑ a ⓒ a + h ⓓ Now evaluate \frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h} Replace the x in the function with each specified value. ⓐ Because the input value is a...
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Evaluating Functions at Specific Values">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$f(x) = x^{2} + 3x - 4$$ at:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$2$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$a$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$a + h$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ Now evaluate $$\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Replace the $$x$$ in the function with each specified value.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ Because the input value is a number, 2, we can use simple algebra to simplify. $$\begin{array}{l} { f(2) = 2^{2} + 3(2) - 4} \\ { = 4 + 6 - 4} \\ { = 6} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ In this case, the input value is a letter so we cannot simplify the answer any further. $$f(a) = a^{2} + 3a - 4$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ With an input value of $$a + h,$$ we must use the distributive property. $$\begin{array}{l} {f(a + h) = {(a + h)}^{2} + 3(a + h) - 4} \\ { = a^{2} + 2ah + h^{2} + 3a + 3h - 4} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ In this case, we apply the input values to the function more than once, and then perform algebraic operations on the result. We already found that $$f\left( {a + h} \right) = a^{2} + 2ah + h^{2} + 3a + 3h - 4$$ and we know that $$f(a) = a^{2} + 3a - 4$$ Now we combine the results and simplify. $$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} \\ {\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h} = \frac{(a^{2} + 2ah + h^{2} + 3a + 3h - 4) - (a^{2} + 3a - 4)}{h}} \end{array} \\ \begin{array}{ll} { = \frac{2ah + h^{2} + 3h}{h}} & \\ { = \frac{h(2a + h + 3)}{h}} & {\begin{array}{ll} \begin{array}{ll} & \end{array} & \end{array} \text{Factor out} h.} \\ { = 2a + h + 3} & {\begin{array}{ll} \begin{array}{ll} & \end{array} & \end{array} \text{Simplify} .} \end{array} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Evaluating Functions: Given the function h(p) = p^{2} + 2p, evaluate h(4). To evaluate h(4), we substitute the value 4 for the input variable p in the given function. \begin{array}{l} { h(p) = p^{2} + 2p} \\ { h(4) = {(4)}^{2} + 2(4)} \\ {...

<example number="7" title="Evaluating Functions">

    </problem>

      <paragraph>To evaluate $$h(4),$$ we substitute the value 4 for the input variable $$p$$ in the given function.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} { h(p) = p^{2} + 2p} \\ { h(4) = {(4)}^{2} + 2(4)} \\ { = 16 + 8} \\ { = 24} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, for an input of 4, we have an output of 24.</paragraph>

title: Solving Functions
snippet: Solving Functions: Given the function h(p) = p^{2} + 2p, solve for h(p) = 3. \begin{array}{llll} {h(p) = 3} & & & \\ {p^{2} + 2p = 3} & & & { \text{Substitute the original function} h(p) = p^{2} + 2p.} \\ {p^{2} + 2p - 3 = 0} & & & {...
body_xml: Given the function $$h(p) = p^{2} + 2p,$$ solve for $$h(p) = 3.$$ $$\begin{array}{llll} {h(p) = 3} & & & \\ {p^{2} + 2p = 3} & & & { \text{Substitute the original function} h(p) = p^{2} + 2p.} \\ {p^{2} + 2p - 3 = 0} & & & { \text{Subtract 3 from each side} .} \\ {(p + 3 \text{)(} p - 1) = 0} & & & { \text{Factor} .} \end{array}$$ If $$\left( {p + 3} \right)\left( {p - 1} \right) = 0,$$ either $$\left( {p + 3} \right) = 0$$ or $$\left( {p - 1} \right) = 0$$ (or both of them equal 0). We will set each factor equal to 0 and solve for $$p$$ in each case. $$\begin{array}{ll} {(p + 3) = 0,} & {p = - 3} \\ {(p - 1) = 0,} & {p = 1} \end{array}$$ This gives us two solutions. The output $$h(p) = 3$$ when the input is either $$p = 1$$ or $$p = - 3.$$ We can also verify by graphing as in Figure 3. The graph verifies that $$h(1) = h\left( {- 3} \right) = 3$$ and $$h(4) = 24.$$

title: Finding the Algebraic Form of a Function
snippet: Finding the Algebraic Form of a Function: Express the relationship 2n + 6p = 12 as a function p = f(n), if possible. To express the relationship in this form, we need to be able to write the relationship where p is a function of n, which...
body_xml:
<example number="9" title="Finding the Algebraic Form of a Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Express the relationship $$2n + 6p = 12$$ as a function $$p = f(n),$$ if possible.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To express the relationship in this form, we need to be able to write the relationship where $$p$$ is a function of $$n,$$ which means writing it as $$p = \lbrack \text{expression} \text{involving} n\rbrack.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {2n + 6p = 12} & \\ { 6p = 12 - 2n} & {\begin{array}{lll} & & \end{array} \text{Subtract} 2n \text{from both sides} .} \\ { p = \frac{12 - 2n}{6}} & {\begin{array}{lll} & & \end{array} \text{Divide both sides by 6 and simplify} .} \\ { p = \frac{12}{6} - \frac{2n}{6}} & \\ { p = 2 - \frac{1}{3}n} & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, $$p$$ as a function of $$n$$ is written as</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$p = f(n) = 2 - \frac{1}{3}n$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>It is important to note that not every relationship expressed by an equation can also be expressed as a function with a formula.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Expressing the Equation of a Circle as a Function
snippet: Expressing the Equation of a Circle as a Function: Does the equation x^{2} + y^{2} = 1 represent a function with x as input and y as output? If so, express the relationship as a function y = f(x). First we subtract x^{2} from both sides....
body_xml:
<example number="10" title="Expressing the Equation of a Circle as a Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Does the equation $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ represent a function with $$x$$ as input and $$y$$ as output? If so, express the relationship as a function $$y = f(x).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First we subtract $$x^{2}$$ from both sides.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y^{2} = 1 - x^{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We now try to solve for $$y$$ in this equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {y = \pm \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}} \\ { = + \sqrt{1 - x^{2}} \text{and} - \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We get two outputs corresponding to the same input, so this relationship cannot be represented as a single function $$y = f(x).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Determining Whether a Relationship Is a One-to-One Function
snippet: Determining Whether a Relationship Is a One-to-One Function: Is the area of a circle a function of its radius? If yes, is the function one-to-one? A circle of radius r has a unique area measure given by A = \pi r^{2}, so for any input, r,...
body_xml:
<example number="13" title="Determining Whether a Relationship Is a One-to-One Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Is the area of a circle a function of its radius? If yes, is the function one-to-one?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>A circle of radius $$r$$ has a unique area measure given by $$A = \pi r^{2},$$ so for any input, $$r,$$ there is only one output, $$A.$$ The area is a function of radius $$r.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>If the function is one-to-one, the output value, the area, must correspond to a unique input value, the radius. Any area measure $$A$$ is given by the formula $$A = \pi r^{2}.$$ Because areas and radii are positive numbers, there is exactly one solution: $$\sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}}.$$ So the area of a circle is a one-to-one function of the circle’s radius.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Finding the Domain of a Function Involving a Denominator: Find the domain of the function f(x) = \frac{x + 1}{2 - x}. When there is a denominator, we want to include only values of the input that do not force the denominator to be zero....
body_xml: Find the domain of the function $$f(x) = \frac{x + 1}{2 - x}.$$ When there is a denominator, we want to include only values of the input that do not force the denominator to be zero. So, we will set the denominator equal to 0 and solve for $$x.$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} {2 - x} & = & 0 \\ {- x} & = & -2 \\ x & = & 2 \end{array}$$ Now, we will exclude 2 from the domain. The answers are all real numbers where $$x < 2$$ or $$x > 2$$ as shown in Figure 4. We can use a symbol known as the union, $$\cup ,$$ to combine the two sets. In interval notation, we write the solution: $$\left( {{-\infty},2} \right) \cup \left( {2,\infty} \right).$$
