    <solution>
      <paragraph>When there is an even root in the formula, we exclude any real numbers that result in a negative number in the radicand.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Set the radicand greater than or equal to zero and solve for $$x.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {7 - x} & \geq & 0 \\ {- x} & \geq & -7 \\ x & \leq & 7 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now, we will exclude any number greater than 7 from the domain. The answers are all real numbers less than or equal to $$7,$$ or $$( - \infty,7\rbrack.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Set-Builder Notation and Interval Notation
snippet: Set-Builder Notation and Interval Notation: Set-builder notation is a method of specifying a set of elements that satisfy a certain condition. It takes the form \left\{ x \middle| \text{statement about} x \right\} which is read as, “the...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Set-Builder Notation and Interval Notation" title="Set-Builder Notation and Interval Notation">
    <paragraph>Set-builder notation is a method of specifying a set of elements that satisfy a certain condition. It takes the form $$\left\{ x \middle| \text{statement about} x \right\}$$ which is read as, “the set of all $$x$$ such that the statement about $$x$$ is true.” For example,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left\{ x \middle| 4 < x \leq 12 \right\}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Interval notation is a way of describing sets that include all real numbers between a lower limit that may or may not be included and an upper limit that may or may not be included. The endpoint values are listed between brackets or parentheses. A square bracket indicates inclusion in the set, and a parenthesis indicates exclusion from the set. For example,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {4,12} \right\rbrack$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given a line graph, describe the set of values using interval notation. Identify the intervals to be included in the set by determining where the heavy line overlays the real line. At the left end of each interval, use [ with each...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given a line graph, describe the set of values using interval notation.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Identify the intervals to be included in the set by determining where the heavy line overlays the real line.</item>
      <item>At the left end of each interval, use [ with each end value to be included in the set (solid dot) or ( for each excluded end value (open dot).</item>
      <item>At the right end of each interval, use ] with each end value to be included in the set (filled dot) or ) for each excluded end value (open dot).</item>
      <item>Use the union symbol $$\cup$$ to combine all intervals into one set.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Describing Sets on the Real-Number Line
snippet: Describing Sets on the Real-Number Line: Describe the intervals of values shown in Figure 6 using inequality notation, set-builder notation, and interval notation. To describe the values, x, included in the intervals shown, we would say, “...
body_xml:
Describe the intervals of values shown in Figure 6 using inequality notation, set-builder notation, and interval notation. To describe the values, $$x,$$ included in the intervals shown, we would say, “ $$x$$ is a real number greater than or equal to 1 and less than or equal to 3, or a real number greater than 5.” Inequality $$1 \leq x \leq 3 \text{or} x > 5$$ Set-builder notation $$\left\{ x \middle| 1 \leq x \leq 3 \text{or} x > 5 \right\}$$ Interval notation $$\lbrack 1,3\rbrack \cup (5,\infty)$$
Remember that, when writing or reading interval notation, using a square bracket means the boundary is included in the set. Using a parenthesis means the boundary is not included in the set.

title: Finding Domain and Range from a Graph
snippet: Finding Domain and Range from a Graph: Find the domain and range of the function f whose graph is shown in Figure 9. We can observe that the horizontal extent of the graph is –3 to 1, so the domain of f is \left( {- 3,1} \right\rbrack. The...
body_xml: Find the domain and range of the function $$f$$ whose graph is shown in Figure 9. We can observe that the horizontal extent of the graph is –3 to 1, so the domain of $$f$$ is $$\left( {- 3,1} \right\rbrack.$$ The vertical extent of the graph is 0 to –4, so the range is $$\left\lbrack {- 4} \right.,\left. 0 \right\rbrack.$$ See Figure 10.

title: Finding Domain and Range from a Graph of Oil Production
snippet: Finding Domain and Range from a Graph of Oil Production: Find the domain and range of the function f whose graph is shown in Figure 11. The input quantity along the horizontal axis is “years,” which we represent with the variable t for...
body_xml: Find the domain and range of the function $$f$$ whose graph is shown in Figure 11. The input quantity along the horizontal axis is “years,” which we represent with the variable $$t$$ for time. The output quantity is “thousands of barrels of oil per day,” which we represent with the variable $$b$$ for barrels. The graph may continue to the left and right beyond what is viewed, but based on the portion of the graph that is visible, we can determine the domain as $$1973 \leq t \leq 2008$$ and the range as approximately $$180 \leq b \leq 2010.$$ In interval notation, the domain is [1973, 2008], and the range is about [180, 2010]. For the domain and the range, we approximate the smallest and largest values since they do not fall exactly on the grid lines.

snippet: Finding the Domain and Range Using Toolkit Functions: Find the domain and range of f(x) = 2x^{3} - x. There are no restrictions on the domain, as any real number may be cubed and then subtracted from the result. The domain is \left( {-...

    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the domain and range of $$f(x) = 2x^{3} - x.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>There are no restrictions on the domain, as any real number may be cubed and then subtracted from the result.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The domain is $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ and the range is also $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right).$$</paragraph>

title: Finding the Domain and Range
snippet: Finding the Domain and Range: Find the domain and range of f(x) = \frac{2}{x + 1}. We cannot evaluate the function at -1 because division by zero is undefined. The domain is \left( {- \infty,-1} \right) \cup \left( {-1,\infty} \right)....
body_xml:
<example number="9" title="Finding the Domain and Range">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the domain and range of $$f(x) = \frac{2}{x + 1}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We cannot evaluate the function at $$-1$$ because division by zero is undefined. The domain is $$\left( {- \infty,-1} \right) \cup \left( {-1,\infty} \right).$$ Because the function is never zero, we exclude 0 from the range. The range is $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right) \cup \left( {0,\infty} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Domain and Range
snippet: Finding the Domain and Range: Find the domain and range of f(x) = 2\sqrt{x + 4}. We cannot take the square root of a negative number, so the value inside the radical must be nonnegative. x + 4 \geq 0 \text{when} x \geq - 4 The domain of...
body_xml: Find the domain and range of $$f(x) = 2\sqrt{x + 4}.$$ We cannot take the square root of a negative number, so the value inside the radical must be nonnegative. $$x + 4 \geq 0 \text{when} x \geq - 4$$ The domain of $$f(x)$$ is $$\lbrack - 4,\infty).$$ We then find the range. We know that $$f\left( {- 4} \right) = 0,$$ and the function value increases as $$x$$ increases without any upper limit. We conclude that the range of $$f$$ is $$\left\lbrack {0,\left. \infty \right)} \right..$$ Figure 22 represents the function $$f.$$

title: Piecewise Function
snippet: Piecewise Function: A piecewise function is a function in which more than one formula is used to define the output. Each formula has its own domain, and the domain of the function is the union of all these smaller domains. We notate this...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Piecewise Function" title="Piecewise Function">
    <paragraph>A piecewise function is a function in which more than one formula is used to define the output. Each formula has its own domain, and the domain of the function is the union of all these smaller domains. We notate this idea like this:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} { \text{formula 1 if} x \text{is in domain 1} } \\ { \text{formula 2 if} x \text{is in domain 2} } \\ { \text{formula 3 if} x \text{is in domain 3} } \end{array} \right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In piecewise notation, the absolute value function is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$|x| = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x \text{if} x \geq 0} \\ {- x \text{if} x < 0} \end{array} \right.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given a piecewise function, write the formula and identify the domain for each interval. Identify the intervals for which different rules apply. Determine formulas that describe how to calculate an output from an input in each...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given a piecewise function, write the formula and identify the domain for each interval.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Identify the intervals for which different rules apply.</item>
      <item>Determine formulas that describe how to calculate an output from an input in each interval.</item>
      <item>Use braces and if-statements to write the function.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Writing a Piecewise Function
snippet: Writing a Piecewise Function: A museum charges \$5 per person for a guided tour with a group of 1 to 9 people or a fixed \$50 fee for a group of 10 or more people. Write a function relating the number of people, n, to the cost, C. Since...
body_xml: A museum charges \$5 per person for a guided tour with a group of 1 to 9 people or a fixed \$50 fee for a group of 10 or more people. Write a function relating the number of people, $$n,$$ to the cost, $$C.$$ Since one cannot have fractions of a person, this is really a discrete function. However, for this exercise we will treat it as a continuous function. Two different formulas will be needed. For n-values under 10, $$C = 5n.$$ For values of $$n$$ that are 10 or greater, $$C = 50.$$ $$C(n) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} {5n} & \text{if} & {0 < n < 10} \\ 50 & \text{if} & {n \geq 10} \end{matrix} \right.$$ The function is represented in Figure 23. The graph is a diagonal line from $$n = 0$$ to $$n = 10$$ and a constant after that. In this example, the two formulas agree at the meeting point where $$n = 10,$$ but not all piecewise functions have this property.

title: Working with a Piecewise Function
snippet: Working with a Piecewise Function: A cell phone company uses the function below to determine the cost, C, in dollars for g gigabytes of data transfer. C(g) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} 25 & \text{if} & {0 < g < 2} \\ {25 + 10(g - 2)} &...
body_xml: A cell phone company uses the function below to determine the cost, $$C,$$ in dollars for $$g$$ gigabytes of data transfer. $$C(g) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} 25 & \text{if} & {0 < g < 2} \\ {25 + 10(g - 2)} & \text{if} & {g \geq 2} \end{matrix} \right.$$ Find the cost of using 1.5 gigabytes of data and the cost of using 4 gigabytes of data. To find the cost of using 1.5 gigabytes of data, $$C(1.5),$$ we first look to see which part of the domain our input falls in. Because 1.5 is less than 2, we use the first formula. $$C(1.5) = \$25$$ To find the cost of using 4 gigabytes of data, $$C(4),$$ we see that our input of 4 is greater than 2, so we use the second formula. $$C(4) = 25 + 10(4 - 2) = \$45$$ The function is represented in Figure 24. We can see where the function changes from a constant to a shifted and stretched identity at $$g = 2.$$ We plot the graphs for the different formulas on a common set of axes, making sure each formula is applied on its proper domain.

title: Graphing a Piecewise Function
snippet: Graphing a Piecewise Function: Sketch a graph of the function. f(x) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} x^{2} & \text{if} & {x \leq 1} \\ 3 & \text{if} & {1 < x \leq 2} \\ x & \text{if} & {x > 2} \end{matrix} \right. Each of the component functions...
body_xml: Sketch a graph of the function. $$f(x) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} x^{2} & \text{if} & {x \leq 1} \\ 3 & \text{if} & {1 < x \leq 2} \\ x & \text{if} & {x > 2} \end{matrix} \right.$$ Each of the component functions is from our library of toolkit functions, so we know their shapes. We can imagine graphing each function and then limiting the graph to the indicated domain. At the endpoints of the domain, we draw open circles to indicate where the endpoint is not included because of a less-than or greater-than inequality; we draw a closed circle where the endpoint is included because of a less-than-or-equal-to or greater-than-or-equal-to inequality. Figure 25 shows the three components of the piecewise function graphed on separate coordinate systems. Now that we have sketched each piece individually, we combine them in the same coordinate plane. See Figure 26. Note that the graph does pass the vertical line test even at $$x = 1$$ and $$x = 2$$ because the points $$\left( {1,3} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2,2} \right)$$ are not part of the graph of the function, though $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2, 3} \right)$$ are.

title: Rate of Change
snippet: Rate of Change: A rate of change describes how an output quantity changes relative to the change in the input quantity. The units on a rate of change are “output units per input units.” The average rate of change between two input values...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Rate of Change" title="Rate of Change">
    <paragraph>A rate of change describes how an output quantity changes relative to the change in the input quantity. The units on a rate of change are “output units per input units.”</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The average rate of change between two input values is the total change of the function values (output values) divided by the change in the input values.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{f\left( x_{2} \right) - f\left( x_{1} \right)}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Calculate the difference $$y_{2} - y_{1} = \text{Δ} y.$$</item>
      <item>Calculate the difference $$x_{2} - x_{1} = \text{Δ} x.$$</item>
      <item>Find the ratio $$\frac{ \text{Δ} y}{ \text{Δ} x}.$$</item>
    </list>

unit_title: Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs
title: Computing an Average Rate of Change
snippet: Computing an Average Rate of Change: Using the data in Table 1, find the average rate of change of the price of gasoline between 2007 and 2009. In 2007, the price of gasoline was \$2.84. In 2009, the cost was \$2.41. The average rate of...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Computing an Average Rate of Change">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Using the data in Table 1, find the average rate of change of the price of gasoline between 2007 and 2009.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>In 2007, the price of gasoline was \$2.84. In 2009, the cost was \$2.41. The average rate of change is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} & = & \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}} \\ & = & \frac{\$ 2.41 - \$ 2.84}{2009 - 2007} \\ & = & \frac{- \$ 0.43}{2 \text{years} } \\ & = & {- \$ 0.22 \text{per year} } \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>Note that a decrease is expressed by a negative change or “negative increase.” A rate of change is negative when the output decreases as the input increases or when the output increases as the input decreases.</paragraph>
  </example>

unit_title: Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs
title: Computing Average Rate of Change from a Graph
snippet: Computing Average Rate of Change from a Graph: Given the function g(t) shown in Figure 1, find the average rate of change on the interval \left\lbrack {- 1,2} \right\rbrack. At t = - 1, Figure 2 shows g(-1) = 4. At t = 2, the graph shows...
body_xml: Given the function $$g(t)$$ shown in Figure 1, find the average rate of change on the interval $$\left\lbrack {- 1,2} \right\rbrack.$$ At $$t = - 1,$$ Figure 2 shows $$g(-1) = 4.$$ At $$t = 2,$$ the graph shows $$g(2) = 1.$$ The horizontal change $$\text{Δ} t = 3$$ is shown by the red arrow, and the vertical change $$\text{Δ} g(t) = - 3$$ is shown by the turquoise arrow. The average rate of change is shown by the slope of the orange line segment. The output changes by –3 while the input changes by 3, giving an average rate of change of $$\frac{1 - 4}{2 - \left( {- 1} \right)} = \frac{- 3}{3} = -1$$ Note that the order we choose is very important. If, for example, we use $$\frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{1} - x_{2}},$$ we will not get the correct answer. Decide which point will be 1 and which point will be 2, and keep the coordinates fixed as $$\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right)$$ and $$\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right).$$

unit_title: Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs
title: Computing Average Rate of Change from a Table
snippet: Computing Average Rate of Change from a Table: After picking up a friend who lives 10 miles away and leaving on a trip, Anna records her distance from home over time. The values are shown in Table 2. Find her average speed over the first 6...
body_xml:
After picking up a friend who lives 10 miles away and leaving on a trip, Anna records her distance from home over time. The values are shown in Table 2. Find her average speed over the first 6 hours. t (hours) 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 D(t) (miles) 10 55 90 153 214 240 292 300
Here, the average speed is the average rate of change. She traveled 282 miles in 6 hours. $$\begin{array}{ccl} \frac{292 - 10}{6 - 0} & = & \frac{282}{6} \\ & = & 47 \end{array}$$ The average speed is 47 miles per hour. Because the speed is not constant, the average speed depends on the interval chosen. For the interval [2,3], the average speed is 63 miles per hour.

unit_title: Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs
title: Computing Average Rate of Change for a Function Expressed as a Formula
snippet: Computing Average Rate of Change for a Function Expressed as a Formula: Compute the average rate of change of f(x) = x^{2} - \frac{1}{x} on the interval \text{[2,} \text{4].} We can start by computing the function values at each endpoint...
body_xml:
<example number="4" title="Computing Average Rate of Change for a Function Expressed as a Formula">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Compute the average rate of change of $$f(x) = x^{2} - \frac{1}{x}$$ on the interval $$\text{[2,} \text{4].}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We can start by computing the function values at each endpoint of the interval.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cclccl} {f(2)} & = & {2^{2} - \frac{1}{2}} & { {f(4)}} & = & {4^{2} - \frac{1}{4}} \\ & = & {4 - \frac{1}{2}} & & = & {16 - \frac{1}{4}} \\ & = & \frac{7}{2} & & = & \frac{63}{4} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now we compute the average rate of change.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} \text{Average rate of change} & = & \frac{f(4) - f(2)}{4 - 2} \\ & = & \frac{\frac{63}{4} - \frac{7}{2}}{4 - 2} \\ & = & \frac{\frac{49}{4}}{2} \\ & = & \frac{49}{8} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

unit_title: Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs
title: Finding the Average Rate of Change of a Force
snippet: Finding the Average Rate of Change of a Force: The electrostatic force F, measured in newtons, between two charged particles can be related to the distance between the particles d, in centimeters, by the formula F(d) = \frac{2}{d^{2}}....
body_xml:
<example number="5" title="Finding the Average Rate of Change of a Force">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The electrostatic force $$F,$$ measured in newtons, between two charged particles can be related to the distance between the particles $$d,$$ in centimeters, by the formula $$F(d) = \frac{2}{d^{2}}.$$ Find the average rate of change of force if the distance between the particles is increased from 2 cm to 6 cm.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We are computing the average rate of change of $$F(d) = \frac{2}{d^{2}}$$ on the interval $$\lbrack 2,6\rbrack.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cclc} \text{Average rate of change} & = & {\frac{F(6) - F(2)}{6 - 2}} & \\ & = & \frac{\frac{2}{6^{2}} - \frac{2}{2^{2}}}{6 - 2} & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ & = & \frac{\frac{2}{36} - \frac{2}{4}}{4} & \\ & = & \frac{- \frac{16}{36}}{4} & { \text{Combine numerator terms} .} \\ & = & {- \frac{1}{9}} & \text{Simplify} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The average rate of change is $$- \frac{1}{9}$$ newton per centimeter.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

unit_title: Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs
title: Finding an Average Rate of Change as an Expression
snippet: Finding an Average Rate of Change as an Expression: Find the average rate of change of g(t) = t^{2} + 3t + 1 on the interval \lbrack 0, a\rbrack. The answer will be an expression involving a in simplest form. We use the average rate of...
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Finding an Average Rate of Change as an Expression">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the average rate of change of $$g(t) = t^{2} + 3t + 1$$ on the interval $$\lbrack 0, a\rbrack.$$ The answer will be an expression involving $$a$$ in simplest form.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We use the average rate of change formula.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cclc} \text{Average rate of change} & = & \frac{g(a) - g(0)}{a - 0} & { \text{Evaluate} .} \\ & = & \frac{\left( a^{2} + 3a + 1 \right) - \left( 0^{2} + 3(0) + 1 \right)}{a - 0} & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ & = & \frac{a^{2} + 3a + 1 - 1}{a} & { \text{Simplify and factor} .} \\ & = & \frac{a(a + 3)}{a} & { \text{Divide by the common factor} a.} \\ & = & {a + 3} & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This result tells us the average rate of change in terms of $$a$$ between $$t = 0$$ and any other point $$t = a.$$ For example, on the interval $$\lbrack 0,5\rbrack,$$ the average rate of change would be $$5 + 3 = 8.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

unit_title: Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs
title: Local Minima and Local Maxima
snippet: Local Minima and Local Maxima: A function f is an increasing function on an open interval if f(b) > f(a) for any two input values a and b in the given interval where b > a. A function f is a decreasing function on an open interval if f(b)...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Local Minima and Local Maxima" title="Local Minima and Local Maxima">
    <paragraph>A function $$f$$ is an increasing function on an open interval if $$f(b) > f(a)$$ for any two input values $$a$$ and $$b$$ in the given interval where $$b > a.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>A function $$f$$ is a decreasing function on an open interval if $$f(b) < f(a)$$ for any two input values $$a$$ and $$b$$ in the given interval where $$b > a.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>A function $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$x = b$$ if there exists an interval $$(a,c)$$ with $$a < b < c$$ such that, for any $$x$$ in the interval $$\left( {a,c} \right),$$ $$f(x) \leq f(b).$$ Likewise, $$f$$ has a local minimum at $$x = b$$ if there exists an interval $$(a,c)$$ with $$a < b < c$$ such that, for any $$x$$ in the interval $$\left( {a,c} \right),$$ $$f(x) \geq f(b).$$</paragraph>
  </note>

unit_title: Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs
title: Finding Increasing and Decreasing Intervals on a Graph
snippet: Finding Increasing and Decreasing Intervals on a Graph: Given the function p(t) in Figure 6, identify the intervals on which the function appears to be increasing. We see that the function is not constant on any interval. The function is...
body_xml: Given the function $$p(t)$$ in Figure 6, identify the intervals on which the function appears to be increasing. We see that the function is not constant on any interval. The function is increasing where it slants upward as we move to the right and decreasing where it slants downward as we move to the right. The function appears to be increasing from $$t = 1$$ to $$t = 3$$ and from $$t = 4$$ on. In interval notation, we would say the function appears to be increasing on the interval (1,3) and the interval $$(4,\infty).$$ Notice in this example that we used open intervals (intervals that do not include the endpoints), because the function is neither increasing nor decreasing at $$t = 1$$ , $$t = 3$$ , and $$t = 4$$ . These points are the local extrema (two minima and a maximum).

unit_title: Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs
title: Finding Local Extrema from a Graph
snippet: Finding Local Extrema from a Graph: Graph the function f(x) = \frac{2}{x} + \frac{x}{3}. Then use the graph to estimate the local extrema of the function and to determine the intervals on which the function is increasing. Using technology,...
body_xml: Graph the function $$f(x) = \frac{2}{x} + \frac{x}{3}.$$ Then use the graph to estimate the local extrema of the function and to determine the intervals on which the function is increasing. Using technology, we find that the graph of the function looks like that in Figure 7. It appears there is a low point, or local minimum, between $$x = 2$$ and $$x = 3,$$ and a mirror-image high point, or local maximum, somewhere between $$x = -3$$ and $$x = -2.$$ Most graphing calculators and graphing utilities can estimate the location of maxima and minima. Figure 8 provides screen images from two different technologies, showing the estimate for the local maximum and minimum. Based on these estimates, the function is increasing on the interval $$( - \infty, - \text{2} \text{.449)}$$ and $$(2.449,\infty).$$ Notice that, while we expect the extrema to be symmetric, the two different technologies agree only up to four decimals due to the differing approximation algorithms used by each. (The exact location of the extrema is at $$\pm \sqrt{6},$$ but determining this requires calculus.)

Observe the graph of $$f.$$ The graph attains a local maximum at $$x = 1$$ because it is the highest point in an open interval around $$x = 1.$$ The local maximum is the $$y$$ -coordinate at $$x = 1,$$ which is $$2.$$ The graph attains a local minimum at $$x = -1$$ because it is the lowest point in an open interval around $$x = -1.$$ The local minimum is the y-coordinate at $$x = -1,$$ which is $$-2.$$

title: Performing Algebraic Operations on Functions
snippet: Performing Algebraic Operations on Functions: Find and simplify the functions \left( {g - f} \right)(x) and \left( \frac{g}{f} \right)(x), given f(x) = x - 1 and g(x) = x^{2} - 1. Are they the same function? Begin by writing the general...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Performing Algebraic Operations on Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find and simplify the functions $$\left( {g - f} \right)(x)$$ and $$\left( \frac{g}{f} \right)(x),$$ given $$f(x) = x - 1$$ and $$g(x) = x^{2} - 1.$$ Are they the same function?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Begin by writing the general form, and then substitute the given functions.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {(g - f)(x)} & = & {g(x) - f(x)} & \\ {(g - f)(x)} & = & {x^{2} - 1 - (x - 1)} & \\ {(g - f)(x)} & = & {x^{2} - x} & \\ {(g - f)(x)} & = & {x(x - 1)} & \\ & & & \\ & & & \\ {\left( \frac{g}{f} \right)(x)} & = & \frac{g(x)}{f(x)} & \\ {\left( \frac{g}{f} \right)(x)} & = & \frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1} & \\ {\left( \frac{g}{f} \right)(x)} & = & \frac{(x + 1)(x - 1)}{x - 1} & { \text{where} x \neq 1} \\ {\left( \frac{g}{f} \right)(x)} & = & {x + 1} & \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>No, the functions are not the same.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Note: For $$\left( \frac{g}{f} \right)(x),$$ the condition $$x \neq 1$$ is necessary because when $$x = 1,$$ the denominator is equal to 0, which makes the function undefined.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Composition of Functions
snippet: Composition of Functions: When the output of one function is used as the input of another, we call the entire operation a composition of functions. For any input x and functions f and g, this action defines a composite function, which we...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Composition of Functions" title="Composition of Functions">
    <paragraph>When the output of one function is used as the input of another, we call the entire operation a composition of functions. For any input $$x$$ and functions $$f$$ and $$g,$$ this action defines a composite function, which we write as $$f \circ g$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {f \circ g} \right)(x) = f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The domain of the composite function $$f \circ g$$ is all $$x$$ such that $$x$$ is in the domain of $$g$$ and $$g(x)$$ is in the domain of $$f.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>It is important to realize that the product of functions $$fg$$ is not the same as the function composition $$f\left( {g(x)} \right),$$ because, in general, $$f(x)g(x) \neq f\left( {g(x)} \right).$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Determining whether Composition of Functions is Commutative
snippet: Determining whether Composition of Functions is Commutative: Using the functions provided, find f\left( {g(x)} \right) and g\left( {f(x)} \right). Determine whether the composition of the functions is commutative. f(x) = 2x + 1 g(x) = 3 -...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Determining whether Composition of Functions is Commutative">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Using the functions provided, find $$f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ and $$g\left( {f(x)} \right).$$ Determine whether the composition of the functions is commutative.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = 2x + 1 g(x) = 3 - x$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let’s begin by substituting $$g(x)$$ into $$f(x).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} {f(g(x))} & = & {2(3 - x) + 1} \\ & = & {6 - 2x + 1} \\ & = & {7 - 2x} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now we can substitute $$f(x)$$ into $$g(x).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} {g(f(x))} & = & {3 - (2x + 1)} \\ & = & {3 - 2x - 1} \\ & = & {-2x + 2} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We find that $$g(f(x)) \neq f(g(x)),$$ so the operation of function composition is not commutative.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Interpreting Composite Functions
snippet: Interpreting Composite Functions: The function c(s) gives the number of calories burned completing s sit-ups, and s(t) gives the number of sit-ups a person can complete in t minutes. Interpret c(s(3)). The inside expression in the...
body_xml:
<example number="3" title="Interpreting Composite Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The function $$c(s)$$ gives the number of calories burned completing $$s$$ sit-ups, and $$s(t)$$ gives the number of sit-ups a person can complete in $$t$$ minutes. Interpret $$c(s(3)).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The inside expression in the composition is $$s(3).$$ Because the input to the s-function is time, $$t = 3$$ represents 3 minutes, and $$s(3)$$ is the number of sit-ups completed in 3 minutes.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Using $$s(3)$$ as the input to the function $$c(s)$$ gives us the number of calories burned during the number of sit-ups that can be completed in 3 minutes, or simply the number of calories burned in 3 minutes (by doing sit-ups).</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Investigating the Order of Function Composition
snippet: Investigating the Order of Function Composition: Suppose f(x) gives miles that can be driven in x hours and g(y) gives the gallons of gas used in driving y miles. Which of these expressions is meaningful: f\left( {g(y)} \right) or g\left(...
body_xml:
<example number="4" title="Investigating the Order of Function Composition">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose $$f(x)$$ gives miles that can be driven in $$x$$ hours and $$g(y)$$ gives the gallons of gas used in driving $$y$$ miles. Which of these expressions is meaningful: $$f\left( {g(y)} \right)$$ or $$g\left( {f(x)} \right)?$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The function $$y = f(x)$$ is a function whose output is the number of miles driven corresponding to the number of hours driven.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\text{number of miles} = f( \text{number of hours} )$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The function $$g(y)$$ is a function whose output is the number of gallons used corresponding to the number of miles driven. This means:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\text{number of gallons} = g( \text{number of miles} )$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The expression $$g(y)$$ takes miles as the input and a number of gallons as the output. The function $$f(x)$$ requires a number of hours as the input. Trying to input a number of gallons does not make sense. The expression $$f\left( {g(y)} \right)$$ is meaningless.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The expression $$f(x)$$ takes hours as input and a number of miles driven as the output. The function $$g(y)$$ requires a number of miles as the input. Using $$f(x)$$ (miles driven) as an input value for $$g(y),$$ where gallons of gas depends on miles driven, does make sense. The expression $$g\left( {f(x)} \right)$$ makes sense, and will yield the number of gallons of gas used, $$g,$$ driving a certain number of miles, $$f(x),$$ in $$x$$ hours.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using a Table to Evaluate a Composite Function
snippet: Using a Table to Evaluate a Composite Function: Using Table 1, evaluate f(g(3)) and g(f(3)). x f(x) g(x) 1 6 3 2 8 5 3 3 2 4 1 7 To evaluate f(g(3) \text{),} we start from the inside with the input value 3. We then evaluate the inside...
body_xml:
Using Table 1, evaluate $$f(g(3))$$ and $$g(f(3)).$$ $$x$$ $$f(x)$$ $$g(x)$$ 1 6 3 2 8 5 3 3 2 4 1 7
To evaluate $$f(g(3) \text{),}$$ we start from the inside with the input value 3. We then evaluate the inside expression $$g(3)$$ using the table that defines the function $$g:$$ $$g(3) = 2.$$ We can then use that result as the input to the function $$f,$$ so $$g(3)$$ is replaced by 2 and we get $$f(2).$$ Then, using the table that defines the function $$f,$$ we find that $$f(2) = 8.$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} {g(3)} & = & 2 \\ {f(g(3))} & = & {f(2) = 8} \end{array}$$ To evaluate $$g(f(3) \text{),}$$ we first evaluate the inside expression $$f(3)$$ using the first table: $$f(3) = 3.$$ Then, using the table for $$g,$$ we can evaluate $$g(f(3)) = g(3) = 2$$ Table 2 shows the composite functions $$f \circ g$$ and $$g \circ f$$ as tables. $$x$$ $$g(x)$$ $$f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ $$f(x)$$ $$g\left( {f(x)} \right)$$ 3 2 8 3 2

title: Using a Graph to Evaluate a Composite Function
snippet: Using a Graph to Evaluate a Composite Function: Using Figure 1, evaluate f(g(1)). To evaluate f(g(1)), we start with the inside evaluation. See Figure 2. We evaluate g(1) using the graph of g(x), finding the input of 1 on the x- axis and...
body_xml: Using Figure 1, evaluate $$f(g(1)).$$ To evaluate $$f(g(1)),$$ we start with the inside evaluation. See Figure 2. We evaluate $$g(1)$$ using the graph of $$g(x),$$ finding the input of 1 on the $$x-$$ axis and finding the output value of the graph at that input. Here, $$g(1) = 3.$$ We use this value as the input to the function $$f.$$ $$f(g(1)) = f(3)$$ We can then evaluate the composite function by looking to the graph of $$f(x),$$ finding the input of 3 on the $$x-$$ axis and reading the output value of the graph at this input. Here, $$f(3) = 6,$$ so $$f(g(1)) = 6.$$ Figure 3 shows how we can mark the graphs with arrows to trace the path from the input value to the output value.

title: Evaluating a Composition of Functions Expressed as Formulas with a Numerical Input
snippet: Evaluating a Composition of Functions Expressed as Formulas with a Numerical Input: Given f(t) = t^{2} - t and h(x) = 3x + 2, evaluate f(h(1)). Because the inside expression is h(1), we start by evaluating h(x) at 1. \begin{array}{rcl}...
body_xml:
<example number="7" title="Evaluating a Composition of Functions Expressed as Formulas with a Numerical Input">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Given $$f(t) = t^{2} - t$$ and $$h(x) = 3x + 2,$$ evaluate $$f(h(1)).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Because the inside expression is $$h(1),$$ we start by evaluating $$h(x)$$ at 1.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {h(1)} & = & {3(1) + 2} \\ {h(1)} & = & 5 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then $$f(h(1)) = f(5),$$ so we evaluate $$f(t)$$ at an input of 5.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {f(h(1))} & = & {f(5)} \\ {f(h(1))} & = & {5^{2} - 5} \\ {f(h(1))} & = & 20 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>It makes no difference what the input variables $$t$$ and $$x$$ were called in this problem because we evaluated for specific numerical values.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Domain of a Composite Function
snippet: Domain of a Composite Function: The domain of a composite function f\left( {g(x)} \right) is the set of those inputs x in the domain of g for which g(x) is in the domain of f.

<note type="rule" source_type="Domain of a Composite Function" title="Domain of a Composite Function">
    <paragraph>The domain of a composite function $$f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ is the set of those inputs $$x$$ in the domain of $$g$$ for which $$g(x)$$ is in the domain of $$f.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given a function composition f(g(x)), determine its domain. Find the domain of g. Find the domain of f. Find those inputs x in the domain of g for which g(x) is in the domain of f. That is, exclude those inputs x from the domain of...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given a function composition $$f(g(x)),$$ determine its domain.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Find the domain of $$g.$$</item>
      <item>Find the domain of $$f.$$</item>
      <item>Find those inputs $$x$$ in the domain of $$g$$ for which $$g(x)$$ is in the domain of $$f.$$ That is, exclude those inputs $$x$$ from the domain of $$g$$ for which $$g(x)$$ is not in the domain of $$f.$$ The resulting set is the domain of $$f \circ g.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Finding the Domain of a Composite Function
snippet: Finding the Domain of a Composite Function: Find the domain of \left( {f \circ g} \right)(x) \text{where} f(x) = \frac{5}{x - 1} \text{and} g(x) = \frac{4}{3x - 2} The domain of g(x) consists of all real numbers except x = \frac{2}{3},...
body_xml:
<example number="8" title="Finding the Domain of a Composite Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the domain of</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {f \circ g} \right)(x) \text{where} f(x) = \frac{5}{x - 1} \text{and} g(x) = \frac{4}{3x - 2}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The domain of $$g(x)$$ consists of all real numbers except $$x = \frac{2}{3},$$ since that input value would cause us to divide by 0. Likewise, the domain of $$f$$ consists of all real numbers except 1. So we need to exclude from the domain of $$g(x)$$ that value of $$x$$ for which $$g(x) = 1.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} \frac{4}{3x - 2} & = & 1 \\ 4 & = & {3x - 2} \\ 6 & = & {3x} \\ x & = & 2 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So the domain of $$f \circ g$$ is the set of all real numbers except $$\frac{2}{3}$$ and $$2.$$ This means that</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x \neq \frac{2}{3} \text{or} x \neq 2$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We can write this in interval notation as</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {- \infty,\frac{2}{3}} \right) \cup \left( {\frac{2}{3},2} \right) \cup \left( {2,\infty} \right)$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Domain of a Composite Function Involving Radicals
snippet: Finding the Domain of a Composite Function Involving Radicals: Find the domain of \left( {f \circ g} \right)(x) \text{where} f(x) = \sqrt{x + 2} \text{and} g(x) = \sqrt{3 - x} Because we cannot take the square root of a negative number,...
body_xml:
<example number="9" title="Finding the Domain of a Composite Function Involving Radicals">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the domain of</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {f \circ g} \right)(x) \text{where} f(x) = \sqrt{x + 2} \text{and} g(x) = \sqrt{3 - x}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Because we cannot take the square root of a negative number, the domain of $$g$$ is $$\left( {- \infty,3} \right\rbrack.$$ Now we check the domain of the composite function</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${(f \circ g)(x)} = \sqrt{\sqrt{3 - x} + 2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>For $${(f \circ g)(x)} = \sqrt{\sqrt{3 - x} + 2},\sqrt{3 - x} + 2 \geq 0,$$ since the radicand of a square root must be positive. Since square roots are positive, $$\sqrt{3 - x} \geq 0,$$ or, $$3 - x \geq 0,$$ which gives a domain of $$\left( \text{-\infty} ,3 \right\rbrack$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>This example shows that knowledge of the range of functions (specifically the inner function) can also be helpful in finding the domain of a composite function. It also shows that the domain of $$f \circ g$$ can contain values that are not in the domain of $$f,$$ though they must be in the domain of $$g.$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Decomposing a Function
snippet: Decomposing a Function: Write f(x) = \sqrt{5 - x^{2}} as the composition of two functions. We are looking for two functions, g and h, so f(x) = g(h(x)). To do this, we look for a function inside a function in the formula for f(x). As one...
body_xml:
<example number="10" title="Decomposing a Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write $$f(x) = \sqrt{5 - x^{2}}$$ as the composition of two functions.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We are looking for two functions, $$g$$ and $$h,$$ so $$f(x) = g(h(x)).$$ To do this, we look for a function inside a function in the formula for $$f(x).$$ As one possibility, we might notice that the expression $$5 - x^{2}$$ is the inside of the square root. We could then decompose the function as</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$h(x) = 5 - x^{2} \text{and} g(x) = \sqrt{x}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We can check our answer by recomposing the functions.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$g(h(x)) = g\left( {5 - x^{2}} \right) = \sqrt{5 - x^{2}}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="rule" source_type="Vertical Shift" title="Vertical Shift">

body_xml: To regulate temperature in a green building, airflow vents near the roof open and close throughout the day. Figure 3 shows the area of open vents $$V$$ (in square feet) throughout the day in hours after midnight, $$t.$$ During the summer, the facilities manager decides to try to better regulate temperature by increasing the amount of open vents by 20 square feet throughout the day and night. Sketch a graph of this new function. We can sketch a graph of this new function by adding 20 to each of the output values of the original function. This will have the effect of shifting the graph vertically up, as shown in Figure 4. Notice that in Figure 4, for each input value, the output value has increased by 20, so if we call the new function $$S(t),$$ we could write $$S(t) = V(t) + 20$$ This notation tells us that, for any value of $$t,S(t)$$ can be found by evaluating the function $$V$$ at the same input and then adding 20 to the result. This defines $$S$$ as a transformation of the function $$V,$$ in this case a vertical shift up 20 units. Notice that, with a vertical shift, the input values stay the same and only the output values change. See Table 1. $$t$$ 0 8 10 17 19 24 $$V(t)$$ 0 0 220 220 0 0 $$S(t)$$ 20 20 240 240 20 20

The formula $$g(x) = f(x) - 3$$ tells us that we can find the output values of $$g$$ by subtracting 3 from the output values of $$f.$$ For example: $$\begin{array}{cclc} {f(2)} & = & 1 & \text{Given} \\ {g(x)} & = & {f(x) - 3} & \text{Given transformation} \\ {g(2)} & = & {f(2) - 3} & \\ & = & {1 - 3} & \\ & = & {- 2} & \end{array}$$ Subtracting 3 from each $$f(x)$$ value, we can complete a table of values for $$g(x)$$ as shown in Table 3. $$x$$ 2 4 6 8 $$f(x)$$ 1 3 7 11 $$g(x)$$ −2 0 4 8

title: Adding a Constant to an Input
snippet: Adding a Constant to an Input: Returning to our building airflow example from Figure 3, suppose that in autumn the facilities manager decides that the original venting plan starts too late, and wants to begin the entire venting program 2...
body_xml: Returning to our building airflow example from Figure 3, suppose that in autumn the facilities manager decides that the original venting plan starts too late, and wants to begin the entire venting program 2 hours earlier. Sketch a graph of the new function. We can set $$V(t)$$ to be the original program and $$F(t)$$ to be the revised program. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {V(t)} & = & \text{the original venting plan} \\ {F(t)} & = & \text{starting 2 hrs sooner} \end{array}$$ In the new graph, at each time, the airflow is the same as the original function $$V$$ was 2 hours later. For example, in the original function $$V,$$ the airflow starts to change at 8 a.m., whereas for the function $$F,$$ the airflow starts to change at 6 a.m. The comparable function values are $$V(8) = F(6).$$ See Figure 6. Notice also that the vents first opened to $$220{ \text{ft} }^{2}$$ at 10 a.m. under the original plan, while under the new plan the vents reach $$220{ \text{ft} }^{ \text{2} }$$ at 8 a.m., so $$V(10) = F(8).$$ In both cases, we see that, because $$F(t)$$ starts 2 hours sooner, $$h = - 2.$$ That means that the same output values are reached when $$F(t) = V(t - \left( {- 2} \right)) = V\left( {t + 2} \right).$$ Note that $$V(t + 2)$$ has the effect of shifting the graph to the left. Horizontal changes or “inside changes” affect the domain of a function (the input) instead of the range and often seem counterintuitive. The new function $$F(t)$$ uses the same outputs as $$V(t),$$ but matches those outputs to inputs 2 hours earlier than those of $$V(t).$$ Said another way, we must add 2 hours to the input of $$V$$ to find the corresponding output for $$F:F(t) = V(t + 2).$$

title: Shifting a Tabular Function Horizontally
snippet: Shifting a Tabular Function Horizontally: A function f(x) is given in Table 4. Create a table for the function g(x) = f(x - 3). x 2 4 6 8 f(x) 1 3 7 11 The formula g(x) = f(x - 3) tells us that the output values of g are the same as the...
body_xml:
A function $$f(x)$$ is given in Table 4. Create a table for the function $$g(x) = f(x - 3).$$ $$x$$ 2 4 6 8 $$f(x)$$ 1 3 7 11
The formula $$g(x) = f(x - 3)$$ tells us that the output values of $$g$$ are the same as the output value of $$f$$ when the input value is 3 less than the original value. For example, we know that $$f(2) = 1.$$ To get the same output from the function $$g,$$ we will need an input value that is 3 larger. We input a value that is 3 larger for $$g(x)$$ because the function takes 3 away before evaluating the function $$f.$$ $$\begin{array}{ccl} {g(5)} & = & {f(5 - 3)} \\ & = & {f(2)} \\ & = & 1 \end{array}$$ We continue with the other values to create Table 5. $$x$$ 5 7 9 11 $$x - 3$$ 2 4 6 8 $$f(x-3)$$ 1 3 7 11 $$g(x)$$ 1 3 7 11
The result is that the function $$g(x)$$ has been shifted to the right by 3. Notice the output values for $$g(x)$$ remain the same as the output values for $$f(x),$$ but the corresponding input values, $$x,$$ have shifted to the right by 3. Specifically, 2 shifted to 5, 4 shifted to 7, 6 shifted to 9, and 8 shifted to 11. Figure 7 represents both of the functions. We can see the horizontal shift in each point.

title: Identifying a Horizontal Shift of a Toolkit Function
snippet: Identifying a Horizontal Shift of a Toolkit Function: Figure 8 represents a transformation of the toolkit function f(x) = x^{2}. Relate this new function g(x) to f(x), and then find a formula for g(x). Notice that the graph is identical in...
body_xml: Figure 8 represents a transformation of the toolkit function $$f(x) = x^{2}.$$ Relate this new function $$g(x)$$ to $$f(x),$$ and then find a formula for $$g(x).$$ Notice that the graph is identical in shape to the $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ function, but the x-values are shifted to the right 2 units. The vertex used to be at (0,0), but now the vertex is at (2,0). The graph is the basic quadratic function shifted 2 units to the right, so $$g(x) = f(x - 2)$$ Notice how we must input the value $$x = 2$$ to get the output value $$y = 0;$$ the x-values must be 2 units larger because of the shift to the right by 2 units. We can then use the definition of the $$f(x)$$ function to write a formula for $$g(x)$$ by evaluating $$f(x - 2).$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} {f(x)} & = & x^{2} \\ {g(x)} & = & {f(x - 2)} \\ {g(x)} & = & {f(x - 2) = {(x - 2)}^{2}} \end{array}$$ To determine whether the shift is $$+ 2$$ or $$- 2$$ , consider a single reference point on the graph. For a quadratic, looking at the vertex point is convenient. In the original function, $$f(0) = 0.$$ In our shifted function, $$g(2) = 0.$$ To obtain the output value of 0 from the function $$f,$$ we need to decide whether a plus or a minus sign will work to satisfy $$g(2) = f(x - 2) = f(0) = 0.$$ For this to work, we will need to subtract 2 units from our input values.

title: Interpreting Horizontal versus Vertical Shifts
snippet: Interpreting Horizontal versus Vertical Shifts: The function G(m) gives the number of gallons of gas required to drive m miles. Interpret G(m) + 10 and G(m + 10). G(m) + 10 can be interpreted as adding 10 to the output, gallons. This is...
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Interpreting Horizontal versus Vertical Shifts">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The function $$G(m)$$ gives the number of gallons of gas required to drive $$m$$ miles. Interpret $$G(m) + 10$$ and $$G(m + 10).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>$$G(m) + 10$$ can be interpreted as adding 10 to the output, gallons. This is the gas required to drive $$m$$ miles, plus another 10 gallons of gas. The graph would indicate a vertical shift.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$G(m + 10)$$ can be interpreted as adding 10 to the input, miles. So this is the number of gallons of gas required to drive 10 miles more than $$m$$ miles. The graph would indicate a horizontal shift.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Graphing Combined Vertical and Horizontal Shifts
snippet: Graphing Combined Vertical and Horizontal Shifts: Given f(x) = |x|, sketch a graph of h(x) = f(x + 1) - 3. The function f is our toolkit absolute value function. We know that this graph has a V shape, with the point at the origin. The...
body_xml: Given $$f(x) = |x|,$$ sketch a graph of $$h(x) = f(x + 1) - 3.$$ The function $$f$$ is our toolkit absolute value function. We know that this graph has a V shape, with the point at the origin. The graph of $$h$$ has transformed $$f$$ in two ways: $$f(x + 1)$$ is a change on the inside of the function, giving a horizontal shift left by 1, and the subtraction by 3 in $$f(x + 1) - 3$$ is a change to the outside of the function, giving a vertical shift down by 3. The transformation of the graph is illustrated in Figure 9. Let us follow one point of the graph of $$f(x) = |x|.$$ The point $$(0,0)$$ is transformed first by shifting left 1 unit: $$(0,0)\rightarrow(-1,0)$$ The point $$(-1,0)$$ is transformed next by shifting down 3 units: $$(-1,0)\rightarrow(-1,-3)$$ Figure 10 shows the graph of $$h.$$

title: Identifying Combined Vertical and Horizontal Shifts
snippet: Identifying Combined Vertical and Horizontal Shifts: Write a formula for the graph shown in Figure 11, which is a transformation of the toolkit square root function. The graph of the toolkit function starts at the origin, so this graph has...
body_xml: Write a formula for the graph shown in Figure 11, which is a transformation of the toolkit square root function. The graph of the toolkit function starts at the origin, so this graph has been shifted 1 to the right and up 2. In function notation, we could write that as $$h(x) = f(x - 1) + 2$$ Using the formula for the square root function, we can write $$h(x) = \sqrt{x - 1} + 2$$ Note that this transformation has changed the domain and range of the function. This new graph has domain $$\lbrack 1,\infty)$$ and range $$\lbrack 2,\infty).$$

title: Reflecting a Graph Horizontally and Vertically
snippet: Reflecting a Graph Horizontally and Vertically: Reflect the graph of s(t) = \sqrt{t} (a) vertically and (b) horizontally. ⓐReflecting the graph vertically means that each output value will be reflected over the horizontal t-axis as shown...
body_xml:
<example number="9" title="Reflecting a Graph Horizontally and Vertically">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Reflect the graph of $$s(t) = \sqrt{t}$$ (a) vertically and (b) horizontally.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐReflecting the graph vertically means that each output value will be reflected over the horizontal t-axis as shown in Figure 13. Figure 13 Vertical reflection of the square root function Because each output value is the opposite of the original output value, we can write $$V(t) = - s(t) \text{or} V(t) = - \sqrt{t}$$ Notice that this is an outside change, or vertical shift, that affects the output $$s(t)$$ values, so the negative sign belongs outside of the function.</item>
        <item>ⓑ Reflecting horizontally means that each input value will be reflected over the vertical axis as shown in Figure 14. Figure 14 Horizontal reflection of the square root function Because each input value is the opposite of the original input value, we can write $$H(t) = s( - t) \text{or} H(t) = \sqrt{- t}$$ Notice that this is an inside change or horizontal change that affects the input values, so the negative sign is on the inside of the function. Note that these transformations can affect the domain and range of the functions. While the original square root function has domain $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ and range $$\lbrack 0,\infty),$$ the vertical reflection gives the $$V(t)$$ function the range $$\left( {- \infty, 0} \right\rbrack$$ and the horizontal reflection gives the $$H(t)$$ function the domain $$\left( {- \infty, 0} \right\rbrack.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Applying a Learning Model Equation
snippet: Applying a Learning Model Equation: A common model for learning has an equation similar to k(t) = - 2^{- t} + 1, where k is the percentage of mastery that can be achieved after t practice sessions. This is a transformation of the function...
body_xml: A common model for learning has an equation similar to $$k(t) = - 2^{- t} + 1,$$ where $$k$$ is the percentage of mastery that can be achieved after $$t$$ practice sessions. This is a transformation of the function $$f(t) = 2^{t}$$ shown in Figure 15. Sketch a graph of $$k(t).$$ This equation combines three transformations into one equation. A horizontal reflection: $$f(-t) = 2^{- t}$$ A vertical reflection: $$- f(-t) = - 2^{- t}$$ A vertical shift: $$- f(-t) + 1 = - 2^{- t} + 1$$ We can sketch a graph by applying these transformations one at a time to the original function. Let us follow two points through each of the three transformations. We will choose the points (0, 1) and (1, 2). First, we apply a horizontal reflection: (0, 1) (–1, 2). Then, we apply a vertical reflection: (0, -1) (-1, –2) Finally, we apply a vertical shift: (0, 0) (-1, -1)). This means that the original points, (0,1) and (1,2) become (0,0) and (-1,-1) after we apply the transformations. In Figure 16, the first graph results from a horizontal reflection. The second results from a vertical reflection. The third results from a vertical shift up 1 unit. As a model for learning, this function would be limited to a domain of $$t \geq 0,$$ with corresponding range $$\lbrack 0,1).$$

    <paragraph>A function is called an odd function if for every input $$x$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = - f( - x)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The graph of an odd function is symmetric about the origin.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given the formula for a function, determine if the function is even, odd, or neither. Determine whether the function satisfies f(x) = f( - x). If it does, it is even. Determine whether the function satisfies f(x) = - f( - x). If it...

<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given the formula for a function, determine if the function is even, odd, or neither.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Determine whether the function satisfies $$f(x) = f( - x).$$ If it does, it is even.</item>
      <item>Determine whether the function satisfies $$f(x) = - f( - x).$$ If it does, it is odd.</item>

title: Determining whether a Function Is Even, Odd, or Neither
snippet: Determining whether a Function Is Even, Odd, or Neither: Is the function f(x) = x^{3} + 2x even, odd, or neither? Without looking at a graph, we can determine whether the function is even or odd by finding formulas for the reflections and...
body_xml: Is the function $$f(x) = x^{3} + 2x$$ even, odd, or neither? Without looking at a graph, we can determine whether the function is even or odd by finding formulas for the reflections and determining if they return us to the original function. Let’s begin with the rule for even functions. $$f( - x) = {( - x)}^{3} + 2( - x) = - x^{3} - 2x$$ This does not return us to the original function, so this function is not even. We can now test the rule for odd functions. $$- f( - x) = - \left( {- x^{3} - 2x} \right) = x^{3} + 2x$$ Because $$- f( - x) = f(x),$$ this is an odd function. Consider the graph of $$f$$ in Figure 18. Notice that the graph is symmetric about the origin. For every point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ on the graph, the corresponding point $$\left( {- x, - y} \right)$$ is also on the graph. For example, (1, 3) is on the graph of $$f,$$ and the corresponding point $$(-1,-3)$$ is also on the graph.

    <list type="unordered">
      <item>If $$a > 1,$$ then the graph will be stretched.</item>
      <item>If $$0 < a < 1,$$ then the graph will be compressed.</item>
      <item>If $$a < 0,$$ then there will be combination of a vertical stretch or compression with a vertical reflection.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Graphing a Vertical Stretch
snippet: Graphing a Vertical Stretch: A function P(t) models the population of fruit flies. The graph is shown in Figure 20. A scientist is comparing this population to another population, Q, whose growth follows the same pattern, but is twice as...
body_xml: A function $$P(t)$$ models the population of fruit flies. The graph is shown in Figure 20. A scientist is comparing this population to another population, $$Q,$$ whose growth follows the same pattern, but is twice as large. Sketch a graph of this population. Because the population is always twice as large, the new population’s output values are always twice the original function’s output values. Graphically, this is shown in Figure 21. If we choose four reference points, (0, 1), (3, 3), (6, 2) and (7, 0) we will multiply all of the outputs by 2. The following shows where the new points for the new graph will be located. $$\begin{array}{l} {\left( {0, 1} \right)\rightarrow\left( {0, 2} \right)} \\ {\left( {3, 3} \right)\rightarrow\left( {3, 6} \right)} \\ {\left( {6, 2} \right)\rightarrow\left( {6, 4} \right)} \\ {\left( {7, 0} \right)\rightarrow\left( {7, 0} \right)} \end{array}$$ Symbolically, the relationship is written as $$Q(t) = 2P(t)$$ This means that for any input $$t,$$ the value of the function $$Q$$ is twice the value of the function $$P.$$ Notice that the effect on the graph is a vertical stretching of the graph, where every point doubles its distance from the horizontal axis. The input values, $$t,$$ stay the same while the output values are twice as large as before.

title: Finding a Vertical Compression of a Tabular Function
snippet: Finding a Vertical Compression of a Tabular Function: A function f is given as Table 10. Create a table for the function g(x) = \frac{1}{2}f(x). x 2 4 6 8 f(x) 1 3 7 11 The formula g(x) = \frac{1}{2}f(x) tells us that the output values of...
body_xml:
A function $$f$$ is given as Table 10. Create a table for the function $$g(x) = \frac{1}{2}f(x).$$ $$x$$ 2 4 6 8 $$f(x)$$ 1 3 7 11
The formula $$g(x) = \frac{1}{2}f(x)$$ tells us that the output values of $$g$$ are half of the output values of $$f$$ with the same inputs. For example, we know that $$f(4) = 3.$$ Then $$g(4) = \frac{1}{2}f(4) = \frac{1}{2}(3) = \frac{3}{2}$$ We do the same for the other values to produce Table 11. $$x$$ $$2$$ $$4$$ $$6$$ $$8$$ $$g(x)$$ $$\frac{1}{2}$$ $$\frac{3}{2}$$ $$\frac{7}{2}$$ $$\frac{11}{2}$$
The result is that the function $$g(x)$$ has been compressed vertically by $$\frac{1}{2}.$$ Each output value is divided in half, so the graph is half the original height.

title: Recognizing a Vertical Stretch
snippet: Recognizing a Vertical Stretch: The graph in Figure 22 is a transformation of the toolkit function f(x) = x^{3}. Relate this new function g(x) to f(x), and then find a formula for g(x). When trying to determine a vertical stretch or shift,...
body_xml: The graph in Figure 22 is a transformation of the toolkit function $$f(x) = x^{3}.$$ Relate this new function $$g(x)$$ to $$f(x),$$ and then find a formula for $$g(x).$$ When trying to determine a vertical stretch or shift, it is helpful to look for a point on the graph that is relatively clear. In this graph, it appears that $$g(2) = 2.$$ With the basic cubic function at the same input, $$f(2) = 2^{3} = 8.$$ Based on that, it appears that the outputs of $$g$$ are $$\frac{1}{4}$$ the outputs of the function $$f$$ because $$g(2) = \frac{1}{4}f(2).$$ From this we can fairly safely conclude that $$g(x) = \frac{1}{4}f(x).$$ We can write a formula for $$g$$ by using the definition of the function $$f.$$ $$g(x) = \frac{1}{4}f(x) = \frac{1}{4}x^{3}$$

title: Graphing a Horizontal Compression
snippet: Graphing a Horizontal Compression: Suppose a scientist is comparing a population of fruit flies to a population that progresses through its lifespan twice as fast as the original population. In other words, this new population, R, will...
body_xml: Suppose a scientist is comparing a population of fruit flies to a population that progresses through its lifespan twice as fast as the original population. In other words, this new population, $$R,$$ will progress in 1 hour the same amount as the original population does in 2 hours, and in 2 hours, it will progress as much as the original population does in 4 hours. Sketch a graph of this population. Symbolically, we could write $$\begin{array}{rcl} {R(1)} & = & {P(2),} \\ {R(2)} & = & {P(4), \text{and in general,} } \\ {R(t)} & = & {P(2t).} \end{array}$$ See Figure 24 for a graphical comparison of the original population and the compressed population. Note that the effect on the graph is a horizontal compression where all input values are half of their original distance from the vertical axis.

title: Finding a Horizontal Stretch for a Tabular Function
snippet: Finding a Horizontal Stretch for a Tabular Function: A function f(x) is given as Table 13. Create a table for the function g(x) = f\left( {\frac{1}{2}x} \right). x 2 4 6 8 f(x) 1 3 7 11 The formula g(x) = f\left( {\frac{1}{2}x} \right)...
body_xml:
A function $$f(x)$$ is given as Table 13. Create a table for the function $$g(x) = f\left( {\frac{1}{2}x} \right).$$ $$x$$ 2 4 6 8 $$f(x)$$ 1 3 7 11
The formula $$g(x) = f\left( {\frac{1}{2}x} \right)$$ tells us that the output values for $$g$$ are the same as the output values for the function $$f$$ at an input half the size. Notice that we do not have enough information to determine $$g(2)$$ because $$g(2) = f\left( {\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2} \right) = f(1),$$ and we do not have a value for $$f(1)$$ in our table. Our input values to $$g$$ will need to be twice as large to get inputs for $$f$$ that we can evaluate. For example, we can determine $$g(4).$$ $$g(4) = f\left( {\frac{1}{2} \cdot 4} \right) = f(2) = 1$$ We do the same for the other values to produce Table 14. $$x$$ 4 8 12 16 $$g(x)$$ 1 3 7 11
Figure 25 shows the graphs of both of these sets of points. Because each input value has been doubled, the result is that the function $$g(x)$$ has been stretched horizontally by a factor of 2.

title: Recognizing a Horizontal Compression on a Graph
snippet: Recognizing a Horizontal Compression on a Graph: Relate the function g(x) to f(x) in Figure 26. The graph of g(x) looks like the graph of f(x) horizontally compressed. Because f(x) ends at (6,4) and g(x) ends at (2,4), we can see that the...
body_xml: Relate the function $$g(x)$$ to $$f(x)$$ in Figure 26. The graph of $$g(x)$$ looks like the graph of $$f(x)$$ horizontally compressed. Because $$f(x)$$ ends at $$(6,4)$$ and $$g(x)$$ ends at $$(2,4),$$ we can see that the $$x-$$ values have been compressed by $$\frac{1}{3},$$ because $$6\left( \frac{1}{3} \right) = 2.$$ We might also notice that $$g(2) = f(6)$$ and $$g(1) = f(3).$$ Either way, we can describe this relationship as $$g(x) = f\left( {3x} \right).$$ This is a horizontal compression by $$\frac{1}{3}.$$ Notice that the coefficient needed for a horizontal stretch or compression is the reciprocal of the stretch or compression. So to stretch the graph horizontally by a scale factor of 4, we need a coefficient of $$\frac{1}{4}$$ in our function: $$f\left( {\frac{1}{4}x} \right).$$ This means that the input values must be four times larger to produce the same result, requiring the input to be larger, causing the horizontal stretching.

title: Combining Transformations
snippet: Combining Transformations: When combining vertical transformations written in the form af(x) + k, first vertically stretch by a and then vertically shift by k. When combining horizontal transformations written in the form f(bx - h), first...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Combining Transformations" title="Combining Transformations">
    <paragraph>When combining vertical transformations written in the form $$af(x) + k,$$ first vertically stretch by $$a$$ and then vertically shift by $$k.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>When combining horizontal transformations written in the form $$f(bx - h),$$ first horizontally shift by $$h$$ and then horizontally stretch by $$1b.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>When combining horizontal transformations written in the form $$f(b(x - h)),$$ first horizontally stretch by $$\frac{1}{b}$$ and then horizontally shift by $$h.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Horizontal and vertical transformations are independent. It does not matter whether horizontal or vertical transformations are performed first.</paragraph>
  </note>

There are three steps to this transformation, and we will work from the inside out. Starting with the horizontal transformations, $$f(3x)$$ is a horizontal compression by $$\frac{1}{3},$$ which means we multiply each $$x-$$ value by $$\frac{1}{3}.$$ See Table 16. $$x$$ 2 4 6 8 $$f(3x)$$ 10 14 15 17
Looking now to the vertical transformations, we start with the vertical stretch, which will multiply the output values by 2. We apply this to the previous transformation. See Table 17. $$x$$ 2 4 6 8 $$2f(3x)$$ 20 28 30 34
Finally, we can apply the vertical shift, which will add 1 to all the output values. See Table 18. $$x$$ 2 4 6 8 $$g(x) = 2f(3x) + 1$$ 21 29 31 35

Remember that twice the size of 0 is still 0, so the point (0,2) remains at (0,2) while the point (2,0) will stretch to (4,0). See Figure 28. title: Using Absolute Value to Determine Resistance
snippet: Using Absolute Value to Determine Resistance: Electrical parts, such as resistors and capacitors, come with specified values of their operating parameters: resistance, capacitance, etc. However, due to imprecision in manufacturing, the...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Using Absolute Value to Determine Resistance">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Electrical parts, such as resistors and capacitors, come with specified values of their operating parameters: resistance, capacitance, etc. However, due to imprecision in manufacturing, the actual values of these parameters vary somewhat from piece to piece, even when they are supposed to be the same. The best that manufacturers can do is to try to guarantee that the variations will stay within a specified range, often $$\text{±1\%,} \pm \text{5\%,}$$ or $$\pm \text{10\%} .$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Suppose we have a resistor rated at 680 ohms, $$\pm 5\%.$$ Use the absolute value function to express the range of possible values of the actual resistance.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We can find that 5% of 680 ohms is 34 ohms. The absolute value of the difference between the actual and nominal resistance should not exceed the stated variability, so, with the resistance $$R$$ in ohms,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left| R - 680 \middle| \leq 34 \right.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Writing an Equation for an Absolute Value Function Given a Graph
snippet: Writing an Equation for an Absolute Value Function Given a Graph: Write an equation for the function graphed in Figure 4. The basic absolute value function changes direction at the origin, so this graph has been shifted to the right 3...
body_xml: Write an equation for the function graphed in Figure 4. The basic absolute value function changes direction at the origin, so this graph has been shifted to the right 3 units and down 2 units from the basic toolkit function. See Figure 5. We also notice that the graph appears vertically stretched, because the width of the final graph on a horizontal line is not equal to 2 times the vertical distance from the corner to this line, as it would be for an unstretched absolute value function. Instead, the width is equal to 1 times the vertical distance as shown in Figure 6. From this information we can write the equation $$\begin{array}{rcll} {f(x)} & = & \left. 2 \middle| x - 3 \middle| - 2, \right. & { \text{treating the stretch as} a \text{vertical stretch,or} } \\ {f(x)} & = & \left| 2(x - 3) \middle| - 2, \right. & { \text{treating the stretch as} a \text{horizontal compression} .} \end{array}$$ Note that these equations are algebraically equivalent—the stretch for an absolute value function can be written interchangeably as a vertical or horizontal stretch or compression. Note also that if the vertical stretch factor is negative, there is also a reflection about the x-axis.

title: Finding the Zeros of an Absolute Value Function
snippet: Finding the Zeros of an Absolute Value Function: For the function \left. f(x) = \middle| 4x + 1 \middle| - 7, \right. find the values of x such that f(x) = 0. \begin{matrix} 0 & = & \left| 4x + 1 \middle| - 7 \right. & & & & & {...
body_xml: For the function $$\left. f(x) = \middle| 4x + 1 \middle| - 7, \right.$$ find the values of $$x$$ such that $$f(x) = 0.$$ $$\begin{matrix} 0 & = & \left| 4x + 1 \middle| - 7 \right. & & & & & { \text{Substitute 0 for} f(x).} \\ 7 & = & |4x + 1| & & & & & { \text{Isolate the absolute value on one side of the equation} .} \\ & & & & & & & \\ & & & & & & & \\ & & & & & & & \\ 7 & = & {4x + 1} & \text{or} & { -7} & = & {4x + 1} & { \text{Break into two separate equations and solve} .} \\ 6 & = & {4x} & & -8 & = & {4x} & \\ & & & & & & & \\ x & = & {\frac{6}{4} = 1.5} & & x & = & {\frac{- 8}{4} = - 2} & \end{matrix}$$ The function outputs 0 when $$x = \frac{3}{2}$$ or $$x = - 2.$$ See Figure 8.

title: Inverse Function
snippet: Inverse Function: For any one-to-one function f(x) = y, a function f^{- 1}(x) is an inverse function of f if f^{- 1}(y) = x. This can also be written as f^{- 1}(f(x)) = x for all x in the domain of f. It also follows that f(f^{- 1}(x)) = x...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Inverse Function" title="Inverse Function">
    <paragraph>For any one-to-one function $$f(x) = y,$$ a function $$f^{- 1}(x)$$ is an inverse function of $$f$$ if $$f^{- 1}(y) = x.$$ This can also be written as $$f^{- 1}(f(x)) = x$$ for all $$x$$ in the domain of $$f.$$ It also follows that $$f(f^{- 1}(x)) = x$$ for all $$x$$ in the domain of $$f^{- 1}$$ if $$f^{- 1}$$ is the inverse of $$f.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The notation $$f^{- 1}$$ is read $$\text{“} f$$ inverse.” Like any other function, we can use any variable name as the input for $$f^{- 1},$$ so we will often write $$f^{- 1}(x),$$ which we read as $$``f$$ inverse of $$x."$$ Keep in mind that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f^{- 1}(x) \neq \frac{1}{f(x)}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and not all functions have inverses.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Identifying an Inverse Function for a Given Input-Output Pair
snippet: Identifying an Inverse Function for a Given Input-Output Pair: If for a particular one-to-one function f(2) = 4 and f(5) = 12, what are the corresponding input and output values for the inverse function? The inverse function reverses the...
body_xml: If for a particular one-to-one function $$f(2) = 4$$ and $$f(5) = 12,$$ what are the corresponding input and output values for the inverse function? The inverse function reverses the input and output quantities, so if $$\begin{array}{rcl} {f(2)} & = & {4, \text{then} f^{-1}(4) = 2;} \\ {f(5)} & = & {12,{ \text{then f} }^{-1}(12) = 5.} \end{array}$$ Alternatively, if we want to name the inverse function $$g,$$ then $$g(4) = 2$$ and $$g(12) = 5.$$ Notice that if we show the coordinate pairs in a table form, the input and output are clearly reversed. See Table 1. $$\left( {x,f(x)} \right)$$ $$\left( {x,g(x)} \right)$$ $$\left( {2,4} \right)$$ $$\left( {4,2} \right)$$ $$\left( {5,12} \right)$$ $$\left( {12,5} \right)$$

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given two functions f(x) and g(x), test whether the functions are inverses of each other. Determine whether f(g(x)) = x or g(f(x)) = x. If both statements are true, then g = f^{- 1} and f = g^{- 1}. If either statement is false,...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given two functions $$f(x)$$ and $$g(x),$$ test whether the functions are inverses of each other.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Determine whether $$f(g(x)) = x$$ or $$g(f(x)) = x.$$</item>
      <item>If both statements are true, then $$g = f^{- 1}$$ and $$f = g^{- 1}.$$ If either statement is false, then both are false, and $$g \neq f^{- 1}$$ and $$f \neq g^{- 1}.$$</item>

title: Testing Inverse Relationships Algebraically
snippet: Testing Inverse Relationships Algebraically: If f(x) = \frac{1}{x + 2} and g(x) = \frac{1}{x} - 2, is g = f^{- 1}? \begin{array}{ccl} {g(f(x))} & = & {\frac{1}{\left( \frac{1}{x + 2} \right)} - 2} \\ & = & {x + 2 - 2} \\ & = & x...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Testing Inverse Relationships Algebraically">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>If $$f(x) = \frac{1}{x + 2}$$ and $$g(x) = \frac{1}{x} - 2,$$ is $$g = f^{- 1}?$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} {g(f(x))} & = & {\frac{1}{\left( \frac{1}{x + 2} \right)} - 2} \\ & = & {x + 2 - 2} \\ & = & x \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We must also verify the other formula.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} {f(g(x))} & = & \frac{1}{\frac{1}{x} - 2 + 2} \\ & = & \frac{1}{\frac{1}{x}} \\ & = & x \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>so</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$g = f^{- 1} \text{and} f = g^{- 1}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>Notice the inverse operations are in reverse order of the operations from the original function.</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="3" title="Determining Inverse Relationships for Power Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>If $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ (the cube function) and $$g(x) = \frac{1}{3}x,$$ is $$g = f^{- 1}?$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {g(x)} \right) = \frac{x^{3}}{27} \neq x$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>No, the functions are not inverses.</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>The correct inverse to the cube is, of course, the cube root $$\sqrt[3]{x} = x^{\frac{1}{3}},$$ that is, the one-third is an exponent, not a multiplier.</paragraph>
  </example>
