title: Finding the Domain of a Rational Function
snippet: Finding the Domain of a Rational Function: Find the domain of f(x) = \frac{x + 3}{x^{2} - 9}. Begin by setting the denominator equal to zero and solving. \begin{array}{rcl} {x^{2} - 9} & = & 0 \\ x^{2} & = & 9 \\ x & = & \pm 3 \end{array}...
body_xml: Find the domain of $$f(x) = \frac{x + 3}{x^{2} - 9}.$$ Begin by setting the denominator equal to zero and solving. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {x^{2} - 9} & = & 0 \\ x^{2} & = & 9 \\ x & = & \pm 3 \end{array}$$ The denominator is equal to zero when $$x = \pm 3.$$ The domain of the function is all real numbers except $$x = \pm 3.$$ A graph of this function, as shown in Figure 8, confirms that the function is not defined when $$x = \pm 3.$$ There is a vertical asymptote at $$x = 3$$ and a hole in the graph at $$x = -3.$$ We will discuss these types of holes in greater detail later in this section.

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given a rational function, identify any vertical asymptotes of its graph. Factor the numerator and denominator. Note any restrictions in the domain of the function. Reduce the expression by canceling common factors in the numerator...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given a rational function, identify any vertical asymptotes of its graph.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Factor the numerator and denominator.</item>
      <item>Note any restrictions in the domain of the function.</item>
      <item>Reduce the expression by canceling common factors in the numerator and the denominator.</item>
      <item>Note any values that cause the denominator to be zero in this simplified version. These are where the vertical asymptotes occur.</item>
      <item>Note any restrictions in the domain where asymptotes do not occur. These are removable discontinuities, or “holes.”</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Identifying Vertical Asymptotes
snippet: Identifying Vertical Asymptotes: Find the vertical asymptotes of the graph of k(x) = \frac{5 + 2x^{2}}{2 - x - x^{2}}. First, factor the numerator and denominator. \begin{array}{ccl} {k(x)} & = & \frac{5 + 2x^{2}}{2 - x - x^{2}} \\ & = &...
body_xml: Find the vertical asymptotes of the graph of $$k(x) = \frac{5 + 2x^{2}}{2 - x - x^{2}}.$$ First, factor the numerator and denominator. $$\begin{array}{ccl} {k(x)} & = & \frac{5 + 2x^{2}}{2 - x - x^{2}} \\ & = & \frac{5 + 2x^{2}}{(2 + x)(1 - x)} \end{array}$$ To find the vertical asymptotes, we determine where this function will be undefined by setting the denominator equal to zero: $$\begin{array}{rcl} {(2 + x)(1 - x)} & = & 0 \\ x & = & {-2,1} \end{array}$$ Neither $$x = -2$$ nor $$x = 1$$ are zeros of the numerator, so the two values indicate two vertical asymptotes. The graph in Figure 9 confirms the location of the two vertical asymptotes.

title: Removable Discontinuities of Rational Functions
snippet: Removable Discontinuities of Rational Functions: A removable discontinuity occurs in the graph of a rational function at x = a if a is a zero for a factor in the denominator that is common with a factor in the numerator. We factor the...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Removable Discontinuities of Rational Functions" title="Removable Discontinuities of Rational Functions">
    <paragraph>A removable discontinuity occurs in the graph of a rational function at $$x = a$$ if $$a$$ is a zero for a factor in the denominator that is common with a factor in the numerator. We factor the numerator and denominator and check for common factors. If we find any, we set the common factor equal to 0 and solve. This is the location of the removable discontinuity. This is true if the multiplicity of this factor is greater than or equal to that in the denominator. If the multiplicity of this factor is greater in the denominator, then there is still an asymptote at that value.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Identifying Vertical Asymptotes and Removable Discontinuities for a Graph
snippet: Identifying Vertical Asymptotes and Removable Discontinuities for a Graph: Find the vertical asymptotes and removable discontinuities of the graph of k(x) = \frac{x - 2}{x^{2} - 4}. Factor the numerator and the denominator. k(x) = \frac{x...
body_xml: Find the vertical asymptotes and removable discontinuities of the graph of $$k(x) = \frac{x - 2}{x^{2} - 4}.$$ Factor the numerator and the denominator. $$k(x) = \frac{x - 2}{(x - 2)(x + 2)}$$ Notice that there is a common factor in the numerator and the denominator, $$x-2.$$ The zero for this factor is $$x = 2.$$ This is the location of the removable discontinuity. Notice that there is a factor in the denominator that is not in the numerator, $$x + 2.$$ The zero for this factor is $$x = -2.$$ The vertical asymptote is $$x = -2.$$ See Figure 11. The graph of this function will have the vertical asymptote at $$x = -2,$$ but at $$x = 2$$ the graph will have a hole.

title: Horizontal Asymptotes of Rational Functions
snippet: Horizontal Asymptotes of Rational Functions: The horizontal asymptote of a rational function can be determined by looking at the degrees of the numerator and denominator. Degree of numerator is less than degree of denominator: horizontal...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Horizontal Asymptotes of Rational Functions" title="Horizontal Asymptotes of Rational Functions">
    <paragraph>The horizontal asymptote of a rational function can be determined by looking at the degrees of the numerator and denominator.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>Degree of numerator is less than degree of denominator: horizontal asymptote at $$y = 0.$$</item>
      <item>Degree of numerator is greater than degree of denominator by one: no horizontal asymptote; slant asymptote.</item>
      <item>Degree of numerator is equal to degree of denominator: horizontal asymptote at ratio of leading coefficients.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Identifying Horizontal and Slant Asymptotes
snippet: Identifying Horizontal and Slant Asymptotes: For the functions listed, identify the horizontal or slant asymptote. ⓐ g(x) = \frac{6x^{3} - 10x}{2x^{3} + 5x^{2}} ⓑ h(x) = \frac{x^{2} - 4x + 1}{x + 2} ⓒ k(x) = \frac{x^{2} + 4x}{x^{3} - 8}...
body_xml:
<example number="7" title="Identifying Horizontal and Slant Asymptotes">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For the functions listed, identify the horizontal or slant asymptote.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$g(x) = \frac{6x^{3} - 10x}{2x^{3} + 5x^{2}}$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$h(x) = \frac{x^{2} - 4x + 1}{x + 2}$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$k(x) = \frac{x^{2} + 4x}{x^{3} - 8}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>For these solutions, we will use $$f(x) = \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}, q(x) \neq 0.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$g(x) = \frac{6x^{3} - 10x}{2x^{3} + 5x^{2}}:$$ The degree of $$p = \text{degree of} q = 3,$$ so we can find the horizontal asymptote by taking the ratio of the leading terms. There is a horizontal asymptote at $$y = \frac{6}{2}$$ or $$y = 3.$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$h(x) = \frac{x^{2} - 4x + 1}{x + 2}:$$ The degree of $$p = 2$$ and degree of $$q = 1.$$ Since $$p > q$$ by 1, there is a slant asymptote found at $$\frac{x^{2} - 4x + 1}{x + 2}.$$ The quotient is $$x-6$$ and the remainder is 13. There is a slant asymptote at $$y = x-6.$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$k(x) = \frac{x^{2} + 4x}{x^{3} - 8}:$$ The degree of $$p = 2 <$$ degree of $$q = 3,$$ so there is a horizontal asymptote $$y = 0.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Identifying Horizontal Asymptotes
snippet: Identifying Horizontal Asymptotes: In the sugar concentration problem earlier, we created the equation C(t) = \frac{5 + t}{100 + 10t}. Find the horizontal asymptote and interpret it in context of the problem. Both the numerator and...
body_xml:
<example number="8" title="Identifying Horizontal Asymptotes">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>In the sugar concentration problem earlier, we created the equation $$C(t) = \frac{5 + t}{100 + 10t}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Find the horizontal asymptote and interpret it in context of the problem.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Both the numerator and denominator are linear (degree 1). Because the degrees are equal, there will be a horizontal asymptote at the ratio of the leading coefficients. In the numerator, the leading term is $$t,$$ with coefficient 1. In the denominator, the leading term is $$10t,$$ with coefficient 10. The horizontal asymptote will be at the ratio of these values:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$t\rightarrow\infty, C(t)\rightarrow\frac{1}{10}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This function will have a horizontal asymptote at $$y = \frac{1}{10}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This tells us that as the values of t increase, the values of $$C$$ will approach $$\frac{1}{10}.$$ In context, this means that, as more time goes by, the concentration of sugar in the tank will approach one-tenth of a pound of sugar per gallon of water or $$\frac{1}{10}$$ pounds per gallon.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Identifying Horizontal and Vertical Asymptotes
snippet: Identifying Horizontal and Vertical Asymptotes: Find the horizontal and vertical asymptotes of the function f(x) = \frac{(x - 2)(x + 3)}{(x - 1)(x + 2)(x - 5)} First, note that this function has no common factors, so there are no potential...
body_xml: Find the horizontal and vertical asymptotes of the function $$f(x) = \frac{(x - 2)(x + 3)}{(x - 1)(x + 2)(x - 5)}$$ First, note that this function has no common factors, so there are no potential removable discontinuities. The function will have vertical asymptotes when the denominator is zero, causing the function to be undefined. The denominator will be zero at $$x = 1,-2, \text{and} 5,$$ indicating vertical asymptotes at these values. The numerator has degree 2, while the denominator has degree 3. Since the degree of the denominator is greater than the degree of the numerator, the denominator will grow faster than the numerator, causing the outputs to tend towards zero as the inputs get large, and so as $$x\rightarrow \pm \infty, f(x)\rightarrow 0.$$ This function will have a horizontal asymptote at $$y = 0.$$ See Figure 15.

title: Intercepts of Rational Functions
snippet: Intercepts of Rational Functions: A rational function will have a y-intercept at f(0) , if the function is defined at zero. A rational function will not have a y-intercept if the function is not defined at zero. Likewise, a rational...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Intercepts of Rational Functions" title="Intercepts of Rational Functions">
    <paragraph>A rational function will have a y-intercept at $$f(0)$$ , if the function is defined at zero. A rational function will not have a y-intercept if the function is not defined at zero.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Likewise, a rational function will have x-intercepts at the inputs that cause the output to be zero. Since a fraction is only equal to zero when the numerator is zero, x-intercepts can only occur when the numerator of the rational function is equal to zero.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding the Intercepts of a Rational Function
snippet: Finding the Intercepts of a Rational Function: Find the intercepts of f(x) = \frac{(x - 2)(x + 3)}{(x - 1)(x + 2)(x - 5)}. We can find the y-intercept by evaluating the function at zero \begin{array}{ccl} {f(0)} & = & \frac{(0 - 2)(0 +...
body_xml: Find the intercepts of $$f(x) = \frac{(x - 2)(x + 3)}{(x - 1)(x + 2)(x - 5)}.$$ We can find the y-intercept by evaluating the function at zero $$\begin{array}{ccl} {f(0)} & = & \frac{(0 - 2)(0 + 3)}{(0 - 1)(0 + 2)(0 - 5)} \\ & = & \frac{- 6}{10} \\ & = & {- \frac{3}{5}} \\ & = & -0.6 \end{array}$$ The x-intercepts will occur when the function is equal to zero: $$\begin{array}{rclc} 0 & = & \frac{(x - 2)(x + 3)}{(x - 1)(x + 2)(x - 5)} & { \text{This is zero when the numerator is zero} .} \\ 0 & = & {(x - 2)(x + 3)} & \\ x & = & {2,-3} & \end{array}$$ The y-intercept is $$(0,-0.6),$$ the x-intercepts are $$(2,0)$$ and $$(-3,0).$$ See Figure 16.

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given a rational function, sketch a graph. Evaluate the function at 0 to find the y-intercept. Factor the numerator and denominator. For factors in the numerator not common to the denominator, determine where each factor of the...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given a rational function, sketch a graph.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Evaluate the function at 0 to find the y-intercept.</item>
      <item>Factor the numerator and denominator.</item>
      <item>For factors in the numerator not common to the denominator, determine where each factor of the numerator is zero to find the x-intercepts.</item>
      <item>Find the multiplicities of the x-intercepts to determine the behavior of the graph at those points.</item>
      <item>For factors in the denominator, note the multiplicities of the zeros to determine the local behavior. For those factors not common to the numerator, find the vertical asymptotes by setting those factors equal to zero and then solve.</item>
      <item>For factors in the denominator common to factors in the numerator, find the removable discontinuities by setting those factors equal to 0 and then solve.</item>
      <item>Compare the degrees of the numerator and the denominator to determine the horizontal or slant asymptotes.</item>
      <item>Sketch the graph.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Graphing a Rational Function
snippet: Graphing a Rational Function: Sketch a graph of f(x) = \frac{(x + 2)(x - 3)}{{(x + 1)}^{2}(x - 2)}. We can start by noting that the function is already factored, saving us a step. Next, we will find the intercepts. Evaluating the function...
body_xml: Sketch a graph of $$f(x) = \frac{(x + 2)(x - 3)}{{(x + 1)}^{2}(x - 2)}.$$ We can start by noting that the function is already factored, saving us a step. Next, we will find the intercepts. Evaluating the function at zero gives the y-intercept: $$\begin{array}{ccl} {f(0)} & = & \frac{(0 + 2)(0 - 3)}{{(0 + 1)}^{2}(0 - 2)} \\ & = & 3 \end{array}$$ To find the x-intercepts, we determine when the numerator of the function is zero. Setting each factor equal to zero, we find x-intercepts at $$x = -2$$ and $$x = 3.$$ At each, the behavior will be linear (multiplicity 1), with the graph passing through the intercept. We have a y-intercept at $$(0,3)$$ and x-intercepts at $$(-2,0)$$ and $$(3,0).$$ To find the vertical asymptotes, we determine when the denominator is equal to zero. This occurs when $$x + 1 = 0$$ and when $$x-2 = 0,$$ giving us vertical asymptotes at $$x = -1$$ and $$x = 2.$$ There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator. This means there are no removable discontinuities. Finally, the degree of denominator is larger than the degree of the numerator, telling us this graph has a horizontal asymptote at $$y = 0.$$ To sketch the graph, we might start by plotting the three intercepts. Since the graph has no x-intercepts between the vertical asymptotes, and the y-intercept is positive, we know the function must remain positive between the asymptotes, letting us fill in the middle portion of the graph as shown in Figure 20. The factor associated with the vertical asymptote at $$x = -1$$ was squared, so we know the behavior will be the same on both sides of the asymptote. The graph heads toward positive infinity as the inputs approach the asymptote on the right, so the graph will head toward positive infinity on the left as well. For the vertical asymptote at $$x = 2,$$ the factor was not squared, so the graph will have opposite behavior on either side of the asymptote. See Figure 21. After passing through the x-intercepts, the graph will then level off toward an output of zero, as indicated by the horizontal asymptote.

title: Writing Rational Functions from Intercepts and Asymptotes
source_type: Writing Rational Functions from Intercepts and Asymptotes
snippet: Writing Rational Functions from Intercepts and Asymptotes: If a rational function has x-intercepts at x = x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}, vertical asymptotes at x = v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{m}, and no x_{i} = \text{any} v_{j}, then the function can be...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Writing Rational Functions from Intercepts and Asymptotes" title="Writing Rational Functions from Intercepts and Asymptotes">
    <paragraph>If a rational function has x-intercepts at $$x = x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n},$$ vertical asymptotes at $$x = v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{m},$$ and no $$x_{i} = \text{any} v_{j},$$ then the function can be written in the form:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = a\frac{{(x - x_{1})}^{p_{1}}{(x - x_{2})}^{p_{2}}\cdots{(x - x_{n})}^{p_{n}}}{{(x - v_{1})}^{q_{1}}{(x - v_{2})}^{q_{2}}\cdots{(x - v_{m})}^{q_{n}}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where the powers $$p_{i}$$ or $$q_{i}$$ on each factor can be determined by the behavior of the graph at the corresponding intercept or asymptote, and the stretch factor $$a$$ can be determined given a value of the function other than the x-intercept or by the horizontal asymptote if it is nonzero.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given a graph of a rational function, write the function. Determine the factors of the numerator. Examine the behavior of the graph at the x-intercepts to determine the zeroes and their multiplicities. (This is easy to do when...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given a graph of a rational function, write the function.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Determine the factors of the numerator. Examine the behavior of the graph at the x-intercepts to determine the zeroes and their multiplicities. (This is easy to do when finding the “simplest” function with small multiplicities—such as 1 or 3—but may be difficult for larger multiplicities—such as 5 or 7, for example.)</item>
      <item>Determine the factors of the denominator. Examine the behavior on both sides of each vertical asymptote to determine the factors and their powers.</item>
      <item>Use any clear point on the graph to find the stretch factor.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Writing a Rational Function from Intercepts and Asymptotes
snippet: Writing a Rational Function from Intercepts and Asymptotes: Write an equation for the rational function shown in Figure 22. The graph appears to have x-intercepts at x = -2 and x = 3. At both, the graph passes through the intercept,...
body_xml: Write an equation for the rational function shown in Figure 22. The graph appears to have x-intercepts at $$x = -2$$ and $$x = 3.$$ At both, the graph passes through the intercept, suggesting linear factors. The graph has two vertical asymptotes. The one at $$x = -1$$ seems to exhibit the basic behavior similar to $$\frac{1}{x},$$ with the graph heading toward positive infinity on one side and heading toward negative infinity on the other. The asymptote at $$x = 2$$ is exhibiting a behavior similar to $$\frac{1}{x^{2}},$$ with the graph heading toward negative infinity on both sides of the asymptote. See Figure 23. We can use this information to write a function of the form $$f(x) = a\frac{(x + 2)(x - 3)}{(x + 1){(x - 2)}^{2}}$$ To find the stretch factor, we can use another clear point on the graph, such as the y-intercept $$(0,-2).$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} -2 & = & {a\frac{(0 + 2)(0 - 3)}{(0 + 1){(0 - 2)}^{2}}} \\ -2 & = & {a\frac{- 6}{4}} \\ a & = & {\frac{- 8}{- 6} = \frac{4}{3}} \end{array}$$ This gives us a final function of $$f(x) = \frac{4(x + 2)(x - 3)}{3(x + 1){(x - 2)}^{2}}.$$

title: Verifying Two Functions Are Inverses of One Another

snippet: Verifying Two Functions Are Inverses of One Another: Two functions, f and g, are inverses of one another if for all x in the domain of f and g. g\left( {f(x)} \right) = f\left( {g(x)} \right) = x
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Verifying Two Functions Are Inverses of One Another" title="Verifying Two Functions Are Inverses of One Another">
    <paragraph>Two functions, $$f$$ and $$g,$$ are inverses of one another if for all $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ and $$g.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$g\left( {f(x)} \right) = f\left( {g(x)} \right) = x$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Verifying Inverse Functions
snippet: Verifying Inverse Functions: Show that f(x) = \frac{1}{x + 1} and f^{- 1}(x) = \frac{1}{x} - 1 are inverses, for x \neq 0,-1 . We must show that f^{- 1}\left( {f(x)} \right) = x and f\left( {f^{- 1}(x)} \right) = x. \begin{matrix} {f^{-...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Verifying Inverse Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Show that $$f(x) = \frac{1}{x + 1}$$ and $$f^{- 1}(x) = \frac{1}{x} - 1$$ are inverses, for $$x \neq 0,-1$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We must show that $$f^{- 1}\left( {f(x)} \right) = x$$ and $$f\left( {f^{- 1}(x)} \right) = x.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {f^{- 1}(f(x))} & = & {f^{- 1}\left( \frac{1}{x + 1} \right)} \\ & = & {\frac{1}{\frac{1}{x + 1}} - 1} \\ & = & {(x + 1) - 1} \\ & = & x \\ {f(f^{-1}(x))} & = & {f\left( {\frac{1}{x} - 1} \right)} \\ & = & \frac{1}{\left( {\frac{1}{x} - 1} \right) + 1} \\ & = & \frac{1}{\frac{1}{x}} \\ & = & x \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, $$f(x) = \frac{1}{x + 1}$$ and $$f^{- 1}(x) = \frac{1}{x} - 1$$ are inverses.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Inverse of a Cubic Function
snippet: Finding the Inverse of a Cubic Function: Find the inverse of the function f(x) = 5x^{3} + 1. This is a transformation of the basic cubic toolkit function, and based on our knowledge of that function, we know it is one-to-one. Solving for...
body_xml: Find the inverse of the function $$f(x) = 5x^{3} + 1.$$ This is a transformation of the basic cubic toolkit function, and based on our knowledge of that function, we know it is one-to-one. Solving for the inverse by solving for $$x.$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {5x^{3} + 1} \\ x & = & {5y^{3} + 1} \\ {x - 1} & = & {5y^{3}} \\ \frac{x - 1}{5} & = & y^{3} \\ {f^{- 1}(x)} & = & \sqrt[3]{\frac{x - 1}{5}} \end{array}$$ Look at the graph of $$f$$ and $$f^{-1}.$$ Notice that one graph is the reflection of the other about the line $$y = x.$$ This is always the case when graphing a function and its inverse function. Also, since the method involved interchanging $$x$$ and $$y,$$ notice corresponding points. If $$(a,b)$$ is on the graph of $$f,$$ then $$(b,a)$$ is on the graph of $$f^{-1}.$$ Since $$(0,1)$$ is on the graph of $$f,$$ then $$(1,0)$$ is on the graph of $$f^{-1}.$$ Similarly, since $$(1,6)$$ is on the graph of $$f,$$ then $$(6,1)$$ is on the graph of $$f^{-1}.$$ See Figure 4.

title: Restricting the Domain
snippet: Restricting the Domain: If a function is not one-to-one, it cannot have an inverse. If we restrict the domain of the function so that it becomes one-to-one, thus creating a new function, this new function will have an inverse.
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Restricting the Domain" title="Restricting the Domain">
    <paragraph>If a function is not one-to-one, it cannot have an inverse. If we restrict the domain of the function so that it becomes one-to-one, thus creating a new function, this new function will have an inverse.</paragraph>
  </note>

      <item>Replace $$f(x)$$ with $$y.$$</item>
      <item>Interchange $$x$$ and $$y.$$</item>
      <item>Solve for $$y,$$ and rename the function or pair of function $$f^{-1}(x).$$</item>
      <item>Revise the formula for $$f^{-1}(x)$$ by ensuring that the outputs of the inverse function correspond to the restricted domain of the original function.</item>

title: Restricting the Domain to Find the Inverse of a Polynomial Function
snippet: Restricting the Domain to Find the Inverse of a Polynomial Function: Find the inverse function of f: ⓐ f(x) = {(x - 4)}^{2}, x \geq 4 ⓑ f(x) = {(x - 4)}^{2}, x \leq 4 The original function f(x) = {(x - 4)}^{2} is not one-to-one, but the...
body_xml: Find the inverse function of $$f:$$ ⓐ $$f(x) = {(x - 4)}^{2}, x \geq 4$$ ⓑ $$f(x) = {(x - 4)}^{2}, x \leq 4$$ The original function $$f(x) = {(x - 4)}^{2}$$ is not one-to-one, but the function is restricted to a domain of $$x \geq 4$$ or $$x \leq 4$$ on which it is one-to-one. See Figure 5. To find the inverse, start by replacing $$f(x)$$ with the simple variable $$y.$$ $$\begin{array}{rclc} y & = & {(x - 4)}^{2} & { \text{Interchange} x \text{and} y.} \\ x & = & {(y - 4)}^{2} & { \text{Take the square root} .} \\ {\pm \sqrt{x}} & = & {y - 4} & { \text{Add} 4 \text{to both sides} .} \\ {4 \pm \sqrt{x}} & = & y & \end{array}$$ This is not a function as written. We need to examine the restrictions on the domain of the original function to determine the inverse. Since we reversed the roles of $$x$$ and $$y$$ for the original $$f(x),$$ we looked at the domain: the values $$x$$ could assume. When we reversed the roles of $$x$$ and $$y,$$ this gave us the values $$y$$ could assume. For this function, $$x \geq 4,$$ so for the inverse, we should have $$y \geq 4,$$ which is what our inverse function gives. ⓐThe domain of the original function was restricted to $$x \geq 4,$$ so the outputs of the inverse need to be the same, $$f(x) \geq 4,$$ and we must use the + case: $$f^{- 1}(x) = 4 + \sqrt{x}$$ ⓑ The domain of the original function was restricted to $$x \leq 4,$$ so the outputs of the inverse need to be the same, $$f(x) \leq 4,$$ and we must use the – case: $$f^{- 1}(x) = 4 - \sqrt{x}$$ On the graphs in Figure 6, we see the original function graphed on the same set of axes as its inverse function. Notice that together the graphs show symmetry about the line $$y = x.$$ The coordinate pair $$(4, 0)$$ is on the graph of $$f$$ and the coordinate pair $$(0, 4)$$ is on the graph of $$f^{- 1}.$$ For any coordinate pair, if $$\left( {a, b} \right)$$ is on the graph of $$f,$$ then $$\left( {b, a} \right)$$ is on the graph of $$f^{- 1}.$$ Finally, observe that the graph of $$f$$ intersects the graph of $$f^{- 1}$$ on the line $$y = x.$$ Points of intersection for the graphs of $$f$$ and $$f^{- 1}$$ will always lie on the line $$y = x.$$

title: Finding the Inverse of a Quadratic Function When the Restriction Is Not Specified
snippet: Finding the Inverse of a Quadratic Function When the Restriction Is Not Specified: Restrict the domain and then find the inverse of f(x) = {(x - 2)}^{2} - 3. We can see this is a parabola with vertex at (2,-3) that opens upward. Because...
body_xml: Restrict the domain and then find the inverse of $$f(x) = {(x - 2)}^{2} - 3.$$ We can see this is a parabola with vertex at $$(2,-3)$$ that opens upward. Because the graph will be decreasing on one side of the vertex and increasing on the other side, we can restrict this function to a domain on which it will be one-to-one by limiting the domain to $$x \geq 2.$$ To find the inverse, we will use the vertex form of the quadratic. We start by replacing $$f(x)$$ with a simple variable, $$y,$$ then solve for $$x.$$ $$\begin{array}{rclc} y & = & {{(x - 2)}^{2} - 3} & { \text{Interchange} x \text{and} y.} \\ x & = & {{(y - 2)}^{2} - 3} & { \text{Add 3 to both sides} .} \\ {x + 3} & = & {(y - 2)}^{2} & { \text{Take the square root} .} \\ {\pm \sqrt{x + 3}} & = & {y - 2} & { \text{Add 2 to both sides} .} \\ {2 \pm \sqrt{x + 3}} & = & y & { \text{Rename the function} .} \\ {f^{- 1}(x)} & = & {2 \pm \sqrt{x + 3}} & \end{array}$$ Now we need to determine which case to use. Because we restricted our original function to a domain of $$x \geq 2,$$ the outputs of the inverse should be the same, telling us to utilize the + case $$f^{- 1}(x) = 2 + \sqrt{x + 3}$$ If the quadratic had not been given in vertex form, rewriting it into vertex form would be the first step. This way we may easily observe the coordinates of the vertex to help us restrict the domain. Notice that we arbitrarily decided to restrict the domain on $$x \geq 2.$$ We could just have easily opted to restrict the domain on $$x \leq 2,$$ in which case $$f^{- 1}(x) = 2 - \sqrt{x + 3}.$$ Observe the original function graphed on the same set of axes as its inverse function in Figure 7. Notice that both graphs show symmetry about the line $$y = x.$$ The coordinate pair $$\left( {2, - 3} \right)$$ is on the graph of $$f$$ and the coordinate pair $$\left( {- 3, 2} \right)$$ is on the graph of $$f^{- 1}.$$ Observe from the graph of both functions on the same set of axes that $$\text{domain of} f = \text{range of} f^{-1} = \left\lbrack {2,\infty} \right)$$ and $$\text{domain of} f^{-1} = \text{range of} f = \left\lbrack {-3,\infty} \right).$$ Finally, observe that the graph of $$f$$ intersects the graph of $$f^{- 1}$$ along the line $$y = x.$$

title: Finding the Inverse of a Radical Function
snippet: Finding the Inverse of a Radical Function: Restrict the domain of the function f(x) = \sqrt{x - 4} and then find the inverse. Note that the original function has range f(x) \geq 0. Replace f(x) with y, then solve for x. \begin{array}{rclc}...
body_xml: Restrict the domain of the function $$f(x) = \sqrt{x - 4}$$ and then find the inverse. Note that the original function has range $$f(x) \geq 0.$$ Replace $$f(x)$$ with $$y,$$ then solve for $$x.$$ $$\begin{array}{rclc} y & = & \sqrt{x - 4} & { \text{Replace} f(x) \text{with} y.} \\ x & = & \sqrt{y - 4} & { \text{Interchange} x \text{and} y.} \\ x & = & \sqrt{y - 4} & { \text{Square each side} .} \\ x^{2} & = & {y - 4} & { \text{Add 4} .} \\ {x^{2} + 4} & = & y & { \text{Rename the function} f^{- 1}(x).} \\ {f^{- 1}(x)} & = & {x^{2} + 4} & \end{array}$$ Recall that the domain of this function must be limited to the range of the original function. $$f^{- 1}(x) = x^{2} + 4,x \geq 0$$ Notice in Figure 8 that the inverse is a reflection of the original function over the line $$y = x.$$ Because the original function has only positive outputs, the inverse function has only positive inputs.

title: Solving an Application with a Cubic Function
snippet: Solving an Application with a Cubic Function: Park rangers construct a mound of gravel in the shape of a cone with the height equal to twice the radius. The volume of the cone in terms of the radius is given by V = \frac{2}{3}\pi r^{3}...
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Solving an Application with a Cubic Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Park rangers construct a mound of gravel in the shape of a cone with the height equal to twice the radius. The volume of the cone in terms of the radius is given by</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$V = \frac{2}{3}\pi r^{3}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Find the inverse of the function $$V = \frac{2}{3}\pi r^{3}$$ that determines the volume $$V$$ of a cone and is a function of the radius $$r.$$ Then use the inverse function to calculate the radius of such a mound of gravel measuring 100 cubic feet. Use $$\pi = 3.14.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Start with the given function for $$V.$$ Notice that the meaningful domain for the function is $$r > 0$$ since negative radii would not make sense in this context nor would a radius of 0. Also note the range of the function (hence, the domain of the inverse function) is $$V > 0.$$ Solve for $$r$$ in terms of $$V,$$ using the method outlined previously. Note that in real-world applications, we do not swap the variables when finding inverses. Instead, we change which variable is considered to be the independent variable.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rclc} V & = & {\frac{2}{3}\pi r^{3}} & \\ r^{3} & = & \frac{3V}{2\pi} & { \text{Solve for} r^{3}.} \\ r & = & \sqrt[3]{\frac{3V}{2\pi}} & { \text{Solve for} r.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This is the result stated in the section opener. Now evaluate this for $$V = 100$$ and $$\pi = 3.14.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} r & = & \sqrt[3]{\frac{3V}{2\pi}} \\ & = & \sqrt[3]{\frac{3 \cdot 100}{2 \cdot 3.14}} \\ & \approx & \sqrt[3]{47.7707} \\ & \approx & 3.63 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, the radius is about 3.63 ft.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Domain of a Radical Function Composed with a Rational Function
snippet: Finding the Domain of a Radical Function Composed with a Rational Function: Find the domain of the function f(x) = \sqrt{\frac{(x + 2)(x - 3)}{(x - 1)}}. Because a square root is only defined when the quantity under the radical is...
body_xml: Find the domain of the function $$f(x) = \sqrt{\frac{(x + 2)(x - 3)}{(x - 1)}}.$$ Because a square root is only defined when the quantity under the radical is non-negative, we need to determine where $$\frac{(x + 2)(x - 3)}{(x - 1)} \geq 0.$$ The output of a rational function can change signs (change from positive to negative or vice versa) at x-intercepts and at vertical asymptotes. For this equation, the graph could change signs at $$x = -2, 1, \text{and} 3.$$ To determine the intervals on which the rational expression is positive, we could test some values in the expression or sketch a graph. While both approaches work equally well, for this example we will use a graph as shown in Figure 9. This function has two x-intercepts, both of which exhibit linear behavior near the x-intercepts. There is one vertical asymptote, corresponding to a linear factor; this behavior is similar to the basic reciprocal toolkit function, and there is no horizontal asymptote because the degree of the numerator is larger than the degree of the denominator. There is a y-intercept at $$(0,\sqrt{6}).$$ From the y-intercept and x-intercept at $$x = -2,$$ we can sketch the left side of the graph. From the behavior at the asymptote, we can sketch the right side of the graph. From the graph, we can now tell on which intervals the outputs will be non-negative, so that we can be sure that the original function $$f(x)$$ will be defined. $$f(x)$$ has domain $$-2 \leq x < 1 \text{or} x \geq 3,$$ or in interval notation, $$\lbrack-2,1) \cup \lbrack 3,\infty).$$

title: Finding the Inverse of a Rational Function
snippet: Finding the Inverse of a Rational Function: The function C = \frac{20 + 0.4n}{100 + n} represents the concentration C of an acid solution after n mL of 40% solution has been added to 100 mL of a 20% solution. First, find the inverse of the...
body_xml:
<example number="8" title="Finding the Inverse of a Rational Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The function $$C = \frac{20 + 0.4n}{100 + n}$$ represents the concentration $$C$$ of an acid solution after $$n$$ mL of 40% solution has been added to 100 mL of a 20% solution. First, find the inverse of the function; that is, find an expression for $$n$$ in terms of $$C.$$ Then use your result to determine how much of the 40% solution should be added so that the final mixture is a 35% solution.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We first want the inverse of the function in order to determine how many mL we need for a given concentration. We will solve for $$n$$ in terms of $$C.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} C & = & \frac{20 + 0.4n}{100 + n} \\ {C(100 + n)} & = & {20 + 0.4n} \\ {100C + Cn} & = & {20 + 0.4n} \\ {100C - 20} & = & {0.4n - Cn} \\ {100C - 20} & = & {(0.4 - C)n} \\ n & = & \frac{100C - 20}{0.4 - C} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now evaluate this function at 35%, which is $$C = 0.35.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} n & = & \frac{100(0.35) - 20}{0.4 - 0.35} \\ & = & \frac{15}{0.05} \\ & = & 300 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We can conclude that 300 mL of the 40% solution should be added.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Direct Variation
snippet: Direct Variation: If x \text{and} y are related by an equation of the form y = kx^{n} then we say that the relationship is direct variation and y varies directly with, or is proportional to, the n th power of x. In direct variation...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Direct Variation" title="Direct Variation">
    <paragraph>If $$x \text{and} y$$ are related by an equation of the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = kx^{n}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>then we say that the relationship is direct variation and $$y$$ varies directly with, or is proportional to, the $$n$$ th power of $$x.$$ In direct variation relationships, there is a nonzero constant ratio $$k = \frac{y}{x^{n}},$$ where $$k$$ is called the constant of variation, which helps to define the relationship between the variables.</paragraph>
  </note>

      <item>Use the constant of variation to write an equation for the relationship.</item>
      <item>Substitute known values into the equation to find the unknown.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Solving a Direct Variation Problem
snippet: Solving a Direct Variation Problem: The quantity y varies directly with the cube of x. If y = 25 when x = 2, find y when x is 6. The general formula for direct variation with a cube is y = kx^{3}. The constant can be found by dividing y by...
body_xml: The quantity $$y$$ varies directly with the cube of $$x.$$ If $$y = 25$$ when $$x = 2,$$ find $$y$$ when $$x$$ is 6. The general formula for direct variation with a cube is $$y = kx^{3}.$$ The constant can be found by dividing $$y$$ by the cube of $$x.$$ $$\begin{array}{ccl} k & = & \frac{y}{x^{3}} \\ & = & \frac{25}{2^{3}} \\ & = & \frac{25}{8} \end{array}$$ Now use the constant to write an equation that represents this relationship. $$y = \frac{25}{8}x^{3}$$ Substitute $$x = 6$$ and solve for $$y.$$ $$\begin{array}{ccl} y & = & {\frac{25}{8}{(6)}^{3}} \\ & = & 675 \end{array}$$ The graph of this equation is a simple cubic, as shown in Figure 2.

title: Inverse Variation
snippet: Inverse Variation: If x and y are related by an equation of the form y = \frac{k}{x^{n}} where k is a nonzero constant, then we say that y varies inversely with the n \text{th} power of x. In inversely proportional relationships, or...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Inverse Variation" title="Inverse Variation">
    <paragraph>If $$x$$ and $$y$$ are related by an equation of the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = \frac{k}{x^{n}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$k$$ is a nonzero constant, then we say that $$y$$ varies inversely with the $$n \text{th}$$ power of $$x.$$ In inversely proportional relationships, or inverse variations, there is a constant multiple $$k = x^{n}y.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Writing a Formula for an Inversely Proportional Relationship
snippet: Writing a Formula for an Inversely Proportional Relationship: A tourist plans to drive 100 miles. Find a formula for the time the trip will take as a function of the speed the tourist drives. Recall that multiplying speed by time gives...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Writing a Formula for an Inversely Proportional Relationship">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A tourist plans to drive 100 miles. Find a formula for the time the trip will take as a function of the speed the tourist drives.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Recall that multiplying speed by time gives distance. If we let $$t$$ represent the drive time in hours, and $$v$$ represent the velocity (speed or rate) at which the tourist drives, then $$vt = \text{distance} .$$ Because the distance is fixed at 100 miles, $$vt = 100$$ so $$t = 100/v.$$ Because time is a function of velocity, we can write $$t(v).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} {t(v)} & = & \frac{100}{v} \\ & = & {100v^{-1}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We can see that the constant of variation is 100 and, although we can write the relationship using the negative exponent, it is more common to see it written as a fraction. We say that time varies inversely with velocity.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given a description of an indirect variation problem, solve for an unknown. Identify the input, x, and the output, y. Determine the constant of variation. You may need to multiply y by the specified power of x to determine the...

title: Solving an Inverse Variation Problem
snippet: Solving an Inverse Variation Problem: A quantity y varies inversely with the cube of x. If y = 25 when x = 2, find y when x is 6. The general formula for inverse variation with a cube is y = \frac{k}{x^{3}}. The constant can be found by...
body_xml: A quantity $$y$$ varies inversely with the cube of $$x.$$ If $$y = 25$$ when $$x = 2,$$ find $$y$$ when $$x$$ is 6. The general formula for inverse variation with a cube is $$y = \frac{k}{x^{3}}.$$ The constant can be found by multiplying $$y$$ by the cube of $$x.$$ $$\begin{array}{ccl} k & = & {x^{3}y} \\ & = & {2^{3} \cdot 25} \\ & = & 200 \end{array}$$ Now we use the constant to write an equation that represents this relationship. $$\begin{array}{ccl} y & = & {\frac{k}{x^{3}}, k = 200} \\ y & = & \frac{200}{x^{3}} \end{array}$$ Substitute $$x = 6$$ and solve for $$y.$$ $$\begin{array}{ccl} y & = & \frac{200}{6^{3}} \\ & = & \frac{25}{27} \end{array}$$ The graph of this equation is a rational function, as shown in Figure 4.

title: Joint Variation
snippet: Joint Variation: Joint variation occurs when a variable varies directly or inversely with multiple variables. For instance, if x varies directly with both y and z, we have x = kyz. If x varies directly with y and inversely with z, we have...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Joint Variation" title="Joint Variation">
    <paragraph>Joint variation occurs when a variable varies directly or inversely with multiple variables.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For instance, if $$x$$ varies directly with both $$y$$ and $$z,$$ we have $$x = kyz.$$ If $$x$$ varies directly with $$y$$ and inversely with $$z,$$ we have $$x = \frac{ky}{z}.$$ Notice that we only use one constant in a joint variation equation.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Solving Problems Involving Joint Variation
snippet: Solving Problems Involving Joint Variation: A quantity x varies directly with the square of y and inversely with the cube root of z. If x = 6 when y = 2 and z = 8, find x when y = 1 and z = 27. Begin by writing an equation to show the...
body_xml:
<example number="4" title="Solving Problems Involving Joint Variation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A quantity $$x$$ varies directly with the square of $$y$$ and inversely with the cube root of $$z.$$ If $$x = 6$$ when $$y = 2$$ and $$z = 8,$$ find $$x$$ when $$y = 1$$ and $$z = 27.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Begin by writing an equation to show the relationship between the variables.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x = \frac{ky^{2}}{\sqrt[3]{z}}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substitute $$x = 6,$$ $$y = 2,$$ and $$z = 8$$ to find the value of the constant $$k.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} 6 & = & \frac{k2^{2}}{\sqrt[3]{8}} \\ 6 & = & \frac{4k}{2} \\ 3 & = & k \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now we can substitute the value of the constant into the equation for the relationship.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x = \frac{3y^{2}}{\sqrt[3]{z}}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To find $$x$$ when $$y = 1$$ and $$z = 27,$$ we will substitute values for $$y$$ and $$z$$ into our equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} x & = & \frac{3{(1)}^{2}}{\sqrt[3]{27}} \\ & = & 1 \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Exponential Function
snippet: Exponential Function: For any real number x, an exponential function is a function with the form f(x) = ab^{x} where a is a non-zero real number called the initial value and b is any positive real number such that b \neq 1. The domain of f...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Exponential Function" title="Exponential Function">
    <paragraph>For any real number $$x,$$ an exponential function is a function with the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = ab^{x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>$$a$$ is a non-zero real number called the initial value and</item>
      <item>$$b$$ is any positive real number such that $$b \neq 1.$$</item>
      <item>The domain of $$f$$ is all real numbers.</item>
      <item>The range of $$f$$ is all positive real numbers if $$a > 0.$$</item>
      <item>The range of $$f$$ is all negative real numbers if $$a < 0.$$</item>
      <item>The y-intercept is $$\left( {0,a} \right),$$ and the horizontal asymptote is $$y = 0.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Identifying Exponential Functions
snippet: Identifying Exponential Functions: Which of the following equations are not exponential functions? f(x) = 4^{3{({x - 2})}} g(x) = x^{3} h(x) = \left( \frac{1}{3} \right)^{x} j(x) = \left( {- 2} \right)^{x} By definition, an exponential...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Identifying Exponential Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Which of the following equations are not exponential functions?</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>$$f(x) = 4^{3{({x - 2})}}$$</item>
        <item>$$g(x) = x^{3}$$</item>
        <item>$$h(x) = \left( \frac{1}{3} \right)^{x}$$</item>
        <item>$$j(x) = \left( {- 2} \right)^{x}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>By definition, an exponential function has a constant as a base and an independent variable as an exponent. Thus, $$g(x) = x^{3}$$ does not represent an exponential function because the base is an independent variable. In fact, $$g(x) = x^{3}$$ is a power function.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Recall that the base b of an exponential function is always a positive constant, and $$b \neq 1.$$ Thus, $$j(x) = (-2)^{x}$$ does not represent an exponential function because the base, $$-2,$$ is less than $$0.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Evaluating Exponential Functions
snippet: Evaluating Exponential Functions: Let f(x) = 5(3)^{x + 1}. Evaluate f(2) without using a calculator. Follow the order of operations. Be sure to pay attention to the parentheses. \begin{array}{lll} {f(x)} & {= 5(3)^{x + 1}} & \\ {f(2)} & {=...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Evaluating Exponential Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$f(x) = 5(3)^{x + 1}.$$ Evaluate $$f(2)$$ without using a calculator.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Follow the order of operations. Be sure to pay attention to the parentheses.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lll} {f(x)} & {= 5(3)^{x + 1}} & \\ {f(2)} & {= 5(3)^{2 + 1}} & { \text{Substitute} x = 2.} \\ & {= 5(3)^{3}} & { \text{Add the exponents} .} \\ & {= 5(27)} & { \text{Simplify the power} .} \\ & {= 135} & { \text{Multiply} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Exponential Growth
snippet: Exponential Growth: A function that models exponential growth grows by a rate proportional to the amount present. For any real number x and any positive real numbers a and b such that b \neq 1, an exponential growth function has the form...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Exponential Growth" title="Exponential Growth">
    <paragraph>A function that models exponential growth grows by a rate proportional to the amount present. For any real number $$x$$ and any positive real numbers $$a$$ and $$b$$ such that $$b \neq 1,$$ an exponential growth function has the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = ab^{x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>$$a$$ is the initial or starting value of the function.</item>
      <item>$$b$$ is the growth factor or growth multiplier per unit $$x$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Evaluating a Real-World Exponential Model
snippet: Evaluating a Real-World Exponential Model: At the beginning of this section, we learned that the population of India was about 1.25 billion in the year 2013, with an annual growth rate of about 1.2\%. This situation is represented by the...
body_xml:
<example number="3" title="Evaluating a Real-World Exponential Model">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>At the beginning of this section, we learned that the population of India was about $$1.25$$ billion in the year 2013, with an annual growth rate of about $$1.2\%.$$ This situation is represented by the growth function $$P(t) = 1.25(1.012)^{t},$$ where $$t$$ is the number of years since $$2013.$$ To the nearest thousandth, what will the population of India be in $$\text{2031?}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To estimate the population in 2031, we evaluate the models for $$t = 18,$$ because 2031 is $$18$$ years after 2013. Rounding to the nearest thousandth,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$P(18) = 1.25(1.012)^{18} \approx 1.549$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>There will be about 1.549 billion people in India in the year 2031.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given two data points, write an exponential model. If one of the data points has the form \left( {0,a} \right), then a is the initial value. Using a, substitute the second point into the equation f(x) = a(b)^{x}, and solve for b....

<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given two data points, write an exponential model.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>If one of the data points has the form $$\left( {0,a} \right),$$ then $$a$$ is the initial value. Using $$a,$$ substitute the second point into the equation $$f(x) = a(b)^{x},$$ and solve for $$b.$$</item>
      <item>If neither of the data points have the form $$\left( {0,a} \right),$$ substitute both points into two equations with the form $$f(x) = a(b)^{x}.$$ Solve the resulting system of two equations in two unknowns to find $$a$$ and $$b.$$</item>
      <item>Using the $$a$$ and $$b$$ found in the steps above, write the exponential function in the form $$f(x) = a(b)^{x}.$$</item>
    </list>

title: Writing an Exponential Model When the Initial Value Is Known
snippet: Writing an Exponential Model When the Initial Value Is Known: In 2006, 80 deer were introduced into a wildlife refuge. By 2012, the population had grown to 180 deer. The population was growing exponentially. Write an exponential function...
body_xml: In 2006, 80 deer were introduced into a wildlife refuge. By 2012, the population had grown to 180 deer. The population was growing exponentially. Write an exponential function $$N(t)$$ representing the population $$(N)$$ of deer over time $$t.$$ We let our independent variable $$t$$ be the number of years after 2006. Thus, the information given in the problem can be written as input-output pairs: (0, 80) and (6, 180). Notice that by choosing our input variable to be measured as years after 2006, we have given ourselves the initial value for the function, $$a = 80.$$ We can now substitute the second point into the equation $$N(t) = 80b^{t}$$ to find $$b:$$ $$\begin{array}{lll} {N(t)} & {= 80b^{t}} & \\ { 180} & {= 80b^{6}} & { \text{Substitute using point} (6, 180).} \\ {\frac{9}{4}} & {= b^{6}} & { \text{Divide and write in lowest terms} .} \\ { b} & {= \left( \frac{9}{4} \right)^{\frac{1}{6}}} & { \text{Isolate} b \text{using properties of exponents} .} \\ { b} & {\approx 1.1447\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{Round to 4 decimal places} .} \end{array}$$ NOTE: Unless otherwise stated, do not round any intermediate calculations. Then round the final answer to four places for the remainder of this section. The exponential model for the population of deer is $$N(t) = 80(1.1447)^{t}.$$ (Note that this exponential function models short-term growth. As the inputs gets large, the output will get increasingly larger, so much so that the model may not be useful in the long term.) We can graph our model to observe the population growth of deer in the refuge over time. Notice that the graph in Figure 3 passes through the initial points given in the problem, $$\left( {0,80} \right)$$ and $$\left( { \text{6} ,180} \right).$$ We can also see that the domain for the function is $$\lbrack 0,\infty),$$ and the range for the function is $$\lbrack 80,\infty).$$

title: Writing an Exponential Model When the Initial Value is Not Known
snippet: Writing an Exponential Model When the Initial Value is Not Known: Find an exponential function that passes through the points \left( {- 2,6} \right) and \left( {2,1} \right). Because we don’t have the initial value, we substitute both...
body_xml: Find an exponential function that passes through the points $$\left( {- 2,6} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2,1} \right).$$ Because we don’t have the initial value, we substitute both points into an equation of the form $$f(x) = ab^{x},$$ and then solve the system for $$a$$ and $$b.$$ Substituting $$\left( {- 2,6} \right)$$ gives $$6 = ab^{- 2}$$ Substituting $$\left( {2,1} \right)$$ gives $$1 = ab^{2}$$ Use the first equation to solve for $$a$$ in terms of $$b:$$ Substitute $$a$$ in the second equation, and solve for $$b:$$ Use the value of $$b$$ in the first equation to solve for the value of $$a:$$ Thus, the equation is $$f(x) = 2.4492{(0.6389)}^{x}.$$ We can graph our model to check our work. Notice that the graph in Figure 4 passes through the initial points given in the problem, $$\left( {- 2, \text{6} } \right)$$ and $$\left( {2, \text{1} } \right).$$ The graph is an example of an exponential decay function.

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given the graph of an exponential function, write its equation. First, identify two points on the graph. Choose the y-intercept as one of the two points whenever possible. Try to choose points that are as far apart as possible to...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given the graph of an exponential function, write its equation.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>First, identify two points on the graph. Choose the y-intercept as one of the two points whenever possible. Try to choose points that are as far apart as possible to reduce round-off error.</item>
      <item>If one of the data points is the y-intercept $$\left( {0,a} \right)$$ , then $$a$$ is the initial value. Using $$a,$$ substitute the second point into the equation $$f(x) = a(b)^{x},$$ and solve for $$b.$$</item>
      <item>If neither of the data points have the form $$\left( {0,a} \right),$$ substitute both points into two equations with the form $$f(x) = a(b)^{x}.$$ Solve the resulting system of two equations in two unknowns to find $$a$$ and $$b.$$</item>
      <item>Write the exponential function, $$f(x) = a(b)^{x}.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Writing an Exponential Function Given Its Graph
snippet: Writing an Exponential Function Given Its Graph: Find an equation for the exponential function graphed in Figure 5. We can choose the y-intercept of the graph, \left( {0,3} \right), as our first point. This gives us the initial value, a =...
body_xml: Find an equation for the exponential function graphed in Figure 5. We can choose the y-intercept of the graph, $$\left( {0,3} \right),$$ as our first point. This gives us the initial value, $$a = 3.$$ Next, choose a point on the curve some distance away from $$\left( {0,3} \right)$$ that has integer coordinates. One such point is $$(2,12).$$ $$\begin{array}{ll} { y = ab^{x}} & { \text{Write the general form of an exponential equation} .} \\ { y = 3b^{x}} & { \text{Substitute the initial value 3 for} a.} \\ {12 = 3b^{2}} & { \text{Substitute in 12 for} y \text{and 2 for} x.} \\ { 4 = b^{2}} & { \text{Divide by 3} .} \\ { b = \pm 2\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{Take the square root} .} \end{array}$$ Because we restrict ourselves to positive values of $$b,$$ we will use $$b = 2.$$ Substitute $$a$$ and $$b$$ into the standard form to yield the equation $$f(x) = 3{(2)}^{x}.$$

title: The Compound Interest Formula
snippet: The Compound Interest Formula: Compound interest can be calculated using the formula A(t) = P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt} where A(t) is the account value, t is measured in years, P is the starting amount of the account, often...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="The Compound Interest Formula" title="The Compound Interest Formula">
    <paragraph>Compound interest can be calculated using the formula</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$A(t) = P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>$$A(t)$$ is the account value,</item>
      <item>$$t$$ is measured in years,</item>
      <item>$$P$$ is the starting amount of the account, often called the principal, or more generally present value,</item>
      <item>$$r$$ is the annual percentage rate (APR) expressed as a decimal, and</item>
      <item>$$n$$ is the number of compounding periods in one year.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Calculating Compound Interest
snippet: Calculating Compound Interest: If we invest \$3,000 in an investment account paying 3% interest compounded quarterly, how much will the account be worth in 10 years? Because we are starting with \$3,000, P = 3000. Our interest rate is 3%,...
body_xml:
<example number="8" title="Calculating Compound Interest">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>If we invest \$3,000 in an investment account paying 3% interest compounded quarterly, how much will the account be worth in 10 years?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Because we are starting with \$3,000, $$P = 3000.$$ Our interest rate is 3%, so $$r = 0.03.$$ Because we are compounding quarterly, we are compounding 4 times per year, so $$n = 4.$$ We want to know the value of the account in 10 years, so we are looking for $$A(10),$$ the value when $$t = 10.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lll} {A(t)} & {= P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt}} & { \text{Use the compound interest formula} .} \\ {A(10)} & {= 3000\left( {1 + \frac{0.03}{4}} \right)^{4\cdot 10}\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{Substitute using given values} .} \\ & {\approx \$4045.05} & { \text{Round to two decimal places} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The account will be worth about \$4,045.05 in 10 years.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using the Compound Interest Formula to Solve for the Principal
snippet: Using the Compound Interest Formula to Solve for the Principal: A 529 Plan is a college-savings plan that allows relatives to invest money to pay for a child’s future college tuition; the account grows tax-free. Lily wants to set up a 529...
body_xml:
<example number="9" title="Using the Compound Interest Formula to Solve for the Principal">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A 529 Plan is a college-savings plan that allows relatives to invest money to pay for a child’s future college tuition; the account grows tax-free. Lily wants to set up a 529 account for her new granddaughter and wants the account to grow to \$40,000 over 18 years. She believes the account will earn 6% compounded semi-annually (twice a year). To the nearest dollar, how much will Lily need to invest in the account now?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The nominal interest rate is 6%, so $$r = 0.06.$$ Interest is compounded twice a year, so $$n = 2.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We want to find the initial investment, $$P,$$ needed so that the value of the account will be worth \$40,000 in $$18$$ years. Substitute the given values into the compound interest formula, and solve for $$P.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lll} { A(t)} & {= P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt}} & { \text{Use the compound interest formula} .} \\ 40,000 & {= P\left( {1 + \frac{0.06}{2}} \right)^{2(18)}\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{Substitute using given values} A , r, n \text{, and} t.} \\ 40,000 & {= P{(1.03)}^{36}} & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ \frac{40,000}{{(1.03)}^{36}} & {= P} & { \text{Isolate} P.} \\ { P} & {\approx \$13,801} & { \text{Divide and round to the nearest dollar} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Lily will need to invest \$13,801 to have \$40,000 in 18 years.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: The Number e e
snippet: The Number e e: The letter e represents the irrational number \left( {1 + \frac{1}{n}} \right)^{n}, \text{as} n \text{increases without bound} The letter e is used as a base for many real-world exponential models. To work with base e, we...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="The Number e e" title="The Number e e">
    <paragraph>The letter e represents the irrational number</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {1 + \frac{1}{n}} \right)^{n}, \text{as} n \text{increases without bound}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The letter e is used as a base for many real-world exponential models. To work with base e, we use the approximation, $$e \approx 2.718282.$$ The constant was named by the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler (1707–1783) who first investigated and discovered many of its properties.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Using a Calculator to Find Powers of e
snippet: Using a Calculator to Find Powers of e: Calculate e^{3.14}. Round to five decimal places. On a calculator, press the button labeled \left\lbrack e^{x} \right\rbrack. The window shows \left\lbrack {e\hat{}(} \right\rbrack. Type 3.14 and...
body_xml:
<example number="10" title="Using a Calculator to Find Powers of e">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate $$e^{3.14}.$$ Round to five decimal places.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>On a calculator, press the button labeled $$\left\lbrack e^{x} \right\rbrack.$$ The window shows $$\left\lbrack {e\hat{}(} \right\rbrack.$$ Type $$3.14$$ and then close parenthesis, $$\left\lbrack ) \right\rbrack.$$ Press [ENTER]. Rounding to $$5$$ decimal places, $$e^{3.14} \approx 23.10387.$$ Caution: Many scientific calculators have an “Exp” button, which is used to enter numbers in scientific notation. It is not used to find powers of $$e.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: The Continuous Growth/Decay Formula
snippet: The Continuous Growth/Decay Formula: For all real numbers t, and all positive numbers a and r, continuous growth or decay is represented by the formula A(t) = ae^{rt} where a is the initial value, r is the continuous growth rate per unit...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="The Continuous Growth/Decay Formula" title="The Continuous Growth/Decay Formula">
    <paragraph>For all real numbers $$t,$$ and all positive numbers $$a$$ and $$r,$$ continuous growth or decay is represented by the formula</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$A(t) = ae^{rt}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>$$a$$ is the initial value,</item>
      <item>$$r$$ is the continuous growth rate per unit time,</item>
      <item>and $$t$$ is the elapsed time.</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>If $$r > 0$$ , then the formula represents continuous growth. If $$r < 0$$ , then the formula represents continuous decay.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For business applications, the continuous growth formula is called the continuous compounding formula and takes the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$A(t) = Pe^{rt}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>$$P$$ is the principal or the initial invested,</item>
      <item>$$r$$ is the growth or interest rate per unit time,</item>
      <item>and $$t$$ is the period or term of the investment.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given the initial value, rate of growth or decay, and time t, solve a continuous growth or decay function. Use the information in the problem to determine a , the initial value of the function. Use the information in the problem to...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given the initial value, rate of growth or decay, and time $$t,$$ solve a continuous growth or decay function.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Use the information in the problem to determine $$a$$ , the initial value of the function.</item>
      <item>Use the information in the problem to determine the growth rate $$r.$$ If the problem refers to continuous growth, then $$r > 0.$$ If the problem refers to continuous decay, then $$r < 0.$$</item>
      <item>Use the information in the problem to determine the time $$t.$$</item>
      <item>Substitute the given information into the continuous growth formula and solve for $$A(t).$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Calculating Continuous Growth
snippet: Calculating Continuous Growth: A person invested \$1,000 in an account earning a nominal 10% per year compounded continuously. How much was in the account at the end of one year? Since the account is growing in value, this is a continuous...
body_xml:
<example number="11" title="Calculating Continuous Growth">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A person invested \$1,000 in an account earning a nominal 10% per year compounded continuously. How much was in the account at the end of one year?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since the account is growing in value, this is a continuous compounding problem with growth rate $$r = 0.10.$$ The initial investment was \$1,000, so $$P = 1000.$$ We use the continuous compounding formula to find the value after $$t = 1$$ year:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lll} {A(t)} & {= Pe^{rt}} & { \text{Use the continuous compounding formula} .} \\ & {= 1000{(e)}^{0.1}\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{Substitute known values for} P, r, \text{and} t.} \\ & {\approx 1105.17} & { \text{Use a calculator to approximate} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The account is worth \$1,105.17 after one year.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Calculating Continuous Decay
snippet: Calculating Continuous Decay: Radon-222 decays at a continuous rate of 17.3% per day. How much will 100 mg of Radon-222 decay to in 3 days? Since the substance is decaying, the rate, 17.3\% , is negative. So, r = - 0.173. The initial...
body_xml:
<example number="12" title="Calculating Continuous Decay">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Radon-222 decays at a continuous rate of 17.3% per day. How much will 100 mg of Radon-222 decay to in 3 days?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since the substance is decaying, the rate, $$17.3\%$$ , is negative. So, $$r = - 0.173.$$ The initial amount of radon-222 was $$100$$ mg, so $$a = 100.$$ We use the continuous decay formula to find the value after $$t = 3$$ days:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lll} {A(t)} & {= ae^{rt}} & { \text{Use the continuous growth formula} .} \\ & {= 100e^{- 0.173(3)}\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{Substitute known values for} a, r, \text{and} t.} \\ & {\approx 59.5115} & { \text{Use a calculator to approximate} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So 59.5115 mg of radon-222 will remain.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="rule" source_type="Shifts of the Parent Function f(x) = b x" title="Shifts of the Parent Function f(x) = b x">
    <paragraph>For any constants $$c$$ and $$d,$$ the function $$f(x) = b^{x + c} + d$$ shifts the parent function $$f(x) = b^{x}$$</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>vertically $$d$$ units, in the same direction of the sign of $$d.$$</item>
      <item>horizontally $$c$$ units, in the opposite direction of the sign of $$c.$$</item>
      <item>The y-intercept becomes $$\left( {0,b^{c} + d} \right).$$</item>
      <item>The horizontal asymptote becomes $$y = d.$$</item>
      <item>The range becomes $$\left( {d,\infty} \right).$$</item>
      <item>The domain, $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right),$$ remains unchanged.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

snippet: Translations of Exponential Functions: A translation of an exponential function has the form f(x) = ab^{x + c} + d Where the parent function, y = b^{x}, b > 1, is shifted horizontally c units to the left. stretched vertically by a factor...

<note type="rule" source_type="Translations of Exponential Functions" title="Translations of Exponential Functions">
    <paragraph>A translation of an exponential function has the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = ab^{x + c} + d$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Where the parent function, $$y = b^{x},$$ $$b > 1,$$ is</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>shifted horizontally $$c$$ units to the left.</item>
      <item>stretched vertically by a factor of $$|a|$$ if $$|a| > 0.$$</item>
      <item>compressed vertically by a factor of $$|a|$$ if $$0 < |a| < 1.$$</item>
      <item>shifted vertically $$d$$ units.</item>
      <item>reflected about the x-axis when $$a < 0.$$</item>
    </list>

  </note>

title: Writing a Function from a Description
snippet: Writing a Function from a Description: Write the equation for the function described below. Give the horizontal asymptote, the domain, and the range. f(x) = e^{x} is vertically stretched by a factor of 2 , reflected across the y-axis, and...
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Writing a Function from a Description">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write the equation for the function described below. Give the horizontal asymptote, the domain, and the range.</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>$$f(x) = e^{x}$$ is vertically stretched by a factor of $$2$$ , reflected across the y-axis, and then shifted up $$4$$ units.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We want to find an equation of the general form $$f(x) = ab^{x + c} + d.$$ We use the description provided to find $$a,$$ $$b,$$ $$c,$$ and $$d.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>We are given the parent function $$f(x) = e^{x},$$ so $$b = e.$$</item>
        <item>The function is stretched by a factor of $$2$$ , so $$a = 2.$$</item>
        <item>The function is reflected about the y-axis. We replace $$x$$ with $$- x$$ to get: $$e^{- x}.$$</item>
        <item>The graph is shifted vertically 4 units, so $$d = 4.$$</item>
      </list>
      <paragraph>Substituting in the general form we get,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} { f(x)} & {= ab^{x + c} + d} \\ & {= 2e^{- x + 0} + 4} \\ & {= 2e^{- x} + 4} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The domain is $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right);$$ the range is $$\left( {4,\infty} \right);$$ the horizontal asymptote is $$y = 4.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Definition of the Logarithmic Function
snippet: Definition of the Logarithmic Function: A logarithm base b of a positive number x satisfies the following definition. For x > 0,b > 0,b \neq 1, y = \log_{b}(x) \text{is equivalent to} b^{y} = x where, we read \log_{b}(x) as, “the logarithm...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Definition of the Logarithmic Function" title="Definition of the Logarithmic Function">
    <paragraph>A logarithm base $$b$$ of a positive number $$x$$ satisfies the following definition.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For $$x > 0,b > 0,b \neq 1,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = \log_{b}(x) \text{is equivalent to} b^{y} = x$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where,</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>we read $$\log_{b}(x)$$ as, “the logarithm with base $$b$$ of $$x$$ ” or the “log base $$b$$ of $$x."$$</item>
      <item>the logarithm $$y$$ is the exponent to which $$b$$ must be raised to get $$x.$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Also, since the logarithmic and exponential functions switch the $$x$$ and $$y$$ values, the domain and range of the exponential function are interchanged for the logarithmic function. Therefore,</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>the domain of the logarithm function with base $$b \text{is} (0,\infty).$$</item>
      <item>the range of the logarithm function with base $$b \text{is} ( - \infty,\infty).$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

    <problem>

      <list type="ordered">

      </list>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, identify the values of $$b,y, \text{and} x.$$ Then, write the equation in the form $$b^{y} = x.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\log_{6}\left( \sqrt{6} \right) = \frac{1}{2}$$ Here, $$b = 6,y = \frac{1}{2}, \text{and} x = \sqrt{6.}$$ Therefore, the equation $$\log_{6}\left( \sqrt{6} \right) = \frac{1}{2}$$ is equivalent to $$6^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{6}.$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\log_{3}(9) = 2$$ Here, $$b = 3,y = 2, \text{and} x = 9.$$ Therefore, the equation $$\log_{3}(9) = 2$$ is equivalent to $$3^{2} = 9.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="2" title="Converting from Exponential Form to Logarithmic Form">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write the following exponential equations in logarithmic form.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$2^{3} = 8$$</item>
        <item>$$5^{2} = 25$$</item>
        <item>$$10^{- 4} = \frac{1}{10,000}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, identify the values of $$b,y, \text{and} x.$$ Then, write the equation in the form $$x = \log_{b}(y).$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$2^{3} = 8$$ Here, $$b = 2,$$ $$x = 3,$$ and $$y = 8.$$ Therefore, the equation $$2^{3} = 8$$ is equivalent to $$\log_{2}(8) = 3.$$</item>
        <item>$$5^{2} = 25$$ Here, $$b = 5,$$ $$x = 2,$$ and $$y = 25.$$ Therefore, the equation $$5^{2} = 25$$ is equivalent to $$\log_{5}(25) = 2.$$</item>
        <item>$$10^{- 4} = \frac{1}{10,000}$$ Here, $$b = 10,$$ $$x = - 4,$$ and $$y = \frac{1}{10,000}.$$ Therefore, the equation $$10^{- 4} = \frac{1}{10,000}$$ is equivalent to $$\log_{10}(\frac{1}{10,000}) = - 4.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="rule" source_type="Definition of the Common Logarithm" title="Definition of the Common Logarithm">
    <paragraph>A common logarithm is a logarithm with base $$10.$$ We can also write $$\log_{10}(x)$$ simply as $$\log(x).$$ The common logarithm of a positive number $$x$$ satisfies the following definition.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For $$x > 0,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = \log(x) \text{is equivalent to} 10^{y} = x$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We read $$\log(x)$$ as, “the logarithm with base $$10$$ of $$x$$ ” or “log base 10 of $$x.$$ ”</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The logarithm $$y$$ is the exponent to which $$10$$ must be raised to get $$x.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

      <paragraph>Rounding to four decimal places, $$\log(321) \approx 2.5065.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>Note that $$10^{2} = 100$$ and that $$10^{3} = 1000.$$ Since 321 is between 100 and 1000, we know that $$\log(321)$$ must be between $$\log(100)$$ and $$\log(1000).$$ This gives us the following:</paragraph>

<example number="7" title="Rewriting and Solving a Real-World Exponential Model">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The amount of energy released from one earthquake was 500 times greater than the amount of energy released from another. The equation $$10^{x} = 500$$ represents this situation, where $$x$$ is the difference in magnitudes on the Richter Scale. To the nearest thousandth, what was the difference in magnitudes?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We begin by rewriting the exponential equation in logarithmic form.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lll} 10^{x} & {= 500} & \\ {\log(500)} & {= x} & { \text{Use the definition of the common log} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next we evaluate the logarithm using a calculator:</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>Press [LOG].</item>
        <item>Enter $$500,$$ followed by [ ) ].</item>
        <item>Press [ENTER].</item>
        <item>To the nearest thousandth, $$\log(500) \approx 2.699.$$</item>
      </list>
      <paragraph>The difference in magnitudes was about $$2.699.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Definition of the Natural Logarithm
snippet: Definition of the Natural Logarithm: A natural logarithm is a logarithm with base e. We write \log_{e}(x) simply as \ln(x). The natural logarithm of a positive number x satisfies the following definition. For x > 0, y = \ln(x) \text{is...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Definition of the Natural Logarithm" title="Definition of the Natural Logarithm">
    <paragraph>A natural logarithm is a logarithm with base $$e.$$ We write $$\log_{e}(x)$$ simply as $$\ln(x).$$ The natural logarithm of a positive number $$x$$ satisfies the following definition.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For $$x > 0,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = \ln(x) \text{is equivalent to} e^{y} = x$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We read $$\ln(x)$$ as, “the logarithm with base $$e$$ of $$x$$ ” or “the natural logarithm of $$x.$$ ”</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The logarithm $$y$$ is the exponent to which $$e$$ must be raised to get $$x.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since the functions $$y = e^{x}$$ and $$y = \ln(x)$$ are inverse functions, $$\ln\left( e^{x} \right) = x$$ for all $$x$$ and $$e{}_{}^{\ln(x)}x$$ for $$x > 0.$$</paragraph>
  </note>
