snippet: Identifying the Domain of a Logarithmic Shift: What is the domain of f(x) = \log_{2}(x + 3)? The logarithmic function is defined only when the input is positive, so this function is defined when x + 3 > 0. Solving this inequality,...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Identifying the Domain of a Logarithmic Shift">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>What is the domain of $$f(x) = \log_{2}(x + 3)?$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The logarithmic function is defined only when the input is positive, so this function is defined when $$x + 3 > 0.$$ Solving this inequality,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {x + 3 > 0} & { \text{The input must be positive} .} \\ {x > - 3\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{Subtract 3} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The domain of $$f(x) = \log_{2}(x + 3)$$ is $$\left( {- 3,\infty} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Identifying the Domain of a Logarithmic Shift and Reflection
snippet: Identifying the Domain of a Logarithmic Shift and Reflection: What is the domain of f(x) = \log(5 - 2x)? The logarithmic function is defined only when the input is positive, so this function is defined when 5-2x > 0. Solving this...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Identifying the Domain of a Logarithmic Shift and Reflection">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>What is the domain of $$f(x) = \log(5 - 2x)?$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The logarithmic function is defined only when the input is positive, so this function is defined when $$5-2x > 0.$$ Solving this inequality,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {5 - 2x > 0} & { \text{The input must be positive} .} \\ {- 2x > - 5} & { \text{Subtract} 5.} \\ {x < \frac{5}{2}\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{Divide by} - 2 \text{and switch the inequality} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The domain of $$f(x) = \log(5 - 2x)$$ is $$\left( {-\infty,\frac{5}{2}} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml: Graph $$f(x) = \log_{5}(x).$$ State the domain, range, and asymptote. Before graphing, identify the behavior and key points for the graph. Since $$b = 5$$ is greater than one, we know the function is increasing. The left tail of the graph will approach the vertical asymptote $$x = 0,$$ and the right tail will increase slowly without bound. The x-intercept is $$\left( {1,0} \right).$$ The key point $$\left( {5,1} \right)$$ is on the graph. We draw and label the asymptote, plot and label the points, and draw a smooth curve through the points (see Figure 5). The domain is $$\left( {0,\infty} \right),$$ the range is $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right),$$ and the vertical asymptote is $$x = 0.$$

      <item>stretches the parent function $$y = \log_{b}(x)$$ vertically by a factor of $$a$$ if $$a > 1.$$</item>
      <item>compresses the parent function $$y = \log_{b}(x)$$ vertically by a factor of $$a$$ if $$0 < a < 1.$$</item>
      <item>has the vertical asymptote $$x = 0.$$</item>
      <item>has the x-intercept $$\left( {1,0} \right).$$</item>
      <item>has domain $$\left( {0,\infty} \right).$$</item>
      <item>has range $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right).$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

body_xml: Sketch a graph of $$f(x) = \log( - x)$$ alongside its parent function. Include the key points and asymptote on the graph. State the domain, range, and asymptote. Before graphing $$f(x) = \log( - x),$$ identify the behavior and key points for the graph. Since $$b = 10$$ is greater than one, we know that the parent function is increasing. Since the input value is multiplied by $$-1,$$ $$f$$ is a reflection of the parent graph about the y-axis. Thus, $$f(x) = \log( - x)$$ will be decreasing as $$x$$ moves from negative infinity to zero, and the right tail of the graph will approach the vertical asymptote $$x = 0.$$ The x-intercept is $$\left( {-1,0} \right).$$ We draw and label the asymptote, plot and label the points, and draw a smooth curve through the points. The domain is $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right),$$ the range is $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right),$$ and the vertical asymptote is $$x = 0.$$

<note type="rule" source_type="Transformations of Logarithmic Functions" title="Transformations of Logarithmic Functions">

    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = a\log_{b}\left( {x + c} \right) + d$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where the parent function, $$y = \log_{b}(x),b > 1,$$ is</paragraph>

      <item>shifted vertically up $$d$$ units.</item>
      <item>shifted horizontally to the left $$c$$ units.</item>
      <item>stretched vertically by a factor of $$|a|$$ if $$|a| > 0.$$</item>
      <item>compressed vertically by a factor of $$|a|$$ if $$0 < |a| < 1.$$</item>
      <item>reflected about the x-axis when $$a < 0.$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>For $$f(x) = \log\left( {- x} \right),$$ the graph of the parent function is reflected about the y-axis.</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Using the Product Rule for Logarithms: Expand \log_{3}\left( {30x\left( {3x + 4} \right)} \right). We begin by factoring the argument completely, expressing 30 as a product of primes. \log_{3}\left( {30x\left( {3x + 4} \right)} \right) =...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Using the Product Rule for Logarithms">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Expand $$\log_{3}\left( {30x\left( {3x + 4} \right)} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We begin by factoring the argument completely, expressing $$30$$ as a product of primes.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{3}\left( {30x\left( {3x + 4} \right)} \right) = \log_{3}\left( {2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot x \cdot \left( {3x + 4} \right)} \right)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next we write the equivalent equation by summing the logarithms of each factor.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{3}\left( {30x\left( {3x + 4} \right)} \right) = \log_{3}(2) + \log_{3}(3) + \log_{3}(5) + \log_{3}(x) + \log_{3}\left( {3x + 4} \right)$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using the Quotient Rule for Logarithms
snippet: Using the Quotient Rule for Logarithms: Expand \log_{2}\left( \frac{15x(x - 1)}{(3x + 4)(2 - x)} \right). First we note that the quotient is factored and in lowest terms, so we apply the quotient rule. \log_{2}\left( \frac{15x(x - 1)}{(3x...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Using the Quotient Rule for Logarithms">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Expand $$\log_{2}\left( \frac{15x(x - 1)}{(3x + 4)(2 - x)} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First we note that the quotient is factored and in lowest terms, so we apply the quotient rule.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{2}\left( \frac{15x(x - 1)}{(3x + 4)(2 - x)} \right) = \log_{2}\left( {15x(x - 1)} \right) - \log_{2}\left( {(3x + 4)(2 - x)} \right)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that the resulting terms are logarithms of products. To expand completely, we apply the product rule, noting that the prime factors of the factor 15 are 3 and 5.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\log_{2}(15x(x - 1)) - \log_{2}((3x + 4)(2 - x)) = \lbrack\log_{2}(3) + \log_{2}(5) + \log_{2}(x) + \log_{2}(x - 1)\rbrack - \lbrack\log_{2}(3x + 4) + \log_{2}(2 - x)\rbrack} \\ { = \log_{2}(3) + \log_{2}(5) + \log_{2}(x) + \log_{2}(x - 1) - \log_{2}(3x + 4) - \log_{2}(2 - x)} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>There are exceptions to consider in this and later examples. First, because denominators must never be zero, this expression is not defined for $$x = - \frac{4}{3}$$ and $$x = 2.$$ Also, since the argument of a logarithm must be positive, we note as we observe the expanded logarithm, that $$x > 0,$$ $$x > 1,$$ $$x > - \frac{4}{3},$$ and $$x < 2.$$ Combining these conditions is beyond the scope of this section, and we will not consider them here or in subsequent exercises.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Using the Power Rule in Reverse
snippet: Using the Power Rule in Reverse: Rewrite 4\ln(x) using the power rule for logs to a single logarithm with a leading coefficient of 1. Because the logarithm of a power is the product of the exponent times the logarithm of the base, it...
body_xml:
<example number="5" title="Using the Power Rule in Reverse">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Rewrite $$4\ln(x)$$ using the power rule for logs to a single logarithm with a leading coefficient of 1.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Because the logarithm of a power is the product of the exponent times the logarithm of the base, it follows that the product of a number and a logarithm can be written as a power. For the expression $$4\ln(x),$$ we identify the factor, 4, as the exponent and the argument, $$x,$$ as the base, and rewrite the product as a logarithm of a power: $$4\ln(x) = \ln(x^{4}).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>

title: Expanding Logarithms Using Product, Quotient, and Power Rules
snippet: Expanding Logarithms Using Product, Quotient, and Power Rules: Rewrite \ln\left( \frac{x^{4}y}{7} \right) as a sum or difference of logs. First, because we have a quotient of two expressions, we can use the quotient rule: \ln\left(...
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Expanding Logarithms Using Product, Quotient, and Power Rules">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Rewrite $$\ln\left( \frac{x^{4}y}{7} \right)$$ as a sum or difference of logs.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, because we have a quotient of two expressions, we can use the quotient rule:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\ln\left( \frac{x^{4}y}{7} \right) = \ln\left( {x^{4}y} \right) - \ln(7)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then seeing the product in the first term, we use the product rule:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\ln\left( {x^{4}y} \right) - \ln(7) = \ln\left( x^{4} \right) + \ln(y) - \ln(7)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Finally, we use the power rule on the first term:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\ln\left( x^{4} \right) + \ln(y) - \ln(7) = 4\ln(x) + \ln(y) - \ln(7)$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Expanding Complex Logarithmic Expressions
snippet: Expanding Complex Logarithmic Expressions: Expand \log_{6}\left( \frac{64x^{3}\left( {4x + 1} \right)}{\left( {2x - 1} \right)} \right). We can expand by applying the Product and Quotient Rules. \begin{array}{lll} {\log_{6}\left(...
body_xml:
<example number="8" title="Expanding Complex Logarithmic Expressions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Expand $$\log_{6}\left( \frac{64x^{3}\left( {4x + 1} \right)}{\left( {2x - 1} \right)} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We can expand by applying the Product and Quotient Rules.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lll} {\log_{6}\left( \frac{64x^{3}(4x + 1)}{(2x - 1)} \right)} & {= \log_{6}64 + \log_{6}x^{3} + \log_{6}(4x + 1) - \log_{6}(2x - 1)} & { \text{Apply the Quotient Rule} .} \\ & {= \log_{6}2^{6} + \log_{6}x^{3} + \log_{6}(4x + 1) - \log_{6}(2x - 1)} & { \text{Simplify by writing 64 as 2} ^{6}.} \\ & {= 6\log_{6}2 + 3\log_{6}x + \log_{6}(4x + 1) - \log_{6}(2x - 1)} & { \text{Apply the Power Rule} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: How To

      <item>Next apply the product property. Rewrite sums of logarithms as the logarithm of a product.</item>

title: Using the Product and Quotient Rules to Combine Logarithms
snippet: Using the Product and Quotient Rules to Combine Logarithms: Write \log_{3}(5) + \log_{3}(8) - \log_{3}(2) as a single logarithm. Using the product and quotient rules \log_{3}(5) + \log_{3}(8) = \log_{3}\left( {5 \cdot 8} \right) =...
body_xml:
<example number="9" title="Using the Product and Quotient Rules to Combine Logarithms">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write $$\log_{3}(5) + \log_{3}(8) - \log_{3}(2)$$ as a single logarithm.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Using the product and quotient rules</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{3}(5) + \log_{3}(8) = \log_{3}\left( {5 \cdot 8} \right) = \log_{3}(40)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This reduces our original expression to</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{3}(40) - \log_{3}(2)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then, using the quotient rule</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{3}(40) - \log_{3}(2) = \log_{3}\left( \frac{40}{2} \right) = \log_{3}(20)$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Condensing Complex Logarithmic Expressions
snippet: Condensing Complex Logarithmic Expressions: Condense \log_{2}\left( x^{2} \right) + \frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left( {x - 1} \right) - 3\log_{2}\left( \left( {x + 3} \right)^{2} \right). We apply the power rule first: \log_{2}\left( x^{2} \right)...
body_xml:
<example number="10" title="Condensing Complex Logarithmic Expressions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Condense $$\log_{2}\left( x^{2} \right) + \frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left( {x - 1} \right) - 3\log_{2}\left( \left( {x + 3} \right)^{2} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We apply the power rule first:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{2}\left( x^{2} \right) + \frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left( {x - 1} \right) - 3\log_{2}\left( \left( {x + 3} \right)^{2} \right) = \log_{2}\left( x^{2} \right) + \log_{2}\left( \sqrt{x - 1} \right) - \log_{2}\left( \left( {x + 3} \right)^{6} \right)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next we apply the product rule to the sum:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{2}\left( x^{2} \right) + \log_{2}\left( \sqrt{x - 1} \right) - \log_{2}\left( \left( {x + 3} \right)^{6} \right) = \log_{2}\left( {x^{2}\sqrt{x - 1}} \right) - \log_{2}\left( \left( {x + 3} \right)^{6} \right)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Finally, we apply the quotient rule to the difference:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{2}\left( {x^{2}\sqrt{x - 1}} \right) - \log_{2}\left( \left( {x + 3} \right)^{6} \right) = \log_{2}\frac{x^{2}\sqrt{x - 1}}{\left( {x + 3} \right)^{6}}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Rewriting as a Single Logarithm
snippet: Rewriting as a Single Logarithm: Rewrite 2\log x - 4\log(x + 5) + \frac{1}{x}\log\left( {3x + 5} \right) as a single logarithm. We apply the power rule first: {2\log x-4\log(x + 5)} + {\frac{1}{x}{\log(3x + 5)}} = \log\left( x^{2} \right)...
body_xml:
<example number="11" title="Rewriting as a Single Logarithm">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Rewrite $$2\log x - 4\log(x + 5) + \frac{1}{x}\log\left( {3x + 5} \right)$$ as a single logarithm.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We apply the power rule first:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${2\log x-4\log(x + 5)} + {\frac{1}{x}{\log(3x + 5)}} = \log\left( x^{2} \right) - \log\left( {x + 5} \right)^{4} + \log\left( {(3x + 5)}^{x^{- 1}} \right)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next we rearrange and apply the product rule to the sum:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\log\left( x^{2} \right) - \log(x + 5)^{4} + \log\left( {(3x + 5)}^{x^{- 1}} \right)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$= \log\left( x^{2} \right) + \log\left( {(3x + 5)}^{x^{- 1}} \right) - \log(x + 5)^{4}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$= \log\left( x^{2}{(3x + 5)}^{x^{- 1}} \right) - \log(x + 5)^{4}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Finally, we apply the quotient rule to the difference:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$= \log{\left( x^{2}(3x + 5)^{x^{-1}} \right) -}{\log(x + 5)}^{4} = \log\frac{x^{2}(3x + 5)^{x^{-1}}}{(x + 5)^{4}}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Applying of the Laws of Logs
snippet: Applying of the Laws of Logs: Recall that, in chemistry, \text{pH} = - \log\lbrack H^{+}\rbrack. If the concentration of hydrogen ions in a liquid is doubled, what is the effect on pH? Suppose C is the original concentration of hydrogen...
body_xml:
<example number="12" title="Applying of the Laws of Logs">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Recall that, in chemistry, $$\text{pH} = - \log\lbrack H^{+}\rbrack.$$ If the concentration of hydrogen ions in a liquid is doubled, what is the effect on pH?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Suppose $$C$$ is the original concentration of hydrogen ions, and $$P$$ is the original pH of the liquid. Then $$P = -\log(C).$$ If the concentration is doubled, the new concentration is $$2C.$$ Then the pH of the new liquid is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\text{pH} = - \log\left( {2C} \right)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Using the product rule of logs</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\text{pH} = - \log\left( {2C} \right) = - \left( {\log(2) + \log(C)} \right) = - \log(2) - \log(C)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$P = -\log(C),$$ the new pH is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\text{pH} = P - \log(2) \approx P - 0.301$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>When the concentration of hydrogen ions is doubled, the pH decreases by about 0.301.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: The Change-of-Base Formula
snippet: The Change-of-Base Formula: The change-of-base formula can be used to evaluate a logarithm with any base. For any positive real numbers M,b, and n, where n \neq 1 and b \neq 1, \log_{b}M=\frac{\log_{n}M}{\log_{n}b}. It follows that the...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="The Change-of-Base Formula" title="The Change-of-Base Formula">
    <paragraph>The change-of-base formula can be used to evaluate a logarithm with any base.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For any positive real numbers $$M,b,$$ and $$n,$$ where $$n \neq 1$$ and $$b \neq 1,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{b}M=\frac{\log_{n}M}{\log_{n}b}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>It follows that the change-of-base formula can be used to rewrite a logarithm with any base as the quotient of common or natural logs.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{b}M = \frac{\ln M}{\ln b}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{b}M = \frac{\log M}{\log b}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given a logarithm with the form \log_{b}M, use the change-of-base formula to rewrite it as a quotient of logs with any positive base n, where n \neq 1. Determine the new base n, remembering that the common log, \log(x), has base...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given a logarithm with the form $$\log_{b}M,$$ use the change-of-base formula to rewrite it as a quotient of logs with any positive base $$n,$$ where $$n \neq 1.$$</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Determine the new base $$n,$$ remembering that the common log, $$\log(x),$$ has base 10, and the natural log, $$\ln(x),$$ has base $$e.$$</item>
      <item>Rewrite the log as a quotient using the change-of-base formula The numerator of the quotient will be a logarithm with base $$n$$ and argument $$M.$$ The denominator of the quotient will be a logarithm with base $$n$$ and argument $$b.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Changing Logarithmic Expressions to Expressions Involving Only Natural Logs
snippet: Changing Logarithmic Expressions to Expressions Involving Only Natural Logs: Change \log_{5}3 to a quotient of natural logarithms. Because we will be expressing \log_{5}3 as a quotient of natural logarithms, the new base, n = e. We rewrite...

<example number="13" title="Changing Logarithmic Expressions to Expressions Involving Only Natural Logs">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Change $$\log_{5}3$$ to a quotient of natural logarithms.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Because we will be expressing $$\log_{5}3$$ as a quotient of natural logarithms, the new base, $$n = e.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We rewrite the log as a quotient using the change-of-base formula. The numerator of the quotient will be the natural log with argument 3. The denominator of the quotient will be the natural log with argument 5.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {\log_{b}M} & {= \frac{\ln M}{\ln b}} \\ {\log_{5}3} & {= \frac{\ln 3}{\ln 5}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using the Change-of-Base Formula with a Calculator
snippet: Using the Change-of-Base Formula with a Calculator: Evaluate \log_{2}(10) using the change-of-base formula with a calculator. According to the change-of-base formula, we can rewrite the log base 2 as a logarithm of any other base. Since...
body_xml:
<example number="14" title="Using the Change-of-Base Formula with a Calculator">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\log_{2}(10)$$ using the change-of-base formula with a calculator.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>According to the change-of-base formula, we can rewrite the log base 2 as a logarithm of any other base. Since our calculators can evaluate the natural log, we might choose to use the natural logarithm, which is the log base $$e.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {\log_{2}10 = \frac{\ln 10}{\ln 2}} & { \text{Apply the change of base formula using base} e.} \\ {\approx 3.3219} & { \text{Use a calculator to evaluate to 4 decimal places} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Solving an Exponential Equation with a Common Base">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve $$2^{x - 1} = 2^{2x - 4}.$$</paragraph>

    <solution>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} { 2^{x - 1} = 2^{2x - 4}} & { \text{The common base is} 2.} \\ {x - 1 = 2x - 4\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{By the one-to-one property the exponents must be equal} .} \\ {x = 3} & { \text{Solve for} x.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

title: Solving an Equation Containing Powers of Different Bases
snippet: Solving an Equation Containing Powers of Different Bases: Solve 5^{x + 2} = 4^{x}. \begin{array}{ll} {5^{x + 2} = 4^{x}} & { \text{There is no easy way to get the powers to have the same base} .} \\ {\ln 5^{x + 2} = \ln 4^{x}} & {...
body_xml:
<example number="5" title="Solving an Equation Containing Powers of Different Bases">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve $$5^{x + 2} = 4^{x}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {5^{x + 2} = 4^{x}} & { \text{There is no easy way to get the powers to have the same base} .} \\ {\ln 5^{x + 2} = \ln 4^{x}} & { \text{Take ln of both sides} .} \\ {(x + 2)\ln 5 = x\ln 4} & { \text{Use laws of logs} .} \\ {x\ln 5 + 2\ln 5 = x\ln 4} & { \text{Use the distributive law} .} \\ {x\ln 5 - x\ln 4 = - 2\ln 5} & { \text{Get terms containing} x \text{on one side, terms without} x \text{on the other} .} \\ {x(\ln 5 - \ln 4) = - 2\ln 5} & { \text{On the left hand side, factor out an} x.} \\ {x\ln\left( \frac{5}{4} \right) = \ln\left( \frac{1}{25} \right)\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & \text{Use the laws of logs.} \\ {x = \frac{\ln\left( \frac{1}{25} \right)}{\ln\left( \frac{5}{4} \right)}} & { \text{Divide by the coefficient of} x.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

Use the fact that} \ln(x) \text{and} e^{x} \text{are inverse functions} .} \\ t & {= \frac{\ln 5}{2}} & { \text{Divide by the coefficient of} t.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

title: Solving Exponential Functions in Quadratic Form
snippet: Solving Exponential Functions in Quadratic Form: Solve e^{2x} - e^{x} = 56. \begin{array}{rll} {e^{2x} - e^{x}} & {= 56} & \\ {e^{2x} - e^{x} - 56} & {= 0} & { \text{Get one side of the equation equal to zero} .} \\ {(e^{x} + 7)(e^{x} -...
body_xml:
<example number="8" title="Solving Exponential Functions in Quadratic Form">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve $$e^{2x} - e^{x} = 56.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {e^{2x} - e^{x}} & {= 56} & \\ {e^{2x} - e^{x} - 56} & {= 0} & { \text{Get one side of the equation equal to zero} .} \\ {(e^{x} + 7)(e^{x} - 8)} & {= 0} & { \text{Factor by the FOIL method} .} \\ {e^{x} + 7} & {= 0 \text{or} e^{x} - 8 = 0\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{If a product is zero, then one factor must be zero} .} \\ e^{x} & {= - 7{ \text{or e} }^{x} = 8} & { \text{Isolate the exponentials} .} \\ e^{x} & {= 8} & { \text{Reject the equation in which the power equals a negative number} .} \\ x & {= \ln 8} & { \text{Solve the equation in which the power equals a positive number} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>When we plan to use factoring to solve a problem, we always get zero on one side of the equation, because zero has the unique property that when a product is zero, one or both of the factors must be zero. We reject the equation $$e^{x} = -7$$ because a positive number never equals a negative number. The solution $$\ln(-7)$$ is not a real number, and in the real number system this solution is rejected as an extraneous solution.</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Using the Definition of a Logarithm to Solve Logarithmic Equations: For any algebraic expression S and real numbers b and c, where b > 0, b \neq 1, \log_{b}(S) = c \text{if and only if} b^{c} = S
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Using the Definition of a Logarithm to Solve Logarithmic Equations" title="Using the Definition of a Logarithm to Solve Logarithmic Equations">
    <paragraph>For any algebraic expression $$S$$ and real numbers $$b$$ and $$c,$$ where $$b > 0, b \neq 1,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{b}(S) = c \text{if and only if} b^{c} = S$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Using Algebra to Solve a Logarithmic Equation

body_xml:
<example number="9" title="Using Algebra to Solve a Logarithmic Equation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve $$2\ln x + 3 = 7.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {2\ln x + 3 = 7} & \\ {2\ln x = 4} & { \text{Subtract 3} .} \\ {\ln x = 2} & { \text{Divide by 2} .} \\ {x = e^{2}} & { \text{Rewrite in exponential form} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="10" title="Using Algebra Before and After Using the Definition of the Natural Logarithm">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve $$2\ln(6x) = 7.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {2\ln(6x) = 7} & \\ {\ln(6x) = \frac{7}{2}} & { \text{Divide by 2} .} \\ {6x = e^{(\frac{7}{2})}} & { \text{Use the definition of} \ln.} \\ {x = \frac{1}{6}e^{(\frac{7}{2})}} & { \text{Divide by 6} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using a Graph to Understand the Solution to a Logarithmic Equation
snippet: Using a Graph to Understand the Solution to a Logarithmic Equation: Solve \ln x = 3. \begin{array}{ll} {\ln x = 3} & \\ {x = e^{3}} & { \text{Use the definition of the natural logarithm} .} \end{array} Figure 3 represents the graph of the...
body_xml: Solve $$\ln x = 3.$$ $$\begin{array}{ll} {\ln x = 3} & \\ {x = e^{3}} & { \text{Use the definition of the natural logarithm} .} \end{array}$$ Figure 3 represents the graph of the equation. On the graph, the x-coordinate of the point at which the two graphs intersect is close to 20. In other words $$e^{3} \approx 20.$$ A calculator gives a better approximation: $$e^{3} \approx 20.0855.$$

title: Using the One-to-One Property of Logarithms to Solve Logarithmic Equations
source_type: Using the One-to-One Property of Logarithms to Solve Logarithmic Equations
snippet: Using the One-to-One Property of Logarithms to Solve Logarithmic Equations: For any algebraic expressions S and T and any positive real number b, where b \neq 1, \log_{b}S = \log_{b}T \text{if and only if} S = T Note, when solving an...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Using the One-to-One Property of Logarithms to Solve Logarithmic Equations" title="Using the One-to-One Property of Logarithms to Solve Logarithmic Equations">
    <paragraph>For any algebraic expressions $$S$$ and $$T$$ and any positive real number $$b,$$ where $$b \neq 1,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\log_{b}S = \log_{b}T \text{if and only if} S = T$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Note, when solving an equation involving logarithms, always check to see if the answer is correct or if it is an extraneous solution.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given an equation containing logarithms, solve it using the one-to-one property. Use the rules of logarithms to combine like terms, if necessary, so that the resulting equation has the form \log_{b}S = \log_{b}T. Use the one-to-one...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given an equation containing logarithms, solve it using the one-to-one property.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Use the rules of logarithms to combine like terms, if necessary, so that the resulting equation has the form $$\log_{b}S = \log_{b}T.$$</item>
      <item>Use the one-to-one property to set the arguments equal.</item>
      <item>Solve the resulting equation, $$S = T,$$ for the unknown.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Solving an Equation Using the One-to-One Property of Logarithms
snippet: Solving an Equation Using the One-to-One Property of Logarithms: Solve \ln(x^{2}) = \ln(2x + 3). \begin{array}{ll} {\ln(x^{2}) = \ln(2x + 3)} & \\ {x^{2} = 2x + 3} & { \text{Use the one-to-one property of the logarithm} .} \\ {x^{2} - 2x -...
body_xml:
<example number="12" title="Solving an Equation Using the One-to-One Property of Logarithms">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve $$\ln(x^{2}) = \ln(2x + 3).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {\ln(x^{2}) = \ln(2x + 3)} & \\ {x^{2} = 2x + 3} & { \text{Use the one-to-one property of the logarithm} .} \\ {x^{2} - 2x - 3 = 0} & { \text{Get zero on one side before factoring} .} \\ {(x - 3)(x + 1) = 0} & { \text{Factor using FOIL} .} \\ {x - 3 = 0 \text{or} x + 1 = 0\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{If a product is zero, one of the factors must be zero} .} \\ {x = 3 \text{or} x = - 1} & { \text{Solve for} x.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>There are two solutions: $$3$$ or $$-1.$$ The solution $$-1$$ is negative, but it checks when substituted into the original equation because the argument of the logarithm functions is still positive.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Using the Formula for Radioactive Decay to Find the Quantity of a Substance
snippet: Using the Formula for Radioactive Decay to Find the Quantity of a Substance: How long will it take for ten percent of a 1000-gram sample of uranium-235 to decay? \begin{array}{ll} {y = \text{1000} e\frac{\ln(0.5)}{ \text{703,800,000} }t} &...
body_xml:
<example number="13" title="Using the Formula for Radioactive Decay to Find the Quantity of a Substance">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>How long will it take for ten percent of a 1000-gram sample of uranium-235 to decay?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {y = \text{1000} e\frac{\ln(0.5)}{ \text{703,800,000} }t} & \\ {900 = 1000e^{\frac{\ln(0.5)}{ \text{703,800,000} }t}} & { \text{After 10\% decays, 900 grams are left} .} \\ {0.9 = e^{\frac{\ln(0.5)}{ \text{703,800,000} }t}} & { \text{Divide by 1000} .} \\ {\ln(0.9) = \ln\left( e^{\frac{\ln(0.5)}{ \text{703,800,000} }t} \right)} & { \text{Take ln of both sides} .} \\ {\ln(0.9) = \frac{\ln(0.5)}{ \text{703,800,000} }t} & {\ln (e^{M}) = M} \\ {t = \text{703,800,000} \times \frac{\ln(0.9)}{\ln(0.5)} \text{years} \begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{Solve for} t.} \\ {t \approx \text{106,979,777 years} } & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>Ten percent of 1000 grams is 100 grams. If 100 grams decay, the amount of uranium-235 remaining is 900 grams.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Graphing Exponential Growth
snippet: Graphing Exponential Growth: A population of bacteria doubles every hour. If the culture started with 10 bacteria, graph the population as a function of time. When an amount grows at a fixed percent per unit time, the growth is...
body_xml: A population of bacteria doubles every hour. If the culture started with 10 bacteria, graph the population as a function of time. When an amount grows at a fixed percent per unit time, the growth is exponential. To find $$A_{0}$$ we use the fact that $$A_{0}$$ is the amount at time zero, so $$A_{0} = 10.$$ To find $$k,$$ use the fact that after one hour $$\left( {t = 1} \right)$$ the population doubles from $$10$$ to $$20.$$ The formula is derived as follows $$\begin{array}{ll} {20 = 10e^{k \cdot 1}} & \\ {2 = e^{k}} & \text{Divide by 10} \\ {\ln 2 = k} & \text{Take the natural logarithm} \end{array}$$ so $$k = \ln(2).$$ Thus the equation we want to graph is $$y = 10e^{(\ln 2)t} = 10{(e^{\ln 2})}^{t} = 10 \cdot 2^{t}.$$ The graph is shown in Figure 5. The population of bacteria after ten hours is 10,240. We could describe this amount is being of the order of magnitude $$10^{4}.$$ The population of bacteria after twenty hours is 10,485,760 which is of the order of magnitude $$10^{7},$$ so we could say that the population has increased by three orders of magnitude in ten hours.

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given the half-life, find the decay rate. Write A = A_{o}e^{kt}. Replace A by \frac{1}{2}A_{0} and replace t by the given half-life. Solve to find k. Express k as an exact value (do not round). Note: It is also possible to find the...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given the half-life, find the decay rate.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Write $$A = A_{o}e^{kt}.$$</item>
      <item>Replace $$A$$ by $$\frac{1}{2}A_{0}$$ and replace $$t$$ by the given half-life.</item>
      <item>Solve to find $$k.$$ Express $$k$$ as an exact value (do not round).</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Note: It is also possible to find the decay rate using $$k = - \frac{\ln(2)}{t}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding the Function that Describes Radioactive Decay
snippet: Finding the Function that Describes Radioactive Decay: The half-life of carbon-14 is 5,730 years. Express the amount of carbon-14 remaining as a function of time, t. This formula is derived as follows. \begin{array}{ll} {A = A_{0}e^{kt}} &...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Finding the Function that Describes Radioactive Decay">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The half-life of carbon-14 is 5,730 years. Express the amount of carbon-14 remaining as a function of time, $$t.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This formula is derived as follows.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {A = A_{0}e^{kt}} & { \text{The continuous growth formula} .} \\ {0.5A_{0} = A_{0}e^{k \cdot 5730}} & { \text{Substitute the half-life for} t \text{and} 0.5A_{0} \text{for} f(t).} \\ {0.5 = e^{5730k}} & { \text{Divide by} A_{0}.} \\ {\ln(0.5) = 5730k} & { \text{Take the natural log of both sides} .} \\ {k = \frac{\ln(0.5)}{5730}} & { \text{Divide by the coefficient of} k.} \\ {A = A_{0}e^{{(\frac{\ln(0.5)}{5730})}t}} & { \text{Substitute for} r \text{in the continuous growth formula} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The function that describes this continuous decay is $$f(t) = A_{0}e^{{(\frac{\ln(0.5)}{5730})}t}.$$ We observe that the coefficient of $$t,$$ $$\frac{\ln(0.5)}{5730} \approx - 1.2097 \times 10^{-4}$$ is negative, as expected in the case of exponential decay.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">

title: Finding the Age of a Bone
snippet: Finding the Age of a Bone: A bone fragment is found that contains 20% of its original carbon-14. To the nearest year, how old is the bone? We substitute 20\% = 0.20 for r in the equation and solve for t: \begin{array}{ll} {t =...
body_xml:
<example number="3" title="Finding the Age of a Bone">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A bone fragment is found that contains 20% of its original carbon-14. To the nearest year, how old is the bone?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We substitute $$20\% = 0.20$$ for $$r$$ in the equation and solve for $$t:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {t = \frac{\ln(r)}{- 0.000121}} & { \text{Use the general form of the equation} .} \\ {= \frac{\ln(0.20)}{- 0.000121}\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{Substitute for} r.} \\ {\approx 13301} & { \text{Round to the nearest year} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The bone fragment is about 13,301 years old.</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>The instruments that measure the percentage of carbon-14 are extremely sensitive and, as we mention above, a scientist will need to do much more work than we did in order to be satisfied. Even so, carbon dating is only accurate to about 1%, so this age should be given as $$\text{13,301 years} \pm \text{1\% or 13,301 years} \pm \text{133 years} .$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Finding a Function That Describes Exponential Growth
snippet: Finding a Function That Describes Exponential Growth: According to Moore’s Law, the doubling time for the number of transistors that can be put on a computer chip is approximately two years. Give a function that describes this behavior....
body_xml:
<example number="4" title="Finding a Function That Describes Exponential Growth">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>According to Moore’s Law, the doubling time for the number of transistors that can be put on a computer chip is approximately two years. Give a function that describes this behavior.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The formula is derived as follows:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {t = \frac{\ln 2}{k}} & { \text{The doubling time formula} .} \\ {2 = \frac{\ln 2}{k}} & { \text{Use a doubling time of two years} .} \\ {k = \frac{\ln 2}{2}} & { \text{Multiply by} k \text{and divide by 2} .} \\ {A = A_{0}e^{\frac{\ln 2}{2}t}\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{Substitute} k \text{into the continuous growth formula} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The function is $$A_{0}e^{\frac{\ln 2}{2}t}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Newton’s Law of Cooling
snippet: Newton’s Law of Cooling: The temperature of an object, T, in surrounding air with temperature T_{s} will behave according to the formula T(t) = Ae^{kt} + T_{s} where t is time A is the difference between the initial temperature of the...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Newton’s Law of Cooling" title="Newton’s Law of Cooling">
    <paragraph>The temperature of an object, $$T,$$ in surrounding air with temperature $$T_{s}$$ will behave according to the formula</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$T(t) = Ae^{kt} + T_{s}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>$$t$$ is time</item>
      <item>$$A$$ is the difference between the initial temperature of the object and the surroundings</item>
      <item>$$k$$ is a constant, the continuous rate of cooling of the object</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Using Newton’s Law of Cooling
snippet: Using Newton’s Law of Cooling: A cheesecake is taken out of the oven with an ideal internal temperature of \text{165°F,} and is placed into a 35{^\circ}F refrigerator. After 10 minutes, the cheesecake has cooled to \text{150°F} . If we...
body_xml:
<example number="5" title="Using Newton’s Law of Cooling">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A cheesecake is taken out of the oven with an ideal internal temperature of $$\text{165°F,}$$ and is placed into a $$35{^\circ}F$$ refrigerator. After 10 minutes, the cheesecake has cooled to $$\text{150°F} .$$ If we must wait until the cheesecake has cooled to $$\text{70°F}$$ before we eat it, how long will we have to wait?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Because the surrounding air temperature in the refrigerator is 35 degrees, the cheesecake’s temperature will decay exponentially toward 35, following the equation</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$T(t) = Ae^{kt} + 35$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We know the initial temperature was 165, so $$T(0) = 165.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {165 = Ae^{k0} + 35} & { \text{Substitute} (0,165).} \\ { A = 130} & { \text{Solve for} A.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We were given another data point, $$T(10) = 150,$$ which we can use to solve for $$k.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {150 = 130e^{k10} + 35} & { \text{Substitute (10, 150)} .} \\ {115 = 130e^{k10}} & { \text{Subtract 35} .} \\ {\frac{115}{130} = e^{10k}} & { \text{Divide by 130} .} \\ {\ln\left( \frac{115}{130} \right) = 10k} & { \text{Take the natural log of both sides} .} \\ {k = \frac{\ln\left( \frac{115}{130} \right)}{10} \approx - 0.0123} & { \text{Divide by the coefficient of} k.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This gives us the equation for the cooling of the cheesecake: $$T(t) = 130e^{-0.0123t} + 35.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now we can solve for the time it will take for the temperature to cool to 70 degrees.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {70 = 130e^{- 0.0123t} + 35} & { \text{Substitute in 70 for} T(t).} \\ {35 = 130e^{- 0.0123t}} & { \text{Subtract 35} .} \\ {\frac{35}{130} = e^{- 0.0123t}} & { \text{Divide by 130} .} \\ {\ln(\frac{35}{130}) = - 0.0123t} & \text{Take the natural log of both sides} \\ {t = \frac{\ln(\frac{35}{130})}{- 0.0123} \approx 106.68} & { \text{Divide by the coefficient of} t.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>It will take about 107 minutes, or one hour and 47 minutes, for the cheesecake to cool to $$\text{70°F} .$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Logistic Growth
snippet: Logistic Growth: The logistic growth model is f(t) = \frac{c}{1 + ae^{- bt}} where \frac{c}{1 + a} is the initial value c is the carrying capacity, or limiting value b is a constant determined by the rate of growth.
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Logistic Growth" title="Logistic Growth">
    <paragraph>The logistic growth model is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(t) = \frac{c}{1 + ae^{- bt}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>$$\frac{c}{1 + a}$$ is the initial value</item>
      <item>$$c$$ is the carrying capacity, or limiting value</item>
      <item>$$b$$ is a constant determined by the rate of growth.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Using the Logistic-Growth Model
snippet: Using the Logistic-Growth Model: An influenza epidemic spreads through a population rapidly, at a rate that depends on two factors: The more people who have the flu, the more rapidly it spreads, and also the more uninfected people there...
body_xml: An influenza epidemic spreads through a population rapidly, at a rate that depends on two factors: The more people who have the flu, the more rapidly it spreads, and also the more uninfected people there are, the more rapidly it spreads. These two factors make the logistic model a good one to study the spread of communicable diseases. And, clearly, there is a maximum value for the number of people infected: the entire population. For example, at time $$t = 0$$ there is one person in a community of 1,000 people who has the flu. So, in that community, at most 1,000 people can have the flu. Researchers find that for this particular strain of the flu, the logistic growth constant is $$b = 0.6030.$$ Estimate the number of people in this community who will have had this flu after ten days. Predict how many people in this community will have had this flu after a long period of time has passed. We substitute the given data into the logistic growth model $$f(t) = \frac{c}{1 + ae^{- bt}}$$ Because at most 1,000 people, the entire population of the community, can get the flu, we know the limiting value is $$c = 1000.$$ To find $$a,$$ we use the formula that the number of cases at time $$t = 0$$ is $$\frac{c}{1 + a} = 1,$$ from which it follows that $$a = 999.$$ This model predicts that, after ten days, the number of people who have had the flu is $$f(t) = \frac{1000}{1 + 999e^{- 0.6030x}} \approx 293.8.$$ Because the actual number must be a whole number (a person has either had the flu or not) we round to 294. In the long term, the number of people who will contract the flu is the limiting value, $$c = 1000.$$ Remember that, because we are dealing with a virus, we cannot predict with certainty the number of people infected. The model only approximates the number of people infected and will not give us exact or actual values. The graph in Figure 7 gives a good picture of how this model fits the data.

title: Choosing a Mathematical Model
snippet: Choosing a Mathematical Model: Does a linear, exponential, logarithmic, or logistic model best fit the values listed in Table 1? Find the model, and use a graph to check your choice. x 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 y 0 1.386 2.197 2.773 3.219 3.584...
body_xml:
Does a linear, exponential, logarithmic, or logistic model best fit the values listed in Table 1? Find the model, and use a graph to check your choice. $$x$$ 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 $$y$$ 0 1.386 2.197 2.773 3.219 3.584 3.892 4.159 4.394
First, plot the data on a graph as in Figure 8. For the purpose of graphing, round the data to two decimal places. Clearly, the points do not lie on a straight line, so we reject a linear model. If we draw a line between any two of the points, most or all of the points between those two points lie above the line, so the graph is concave down, suggesting a logarithmic model. We can try $$y = a\ln(bx).$$ Plugging in the first point, $$\left( \text{1,0} \right),$$ gives $$0 = a\ln b.$$ We reject the case that $$a = 0$$ (if it were, all outputs would be 0), so we know $$\ln(b) = 0.$$ Thus $$b = 1$$ and $$y = a\ln\left( \text{x} \right).$$ Next we can use the point $$\left( { \text{9,4} \text{.394} } \right)$$ to solve for $$a:$$ $$\begin{array}{l} {y = a\ln(x)} \\ {4.394 = a\ln(9)} \\ {a = \frac{4.394}{\ln(9)}} \end{array}$$ Because $$a = \frac{4.394}{\ln(9)} \approx 2,$$ an appropriate model for the data is $$y = 2\ln(x).$$ To check the accuracy of the model, we graph the function together with the given points as in Figure 9. We can conclude that the model is a good fit to the data. Compare Figure 9 to the graph of $$y = \ln\left( x^{2} \right)$$ shown in Figure 10. The graphs appear to be identical when $$x > 0.$$ A quick check confirms this conclusion: $$y = \ln\left( x^{2} \right) = 2\ln(x)$$ for $$x > 0.$$ However, if $$x < 0,$$ the graph of $$y = \ln\left( x^{2} \right)$$ includes a “extra” branch, as shown in Figure 11. This occurs because, while $$y = 2\ln(x)$$ cannot have negative values in the domain (as such values would force the argument to be negative), the function $$y = \ln\left( x^{2} \right)$$ can have negative domain values.

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given a model with the form y = ab^{x}, change it to the form y = A_{0}e^{kx}. Rewrite y = ab^{x} as y = ae^{\ln{(b^{x})}}. Use the power rule of logarithms to rewrite y as y = ae^{x\ln{(b)}} = ae^{\ln{(b)}x}. Note that a = A_{0}...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given a model with the form $$y = ab^{x},$$ change it to the form $$y = A_{0}e^{kx}.$$</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Rewrite $$y = ab^{x}$$ as $$y = ae^{\ln{(b^{x})}}.$$</item>
      <item>Use the power rule of logarithms to rewrite y as $$y = ae^{x\ln{(b)}} = ae^{\ln{(b)}x}.$$</item>
      <item>Note that $$a = A_{0}$$ and $$k = \ln(b)$$ in the equation $$y = A_{0}e^{kx}.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Changing to base e

    <paragraph>Exponential regression is used to model situations in which growth begins slowly and then accelerates rapidly without bound, or where decay begins rapidly and then slows down to get closer and closer to zero. We use the command “ExpReg” on a graphing utility to fit an exponential function to a set of data points. This returns an equation of the form, $$y = ab^{x}$$</paragraph>

    <list type="unordered">
      <item>$$b$$ must be non-negative.</item>
      <item>when $$b > 1,$$ we have an exponential growth model.</item>
      <item>when $$0 < b < 1,$$ we have an exponential decay model.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Using Exponential Regression to Fit a Model to Data
snippet: Using Exponential Regression to Fit a Model to Data: In 2007, a university study was published investigating the crash risk of alcohol impaired driving. Data from 2,871 crashes were used to measure the association of a person’s blood...
body_xml:
In 2007, a university study was published investigating the crash risk of alcohol impaired driving. Data from 2,871 crashes were used to measure the association of a person’s blood alcohol level (BAC) with the risk of being in an accident. Table 1 shows results from the study 9. The relative risk is a measure of how many times more likely a person is to crash. So, for example, a person with a BAC of 0.09 is 3.54 times as likely to crash as a person who has not been drinking alcohol. BAC 0 0.01 0.03 0.05 0.07 0.09 Relative Risk of Crashing 1 1.03 1.06 1.38 2.09 3.54 BAC 0.11 0.13 0.15 0.17 0.19 0.21 Relative Risk of Crashing 6.41 12.6 22.1 39.05 65.32 99.78
Let $$x$$ represent the BAC level, and let $$y$$ represent the corresponding relative risk. Use exponential regression to fit a model to these data. After 6 drinks, a person weighing 160 pounds will have a BAC of about $$0.16.$$ How many times more likely is a person with this weight to crash if they drive after having a 6-pack of beer? Round to the nearest hundredth. Using the STAT then EDIT menu on a graphing utility, list the BAC values in L1 and the relative risk values in L2. Then use the STATPLOT feature to verify that the scatterplot follows the exponential pattern shown in Figure 1: Figure 1 Use the “ExpReg” command from the STAT then CALC menu to obtain the exponential model, $$y = 0.58304829\left( {2.20720213 \text{E} 10} \right)^{x}$$ Converting from scientific notation, we have: $$y = 0.58304829\left( \text{22,072,021,300} \right)^{x}$$ Notice that $$r^{2} \approx 0.97$$ which indicates the model is a good fit to the data. To see this, graph the model in the same window as the scatterplot to verify it is a good fit as shown in Figure 2: Figure 2 Use the model to estimate the risk associated with a BAC of $$0.16.$$ Substitute $$0.16$$ for $$x$$ in the model and solve for $$y.$$ $$\begin{array}{lll} y & {= 0.58304829\left( \text{22,072,021,300} \right)^{x}} & { \text{Use the regression model found in part (a)} .} \\ & {= 0.58304829\left( \text{22,072,021,300} \right)^{0.16}} & { \text{Substitute 0} \text{.16 for} x.} \\ & {\approx \text{26} \text{.35} } & { \text{Round to the nearest hundredth} .} \end{array}$$ If a 160-pound person drives after having 6 drinks, they are about 26.35 times more likely to crash than if driving while sober.

title: Using Logarithmic Regression to Fit a Model to Data
snippet: Using Logarithmic Regression to Fit a Model to Data: Due to advances in medicine and higher standards of living, life expectancy has been increasing in most developed countries since the beginning of the 20th century. Table 3 shows the...
body_xml:
Due to advances in medicine and higher standards of living, life expectancy has been increasing in most developed countries since the beginning of the 20th century. Table 3 shows the average life expectancies, in years, of Americans from 1900–201010. Year 1900 1910 1920 1930 1940 1950 Life Expectancy(Years) 47.3 50.0 54.1 59.7 62.9 68.2 Year 1960 1970 1980 1990 2000 2010 Life Expectancy(Years) 69.7 70.8 73.7 75.4 76.8 78.7
ⓐ Let $$x$$ represent time in decades starting with $$x = 1$$ for the year 1900, $$x = 2$$ for the year 1910, and so on. Let $$y$$ represent the corresponding life expectancy. Use logarithmic regression to fit a model to these data. ⓑ Use the model to predict the average American life expectancy for the year 2030. ⓐ Using the STAT then EDIT menu on a graphing utility, list the years using values 1–12 in L1 and the corresponding life expectancy in L2. Then use the STATPLOT feature to verify that the scatterplot follows a logarithmic pattern as shown in Figure 3: Figure 3 Use the “LnReg” command from the STAT then CALC menu to obtain the logarithmic model, $$y = 42.52722583 + 13.85752327\ln(x)$$ Next, graph the model in the same window as the scatterplot to verify it is a good fit as shown in Figure 4: Figure 4 ⓑ To predict the life expectancy of an American in the year 2030, substitute $$x = 14$$ for the in the model and solve for $$y:$$ $$\begin{array}{lll} y & {= 42.52722583 + 13.85752327\ln(x)} & { \text{Use the regression model found in part (a)} .} \\ & {= 42.52722583 + 13.85752327\ln(14)} & { \text{Substitute 14 for} x.} \\ & {\approx \text{79} \text{.1} } & \text{Round to the nearest tenth.} \end{array}$$ If life expectancy continues to increase at this pace, the average life expectancy of an American will be 79.1 by the year 2030.

title: Using Logistic Regression to Fit a Model to Data
snippet: Using Logistic Regression to Fit a Model to Data: Mobile telephone service has increased rapidly in America since the mid 1990s. Today, almost all residents have cellular service. Table 5 shows the percentage of Americans with cellular...
body_xml:
Mobile telephone service has increased rapidly in America since the mid 1990s. Today, almost all residents have cellular service. Table 5 shows the percentage of Americans with cellular service between the years 1995 and 2012 11. Year Americans with Cellular Service (%) Year Americans with Cellular Service (%) 1995 12.69 2004 62.852 1996 16.35 2005 68.63 1997 20.29 2006 76.64 1998 25.08 2007 82.47 1999 30.81 2008 85.68 2000 38.75 2009 89.14 2001 45.00 2010 91.86 2002 49.16 2011 95.28 2003 55.15 2012 98.17
ⓐ Let $$x$$ represent time in years starting with $$x = 0$$ for the year 1995. Let $$y$$ represent the corresponding percentage of residents with cellular service. Use logistic regression to fit a model to these data. ⓑ Use the model to calculate the percentage of Americans with cell service in the year 2013. Round to the nearest tenth of a percent. ⓒ Discuss the value returned for the upper limit, $$c.$$ What does this tell you about the model? What would the limiting value be if the model were exact? ⓐ Using the STAT then EDIT menu on a graphing utility, list the years using values 0–15 in L1 and the corresponding percentage in L2. Then use the STATPLOT feature to verify that the scatterplot follows a logistic pattern as shown in Figure 5: Figure 5 Use the “Logistic” command from the STAT then CALC menu to obtain the logistic model, $$y = \frac{105.7379526}{1 + 6.88328979e^{- 0.2595440013x}}$$ Next, graph the model in the same window as shown in Figure 6 the scatterplot to verify it is a good fit: Figure 6 ⓑ To approximate the percentage of Americans with cellular service in the year 2013, substitute $$x = 18$$ for the in the model and solve for $$y:$$ $$\begin{array}{lll} y & {= \frac{105.7379526}{1 + 6.88328979e^{- 0.2595440013x}}} & { \text{Use the regression model found in part (a)} .} \\ & {= \frac{105.7379526}{1 + 6.88328979e^{- 0.2595440013(18)}}} & { \text{Substitute 18 for} x.} \\ & {\approx \text{99} \text{.3} } & \text{Round to the nearest tenth} \end{array}$$ According to the model, about 99.3% of Americans had cellular service in 2013. ⓒ The model gives a limiting value of about 105. This means that the maximum possible percentage of Americans with cellular service would be 105%, which is impossible. (How could over 100% of a population have cellular service?) If the model were exact, the limiting value would be $$c = 100$$ and the model’s outputs would get very close to, but never actually reach 100%. After all, there will always be someone out there without cellular service!

title: Types of Linear Systems
snippet: Types of Linear Systems: There are three types of systems of linear equations in two variables, and three types of solutions. An independent system has exactly one solution pair \left( {x,y} \right). The point where the two lines intersect...
body_xml: There are three types of systems of linear equations in two variables, and three types of solutions. An independent system has exactly one solution pair $$\left( {x,y} \right).$$ The point where the two lines intersect is the only solution. An inconsistent system has no solution. Notice that the two lines are parallel and will never intersect. A dependent system has infinitely many solutions. The lines are coincident. They are the same line, so every coordinate pair on the line is a solution to both equations. Figure 2 compares graphical representations of each type of system.

title: Determining Whether an Ordered Pair Is a Solution to a System of Equations
snippet: Determining Whether an Ordered Pair Is a Solution to a System of Equations: Determine whether the ordered pair \left( {5,1} \right) is a solution to the given system of equations. \begin{array}{l} { x + 3y = 8} \\ { 2x - 9 = y} \end{array}...
body_xml: Determine whether the ordered pair $$\left( {5,1} \right)$$ is a solution to the given system of equations. $$\begin{array}{l} { x + 3y = 8} \\ { 2x - 9 = y} \end{array}$$ Substitute the ordered pair $$\left( {5,1} \right)$$ into both equations. $$\begin{array}{ll} {(5) + 3(1) = 8} & \\ {8 = 8} & \text{True} \\ {2(5) - 9 = (1)} & \\ \text{1=1} & \text{True} \end{array}$$ The ordered pair $$\left( {5,1} \right)$$ satisfies both equations, so it is the solution to the system. We can see the solution clearly by plotting the graph of each equation. Since the solution is an ordered pair that satisfies both equations, it is a point on both of the lines and thus the point of intersection of the two lines. See Figure 3.

title: Solving a System of Equations in Two Variables by Graphing
snippet: Solving a System of Equations in Two Variables by Graphing: Solve the following system of equations by graphing. Identify the type of system. \begin{matrix} {2x + y = -8} \\ {x - y = -1} \end{matrix} Solve the first equation for y....
body_xml: Solve the following system of equations by graphing. Identify the type of system. $$\begin{matrix} {2x + y = -8} \\ {x - y = -1} \end{matrix}$$ Solve the first equation for $$y.$$ $$\begin{matrix} {2x + y = -8} \\ {y = -2x-8} \end{matrix}$$ Solve the second equation for $$y.$$ $$\begin{matrix} {x - y = -1} \\ {y = x + 1} \end{matrix}$$ Graph both equations on the same set of axes as in Figure 4. The lines appear to intersect at the point $$\left( {-3,-2} \right).$$ We can check to make sure that this is the solution to the system by substituting the ordered pair into both equations. $$\begin{array}{ll} {2(-3) + (-2) = -8} & \\ {-8 = -8} & \text{True} \\ {(-3) - (-2) = -1} & \\ {-1 = -1} & \text{True} \end{array}$$ The solution to the system is the ordered pair $$\left( {-3,-2} \right),$$ so the system is independent.

title: Solving a System of Equations in Two Variables by Substitution
snippet: Solving a System of Equations in Two Variables by Substitution: Solve the following system of equations by substitution. \begin{array}{l} {- x + y = -5} \\ {2x - 5y = 1} \end{array} First, we will solve the first equation for y....
body_xml:
<example number="3" title="Solving a System of Equations in Two Variables by Substitution">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the following system of equations by substitution.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {- x + y = -5} \\ {2x - 5y = 1} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, we will solve the first equation for $$y.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {- x + y = -5} \\ {y = x-5} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now we can substitute the expression $$x-5$$ for $$y$$ in the second equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {2x - 5y = 1} \\ {2x - 5(x - 5) = 1} \\ {2x - 5x + 25 = 1} \\ {- 3x = -24} \\ {x = 8} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now, we substitute $$x = 8$$ into the first equation and solve for $$y.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {- (8) + y = -5} \\ {y = 3} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Our solution is $$\left( {8,3} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Check the solution by substituting $$\left( {8,3} \right)$$ into both equations.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{llll} {- x + y = - 5} & & & \\ {- (8) + (3) = - 5} & & & \text{True} \\ {2x - 5y = 1} & & & \\ {2(8) - 5(3) = 1} & & & \text{True} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

If one of the variables in the top equation has the opposite coefficient of the same variable in the bottom equation, add the equations together, eliminating one variable. If not, use multiplication by a nonzero number so that one of the variables in the top equation has the opposite coefficient of the same variable in the bottom equation, then add the equations to eliminate the variable.</item>

unit_title: Systems of Linear Equations: Two Variables
title: Solving a System by the Addition Method
snippet: Solving a System by the Addition Method: Solve the given system of equations by addition. \begin{array}{l} {x + 2y = -1} \\ {- x + y = 3} \end{array} Both equations are already set equal to a constant. Notice that the coefficient of x in...
body_xml: Solve the given system of equations by addition. $$\begin{array}{l} {x + 2y = -1} \\ {- x + y = 3} \end{array}$$ Both equations are already set equal to a constant. Notice that the coefficient of $$x$$ in the second equation, –1, is the opposite of the coefficient of $$x$$ in the first equation, 1. We can add the two equations to eliminate $$x$$ without needing to multiply by a constant. $$\frac{\begin{array}{l} \\ {x + 2y = - 1} \\ {- x + y = 3} \end{array}}{3y = 2}$$ Now that we have eliminated $$x,$$ we can solve the resulting equation for $$y.$$ $$\begin{array}{l} {3y = 2} \\ {y = \frac{2}{3}} \end{array}$$ Then, we substitute this value for $$y$$ into one of the original equations and solve for $$x.$$ $$\begin{array}{l} {- x + y = 3} \\ {- x + \frac{2}{3} = 3} \\ {- x = 3 - \frac{2}{3}} \\ {- x = \frac{7}{3}} \\ {x = - \frac{7}{3}} \end{array}$$ The solution to this system is $$\left( {- \frac{7}{3},\frac{2}{3}} \right).$$ Check the solution in the first equation. $$\begin{array}{llll} {x + 2y = -1} & & & \\ {\left( {- \frac{7}{3}} \right) + 2\left( \frac{2}{3} \right) =} & & & \\ {- \frac{7}{3} + \frac{4}{3} =} & & & \\ {- \frac{3}{3} =} & & & \\ {-1 = -1} & & & \text{True} \end{array}$$ We gain an important perspective on systems of equations by looking at the graphical representation. See Figure 5 to find that the equations intersect at the solution. We do not need to ask whether there may be a second solution because observing the graph confirms that the system has exactly one solution.

unit_title: Systems of Linear Equations: Two Variables
title: Using the Addition Method When Multiplication of One Equation Is Required
snippet: Using the Addition Method When Multiplication of One Equation Is Required: Solve the given system of equations by the addition method. \begin{array}{l} {3x + 5y = -11} \\ \\ { x - 2y = 11} \end{array} Adding these equations as presented...
body_xml: Solve the given system of equations by the addition method. $$\begin{array}{l} {3x + 5y = -11} \\ \\ { x - 2y = 11} \end{array}$$ Adding these equations as presented will not eliminate a variable. However, we see that the first equation has $$3x$$ in it and the second equation has $$x.$$ So if we multiply the second equation by $$-3,$$ the x-terms will add to zero. $$\begin{array}{llll} {x-2y = 11} & & & \\ {-3(x-2y) = -3(11)} & & & { \text{Multiply both sides by} -3.} \\ {-3x + 6y = -33} & & & { \text{Use the distributive property} .} \end{array}$$ Now, let’s add them. $$\begin{array}{l} \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{\begin{array}{l} \\ \begin{array}{l} {3x + 5y = -11} \\ {-3x + 6y = -33} \end{array} \end{array}} \\ {11y = -44} \\ {y = -4} \end{array}$$ For the last step, we substitute $$y = -4$$ into one of the original equations and solve for $$x.$$ $$\begin{matrix} { 3x + 5y = - 11} \\ { 3x + 5( - 4) = - 11} \\ { 3x - 20 = - 11} \\ { 3x = 9} \\ { x = 3} \end{matrix}$$ Our solution is the ordered pair $$\left( {3,-4} \right).$$ See Figure 6. Check the solution in the original second equation. $$\begin{array}{llll} { x - 2y = 11} & & & \\ {(3) - 2( - 4) = 3 + 8} & & & \\ { 11 = 11} & & & \text{True} \end{array}$$

unit_title: Systems of Linear Equations: Two Variables
title: Using the Addition Method When Multiplication of Both Equations Is Required
snippet: Using the Addition Method When Multiplication of Both Equations Is Required: Solve the given system of equations in two variables by addition. \begin{matrix} {2x + 3y = -16} \\ {5x-10y = 30} \end{matrix} One equation has 2x and the other...
body_xml: Solve the given system of equations in two variables by addition. $$\begin{matrix} {2x + 3y = -16} \\ {5x-10y = 30} \end{matrix}$$ One equation has $$2x$$ and the other has $$5x.$$ The least common multiple is $$10x$$ so we will have to multiply both equations by a constant in order to eliminate one variable. Let’s eliminate $$x$$ by multiplying the first equation by $$-5$$ and the second equation by $$2.$$ $$\begin{array}{l} { - 5(2x + 3y) = - 5(-16)} \\ { - 10x - 15y = 80} \\ {2(5x - 10y) = 2(30)} \\ {10x - 20y = 60} \end{array}$$ Then, we add the two equations together. $$\begin{array}{l} \underset{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_}{\begin{array}{l} \\ \begin{array}{l} {-10x-15y=80} \\ {10x-20y=60} \end{array} \end{array}} \\ {-35y = 140} \\ {y = -4} \end{array}$$ Substitute $$y = -4$$ into the original first equation. $$\begin{matrix} {2x + 3(-4) = -16} \\ { 2x - 12 = -16} \\ { 2x = -4} \\ { x = -2} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is $$\left( {-2,-4} \right).$$ Check it in the other equation. $$\begin{array}{r} {5x-10y = 30} \\ {5(-2)-10(-4) = 30} \\ {-10 + 40 = 30} \\ {30 = 30} \end{array}$$ See Figure 7.

title: Using the Addition Method in Systems of Equations Containing Fractions
snippet: Using the Addition Method in Systems of Equations Containing Fractions: Solve the given system of equations in two variables by addition. \begin{array}{l} {\frac{x}{3} + \frac{y}{6} = 3} \\ {\frac{x}{2} - \frac{y}{4} = 1} \end{array} First...
body_xml:
<example number="7" title="Using the Addition Method in Systems of Equations Containing Fractions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the given system of equations in two variables by addition.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{x}{3} + \frac{y}{6} = 3} \\ {\frac{x}{2} - \frac{y}{4} = 1} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First clear each equation of fractions by multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {6\left( {\frac{x}{3} + \frac{y}{6}} \right) = 6(3)} \\ {2x + y = 18} \\ {4\left( {\frac{x}{2} - \frac{y}{4}} \right) = 4(1)} \\ {2x - y = 4} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now multiply the second equation by $$-1$$ so that we can eliminate the x-variable.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {-1(2x - y) = -1(4)} \\ {-2x + y = -4} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Add the two equations to eliminate the x-variable and solve the resulting equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {2x + y = 18} \\ \underset{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_}{-2x+y=-4} \\ {2y = 14} \\ {y = 7} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substitute $$y = 7$$ into the first equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {2x + (7) = 18} \\ {2x = 11} \\ {x = \frac{11}{2}} \\ { = 5.5} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solution is $$\left( {\frac{11}{2},7} \right).$$ Check it in the other equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {\frac{x}{2} - \frac{y}{4} = 1} \\ {\frac{\frac{11}{2}}{2} - \frac{7}{4} = 1} \\ {\frac{11}{4} - \frac{7}{4} = 1} \\ {\frac{4}{4} = 1} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving an Inconsistent System of Equations
snippet: Solving an Inconsistent System of Equations: Solve the following system of equations. \begin{array}{l} {x = 9-2y} \\ {x + 2y = 13} \end{array} We can approach this problem in two ways. Because one equation is already solved for x, the most...
body_xml: Solve the following system of equations. $$\begin{array}{l} {x = 9-2y} \\ {x + 2y = 13} \end{array}$$ We can approach this problem in two ways. Because one equation is already solved for $$x,$$ the most obvious step is to use substitution. $$\begin{array}{l} { x + 2y = 13} \\ {(9 - 2y) + 2y = 13} \\ { 9 + 0y = 13} \\ { 9 = 13} \end{array}$$ Clearly, this statement is a contradiction because $$9 \neq 13.$$ Therefore, the system has no solution. The second approach would be to first manipulate the equations so that they are both in slope-intercept form. We manipulate the first equation as follows. $$\begin{array}{l} { x = 9-2y} \\ {2y = - x + 9} \\ { y = - \frac{1}{2}x + \frac{9}{2}} \end{array}$$ We then convert the second equation expressed to slope-intercept form. $$\begin{array}{l} {x + 2y = 13} \\ { 2y = - x + 13} \\ { y = - \frac{1}{2}x + \frac{13}{2}} \end{array}$$ Comparing the equations, we see that they have the same slope but different y-intercepts. Therefore, the lines are parallel and do not intersect. $$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} \\ {y = - \frac{1}{2}x + \frac{9}{2}} \end{array} \\ {y = - \frac{1}{2}x + \frac{13}{2}} \end{array}$$ Writing the equations in slope-intercept form confirms that the system is inconsistent because all lines will intersect eventually unless they are parallel. Parallel lines will never intersect; thus, the two lines have no points in common. The graphs of the equations in this example are shown in Figure 8.

title: Finding a Solution to a Dependent System of Linear Equations
snippet: Finding a Solution to a Dependent System of Linear Equations: Find a solution to the system of equations using the addition method. \begin{matrix} { x + 3y = 2} \\ {3x + 9y = 6} \end{matrix} With the addition method, we want to eliminate...
body_xml: Find a solution to the system of equations using the addition method. $$\begin{matrix} { x + 3y = 2} \\ {3x + 9y = 6} \end{matrix}$$ With the addition method, we want to eliminate one of the variables by adding the equations. In this case, let’s focus on eliminating $$x.$$ If we multiply both sides of the first equation by $$-3,$$ then we will be able to eliminate the $$x$$ -variable. $$\begin{array}{l} { x + 3y = 2} \\ { (-3)(x + 3y) = (-3)(2)} \\ {-3x - 9y = - 6} \end{array}$$ Now add the equations. $$\begin{array}{l} \underset{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_}{\begin{array}{ll} {-3x-9y} & {=-6} \\ {+ 3x+9y} & {=6} \end{array}} \\ \begin{array}{ll} { 0} & {= 0} \end{array} \end{array}$$ We can see that there will be an infinite number of solutions that satisfy both equations. If we rewrote both equations in the slope-intercept form, we might know what the solution would look like before adding. Let’s look at what happens when we convert the system to slope-intercept form. $$\begin{array}{l} { x + 3y = 2} \\ {3y = - x + 2} \\ {y = - \frac{1}{3}x + \frac{2}{3}} \\ {3x + 9y = 6} \\ {9y = -3x + 6} \\ {y = - \frac{3}{9}x + \frac{6}{9}} \\ {y = - \frac{1}{3}x + \frac{2}{3}} \end{array}$$ See Figure 9. Notice the results are the same. The general solution to the system is $$\left( {x \text{,\ -} \frac{1}{3}x + \frac{2}{3}} \right).$$

title: Finding the Break-Even Point and the Profit Function Using Substitution
snippet: Finding the Break-Even Point and the Profit Function Using Substitution: Given the cost function C(x) = 0.85x + 35,000 and the revenue function R(x) = 1.55x, find the break-even point and the profit function. Write the system of equations...
body_xml: Given the cost function $$C(x) = 0.85x + 35,000$$ and the revenue function $$R(x) = 1.55x,$$ find the break-even point and the profit function. Write the system of equations using $$y$$ to replace function notation. $$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} \\ {y = 0.85x + 35,000} \end{array} \\ {y = 1.55x} \end{array}$$ Substitute the expression $$0.85x + 35,000$$ from the first equation into the second equation and solve for $$x.$$ $$\begin{matrix} {0.85x + 35,000 = 1.55x} \\ { 35,000 = 0.7x} \\ { 50,000 = x} \end{matrix}$$ Then, we substitute $$x = 50,000$$ into either the cost function or the revenue function. $$1.55(50,000) = 77,500$$ The break-even point is $$\left( {50,000,77,500} \right).$$ The profit function is found using the formula $$P(x) = R(x) - C(x).$$ $$\begin{array}{l} {P(x) = 1.55x - (0.85x + 35,000)} \\ { = 0.7x - 35,000} \end{array}$$ The profit function is $$P(x) = 0.7x-35,000.$$ The cost to produce 50,000 units is \$77,500, and the revenue from the sales of 50,000 units is also \$77,500. To make a profit, the business must produce and sell more than 50,000 units. See Figure 11. We see from the graph in Figure 12 that the profit function has a negative value until $$x = 50,000,$$ when the graph crosses the x-axis. Then, the graph emerges into positive y-values and continues on this path as the profit function is a straight line. This illustrates that the break-even point for businesses occurs when the profit function is 0. The area to the left of the break-even point represents operating at a loss.

title: Writing and Solving a System of Equations in Two Variables
snippet: Writing and Solving a System of Equations in Two Variables: The cost of a ticket to the circus is $$\$25.00 for children and \$50.00 for adults. On a certain day, attendance at the circus is 2,000 and the total gate revenue is \$70,000....
body_xml:
<example number="11" title="Writing and Solving a System of Equations in Two Variables">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The cost of a ticket to the circus is $$\$25.00$$ for children and $$\$50.00$$ for adults. On a certain day, attendance at the circus is $$2,000$$ and the total gate revenue is $$\$70,000.$$ How many children and how many adults bought tickets?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let c = the number of children and a = the number of adults in attendance.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The total number of people is $$2,000.$$ We can use this to write an equation for the number of people at the circus that day.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$c + a = 2,000$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The revenue from all children can be found by multiplying $$\$25.00$$ by the number of children, $$25c.$$ The revenue from all adults can be found by multiplying $$\$50.00$$ by the number of adults, $$50a.$$ The total revenue is $$\$70,000.$$ We can use this to write an equation for the revenue.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$25c + 50a = 70,000$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We now have a system of linear equations in two variables.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} { c + a = 2,000} \\ {25c + 50a = 70,000} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>In the first equation, the coefficient of both variables is 1. We can quickly solve the first equation for either $$c$$ or $$a.$$ We will solve for $$a.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {c + a = 2,000} \\ {a = 2,000 - c} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substitute the expression $$2,000 - c$$ in the second equation for $$a$$ and solve for $$c.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {25c + 50(2,000 - c) = 70,000} \\ {25c + 100,000 - 50c = 70,000} \\ {- 25c = -30,000} \\ {c = 1,200} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substitute $$c = 1,200$$ into the first equation to solve for $$a.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {1,200 + a = 2,000} \\ {a = 800} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We find that $$1,200$$ children and $$800$$ adults bought tickets to the circus that day.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Number of Possible Solutions
snippet: Number of Possible Solutions: Figure 2 and Figure 3 illustrate possible solution scenarios for three-by-three systems. Systems that have a single solution are those which, after elimination, result in a solution set consisting of an...
body_xml: Figure 2 and Figure 3 illustrate possible solution scenarios for three-by-three systems. Systems that have a single solution are those which, after elimination, result in a solution set consisting of an ordered triple $$\left\{ \left( {x,y,z} \right) \right\}.$$ Graphically, the ordered triple defines a point that is the intersection of three planes in space. Systems that have an infinite number of solutions are those which, after elimination, result in an expression that is always true, such as $$0 = 0.$$ Graphically, an infinite number of solutions represents a line or coincident plane that serves as the intersection of three planes in space. Systems that have no solution are those that, after elimination, result in a statement that is a contradiction, such as $$3 = 0.$$ Graphically, a system with no solution is represented by three planes with no point in common.

title: Determining Whether an Ordered Triple Is a Solution to a System
snippet: Determining Whether an Ordered Triple Is a Solution to a System: Determine whether the ordered triple \left( {3,-2,1} \right) is a solution to the system. \begin{array}{l} { x + y + z = 2} \\ { 6x - 4y + 5z = 31} \\ {5x + 2y + 2z = 13}...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Determining Whether an Ordered Triple Is a Solution to a System">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine whether the ordered triple $$\left( {3,-2,1} \right)$$ is a solution to the system.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} { x + y + z = 2} \\ { 6x - 4y + 5z = 31} \\ {5x + 2y + 2z = 13} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We will check each equation by substituting in the values of the ordered triple for $$x,y,$$ and $$z.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{r} {x + y + z = 2} \\ {(3) + (-2) + (1) = 2} \\ { \text{True} } \end{array} & & \begin{array}{r} { 6x-4y + 5z = 31} \\ {6(3)-4(-2) + 5(1) = 31} \\ {18 + 8 + 5 = 31} \\ { \text{True} } \end{array} & & \begin{array}{r} { 5x + 2y + 2z = 13} \\ {5(3) + 2(-2) + 2(1) = 13} \\ { 15-4 + 2 = 13} \\ { \text{True} } \end{array} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The ordered triple $$\left( {3,-2,1} \right)$$ is indeed a solution to the system.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>
