<example number="8" title="Solving a 3 × 3 System Using the Inverse of a Matrix">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the following system using the inverse of a matrix.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{r} {\left( A^{-1} \right)AX = \left( A^{-1} \right)B} \\ {\left\lbrack {\left( A^{-1} \right)A} \right\rbrack X = \left( A^{-1} \right)B} \\ {IX = \left( A^{-1} \right)B} \\ {X = \left( A^{-1} \right)B} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Write the equation $$A^{-1},$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$A^{-1}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>First, we will find the inverse of $$A$$ by augmenting with the identity.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$B$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Multiply row 1 by $$\begin{array}{r} {5x + 15y + 56z = 35} \\ {-4x-11y-41z = -26} \\ {- x-3y-11z = -7} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$AX = B.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Multiply row 1 by 4 and add to row 2.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 15 & 56 \\ -4 & -11 & -41 \\ -1 & -3 & -11 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 35 \\ -26 \\ -7 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Add row 1 to row 3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$A$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Multiply row 2 by −3 and add to row 1.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\lbrack {\left. {\begin{array}{rrr} 5 & 15 & 56 \\ -4 & -11 & -41 \\ -1 & -3 & -11 \end{array}} \right|\begin{matrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{matrix}} \right\rbrack$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Multiply row 3 by 5.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{1}{5}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Multiply row 3 by $$\left\lbrack {\begin{matrix} 1 & 3 & \frac{56}{5} \\ -4 & -11 & -41 \\ -1 & -3 & -11 \end{matrix}\left| {\begin{matrix} \frac{1}{5} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{matrix}} \right.} \right\rbrack$$ and add to row 1.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\lbrack {\begin{matrix} 1 & 3 & \frac{56}{5} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{19}{5} \\ -1 & -3 & -11 \end{matrix}\left| {\begin{matrix} \frac{1}{5} & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{matrix}} \right.} \right\rbrack$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Multiply row 3 by $$\left\lbrack {\begin{matrix} 1 & 3 & \frac{56}{5} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{19}{5} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{5} \end{matrix}\left| {\begin{matrix} \frac{1}{5} & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{5} & 0 & 1 \end{matrix}} \right.} \right\rbrack$$ and add to row 2.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\lbrack {\begin{matrix} 1 & 0 & {- \frac{1}{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{19}{5} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{5} \end{matrix}\left| {\begin{matrix} {- \frac{11}{5}} & -3 & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{5} & 0 & 1 \end{matrix}} \right.} \right\rbrack$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\lbrack {\begin{matrix} 1 & 0 & {- \frac{1}{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{19}{5} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\left| {\begin{matrix} {- \frac{11}{5}} & -3 & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 5 \end{matrix}} \right.} \right\rbrack$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Multiply both sides of the equation by $$\frac{1}{5}$$ We want $$\left\lbrack {\begin{matrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{19}{5} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\left| {\begin{matrix} -2 & -3 & 1 \\ \frac{4}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 5 \end{matrix}} \right.} \right\rbrack$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$- \frac{19}{5}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\lbrack {\begin{matrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\left| {\begin{matrix} -2 & -3 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & -19 \\ 1 & 0 & 5 \end{matrix}} \right.} \right\rbrack$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solution is $$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & -3 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & -19 \\ 1 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="rule" source_type="Cramer’s Rule for 2×2 Systems" title="Cramer’s Rule for 2×2 Systems">
    <paragraph>Cramer’s Rule is a method that uses determinants to solve systems of equations that have the same number of equations as variables.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Consider a system of two linear equations in two variables.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {a_{1}x + b_{1}y = c_{1}} \\ {a_{2}x + b_{2}y = c_{2}} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The solution using Cramer’s Rule is given as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$x = \frac{D_{x}}{D} = \frac{\left| \begin{matrix} c_{1} & b_{1} \\ c_{2} & b_{2} \end{matrix} \right|}{\left| \begin{matrix} a_{1} & b_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} \end{matrix} \right|}, D \neq 0; y = \frac{D_{y}}{D} = \frac{\left| \begin{matrix} a_{1} & c_{1} \\ a_{2} & c_{2} \end{matrix} \right|}{\left| \begin{matrix} a_{1} & b_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} \end{matrix} \right|}, D \neq 0.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If we are solving for $$x,$$ the $$x$$ column is replaced with the constant column. If we are solving for $$y,$$ the $$y$$ column is replaced with the constant column.</paragraph>
  </note>

      <paragraph>Solve for $$x.$$</paragraph>

      <paragraph>Solve for $$y.$$</paragraph>

<example number="4" title="Solving a 3 × 3 System Using Cramer’s Rule">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the solution to the given 3 × 3 system using Cramer’s Rule.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {x + y - z = 6} \\ {3x - 2y + z = -5} \\ {x + 3y - 2z = 14} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use Cramer’s Rule.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$D = \left| \begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & {- 1} \\ 3 & {- 2} & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & {- 2} \end{matrix} \right|,D_{x} = \left| \begin{matrix} 6 & 1 & {- 1} \\ {- 5} & {- 2} & 1 \\ 14 & 3 & {- 2} \end{matrix} \right|,D_{y} = \left| \begin{matrix} 1 & 6 & {- 1} \\ 3 & {- 5} & 1 \\ 1 & 14 & {- 2} \end{matrix} \right|,D_{z} = \left| \begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 3 & {- 2} & {- 5} \\ 1 & 3 & 14 \end{matrix} \right|$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {x = \frac{D_{x}}{D} = \frac{- 3}{- 3} = 1} \\ {y = \frac{D_{y}}{D} = \frac{- 9}{- 3} = 3} \\ {z = \frac{D_{z}}{D} = \frac{6}{- 3} = - 2} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solution is $$\left( {1,3,-2} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using Cramer’s Rule to Solve an Inconsistent System
snippet: Using Cramer’s Rule to Solve an Inconsistent System: Solve the system of equations using Cramer’s Rule. \begin{array}{l} {3x - 2y = 4 (1)} \\ {6x - 4y = 0 (2)} \end{array} We begin by finding the determinants D,D_{x}, \text{and} D_{y}. D =...
body_xml: Solve the system of equations using Cramer’s Rule. $$\begin{array}{l} {3x - 2y = 4 (1)} \\ {6x - 4y = 0 (2)} \end{array}$$ We begin by finding the determinants $$D,D_{x}, \text{and} D_{y}.$$ $$D = \left| \begin{matrix} 3 & {- 2} \\ 6 & {- 4} \end{matrix} \right| = 3\left( {- 4} \right) - 6\left( {- 2} \right) = 0$$ We know that a determinant of zero means that either the system has no solution or it has an infinite number of solutions. To see which one, we use the process of elimination. Our goal is to eliminate one of the variables. Multiply equation (1) by $$-2.$$ Add the result to equation $$(2).$$ $$\begin{array}{l} \underset{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_}{\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} \\ {-6x+4y=-8} \end{array} \\ {6x-4y=0} \end{array}} \\ {0 = -8} \end{array}$$ We obtain the equation $$0 = -8,$$ which is false. Therefore, the system has no solution. Graphing the system reveals two parallel lines. See Figure 1.

title: Use Cramer’s Rule to Solve a Dependent System
snippet: Use Cramer’s Rule to Solve a Dependent System: Solve the system with an infinite number of solutions. \begin{array}{rr} {x - 2y + 3z = 0} & {(1)} \\ {3x + y - 2z = 0} & {(2)} \\ {2x - 4y + 6z = 0} & {(3)} \end{array} Let’s find the...
body_xml: Solve the system with an infinite number of solutions. $$\begin{array}{rr} {x - 2y + 3z = 0} & {(1)} \\ {3x + y - 2z = 0} & {(2)} \\ {2x - 4y + 6z = 0} & {(3)} \end{array}$$ Let’s find the determinant first. Set up a matrix augmented by the first two columns. $$\left| {\begin{array}{rrr} 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -4 & 6 \end{array}\left| {\begin{array}{rr} 1 & -2 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 2 & -4 \end{array}} \right.} \right|$$ Then, $$1(1)(6) + \left( {- 2} \right)\left( {- 2} \right)(2) + 3(3)\left( {- 4} \right) - 2(1)(3) - \left( {- 4} \right)\left( {- 2} \right)(1) - 6(3)\left( {- 2} \right) = 0$$ As the determinant equals zero, there is either no solution or an infinite number of solutions. We have to perform elimination to find out. Multiply equation (1) by $$-2$$ and add the result to equation (3): $$\frac{\begin{array}{r} {- 2x + 4y - 6z = 0} \\ {2x - 4y + 6z = 0} \end{array}}{0 = 0}$$ Obtaining an answer of $$0 = 0,$$ a statement that is always true, means that the system has an infinite number of solutions. Graphing the system, we can see that two of the planes are the same and they both intersect the third plane on a line. See Figure 2.

title: Properties of Determinants
snippet: Properties of Determinants: If the matrix is in upper triangular form, the determinant equals the product of entries down the main diagonal. When two rows are interchanged, the determinant changes sign. If either two rows or two columns...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Properties of Determinants" title="Properties of Determinants">
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>If the matrix is in upper triangular form, the determinant equals the product of entries down the main diagonal.</item>
      <item>When two rows are interchanged, the determinant changes sign.</item>
      <item>If either two rows or two columns are identical, the determinant equals zero.</item>
      <item>If a matrix contains either a row of zeros or a column of zeros, the determinant equals zero.</item>
      <item>The determinant of an inverse matrix $$A^{- 1}$$ is the reciprocal of the determinant of the matrix $$A.$$</item>
      <item>If any row or column is multiplied by a constant, the determinant is multiplied by the same factor.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Illustrating Properties of Determinants
snippet: Illustrating Properties of Determinants: Illustrate each of the properties of determinants. Property 1 states that if the matrix is in upper triangular form, the determinant is the product of the entries down the main diagonal. A =...
body_xml:
<example number="7" title="Illustrating Properties of Determinants">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Illustrate each of the properties of determinants.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Property 1 states that if the matrix is in upper triangular form, the determinant is the product of the entries down the main diagonal.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Augment $$A$$ with the first two columns.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$A = \left\lbrack {\begin{matrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & {- 1} \end{matrix}\left| \begin{matrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{matrix} \right.\begin{matrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{matrix}} \right\rbrack$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\det(A) = 1(2)(-1) + 2(1)(0) + 3(0)(0) - 0(2)(3) - 0(1)(1) + 1(0)(2)} \\ {= -2} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Property 2 states that interchanging rows changes the sign. Given</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} \\ {A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} -1 & 5 \\ 4 & -3 \end{array} \right\rbrack,\det(A) = (-1)(-3) - (4)(5) = 3 - 20 = -17} \end{array} \\ \\ {B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} 4 & {- 3} \\ {- 1} & 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack,\det(B) = (4)(5) - (-1)(-3) = 20 - 3 = 17} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Property 3 states that if two rows or two columns are identical, the determinant equals zero.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {A = \left\lbrack {\begin{array}{lll} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 2 \end{array} \left| { \begin{array}{l} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{array} \begin{array}{l} 2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{array}} \right.} \right\rbrack} \\ \\ {\det(A) = 1(2)(2) + 2(2)(-1) + 2(2)(2) + 1(2)(2) - 2(2)(1) - 2(2)(2)} \\ {= 4 - 4 + 8 + 4 - 4 - 8 = 0} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Property 4 states that if a row or column equals zero, the determinant equals zero. Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix},\det(A) = 1(0) - 2(0) = 0$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Property 5 states that the determinant of an inverse matrix $$A^{- 1}$$ is the reciprocal of the determinant $$A.$$ Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack,\det(A) = 1(4) - 3(2) = -2} \\ \\ {A^{- 1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} {- 2} & 1 \\ \frac{3}{2} & {- \frac{1}{2}} \end{array} \right\rbrack,\det\left( A^{- 1} \right) = - 2\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right) - \left( \frac{3}{2} \right)(1) = - \frac{1}{2}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Property 6 states that if any row or column of a matrix is multiplied by a constant, the determinant is multiplied by the same factor. Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack,\det(A) = 1(4) - 2(3) = -2} \\ \\ {B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} {2(1)} & {2(2)} \\ 3 & 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack,\det(B) = 2(4) - 3(4) = -4} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using Cramer’s Rule and Determinant Properties to Solve a System
snippet: Using Cramer’s Rule and Determinant Properties to Solve a System: Find the solution to the given 3 × 3 system. \begin{array}{ll} {2x + 4y + 4z = 2} & {(1)} \\ {3x + 7y + 7z = -5} & {(2)} \\ { x + 2y + 2z = 4} & {(3)} \end{array} Using...
body_xml:
<example number="8" title="Using Cramer’s Rule and Determinant Properties to Solve a System">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the solution to the given 3 × 3 system.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {2x + 4y + 4z = 2} & {(1)} \\ {3x + 7y + 7z = -5} & {(2)} \\ { x + 2y + 2z = 4} & {(3)} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Using Cramer’s Rule, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$D = \left| \begin{matrix} 2 & 4 & 4 \\ 3 & 7 & 7 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \end{matrix} \right|$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that the second and third columns are identical. According to Property 3, the determinant will be zero, so there is either no solution or an infinite number of solutions. We have to perform elimination to find out.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Multiply equation (3) by –2 and add the result to equation (1). $$\frac{\begin{array}{l} {- 2x - 4y - 4x = - 8} \\ {2x + 4y + 4z = 2} \end{array}}{ 0 = - 6}$$</item>
      </list>
      <paragraph>Obtaining a statement that is a contradiction means that the system has no solution.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Standard Forms of the Equation of an Ellipse with Center (0,0)
source_type: Standard Forms of the Equation of an Ellipse with Center (0,0)
snippet: Standard Forms of the Equation of an Ellipse with Center (0,0): The standard form of the equation of an ellipse with center \left( {0,0} \right) and major axis on the x-axis is \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1 where a > b the...
body_xml: The standard form of the equation of an ellipse with center $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and major axis on the x-axis is $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1$$ where $$a > b$$ the length of the major axis is $$2a$$ the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {\pm a,0} \right)$$ the length of the minor axis is $$2b$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {0, \pm b} \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {\pm c,0} \right)$$ , where $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$ See Figure 6 a The standard form of the equation of an ellipse with center $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and major axis on the y-axis is $$\frac{x^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{a^{2}} = 1$$ where $$a > b$$ the length of the major axis is $$2a$$ the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {0, \pm a} \right)$$ the length of the minor axis is $$2b$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {\pm b,0} \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {0, \pm c} \right)$$ , where $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$ See Figure 6 b Note that the vertices, co-vertices, and foci are related by the equation $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$ When we are given the coordinates of the foci and vertices of an ellipse, we can use this relationship to find the equation of the ellipse in standard form.

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given the vertices and foci of an ellipse centered at the origin, write its equation in standard form. Determine whether the major axis lies on the x- or y-axis. If the given coordinates of the vertices and foci have the form...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given the vertices and foci of an ellipse centered at the origin, write its equation in standard form.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Determine whether the major axis lies on the x- or y-axis. If the given coordinates of the vertices and foci have the form $$\left( {\pm a,0} \right)$$ and $$( \pm c,0)$$ respectively, then the major axis is the x-axis. Use the standard form $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1.$$ If the given coordinates of the vertices and foci have the form $$\left( {0, \pm a} \right)$$ and $$(0, \pm c),$$ respectively, then the major axis is the y-axis. Use the standard form $$\frac{x^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{a^{2}} = 1.$$</item>
      <item>Use the equation $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2},$$ along with the given coordinates of the vertices and foci, to solve for $$b^{2}.$$</item>
      <item>Substitute the values for $$a^{2}$$ and $$b^{2}$$ into the standard form of the equation determined in Step 1.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Writing the Equation of an Ellipse Centered at the Origin in Standard Form
snippet: Writing the Equation of an Ellipse Centered at the Origin in Standard Form: What is the standard form equation of the ellipse that has vertices \left( {\pm 8,0} \right) and foci \left( {\pm 5,0} \right)? The foci are on the x-axis, so the...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Writing the Equation of an Ellipse Centered at the Origin in Standard Form">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>What is the standard form equation of the ellipse that has vertices $$\left( {\pm 8,0} \right)$$ and foci $$\left( {\pm 5,0} \right)?$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The foci are on the x-axis, so the major axis is the x-axis. Thus, the equation will have the form</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The vertices are $$\left( {\pm 8,0} \right),$$ so $$a = 8$$ and $$a^{2} = 64.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The foci are $$\left( {\pm 5,0} \right),$$ so $$c = 5$$ and $$c^{2} = 25.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We know that the vertices and foci are related by the equation $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$ Solving for $$b^{2},$$ we have:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}} & \\ {25 = 64 - b^{2}\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array}} & { \text{Substitute for} c^{2} \text{and} a^{2}.} \\ {b^{2} = 39} & { \text{Solve for} b^{2}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now we need only substitute $$a^{2} = 64$$ and $$b^{2} = 39$$ into the standard form of the equation. The equation of the ellipse is $$\frac{x^{2}}{64} + \frac{y^{2}}{39} = 1.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Standard Forms of the Equation of an Ellipse with Center (h, k)
source_type: Standard Forms of the Equation of an Ellipse with Center (h, k)
snippet: Standard Forms of the Equation of an Ellipse with Center (h, k): The standard form of the equation of an ellipse with center \left( {h, k} \right) and major axis parallel to the x-axis is \frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} +...
body_xml: The standard form of the equation of an ellipse with center $$\left( {h, k} \right)$$ and major axis parallel to the x-axis is $$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1$$ where $$a > b$$ the length of the major axis is $$2a$$ the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {h \pm a,k} \right)$$ the length of the minor axis is $$2b$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {h,k \pm b} \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {h \pm c,k} \right),$$ where $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$ See Figure 7a The standard form of the equation of an ellipse with center $$\left( {h,k} \right)$$ and major axis parallel to the y-axis is $$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} = 1$$ where $$a > b$$ the length of the major axis is $$2a$$ the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {h,k \pm a} \right)$$ the length of the minor axis is $$2b$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {h \pm b,k} \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {h,k \pm c} \right),$$ where $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$ See Figure 7b Just as with ellipses centered at the origin, ellipses that are centered at a point $$\left( {h,k} \right)$$ have vertices, co-vertices, and foci that are related by the equation $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$ We can use this relationship along with the midpoint and distance formulas to find the equation of the ellipse in standard form when the vertices and foci are given.

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given the vertices and foci of an ellipse not centered at the origin, write its equation in standard form. Determine whether the major axis is parallel to the x- or y-axis. If the y-coordinates of the given vertices and foci are...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given the vertices and foci of an ellipse not centered at the origin, write its equation in standard form.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Determine whether the major axis is parallel to the x- or y-axis. If the y-coordinates of the given vertices and foci are the same, then the major axis is parallel to the x-axis. Use the standard form $$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1.$$ If the x-coordinates of the given vertices and foci are the same, then the major axis is parallel to the y-axis. Use the standard form $$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} = 1.$$</item>
      <item>Identify the center of the ellipse $$\left( {h,k} \right)$$ using the midpoint formula and the given coordinates for the vertices.</item>
      <item>Find $$a^{2}$$ by solving for the length of the major axis, $$2a,$$ which is the distance between the given vertices.</item>
      <item>Find $$c^{2}$$ using $$h$$ and $$k,$$ found in Step 2, along with the given coordinates for the foci.</item>
      <item>Solve for $$b^{2}$$ using the equation $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$</item>
      <item>Substitute the values for $$h,k,a^{2},$$ and $$b^{2}$$ into the standard form of the equation determined in Step 1.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Writing the Equation of an Ellipse Centered at a Point Other Than the Origin
snippet: Writing the Equation of an Ellipse Centered at a Point Other Than the Origin: What is the standard form equation of the ellipse that has vertices \left( {-2,-8} \right) and \left( {-2, \text{2} } \right) and foci \left( {-2,-7} \right) and...
body_xml:
<example number="2" title="Writing the Equation of an Ellipse Centered at a Point Other Than the Origin">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>What is the standard form equation of the ellipse that has vertices $$\left( {-2,-8} \right)$$ and $$\left( {-2, \text{2} } \right)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and foci $$\left( {-2,-7} \right)$$ and $$\left( {-2, \text{1} } \right)?$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The x-coordinates of the vertices and foci are the same, so the major axis is parallel to the y-axis. Thus, the equation of the ellipse will have the form</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} = 1$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>First, we identify the center, $$\left( {h,k} \right).$$ The center is halfway between the vertices, $$\left( {- 2, - 8} \right)$$ and $$\left( {- 2, \text{2} } \right).$$ Applying the midpoint formula, we have:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {(h,k) = \left( {\frac{-2 + (-2)}{2},\frac{-8 + 2}{2}} \right)} \\ { = (-2,-3)} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, we find $$a^{2}.$$ The length of the major axis, $$2a,$$ is bounded by the vertices. We solve for $$a$$ by finding the distance between the y-coordinates of the vertices.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {2a = 2 - (-8)} \\ {2a = 10} \\ {a = 5} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So $$a^{2} = 25.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now we find $$c^{2}.$$ The foci are given by $$\left( {h,k \pm c} \right).$$ So, $$\left( {h,k - c} \right) = \left( {-2,-7} \right)$$ and $$\left( {h,k + c} \right) = \left( {-2, \text{1} } \right).$$ We substitute $$k = -3$$ using either of these points to solve for $$c.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {k + c = 1} \\ {-3 + c = 1} \\ {c = 4} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So $$c^{2} = 16.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, we solve for $$b^{2}$$ using the equation $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}} \\ {16 = 25 - b^{2}} \\ {b^{2} = 9} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Finally, we substitute the values found for $$h,k,a^{2},$$ and $$b^{2}$$ into the standard form equation for an ellipse:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\left( {x + 2} \right)^{2}}{9} + \frac{\left( {y + 3} \right)^{2}}{25} = 1$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

If the equation is in the form $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1,$$ where $$a > b,$$ then the major axis is the x-axis the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {\pm a,0} \right)$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {0, \pm b} \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {\pm c,0} \right)$$ If the equation is in the form $$\frac{x^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{a^{2}} = 1,$$ where $$a > b,$$ then the major axis is the y-axis the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {0, \pm a} \right)$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {\pm b,0} \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {0, \pm c} \right)$$</item>
      <item>Solve for $$c$$ using the equation $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$</item>
      <item>Plot the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci in the coordinate plane, and draw a smooth curve to form the ellipse.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Graphing an Ellipse Centered at the Origin
snippet: Graphing an Ellipse Centered at the Origin: Graph the ellipse given by the equation, \frac{x^{2}}{9} + \frac{y^{2}}{25} = 1. Identify and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci. First, we determine the position of the major...
body_xml: Graph the ellipse given by the equation, $$\frac{x^{2}}{9} + \frac{y^{2}}{25} = 1.$$ Identify and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci. First, we determine the position of the major axis. Because $$25 > 9,$$ the major axis is on the y-axis. Therefore, the equation is in the form $$\frac{x^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{a^{2}} = 1,$$ where $$b^{2} = 9$$ and $$a^{2} = 25.$$ It follows that: the center of the ellipse is $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {0, \pm a} \right) = \left( {0, \pm \sqrt{25}} \right) = \left( {0, \pm 5} \right)$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {\pm b,0} \right) = \left( {\pm \sqrt{9},0} \right) = \left( {\pm 3,0} \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {0, \pm c} \right),$$ where $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}$$ Solving for $$c,$$ we have: $$\begin{array}{l} {c = \pm \sqrt{a^{2} - b^{2}}} \\ {= \pm \sqrt{25 - 9}} \\ {= \pm \sqrt{16}} \\ {= \pm 4} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {0, \pm 4} \right).$$ Next, we plot and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci, and draw a smooth curve to form the ellipse. See Figure 8.

snippet: Graphing an Ellipse Centered at the Origin from an Equation Not in Standard Form: Graph the ellipse given by the equation 4x^{2} + 25y^{2} = 100. Rewrite the equation in standard form. Then identify and label the center, vertices,...
body_xml: Graph the ellipse given by the equation $$4x^{2} + 25y^{2} = 100.$$ Rewrite the equation in standard form. Then identify and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci. First, use algebra to rewrite the equation in standard form. $$\begin{array}{l} { 4x^{2} + 25y^{2} = 100} \\ { \frac{4x^{2}}{100} + \frac{25y^{2}}{100} = \frac{100}{100}} \\ {\frac{x^{2}}{25} + \frac{y^{2}}{4} = 1} \end{array}$$ Next, we determine the position of the major axis. Because $$25 > 4,$$ the major axis is on the x-axis. Therefore, the equation is in the form $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1,$$ where $$a^{2} = 25$$ and $$b^{2} = 4.$$ It follows that: the center of the ellipse is $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {\pm a,0} \right) = \left( {\pm \sqrt{25},0} \right) = \left( {\pm 5,0} \right)$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {0, \pm b} \right) = \left( {0, \pm \sqrt{4}} \right) = \left( {0, \pm 2} \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {\pm c,0} \right),$$ where $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$ Solving for $$c,$$ we have: $$\begin{array}{l} {c = \pm \sqrt{a^{2} - b^{2}}} \\ {= \pm \sqrt{25 - 4}} \\ {= \pm \sqrt{21}} \end{array}$$ Therefore the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {\pm \sqrt{21},0} \right).$$ Next, we plot and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci, and draw a smooth curve to form the ellipse.

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given the standard form of an equation for an ellipse centered at \left( {h,k} \right), sketch the graph. Use the standard forms of the equations of an ellipse to determine the center, position of the major axis, vertices,...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given the standard form of an equation for an ellipse centered at $$\left( {h,k} \right),$$ sketch the graph.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Use the standard forms of the equations of an ellipse to determine the center, position of the major axis, vertices, co-vertices, and foci. If the equation is in the form $$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1,$$ where $$a > b,$$ then the center is $$\left( {h,k} \right)$$ the major axis is parallel to the x-axis the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {h \pm a,k} \right)$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {h,k \pm b} \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {h \pm c,k} \right)$$ If the equation is in the form $$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} = 1,$$ where $$a > b,$$ then the center is $$\left( {h,k} \right)$$ the major axis is parallel to the y-axis the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {h,k \pm a} \right)$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {h \pm b,k} \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {h,k \pm c} \right)$$</item>
      <item>Solve for $$c$$ using the equation $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$</item>
      <item>Plot the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci in the coordinate plane, and draw a smooth curve to form the ellipse.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Graphing an Ellipse Centered at (h, k)
snippet: Graphing an Ellipse Centered at (h, k): Graph the ellipse given by the equation, \frac{\left( {x + 2} \right)^{2}}{4} + \frac{\left( {y - 5} \right)^{2}}{9} = 1. Identify and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci. First, we...
body_xml: Graph the ellipse given by the equation, $$\frac{\left( {x + 2} \right)^{2}}{4} + \frac{\left( {y - 5} \right)^{2}}{9} = 1.$$ Identify and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci. First, we determine the position of the major axis. Because $$9 > 4,$$ the major axis is parallel to the y-axis. Therefore, the equation is in the form $$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} = 1,$$ where $$b^{2} = 4$$ and $$a^{2} = 9.$$ It follows that: the center of the ellipse is $$\left( {h,k} \right) = \left( {-2, \text{5} } \right)$$ the coordinates of the vertices are $$(h,k \pm a) = ( - 2,5 \pm \sqrt{9}) = ( - 2,5 \pm 3),$$ or $$\left( {-2, \text{2} } \right)$$ and $$\left( {-2, \text{8} } \right)$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$(h \pm b,k) = ( - 2 \pm \sqrt{4},5) = ( - 2 \pm 2,5),$$ or $$\left( {-4,5} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0, \text{5} } \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {h,k \pm c} \right),$$ where $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$ Solving for $$c,$$ we have: $$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} \\ {c = \pm \sqrt{a^{2} - b^{2}}} \end{array} \\ {= \pm \sqrt{9 - 4}} \\ {= \pm \sqrt{5}} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {-2, \text{5} - \sqrt{5}} \right)$$ and $$\left( {-2, \text{5+} \sqrt{5}} \right).$$ Next, we plot and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci, and draw a smooth curve to form the ellipse.

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given the general form of an equation for an ellipse centered at (h, k), express the equation in standard form. Recognize that an ellipse described by an equation in the form ax^{2} + by^{2} + cx + dy + e = 0 is in general form....
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given the general form of an equation for an ellipse centered at (h, k), express the equation in standard form.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Recognize that an ellipse described by an equation in the form $$ax^{2} + by^{2} + cx + dy + e = 0$$ is in general form.</item>
      <item>Rearrange the equation by grouping terms that contain the same variable. Move the constant term to the opposite side of the equation.</item>
      <item>Factor out the coefficients of the $$x^{2}$$ and $$y^{2}$$ terms in preparation for completing the square.</item>
      <item>Complete the square for each variable to rewrite the equation in the form of the sum of multiples of two binomials squared set equal to a constant, $$m_{1}\left( {x - h} \right)^{2} + m_{2}\left( {y - k} \right)^{2} = m_{3},$$ where $$m_{1},m_{2},$$ and $$m_{3}$$ are constants.</item>
      <item>Divide both sides of the equation by the constant term to express the equation in standard form.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Graphing an Ellipse Centered at (h, k) by First Writing It in Standard Form
snippet: Graphing an Ellipse Centered at (h, k) by First Writing It in Standard Form: Graph the ellipse given by the equation 4x^{2} + 9y^{2} - 40x + 36y + 100 = 0. Identify and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci. We must begin by...
body_xml: Graph the ellipse given by the equation $$4x^{2} + 9y^{2} - 40x + 36y + 100 = 0.$$ Identify and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci. We must begin by rewriting the equation in standard form. $$4x^{2} + 9y^{2} - 40x + 36y + 100 = 0$$ Group terms that contain the same variable, and move the constant to the opposite side of the equation. $$\left( {4x^{2} - 40x} \right) + \left( {9y^{2} + 36y} \right) = -100$$ Factor out the coefficients of the squared terms. $$4\left( {x^{2} - 10x} \right) + 9\left( {y^{2} + 4y} \right) = -100$$ Complete the square twice. Remember to balance the equation by adding the same constants to each side. $$4\left( {x^{2} - 10x + 25} \right) + 9\left( {y^{2} + 4y + 4} \right) = -100 + 100 + 36$$ Rewrite as perfect squares. $$4\left( {x - 5} \right)^{2} + 9\left( {y + 2} \right)^{2} = 36$$ Divide both sides by the constant term to place the equation in standard form. $$\frac{\left( {x - 5} \right)^{2}}{9} + \frac{\left( {y + 2} \right)^{2}}{4} = 1$$ Now that the equation is in standard form, we can determine the position of the major axis. Because $$9 > 4,$$ the major axis is parallel to the x-axis. Therefore, the equation is in the form $$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1,$$ where $$a^{2} = 9$$ and $$b^{2} = 4.$$ It follows that: the center of the ellipse is $$\left( {h,k} \right) = \left( {5,-2} \right)$$ the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {h \pm a,k} \right) = \left( {5 \pm \sqrt{9},-2} \right) = \left( {5 \pm 3,-2} \right),$$ or $$\left( {2,-2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {8,-2} \right)$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {h,k \pm b} \right) = \left( { \text{5} ,-2 \pm \sqrt{4}} \right) = \left( { \text{5} ,-2 \pm 2} \right),$$ or $$\left( {5,-4} \right)$$ and $$\left( {5, \text{0} } \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {h \pm c,k} \right),$$ where $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$ Solving for $$c,$$ we have: $$\begin{array}{l} {c = \pm \sqrt{a^{2} - b^{2}}} \\ {= \pm \sqrt{9 - 4}} \\ {= \pm \sqrt{5}} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( { \text{5} - \sqrt{5},-2} \right)$$ and $$\left( { \text{5+} \sqrt{5},-2} \right).$$ Next we plot and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci, and draw a smooth curve to form the ellipse as shown in Figure 11.

title: Locating the Foci of a Whispering Chamber
snippet: Locating the Foci of a Whispering Chamber: A large room in an art gallery is a whispering chamber. Its dimensions are 46 feet wide by 96 feet long as shown in Figure 13. What is the standard form of the equation of the ellipse representing...
body_xml: A large room in an art gallery is a whispering chamber. Its dimensions are 46 feet wide by 96 feet long as shown in Figure 13. What is the standard form of the equation of the ellipse representing the outline of the room? Hint: assume a horizontal ellipse, and let the center of the room be the point $$\left( {0,0} \right).$$ If two visitors standing at the foci of this room can hear each other whisper, how far apart are the two visitors? Round to the nearest foot. We are assuming a horizontal ellipse with center $$\left( {0,0} \right),$$ so we need to find an equation of the form $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1,$$ where $$a > b.$$ We know that the length of the major axis, $$2a,$$ is longer than the length of the minor axis, $$2b.$$ So the length of the room, 96, is represented by the major axis, and the width of the room, 46, is represented by the minor axis. Solving for $$a,$$ we have $$2a = 96,$$ so $$a = 48,$$ and $$a^{2} = 2304.$$ Solving for $$b,$$ we have $$2b = 46,$$ so $$b = 23,$$ and $$b^{2} = 529.$$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is $$\frac{x^{2}}{2304} + \frac{y^{2}}{529} = 1.$$ To find the distance between the senators, we must find the distance between the foci, $$\left( {\pm c,0} \right),$$ where $$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}.$$ Solving for $$c,$$ we have: $$\begin{array}{ll} {c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}} & \\ {c^{2} = 2304 - 529} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Substitute using the values found in part (a)} .} \\ {c = \pm \sqrt{2304 - 529}} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Take the square root of both sides} .} \\ {c = \pm \sqrt{1775} } & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Subtract} .} \\ {c \approx \pm 42} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Round to the nearest foot} .} \end{array}$$ The points $$\left( {\pm 42,0} \right)$$ represent the foci. Thus, the distance between the senators is $$2(42) = 84$$ feet.

snippet: Standard Forms of the Equation of a Hyperbola with Center (0,0): The standard form of the equation of a hyperbola with center \left( {0,0} \right) and transverse axis on the x-axis is \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1 where the...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Standard Forms of the Equation of a Hyperbola with Center (0,0)" title="Standard Forms of the Equation of a Hyperbola with Center (0,0)">
    <paragraph>The standard form of the equation of a hyperbola with center $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and transverse axis on the x-axis is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>the length of the transverse axis is $$2a$$</item>
      <item>the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {\pm a,0} \right)$$</item>
      <item>the length of the conjugate axis is $$2b$$</item>
      <item>the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {0, \pm b} \right)$$</item>
      <item>the distance between the foci is $$2c,$$ where $$c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}$$</item>
      <item>the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {\pm c,0} \right)$$</item>
      <item>the equations of the asymptotes are $$y = \pm \frac{b}{a}x$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>See Figure 5a.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The standard form of the equation of a hyperbola with center $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and transverse axis on the y-axis is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{y^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{x^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>the length of the transverse axis is $$2a$$</item>
      <item>the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {0, \pm a} \right)$$</item>
      <item>the length of the conjugate axis is $$2b$$</item>
      <item>the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {\pm b,0} \right)$$</item>
      <item>the distance between the foci is $$2c,$$ where $$c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}$$</item>
      <item>the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {0, \pm c} \right)$$</item>
      <item>the equations of the asymptotes are $$y = \pm \frac{a}{b}x$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>See Figure 5b.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Note that the vertices, co-vertices, and foci are related by the equation $$c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}.$$ When we are given the equation of a hyperbola, we can use this relationship to identify its vertices and foci.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given the equation of a hyperbola in standard form, locate its vertices and foci. Determine whether the transverse axis lies on the x- or y-axis. Notice that a^{2} is always under the variable with the positive coefficient. So, if...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given the equation of a hyperbola in standard form, locate its vertices and foci.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Determine whether the transverse axis lies on the x- or y-axis. Notice that $$a^{2}$$ is always under the variable with the positive coefficient. So, if you set the other variable equal to zero, you can easily find the intercepts. In the case where the hyperbola is centered at the origin, the intercepts coincide with the vertices. If the equation has the form $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1,$$ then the transverse axis lies on the x-axis. The vertices are located at $$( \pm a,0),$$ and the foci are located at $$\left( {\pm c,0} \right).$$ If the equation has the form $$\frac{y^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{x^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1,$$ then the transverse axis lies on the y-axis. The vertices are located at $$(0, \pm a),$$ and the foci are located at $$\left( {0, \pm c} \right).$$</item>
      <item>Solve for $$a$$ using the equation $$a = \sqrt{a^{2}}.$$</item>
      <item>Solve for $$c$$ using the equation $$c = \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Locating a Hyperbola’s Vertices and Foci
snippet: Locating a Hyperbola’s Vertices and Foci: Identify the vertices and foci of the hyperbola with equation \frac{y^{2}}{49} - \frac{x^{2}}{32} = 1. The equation has the form \frac{y^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{x^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1, so the transverse...
body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Locating a Hyperbola’s Vertices and Foci">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Identify the vertices and foci of the hyperbola with equation $$\frac{y^{2}}{49} - \frac{x^{2}}{32} = 1.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The equation has the form $$\frac{y^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{x^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1,$$ so the transverse axis lies on the y-axis. The hyperbola is centered at the origin, so the vertices serve as the y-intercepts of the graph. To find the vertices, set $$x = 0,$$ and solve for $$y.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {1 = \frac{y^{2}}{49} - \frac{x^{2}}{32}} \\ {1 = \frac{y^{2}}{49} - \frac{0^{2}}{32}} \\ {1 = \frac{y^{2}}{49}} \\ {y^{2} = 49} \\ {y = \pm \sqrt{49} = \pm 7} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The foci are located at $$\left( {0, \pm c} \right).$$ Solving for $$c,$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$c = \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}} = \sqrt{49 + 32} = \sqrt{81} = 9$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, the vertices are located at $$\left( {0, \pm 7} \right),$$ and the foci are located at $$\left( {0, \pm 9} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given the vertices and foci of a hyperbola centered at $$\left( {0, \text{0} } \right),$$ write its equation in standard form.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Determine whether the transverse axis lies on the x- or y-axis. If the given coordinates of the vertices and foci have the form $$\left( {\pm a,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {\pm c,0} \right),$$ respectively, then the transverse axis is the x-axis. Use the standard form $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1.$$ If the given coordinates of the vertices and foci have the form $$\left( {0, \pm a} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0, \pm c} \right),$$ respectively, then the transverse axis is the y-axis. Use the standard form $$\frac{y^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{x^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1.$$</item>
      <item>Find $$b^{2}$$ using the equation $$b^{2} = c^{2} - a^{2}.$$</item>
      <item>Substitute the values for $$a^{2}$$ and $$b^{2}$$ into the standard form of the equation determined in Step 1.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Finding the Equation of a Hyperbola Centered at (0,0) Given its Foci and Vertices
snippet: Finding the Equation of a Hyperbola Centered at (0,0) Given its Foci and Vertices: What is the standard form equation of the hyperbola that has vertices \left( {\pm 6,0} \right) and foci \left( {\pm 2\sqrt{10},0} \right)? The vertices and...
body_xml: What is the standard form equation of the hyperbola that has vertices $$\left( {\pm 6,0} \right)$$ and foci $$\left( {\pm 2\sqrt{10},0} \right)?$$ The vertices and foci are on the x-axis. Thus, the equation for the hyperbola will have the form $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1.$$ The vertices are $$\left( {\pm 6,0} \right),$$ so $$a = 6$$ and $$a^{2} = 36.$$ The foci are $$\left( {\pm 2\sqrt{10},0} \right),$$ so $$c = 2\sqrt{10}$$ and $$c^{2} = 40.$$ Solving for $$b^{2},$$ we have $$\begin{array}{ll} {b^{2} = c^{2} - a^{2}} & \\ {b^{2} = 40 - 36} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Substitute for} c^{2} \text{and} a^{2}.} \\ {b^{2} = 4} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Subtract} .} \end{array}$$ Finally, we substitute $$a^{2} = 36$$ and $$b^{2} = 4$$ into the standard form of the equation, $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1.$$ The equation of the hyperbola is $$\frac{x^{2}}{36} - \frac{y^{2}}{4} = 1,$$ as shown in Figure 6.

title: Standard Forms of the Equation of a Hyperbola with Center (h, k)

snippet: Standard Forms of the Equation of a Hyperbola with Center (h, k): The standard form of the equation of a hyperbola with center \left( {h,k} \right) and transverse axis parallel to the x-axis is \frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} -...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Standard Forms of the Equation of a Hyperbola with Center (h, k)" title="Standard Forms of the Equation of a Hyperbola with Center (h, k)">
    <paragraph>The standard form of the equation of a hyperbola with center $$\left( {h,k} \right)$$ and transverse axis parallel to the x-axis is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>the length of the transverse axis is $$2a$$</item>
      <item>the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {h \pm a,k} \right)$$</item>
      <item>the length of the conjugate axis is $$2b$$</item>
      <item>the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {h,k \pm b} \right)$$</item>
      <item>the distance between the foci is $$2c,$$ where $$c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}$$</item>
      <item>the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {h \pm c,k} \right)$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>The asymptotes of the hyperbola coincide with the diagonals of the central rectangle. The length of the rectangle is $$2a$$ and its width is $$2b.$$ The slopes of the diagonals are $$\pm \frac{b}{a},$$ and each diagonal passes through the center $$\left( {h,k} \right).$$ Using the point-slope formula, it is simple to show that the equations of the asymptotes are $$y = \pm \frac{b}{a}\left( {x - h} \right) + k.$$ See Figure 7a</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The standard form of the equation of a hyperbola with center $$\left( {h,k} \right)$$ and transverse axis parallel to the y-axis is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>the length of the transverse axis is $$2a$$</item>
      <item>the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {h,k \pm a} \right)$$</item>
      <item>the length of the conjugate axis is $$2b$$</item>
      <item>the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {h \pm b,k} \right)$$</item>
      <item>the distance between the foci is $$2c,$$ where $$c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}$$</item>
      <item>the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {h,k \pm c} \right)$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Using the reasoning above, the equations of the asymptotes are $$y = \pm \frac{a}{b}\left( {x - h} \right) + k.$$ See Figure 7b.</paragraph>
  </note>

<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given the vertices and foci of a hyperbola centered at $$\left( {h,k} \right),$$ write its equation in standard form.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Determine whether the transverse axis is parallel to the x- or y-axis. If the y-coordinates of the given vertices and foci are the same, then the transverse axis is parallel to the x-axis. Use the standard form $$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1.$$ If the x-coordinates of the given vertices and foci are the same, then the transverse axis is parallel to the y-axis. Use the standard form $$\frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1.$$</item>
      <item>Identify the center of the hyperbola, $$\left( {h,k} \right),$$ using the midpoint formula and the given coordinates for the vertices.</item>
      <item>Find $$a^{2}$$ by solving for the length of the transverse axis, $$2a$$ , which is the distance between the given vertices.</item>
      <item>Find $$c^{2}$$ using $$h$$ and $$k$$ found in Step 2 along with the given coordinates for the foci.</item>
      <item>Solve for $$b^{2}$$ using the equation $$b^{2} = c^{2} - a^{2}.$$</item>
      <item>Substitute the values for $$h,k,a^{2},$$ and $$b^{2}$$ into the standard form of the equation determined in Step 1.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

<example number="3" title="Finding the Equation of a Hyperbola Centered at (h, k) Given its Foci and Vertices">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>What is the standard form equation of the hyperbola that has vertices at $$(0,-2)$$ and $$(6,-2)$$ and foci at $$(-2,-2)$$ and $$(8,-2)?$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The y-coordinates of the vertices and foci are the same, so the transverse axis is parallel to the x-axis. Thus, the equation of the hyperbola will have the form</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>First, we identify the center, $$\left( {h,k} \right).$$ The center is halfway between the vertices $$\left( {0,-2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {6,-2} \right).$$ Applying the midpoint formula, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {h,k} \right) = \left( {\frac{0 + 6}{2},\frac{-2 + (-2)}{2}} \right) = \left( {3,-2} \right)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, we find $$a^{2}.$$ The length of the transverse axis, $$2a,$$ is bounded by the vertices. So, we can find $$a^{2}$$ by finding the distance between the x-coordinates of the vertices.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {2a = \left| {0 - 6} \right|} \\ {2a = 6} \\ { a = 3} \\ {a^{2} = 9} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now we need to find $$c^{2}.$$ The coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {h \pm c,k} \right).$$ So $$\left( {h - c,k} \right) = \left( {- 2,-2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {h + c,k} \right) = \left( {8,-2} \right).$$ We can use the x-coordinate from either of these points to solve for $$c.$$ Using the point $$\left( {8,-2} \right),$$ and substituting $$h = 3,$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {h + c = 8} \\ {3 + c = 8} \\ {c = 5} \\ {c^{2} = 25} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, solve for $$b^{2}$$ using the equation $$b^{2} = c^{2} - a^{2}:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {b^{2} = c^{2} - a^{2}} \\ { = 25 - 9} \\ { = 16} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Finally, substitute the values found for $$h,k,a^{2},$$ and $$b^{2}$$ into the standard form of the equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{{(x - 3)}^{2}}{9} - \frac{{(y + 2)}^{2}}{16} = 1$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

      <item>Solve for the coordinates of the foci using the equation $$c = \pm \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}.$$</item>
      <item>Plot the vertices, co-vertices, foci, and asymptotes in the coordinate plane, and draw a smooth curve to form the hyperbola.</item>

snippet: Graphing a Hyperbola Centered at (0, 0) Given an Equation in Standard Form: Graph the hyperbola given by the equation \frac{y^{2}}{64} - \frac{x^{2}}{36} = 1. Identify and label the vertices, co-vertices, foci, and asymptotes. The standard...
body_xml: Graph the hyperbola given by the equation $$\frac{y^{2}}{64} - \frac{x^{2}}{36} = 1.$$ Identify and label the vertices, co-vertices, foci, and asymptotes. The standard form that applies to the given equation is $$\frac{y^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{x^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1.$$ Thus, the transverse axis is on the y-axis The coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {0, \pm a} \right) = \left( {0, \pm \sqrt{64}} \right) = \left( {0, \pm 8} \right)$$ The coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {\pm b,0} \right) = \left( {\pm \sqrt{36}, 0} \right) = \left( {\pm 6,0} \right)$$ The coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {0, \pm c} \right),$$ where $$c = \pm \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}.$$ Solving for $$c,$$ we have $$c = \pm \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}} = \pm \sqrt{64 + 36} = \pm \sqrt{100} = \pm 10$$ Therefore, the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {0, \pm 10} \right)$$ The equations of the asymptotes are $$y = \pm \frac{a}{b}x = \pm \frac{8}{6}x = \pm \frac{4}{3}x$$ Plot and label the vertices and co-vertices, and then sketch the central rectangle. Sides of the rectangle are parallel to the axes and pass through the vertices and co-vertices. Sketch and extend the diagonals of the central rectangle to show the asymptotes. The central rectangle and asymptotes provide the framework needed to sketch an accurate graph of the hyperbola. Label the foci and asymptotes, and draw a smooth curve to form the hyperbola, as shown in Figure 8.

snippet: Graphing a Hyperbola Centered at (h, k) Given an Equation in General Form: Graph the hyperbola given by the equation 9x^{2} - 4y^{2} - 36x - 40y - 388 = 0. Identify and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, foci, and asymptotes. Start...
body_xml: Graph the hyperbola given by the equation $$9x^{2} - 4y^{2} - 36x - 40y - 388 = 0.$$ Identify and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, foci, and asymptotes. Start by expressing the equation in standard form. Group terms that contain the same variable, and move the constant to the opposite side of the equation. $$\left( {9x^{2} - 36x} \right) - \left( {4y^{2} + 40y} \right) = 388$$ Factor the leading coefficient of each expression. $$9\left( {x^{2} - 4x} \right) - 4\left( {y^{2} + 10y} \right) = 388$$ Complete the square twice. Remember to balance the equation by adding the same constants to each side. $$9\left( {x^{2} - 4x + 4} \right) - 4\left( {y^{2} + 10y + 25} \right) = 388 + 36 - 100$$ Rewrite as perfect squares. $$9\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2} - 4\left( {y + 5} \right)^{2} = 324$$ Divide both sides by the constant term to place the equation in standard form. $$\frac{\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2}}{36} - \frac{\left( {y + 5} \right)^{2}}{81} = 1$$ The standard form that applies to the given equation is $$\frac{\left( {x - h} \right)^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{\left( {y - k} \right)^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1,$$ where $$a^{2} = 36$$ and $$b^{2} = 81,$$ or $$a = 6$$ and $$b = 9.$$ Thus, the transverse axis is parallel to the x-axis. It follows that: the center of the ellipse is $$\left( {h,k} \right) = \left( {2,-5} \right)$$ the coordinates of the vertices are $$\left( {h \pm a,k} \right) = \left( {2 \pm 6,-5} \right),$$ or $$\left( {- 4,-5} \right)$$ and $$\left( {8,-5} \right)$$ the coordinates of the co-vertices are $$\left( {h,k \pm b} \right) = \left( {2, - 5 \pm 9} \right),$$ or $$\left( {2, - 14} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2,4} \right)$$ the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {h \pm c,k} \right),$$ where $$c = \pm \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}.$$ Solving for $$c,$$ we have $$c = \pm \sqrt{36 + 81} = \pm \sqrt{117} = \pm 3\sqrt{13}$$ Therefore, the coordinates of the foci are $$\left( {2 - 3\sqrt{13},-5} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2 + 3\sqrt{13},-5} \right).$$ The equations of the asymptotes are $$y = \pm \frac{b}{a}\left( {x - h} \right) + k = \pm \frac{3}{2}\left( {x - 2} \right) - 5.$$ Next, we plot and label the center, vertices, co-vertices, foci, and asymptotes and draw smooth curves to form the hyperbola, as shown in Figure 9.

title: Solving Applied Problems Involving Hyperbolas
snippet: Solving Applied Problems Involving Hyperbolas: The design layout of a cooling tower is shown in Figure 11. The tower stands 179.6 meters tall. The diameter of the top is 72 meters. At their closest, the sides of the tower are 60 meters...
body_xml: The design layout of a cooling tower is shown in Figure 11. The tower stands 179.6 meters tall. The diameter of the top is 72 meters. At their closest, the sides of the tower are 60 meters apart. Find the equation of the hyperbola that models the sides of the cooling tower. Assume that the center of the hyperbola—indicated by the intersection of dashed perpendicular lines in the figure—is the origin of the coordinate plane. Round final values to four decimal places. We are assuming the center of the tower is at the origin, so we can use the standard form of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin: $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1,$$ where the branches of the hyperbola form the sides of the cooling tower. We must find the values of $$a^{2}$$ and $$b^{2}$$ to complete the model. First, we find $$a^{2}.$$ Recall that the length of the transverse axis of a hyperbola is $$2a.$$ This length is represented by the distance where the sides are closest, which is given as $$60$$ meters. So, $$2a = 60.$$ Therefore, $$a = 30$$ and $$a^{2} = 900.$$ To solve for $$b^{2},$$ we need to substitute for $$x$$ and $$y$$ in our equation using a known point. To do this, we can use the dimensions of the tower to find some point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ that lies on the hyperbola. We will use the top right corner of the tower to represent that point. Since the y-axis bisects the tower, our x-value can be represented by the radius of the top, or 36 meters. The y-value is represented by the distance from the origin to the top, which is given as 79.6 meters. Therefore, $$\begin{array}{ll} {\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Standard form of horizontal hyperbola} .} \\ {b^{2} = \frac{y^{2}}{\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - 1}} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Isolate} b^{2}} \\ { = \frac{{(79.6)}^{2}}{\frac{{(36)}^{2}}{900} - 1}} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Substitute for} a^{2},x, \text{and} y} \\ { \approx 14400.3636} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Round to four decimal places} } \end{array}$$ The sides of the tower can be modeled by the hyperbolic equation $$\frac{x^{2}}{900} - \frac{y^{2}}{14400.3636 } = 1, \text{or} \frac{x^{2}}{30^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{120.0015^{2} } = 1$$

<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given a standard form equation for a parabola centered at (0, 0), sketch the graph.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Determine which of the standard forms applies to the given equation: $$y^{2} = 4px$$ or $$x^{2} = 4py.$$</item>
      <item>Use the standard form identified in Step 1 to determine the axis of symmetry, focus, equation of the directrix, and endpoints of the latus rectum. If the equation is in the form $$y^{2} = 4px,$$ then the axis of symmetry is the x-axis, $$y = 0$$ set $$4p$$ equal to the coefficient of x in the given equation to solve for $$p.$$ If $$p > 0,$$ the parabola opens right. If the equation is in the form $$x^{2} = 4py,$$ then the axis of symmetry is the y-axis, $$x = 0$$ set $$4p$$ equal to the coefficient of y in the given equation to solve for $$p.$$ If $$p > 0,$$ the parabola opens up. If $$p < 0,$$ the parabola opens down. use $$p$$ to find the coordinates of the focus, $$\left( {0,p} \right)$$ use $$p$$ to find equation of the directrix, $$y = - p$$ use $$p$$ to find the endpoints of the latus rectum, $$\left( {\pm 2p,p} \right)$$</item>

    </list>

<example number="3" title="Writing the Equation of a Parabola in Standard Form Given its Focus and Directrix">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>What is the equation for the parabola with focus $$\left( {- \frac{1}{2},0} \right)$$ and directrix $$x = \frac{1}{2}?$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The focus has the form $$\left( {p,0} \right),$$ so the equation will have the form $$y^{2} = 4px.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>Multiplying $$4p,$$ we have $$4p = 4\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right) = -2.$$</item>
        <item>Substituting for $$4p,$$ we have $$y^{2} = 4px = -2x.$$</item>
      </list>
      <paragraph>Therefore, the equation for the parabola is $$y^{2} = -2x.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

Start by writing the equation of the parabola in standard form. The standard form that applies to the given equation is $$\left( {x - h} \right)^{2} = 4p\left( {y - k} \right).$$ Thus, the axis of symmetry is parallel to the y-axis. To express the equation of the parabola in this form, we begin by isolating the terms that contain the variable $$x$$ in order to complete the square. $$\begin{array}{l} {x^{2} - 8x - 28y - 208 = 0} \\ {x^{2} - 8x = 28y + 208} \\ {x^{2} - 8x + 16 = 28y + 208 + 16} \\ {{(x - 4)}^{2} = 28y + 224} \\ {{(x - 4)}^{2} = 28(y + 8)} \\ {{(x - 4)}^{2} = 4 \cdot 7 \cdot (y + 8)} \end{array}$$ It follows that: the vertex is $$\left( {h,k} \right) = \left( {4,-8} \right)$$ the axis of symmetry is $$x = h = 4$$ since $$p = 7,p > 0$$ and so the parabola opens up the coordinates of the focus are $$\left( {h,k + p} \right) = \left( {4,-8 + 7} \right) = \left( {4,-1} \right)$$ the equation of the directrix is $$y = k - p = -8 - 7 = -15$$ the endpoints of the latus rectum are $$\left( {h \pm 2p,k + p} \right) = \left( {4 \pm 2(7),-8 + 7} \right),$$ or $$\left( {-10,-1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {18,-1} \right)$$ Next we plot the vertex, axis of symmetry, focus, directrix, and latus rectum, and draw a smooth curve to form the parabola. See Figure 11.

title: Solving Applied Problems Involving Parabolas
snippet: Solving Applied Problems Involving Parabolas: A cross-section of a design for a travel-sized solar fire starter is shown in Figure 13. The sun’s rays reflect off the parabolic mirror toward an object attached to the igniter. Because the...
body_xml: A cross-section of a design for a travel-sized solar fire starter is shown in Figure 13. The sun’s rays reflect off the parabolic mirror toward an object attached to the igniter. Because the igniter is located at the focus of the parabola, the reflected rays cause the object to burn in just seconds. ⓐ Find the equation of the parabola that models the fire starter. Assume that the vertex of the parabolic mirror is the origin of the coordinate plane. ⓑ Use the equation found in part ⓐ to find the depth of the fire starter. ⓐ The vertex of the dish is the origin of the coordinate plane, so the parabola will take the standard form $$x^{2} = 4py,$$ where $$p > 0.$$ The igniter, which is the focus, is 1.7 inches above the vertex of the dish. Thus we have $$p = 1.7.$$ $$\begin{array}{ll} {x^{2} = 4py} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Standard form of upward-facing parabola with vertex (0,0)} } \\ {x^{2} = 4(1.7)y} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Substitute 1} \text{.7 for} p.} \\ {x^{2} = 6.8y} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Multiply} .} \end{array}$$ ⓑ The dish extends $$\frac{4.5}{2} = 2.25$$ inches on either side of the origin. We can substitute 2.25 for $$x$$ in the equation from part (a) to find the depth of the dish. $$\begin{array}{ll} {x^{2} = 6.8y} & { \text{Equation found in part (a)} .} \\ {{(2.25)}^{2} = 6.8y} & { \text{Substitute 2} \text{.25 for} x.} \\ {y \approx 0.74 } & { \text{Solve for} y.} \end{array}$$ The dish is about 0.74 inches deep.

title: General Form of Conic Sections
snippet: General Form of Conic Sections: A conic section has the general form Ax^{2} + Bxy + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0 where A,B, and C are not all zero. Table 2 summarizes the different conic sections where B = 0, and A and C are nonzero real...
body_xml: A conic section has the general form $$Ax^{2} + Bxy + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0$$ where $$A,B,$$ and $$C$$ are not all zero. Table 2 summarizes the different conic sections where $$B = 0,$$ and $$A$$ and $$C$$ are nonzero real numbers. This indicates that the conic has not been rotated. ellipse $$Ax^{2} + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0, A \neq C \text{and} AC > 0$$ circle $$Ax^{2} + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0, A = C$$ hyperbola $$Ax^{2} - Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0 \text{or} - Ax^{2} + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0,$$ where $$A$$ and $$C$$ are positive parabola $$Ax^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0 \text{or} Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0$$

title: How To
snippet: How To: Given the equation of a conic, identify the type of conic. Rewrite the equation in the general form, Ax^{2} + Bxy + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0. Identify the values of A and C from the general form. If A and C are nonzero, have the...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="How To" title="How To">
    <paragraph>Given the equation of a conic, identify the type of conic.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Rewrite the equation in the general form, $$Ax^{2} + Bxy + Cy^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0.$$</item>
      <item>Identify the values of $$A$$ and $$C$$ from the general form. If $$A$$ and $$C$$ are nonzero, have the same sign, and are not equal to each other, then the graph may be an ellipse. If $$A$$ and $$C$$ are equal and nonzero and have the same sign, then the graph may be a circle. If $$A$$ and $$C$$ are nonzero and have opposite signs, then the graph may be a hyperbola. If either $$A$$ or $$C$$ is zero, then the graph may be a parabola.If B = 0, the conic section will have a vertical and/or horizontal axes. If B does not equal 0, as shown below, the conic section is rotated. Notice the phrase “may be” in the definitions. That is because the equation may not represent a conic section at all, depending on the values of A, B, C, D, E, and F. For example, the degenerate case of a circle or an ellipse is a point: $$Ax^{2} + By^{2} = 0,$$ when A and B have the same sign. The degenerate case of a hyperbola is two intersecting straight lines: $$Ax^{2} + By^{2} = 0,$$ when A and B have opposite signs. On the other hand, the equation, $$Ax^{2} + By^{2} + 1 = 0,$$ when A and B are positive does not represent a graph at all, since there are no real ordered pairs which satisfy it.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

body_xml:
<example number="1" title="Identifying a Conic from Its General Form">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Identify the graph of each of the following nondegenerate conic sections.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$4x^{2} - 9y^{2} + 36x + 36y - 125 = 0$$</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$9y^{2} + 16x + 36y - 10 = 0$$</item>
        <item>ⓒ $$3x^{2} + 3y^{2} - 2x - 6y - 4 = 0$$</item>
        <item>ⓓ $$- 25x^{2} - 4y^{2} + 100x + 16y + 20 = 0$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>ⓐ Rewriting the general form, we have $$A = 4$$ and $$C = -9,$$ so we observe that $$A$$ and $$C$$ have opposite signs. The graph of this equation is a hyperbola.</item>
        <item>ⓑ Rewriting the general form, we have $$A = 0$$ and $$C = 9.$$ We can determine that the equation is a parabola, since $$A$$ is zero.</item>
        <item>ⓒ Rewriting the general form, we have $$A = 3$$ and $$C = 3.$$ Because $$A = C,$$ the graph of this equation is a circle.</item>
        <item>ⓓ Rewriting the general form, we have $$A = -25$$ and $$C = -4.$$ Because $$AC > 0$$ and $$A \neq C,$$ the graph of this equation is an ellipse.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Equations of Rotation
snippet: Equations of Rotation: If a point \left( {x,y} \right) on the Cartesian plane is represented on a new coordinate plane where the axes of rotation are formed by rotating an angle \theta from the positive x-axis, then the coordinates of the...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Equations of Rotation" title="Equations of Rotation">
    <paragraph>If a point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ on the Cartesian plane is represented on a new coordinate plane where the axes of rotation are formed by rotating an angle $$\theta$$ from the positive x-axis, then the coordinates of the point with respect to the new axes are $$\left( {x^{\prime},y^{\prime}} \right).$$ We can use the following equations of rotation to define the relationship between $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and $$\left( {x^{\prime},y^{\prime}} \right):$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$x = x^{\prime}\cos\theta - y^{\prime}\sin\theta$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = x^{\prime}\sin\theta + y^{\prime}\cos\theta$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding a New Representation of an Equation after Rotating through a Given Angle
snippet: Finding a New Representation of an Equation after Rotating through a Given Angle: Find a new representation of the equation 2x^{2} - xy + 2y^{2} - 30 = 0 after rotating through an angle of \theta = 45{^\circ}. Find x and y, where x =...
body_xml: Find a new representation of the equation $$2x^{2} - xy + 2y^{2} - 30 = 0$$ after rotating through an angle of $$\theta = 45{^\circ}.$$ Find $$x$$ and $$y,$$ where $$x = x^{\prime}\cos\theta - y^{\prime}\sin\theta$$ and $$y = x^{\prime}\sin\theta + y^{\prime}\cos\theta.$$ Because $$\theta = 45{^\circ},$$ $$\begin{array}{l} \\ {x = x^{\prime}\cos(45{^\circ}) - y^{\prime}\sin(45{^\circ})} \\ {x = x^{\prime}\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) - y^{\prime}\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right)} \\ {x = \frac{x^{\prime} - y^{\prime}}{\sqrt{2}}} \end{array}$$ and $$\begin{array}{l} \\ \begin{array}{l} {y = x^{\prime}\sin(45{^\circ}) + y^{\prime}\cos(45{^\circ})} \\ {y = x^{\prime}\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) + y^{\prime}\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right)} \\ {y = \frac{x^{\prime} + y^{\prime}}{\sqrt{2}}} \end{array} \end{array}$$ Substitute $$x = x^{\prime}\cos\theta - y^{\prime}\sin\theta$$ and $$y = x^{\prime}\sin\theta + y^{\prime}\cos\theta$$ into $$2x^{2} - xy + 2y^{2} - 30 = 0.$$ $$2\left( \frac{x^{\prime} - y^{\prime}}{\sqrt{2}} \right)^{2} - \left( \frac{x^{\prime} - y^{\prime}}{\sqrt{2}} \right)\left( \frac{x^{\prime} + y^{\prime}}{\sqrt{2}} \right) + 2\left( \frac{x^{\prime} + y^{\prime}}{\sqrt{2}} \right)^{2} - 30 = 0$$ Simplify. $$\begin{array}{ll} {2\frac{(x^{\prime} - y^{\prime})(x^{\prime} - y^{\prime})}{2} - \frac{(x^{\prime} - y^{\prime})(x^{\prime} + y^{\prime})}{2} + 2\frac{(x^{\prime} + y^{\prime})(x^{\prime} + y^{\prime})}{2} - 30 = 0} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{FOIL method} } \\ {x^{\prime}{}^{2}{- 2x^{\prime}y}^{\prime} + y^{\prime}{}^{2} - \frac{(x^{\prime}{}^{2} - y^{\prime}{}^{2})}{2} + x^{\prime}{}^{2}{+ 2x^{\prime}y^{\prime}} + y^{\prime}{}^{2} - 30 = 0} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Combine like terms} .} \\ {2x^{\prime}{}^{2} + 2y^{\prime}{}^{2} - \frac{(x^{\prime}{}^{2} - y^{\prime}{}^{2})}{2} = 30} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Combine like terms} .} \\ {2\left( {2x^{\prime}{}^{2} + 2y^{\prime}{}^{2} - \frac{(x^{\prime}{}^{2} - y^{\prime}{}^{2})}{2}} \right) = 2(30)} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Multiply both sides by 2} .} \\ {4x^{\prime}{}^{2} + 4y^{\prime}{}^{2} - (x^{\prime}{}^{2} - y^{\prime}{}^{2}) = 60} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Simplify} .} \\ {4x^{\prime}{}^{2} + 4y^{\prime}{}^{2} - x^{\prime}{}^{2} + y^{\prime}{}^{2} = 60} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Distribute} .} \\ {\frac{3x^{\prime}{}^{2}}{60} + \frac{5y^{\prime}{}^{2}}{60} = \frac{60}{60}} & {\begin{array}{llll} & & & \end{array} \text{Set equal to 1} .} \end{array}$$ Write the equations with $$x^{\prime}$$ and $$y^{\prime}$$ in the standard form. $$\frac{{x^{\prime}}^{2}}{20} + \frac{{y^{\prime}}^{2}}{12} = 1$$ This equation is an ellipse. Figure 6 shows the graph.
