<example number="2" title="Computing the Probability of an Event with Equally Likely Outcomes">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A six-sided number cube is rolled. Find the probability of rolling an odd number.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The event “rolling an odd number” contains three outcomes. There are 6 equally likely outcomes in the sample space. Divide to find the probability of the event.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$P(E) = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Probability of the Union of Two Events
source_type: Probability of the Union of Two Events
snippet: Probability of the Union of Two Events: The probability of the union of two events E and F (written E \cup F ) equals the sum of the probability of E and the probability of F minus the probability of E and F occurring together ( which is...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Probability of the Union of Two Events" title="Probability of the Union of Two Events">
    <paragraph>The probability of the union of two events $$E$$ and $$F$$ (written $$E \cup F$$ ) equals the sum of the probability of $$E$$ and the probability of $$F$$ minus the probability of $$E$$ and $$F$$ occurring together $$($$ which is called the intersection of $$E$$ and $$F$$ and is written as $$E \cap F$$ ).</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$P(E \cup F) = P(E) + P(F) - P(E \cap F)$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Computing the Probability of the Union of Two Events
snippet: Computing the Probability of the Union of Two Events: A card is drawn from a standard deck. Find the probability of drawing a heart or a 7. A standard deck contains an equal number of hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades. So the probability...
body_xml:
<example number="3" title="Computing the Probability of the Union of Two Events">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A card is drawn from a standard deck. Find the probability of drawing a heart or a 7.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>A standard deck contains an equal number of hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades. So the probability of drawing a heart is $$\frac{1}{4}.$$ There are four 7s in a standard deck, and there are a total of 52 cards. So the probability of drawing a 7 is $$\frac{1}{13}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The only card in the deck that is both a heart and a 7 is the 7 of hearts, so the probability of drawing both a heart and a 7 is $$\frac{1}{52}.$$ Substitute $$P(H) = \frac{1}{4}, P(7) = \frac{1}{13}, \text{and} P(H \cap 7) = \frac{1}{52}$$ into the formula.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {P(E \cup^{}F) = P(E) + P(F) - P(E \cap^{}F)} \\ { = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{13} - \frac{1}{52}} \\ { = \frac{4}{13}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The probability of drawing a heart or a 7 is $$\frac{4}{13}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Computing the Probability of the Union of Mutually Exclusive Events
snippet: Computing the Probability of the Union of Mutually Exclusive Events: A card is drawn from a standard deck. Find the probability of drawing a heart or a spade. The events “drawing a heart” and “drawing a spade” are mutually exclusive...

<example number="4" title="Computing the Probability of the Union of Mutually Exclusive Events">

      <paragraph>A card is drawn from a standard deck. Find the probability of drawing a heart or a spade.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The events “drawing a heart” and “drawing a spade” are mutually exclusive because they cannot occur at the same time. The probability of drawing a heart is $$\frac{1}{4},$$ and the probability of drawing a spade is also $$\frac{1}{4},$$ so the probability of drawing a heart or a spade is</paragraph>

title: Using the Complement Rule to Calculate Probabilities
snippet: Using the Complement Rule to Calculate Probabilities: Two six-sided number cubes are rolled. ⓐFind the probability that the sum of the numbers rolled is less than or equal to 3. ⓑFind the probability that the sum of the numbers rolled is...
body_xml:
Two six-sided number cubes are rolled. ⓐFind the probability that the sum of the numbers rolled is less than or equal to 3. ⓑFind the probability that the sum of the numbers rolled is greater than 3. The first step is to identify the sample space, which consists of all the possible outcomes. There are two number cubes, and each number cube has six possible outcomes. Using the Multiplication Principle, we find that there are $$6 \times 6,$$ or $$\text{36}$$ total possible outcomes. So, for example, 1-1 represents a 1 rolled on each number cube. $$\text{1-1}$$ $$\text{1-2}$$ $$\text{1-3}$$ $$\text{1-4}$$ $$\text{1-5}$$ $$\text{1-6}$$ $$\text{2-1}$$ $$\text{2-2}$$ $$\text{2-3}$$ $$\text{2-4}$$ $$\text{2-5}$$ $$\text{2-6}$$ $$\text{3-1}$$ $$\text{3-2}$$ $$\text{3-3}$$ $$\text{3-4}$$ $$\text{3-5}$$ $$\text{3-6}$$ $$\text{4-1}$$ $$\text{4-2}$$ $$\text{4-3}$$ $$\text{4-4}$$ $$\text{4-5}$$ $$\text{4-6}$$ $$\text{5-1}$$ $$\text{5-2}$$ $$\text{5-3}$$ $$\text{5-4}$$ $$\text{5-5}$$ $$\text{5-6}$$ $$\text{6-1}$$ $$\text{6-2}$$ $$\text{6-3}$$ $$\text{6-4}$$ $$\text{6-5}$$ $$\text{6-6}$$ $$\frac{3}{36} = \frac{1}{12}$$
ⓐWe need to count the number of ways to roll a sum of 3 or less. These would include the following outcomes: 1-1, 1-2, and 2-1. So there are only three ways to roll a sum of 3 or less. The probability is $$\begin{array}{l} {P(E^{\prime}) = 1 - P(E)} \\ { = 1 - \frac{1}{12}} \\ { = \frac{11}{12}} \end{array}$$ ⓑRather than listing all the possibilities, we can use the Complement Rule. Because we have already found the probability of the complement of this event, we can simply subtract that probability from 1 to find the probability that the sum of the numbers rolled is greater than 3. $$C(5,2)$$

title: Computing Probability Using Counting Theory
snippet: Computing Probability Using Counting Theory: A child randomly selects 5 toys from a bin containing 3 bunnies, 5 dogs, and 6 bears. ⓐFind the probability that only bears are chosen. ⓑFind the probability that 2 bears and 3 dogs are chosen....
body_xml:
<example number="6" title="Computing Probability Using Counting Theory">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A child randomly selects 5 toys from a bin containing 3 bunnies, 5 dogs, and 6 bears.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐFind the probability that only bears are chosen.</item>
        <item>ⓑFind the probability that 2 bears and 3 dogs are chosen.</item>
        <item>ⓒFind the probability that at least 2 dogs are chosen.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐWe need to count the number of ways to choose only bears and the total number of possible ways to select 5 toys. There are 6 bears, so there are $$C(14,5)$$ ways to choose 5 bears. There are 14 toys, so there are $$\frac{C(6,5)}{C(14,5)} = \frac{6}{2,002} = \frac{3}{1,001}$$ ways to choose any 5 toys. $$C(6,2)$$</item>
        <item>ⓑWe need to count the number of ways to choose 2 bears and 3 dogs and the total number of possible ways to select 5 toys. There are 6 bears, so there are $$C(5,3)$$ ways to choose 2 bears. There are 5 dogs, so there are $$C(6,2) \cdot C(5,3)$$ ways to choose 3 dogs. Since we are choosing both bears and dogs at the same time, we will use the Multiplication Principle. There are $$\frac{C(6,2)C(5,3)}{C(14,5)} = \frac{15 \cdot 10}{2,002} = \frac{75}{1,001}$$ ways to choose 2 bears and 3 dogs. We can use this result to find the probability. $$C(9,5)$$</item>
        <item>ⓒIt is often easiest to solve “at least” problems using the Complement Rule. We will begin by finding the probability that fewer than 2 dogs are chosen. If less than 2 dogs are chosen, then either no dogs could be chosen, or 1 dog could be chosen. When no dogs are chosen, all 5 toys come from the 9 toys that are not dogs. There are $$C(14,5)$$ ways to choose toys from the 9 toys that are not dogs. Since there are 14 toys, there are $$\frac{C(9,5)}{C(14,5)} = \frac{63}{1,001}$$ ways to choose the 5 toys from all of the toys. $$C(5,1) \cdot C(9,4)$$ If there is 1 dog chosen, then 4 toys must come from the 9 toys that are not dogs, and 1 must come from the 5 dogs. Since we are choosing both dogs and other toys at the same time, we will use the Multiplication Principle. There are $$\frac{C(5,1)C(9,4)}{C(14,5)} = \frac{5 \cdot 126}{2,002} = \frac{315}{1,001}$$ ways to choose 1 dog and 1 other toy. $$\frac{63}{1,001} + \frac{315}{1,001} = \frac{378}{1,001}$$ Because these events would not occur together and are therefore mutually exclusive, we add the probabilities to find the probability that fewer than 2 dogs are chosen. $$1 - \frac{378}{1,001} = \frac{623}{1,001}$$ We then subtract that probability from 1 to find the probability that at least 2 dogs are chosen. $$52$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>
